ALPHABETICAL EXPLANATION OF BOTANICAL TERMS

Pages 340-344

A. Abrupt (abruptus), when a winged <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> ends without a little leaf. Acorn, the seed of the oak. Acotyledones, seeds without lobes, which produce no seminal leaves. Acute (acutus), tapering to a slender, but not thorny termination. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a>-bag (folliculus), a distended seed-vessel opening on one side. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">Alternate</a> (alternans), applied to branches, leaves, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, springing out regularly one above another. Androgynous, having some flowers on the same plant, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> stamens, but no pistils; and other flowers bearing pistils, but no stamens. Angiosperma, seeds in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPSULE">capsule</a>. Angular (angulatus) having corners; opposed to cylindrical. — capsule, as in flower-de-luce. Annual (annuus), living only one year. Anomalous (anomalus), <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANTHER">Anther</a> (anthera), the top of the stamen fixed on the filament, and containing the pollen. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">Apex</a>, termination. Apophysis, excrescence. Approaching, see Converging. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">Arrow</a>-shaped, (sagittatus), leaf shaped like an arrow head, as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>. Ascending, growing first horizontally, and then bent upwards. Attenuate (attenuatus), tapering. Awl-shaped (subulatus), slender. Awn (arista) or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, the sharp substance growing to the valves of corn or grass. Awnless (muticus), without awns. Axillary (axillaris) at the base of the leaves or branches. B. Bark (cortex), the covering of the stems, roots, and branches of vegetables. Barren (masculi, abortivi), flowers or florets which produce no perfect seeds; generally wanting pistils. Base, see Axillary. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">Battle</a>-dore-shaped (spatulatum), rounded with a neck. Beaded (granulatus), consisting of many little knobs, connected by small strings. Beak or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> (rostrum), a projecting appendage to some seeds. Bearded (barbatus), beset with straight <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> hairs. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">Bell</a>-shaped (campanulatus), like the blossom of the convolvulus. Beltying (ventricosus) distended. Beneath (inferus). A blossom is beneath, when it includes the germen, and is attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> immediately below it. A germen is said to be beneath when it is not included in the corolla or blossom. Berry (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BACCA">bacca</a>), a pulpy seed-vessel without valves. Biennial, continuing alive for two years. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>-footed (pedatus), resembling the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fowl. Bitten, ending in no regular form, not tapering. Bill (rostrum), a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> substance attached to a seed. Bladders, air-bags on some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUCUS">fucus</a>. Bladder-shaped (inflatus), inflated or distended. Blistered, when the surface of a leaf rises <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above the veins. Blossoms (corolla), part of a flower, consisting of one or more leaves called petals. It is an expansion of the inner bark of the plant, and is the ornamented cover of the stamens and pistils. Blunt (obtusus), opposed to acute. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>-shaped (navicularis), like a little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>-bottomed boat. Border (limbus), the upper part of a corolla of one petal. Bowed (arcuatus), bent. Branched (ramosus), having lateral divisions. Bristles (setae), stiff cylindrical hairs. Bristle-shaped (setaceus), slender, and like a bristle. Bud (gemma), a protuberance on the stem or branches, containing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the leaves or flowers to be expanded the following year. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">Bulb</a> (bulbus), a bud placed on the root or stem. Bulging (gibbus) irregularly swollen out. Bunch Bunch (racemus), a fruitstalk with short lateral branches. Bundle (fasciculus), several flowers rising to the same point from their respective fruitstalks, as in sweet-william. Bundled, applied to leaves, as in the larch. Butterfly-shaped (papilionaceus), as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a> flowers. C. Calycled (calyculatus), having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> calyx. Calypre, veil. Calyx, or empalement, a continuation of the outer bark of the plant, forming part of the flower, is called a cup, as in primrose, involucrem in carrot, catkin in hazel, calypre in the mosses, a husk in oats, a sheath in the narcissus, and a curtain in some fungs. Capsule, a dry hollow seed-vessel opening in some determinate manner. Catkin (amentum), a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of flowers and chaff on a long thread-shaped receptacle; the whole like a cat's tail; e.g., the willow. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CELL">Cell</a> (loculumentum), vacuity in the capsule to lodge the seed. Central florets (flores flosculosi); those which occupy the middle part of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> flower, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> ones in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> daisy. Chaff (palea), thin membranaceous substance separating the florets from each other, and growing on a common receptacle. Channelled (canaliculatus), having a furrow from the base to the end. Cicatrised, scarred. Ciliate, fringed. Circumference, the florets farthest from the centre of a compound flower, as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> ones in the common daisy. Clammy (viscosus), adhesive like bird-lime. Claw (unguis), the part of a petal next the base, distinguished from the limb or upper part. Cleft, divided half-way <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Climbing (scandens), <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> that rise by the aid of others. Clothing (pubes), hairiness on the surface of plants. Cloven, see Cleft. Club-shaped (clavatus), thinner at the base, and thicker upwards. Cluster (thyrsus), flowers collected in somewhat of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>-shaped form, like the lilac. Coated (tunicatus), root, composed of layers like the onion. Cobwebbed (arachnoideus), covered with a substance resembling a cobweb. Coloured (coloratus), not green. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">Column</a> (columella), the little pillar in the centre of some capsules to which the seeds are fixed. Comb (coma), a collection of floral leaves terminating the flowering stem, as in the pine-apple. Comb-like (pectinatum), a sort of winged leaf; the leaflets of which are like the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of a comb. Common calyx, including several flowers, as in thistles. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPACT">Compact</a>, growing <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together. Compound flowers (compositi flores) consist of many florets or little flowers, on a receptacle or seat, as in thistles. Compressed (compressus), a cylindrical substance, more or less flatted. Cone (strobilus), a seed-vessel, formed by a catkin, with hardened scales, as in the pine and fir. Cone-shaped (cucullatus), applied to leaves rolled up, as the grocers roll up <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> to hold spices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, &c. Confluent (confluentia folia), running into one another at the base. Congregated (glomeratus), spikes, &c., crowded together, somewhat in a globular form. Connected (adnatus) leaves, having their upper surface at the base, growing to the stem or branch. Contiguous (adpressus) leaves, &c., close to the stem. Converging (connivens), approaching at the top. Convex, rising like the surface of a globe. Convolute, twisted spirally. Corolla, blossom. Corymb, a collection of flowers standing each on its own fruitstalk, with fruitstalks of such a length, that the whole collection forms a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> surface at the top, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-tree. Cotton, Cottony (tomentosum, tomentosus), downy, covered with a whitish soft substance. Cotyledones, seed-lobes. Creeping (repens) stem; creeping along the ground, as ivy. ——— root, as spearmint. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">Crescent</a>-shaped (lunaris, lunatus), shaped like a waxing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, like the anthers of the strawberry. Crested (cristatus) flowers, tufted. Crooked (cernuous) fruitstalk, with the flower facing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and so stiff, that it cannot be straightened without breaking; as in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> imperial. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a>-pairs (decussatus), leaves in pairs, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> pointing in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> different from the pair above or below it. Cross-shaped (cruciatus, cruciformis) flowers, having four petals in a form of a cross; called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRUCIFORM">cruciform</a> plants. Crowned (coronatus) seed, a seed to which the calyx adheres, e.g., teazel. Cruciform, see Cross-shaped. Cryptogonia, stamens and pistils indistinct. Cup (perianthium), a calyx contiguous to the other parts of the flower. ——— double (calyculatus), when the base of one cup is surrounded by another cup. Curtain (volva), the calyx of agarics and boleti. Cut-round (circumscissus), when a seed-vessel opens in a circle, and not longways. Cylindrical (teres), round like a walking stick. D. Dagger-pointed (mucronatus), ending, not gradually, but suddenly in a sharp point. Deciduous (deciduus) leaves, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> at the approach of winter. ——— cup or calyx, falling off before the blossom. ——— seed-vessel, falling off before it opens. Declining (declinatus), bent like a bow, with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> downwards. Decurrent (decurrens) leaf, without a leafstalk, but where the leaf runs down the stem. Dented (retusus), a blunt leaf with a blunt notch at the end. Depressed (depressus), when the surface of a leaf is slightly sunk. Diadelphia, the 17th class of plants, having the filaments united into two sets. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">Diamond</a>-shaped (rhombeus), applied to leaves resembling a diamond on <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>. Diandra, two stamens. Didynamia, the 14th class, having two stamens longer. Digynia, two pistils. Dimpled (umbilicatus), having a hollow dot. Dicoccia, dioecious, having the flowers bearing stamens and those bearing pistils on different plants. Disk (discus) of a leaf is its surface: of a compound flower is its central florets; thus, in a daisy, the minute yellow florets form the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DISC">disc</a>, and the larger white-shaped florets form the ray. Distant (distans,) far asunder, as the stamens of mint. Distended (ventricosus), as the cup of the rose. Diverging (divergens), spreading wide from the stem almost horizontally, opposed to compact. Divided (partitus), or parted, partite, signifies that a cup, leaf, or petal, is parted more than half way down. Dodecandria, 12 stamens. Dorsal, fixed to the back. Dotted (punctatus), marked with little hollow dots. Double (didymus), applied to two anthers on one filament. Doubly-compound (decompositus) leaves, having the primary leaf-stalk divided, so that each <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> forms a compound leaf. They are twin-fork (begeminius), when a forked leaf-stalk has several leaflets at the end of each fork; or, doubly-threefold (bi-ternatus), when a leaf-stalk, with three divisions, has three leaflets on the end of each division or fork; or doubly winged (duplicato-pinnatum, bi-pinnatum), when a leaf-stalk has lateral ribs, each of which forms a winged leaf. Down (pappus), the fine <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> or feather-like substance, crowning the seeds of some plants, and wafting them abroad. Downy leaf, see Cottony. Drupe, a pulpy seed-vessel, without valves, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a> surrounded by a pulpy substance, ex gr. a cherry. Dusted (pulveratus), applied to some plants which appear covered with a kind of powder. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">Ear</a>-shaped (auriculatus), somewhat resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> ear. Egg-shaped (ovatus), in form of an egg. Egg-spear-shaped (ovato-lanceolatum), see Spear-egg-shaped. Elliptic, oval. Embracing (amplexicaulis) the stem, when the base of a leaf nearly surrounds the stem. Entire (integer), opposed to cleft, gashed, &c. Equal (æqualis), regular. Erect, upright. Even (levis) surface; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, regular. Excrecence (apophysis), a substance growing on some of the mosses from the seat of the flower. Expanding (patens), between upright and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a>. Eye (hilum), the scar by which a seed is fixed to the seed-vessel. Feathered (plumosum), the down of seeds when it sends out lateral hairs. Feeble (debilis), unable to stand upright. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> flowers or florets, such as have one or more pistils, but no stamens. Ferns, the first order of the class of cryptogamia. Fertile (fertiles vel feminæi) flowers, those that produce seed capable of vegetation. Those that have stamens only are always barren. Those that have pistils only, are only barren when placed beyond the reach of the pollen coming from the anthers of staminiferous flowers. Fibres (nervi), woody strings running along a leaf. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">Fibrous</a> (fibrosus) roots, composed of small threads or fibres. Fiddle-shaped (panduriformis), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, but narrow in the middle, and broader below. Filament or thread (filamentum) the slender part of a stamen supporting the anther. Fistulous, hollow. Finger-like (digitatus) leaves, expanded like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, in pairs, threes and fives. Flat-topped (fastigiatus), rising to the same height, so as to form a flat surface. Fleshy seed-vessel, ex gr. an apple. Floral leaves (bracteæ) are generally on the fruitstalk, so that they are sometimes mistaken for the calyx; but the calyx withers when the fruit is ripe, whereas the floral leaves endure as long as the other leaves of the plant. Floret (floceulus), one of the small flowers forming a compound or incorporated flower. Flower (flos), a temporary part of a plant subservient to the formation of the seed. It consists of eight parts, a calyx, corolla or blossom, stamens, pistils, seed-vessel, seeds, receptacle, and a nectary. Wanting any of these parts, a flower is incomplete. Forked (furcatus, dichotomus), divided. Fringed (alatus), as the blossom of the buck-bean. Fruit (fructus), a part of a flower consisting of the seed-vessel, seed, and receptacle. Fruitstalk (pedunculus), a part of a branch or stem bearing flowers, but not leaves. Fungus, the last order of the class of cryptogamia. Funnel-shaped (infundibuliformis), when a one-petaled blossom is tubular at the base, and conical at the top. Furrowed (sulcatus), marked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> running lengthwise. Gaping (ringens, personatus) blossom, so called from its resemblance to a gaping mouth. Gashed (lobatus), divided nearly half way down into lobes, convex at the edges, and distant from each other. Gelatinous, jelly-like. Gem, a bud. General involucrem, a calyx at the base of a general umbel, as in carrot. Germ, germen, seed-bud. Gibbous, bulged, or bulging. Gills (lamellæ), thin plates on the under side of the pileus. pileus or hat of an agaric; remarkable in the common mushroom. Glass-shaped (cyathiformis), tubular, but widening towards the mouth. Glaucous (glaucus), hoary, as the back of a cabbage-leaf. Globose (globosus), like a round <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. Glume (gluma), husk. Guarved (erosum), when an indented leaf seems as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> bitten at the edges. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANULATED">Granulated</a>, resembling beads. Gymnospermia, naked seeds. Gynandria, stamens on the pistils. H. Hair-like (capillaris), slender, undivided, and cylindrical. Hairs (pili), by some thought secretory ducts. Hand-shaped (palmatus), like the human hand with the fingers expanded. Hat (pileus), the upper broad part of funguses. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHET">Hatchet</a>-shaped (dolabriforme) leaf, like an axe of unequal thickness. Headed (capitulus) stalk, supporting one compact knob of flowers at its extremity. Heads (capitatus) of flowers, growing in compact knobs, as in peppermint. Heart (corculum), that part of a seed which is the future plant in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">Helmet</a> (galea), the upper part of a gaping blossom. Hemispherical, like a half globe. Herbacous stem, succulent, opposed to woody. Hermaphrodite flowers or florets, such as contain both a stamen or stamens, and a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a> or pistils, as the greater part of flowers. Hexagonal, or six-sided. Hexagynia, having six pistils. Hexandria, six-stamened. Hoary (incanus), covered with a silvery-looking substance. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">Honey</a>-combed (favosum), a receptacle with cells open at the top, and having a seed in each. Husk (gluma), the calyx of a grass plant. Hybrid (hybrida), a plant produced by the pollen of one plant fertilizing the germs of a plant of a different species. A <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>. J. Jagged (laciniatus) leaves, irregularly divided and subdivided into lobes. Icosandra, 20-stamened. Imperfect flowers, wanting anther or pistil, or both. Incomplete flowers want the cup, the corolla, or some other important part. See Flower. The tulip wants a cup, and the nettle has no blossom or corolla. Incorporated (aggregatus), when little flowers or florets form a compound flower, as a daisy. Incumbent, anthers fixed by the side, or stamens leaning or resting against. Indented leaf, having the edges deeply scolloped, and the lobes far asunder. Inflated, as if blown up like a bladder. Inferior, see Beneath. Interrupted, broken in its regular form, as a spike by leaves intervening. Inversely heart-shaped (obcordatus), with the point of the heart next the stem. Involutellum, a partial involucrem. Involucrem or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a>, the calyx of an umbel placed at a distance from the flowers. Jointed (articulatus), ex gr. a wheat straw. K. Keel, the lowest petal in a butterfly-shaped corolla. Keeled (carinatus), bent. Knob, see Heads. L. Lactescent, having a milky juice. Laminated, when the flat surfaces of leaves <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> close on each other. Lateral branches, growing from the sides of the stem, opposed to terminating. Leaf, the part of a plant corresponding to the lungs, and also to the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of animals. Leaflet, or little leaf, one of the single leaves of a compound leaf. Leaf-stalk (petiolus), the footstalk of a leaf. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">Leather</a>-like (coriaceus), tough like leather. Legume (legumen) or shell, a seed-vessel of two valves with the seeds fixed to one seam, as in the pea. Level, when several branches or fruitstalks grow to equal heights. Lid (operculum), a cover to the capsules of several mosses. Ligulate, strap-shaped. Limb, the upper spreading part of a petal. Limber (flaccidus) <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> with its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Lip, the upper or under division of a gaping corolla. Lobes, the division of a gashed leaf. Lopped (truncatus), looking as if cut off by scissors. M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">Male</a> flowers, which have stamens, but no pistils. Matte (caespitosus), thickly interwoven. Membranous (membranaceus), thin, skinny, and semi-transparent. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONADELPHIA">Monadelphia</a>, united filaments. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONANDRIA">Monandria</a>, one stamen. Monoeccia, one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, or plants having the stamens and pistils in different flowers, but on the same plant. Monogynia, one pistil in each flower. Monopetalous, one-petaled. Mouth (faux), the upper or opening part of the tube in a one-petaled corolla. Mules, see Hybrid. N. Naked, without leaves or hairs. Nectary, or honey-cup, the part of the flower which secretes the honey. Nut, a seed covered by a hard woody shell. O. Oblong-egg-shaped, oblong at the base, but egg-shaped towards the end. Octandra, eight-stamened. Octagynia, eight pistils. P. Paleaceous, chalky. Panicle, an irregular assemblage of flowers. Papilionaceous flowers, butterfly-shaped, as the pea. Parasitical plants, which grow not on the earth, but on other plants. Pedicle, a little fruitstalk. Pentagon, five-cornered. Pentagynia, five pistils. Pentandra, Pentandria, five stamened. Perennial, continuing more than two years. Petals (petala), the leaves which constitute the corolla or blossom. Pillar (stipes), the pedicle of the down of some seeds, as in dandelion. Pimpled (papillosus), beset with little hard protuberances. Pistil, a part of a flower consisting of the germen, the style, and the summit. Pitcher-shaped (urceolatus), bellying like a jug. Pith, a soft substance filling the cavities of some plants. Plaited, folded. Pod (siliqua), seed-vessel of two valves, within which the seeds are alternately fixed to each seam. Pollen (farina), a fine powder in the anthers of flowers. Polyadelphia, stamens in three or more sets. Polyandra, many stamens. Polygamia, see introduction to the 23rd class. Pores, little holes. Pouch, a short pod. Prism-shaped, different from cylindrical, in having the circumference angular. Proliferous, when one flower, &c., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> out of another. Pubescent, clothed with soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> or hair. R. Radiate, compound flowers in which the florets of the centre differ from those of the circumference. See Disk. Rafts (radii), outer florets of a radiate compound flower. See Disk. Receptacle, the seat or base of a flower. Reflected, bent back. Remote whorls, having a considerable length of stem between each. Rhomboidal, nearly diamond-shaped. Rigid, inflexible. Root-leaves (radicalia), those which proceed immediately from the root. Ruffle or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>, the part of the curtain of an agaric which adheres to the stem after the outer part is gone. S. Salver-shaped (hypocrateriformis), when a one-petaled corolla has its lower part tubular, and its higher part flat and expanded. Scaly (squamous), like the skin of a fish. Scurfy (squarrosus), applied to the rough cup of some compound flowers. Seed, that which contains the rudiments of the new plant. Seed-lobes (cotyledones), the perishable part of a seed which affords food to the rest in germination. Seminal leaves, those which rise from the seed-lobes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERRATED">Serrated</a>, like the teeth of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>. Sheath (spatha), a kind of calyx like that of the crocus. Simple, undivided. Sitting leaves or flowers, without leaf or flower-stalks. Solitary, only one in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Spear-egg-shaped, like a spear at the base, and an egg at the extremity. Spike (spica), a collection of flowers placed alternately on each side of a common fruitstalk without little fruitstalks. Stamen, consists of a filament and anther. Staminiferous, bearing stamens. Streaked, marked with depressed lines. Syngenesia, united anthers. T. Target-shaped leaf, having the stalk fixed, not in the edge, but the centre. Tetragnia, four pistils. Tetradynamia, four stamens longer. Tiled, one leaf or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> partly covering another. Tooth-serrated, when the edge of a leaf is marked with little serrated teeth. Triandra, three stamens. Trigynia, three pistils. Tubercled, having <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> warts; applied to certain <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LICHENS">lichens</a>. Tuberous root, having many roundish knobs in a bundle. Tubular, hollow like a tube. U. Umbel (umbella), an assemblage of flowers in which a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of slender fruitstalks, proceeding from the same centre, rise to nearly the same height, so as to form a regular surface at the top, as in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HEMLOCK">hemlock</a> or carrot. Unequal florets (radiati), when the florets of an umbel are larger in the circumference than in the centre. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALVE">Valve</a>, the pieces of a capsule are called valves. Vaulted (fornicatus), like the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the mouth. Veil (calyptra), the calyx of mosses. W. Wheel-shaped, a corolla of one petal, with a flat border and a short tube. Whirls of branches, leaves or flowers; ex gr. the branches of the fir. Wings, the lateral petals of a butterfly-shaped blossom. Winged leaf-stalk, with a thin membrane on each side. leaf; when an undivided leaf-stalk has many little leaves growing from each side. Wing-cleft, a leaf deeply cut. Woody, opposed to herbaceous. Woolly, curly haired clothing on some plants. Z. Zigzag, having many contrary bendings.

BOOM

Pages 38-40

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> with. with which the clew of the studding-sail is spread out; and sometimes the boom is used to spread <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boom out the clew of the main-sail. **Boom**, denotes also a cable stretched athwart the mouth of a river or harbour; with yards, top-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, battling or spars of wood lashed to it, to prevent an enemy's coming in. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOMING">Booming</a>**, among sailors, denotes the application of a boom to the sails. A ship is said to come booming forwards, when she comes with all the sail she can make. **Boonen, Arnold**, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORT">Dort</a> in 1669, and at first was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Arnold Verhuis, a painter of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and portrait. Afterwards he placed himself with Godfrey Schalcken, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> with that <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> for six years. The sweetness of his colouring, and the neatness of his touch, with a striking likeness in his portraits, procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of admirers. He painted in the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, particularly subjects by candlelight, which were very delicate, and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and much more of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was requested by the lovers of the art than it was possible for him to undertake. He had the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to paint the portraits of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">czar</a> of Muscovy; of Frederick I., <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; of the victorious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, as well as many of the princes of Germany; and most of the noblemen who attended the czar. His style of colouring was extremely good, and he had an elegant manner of disposing the attitudes of his figures: his handling was neat, and the whole had so much <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> that he was justly ranked among the ablest artists of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The small pictures of Boonen are in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of his master Schalcken; but his excessive application, to answer the multitude of his engagements, impaired his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, and destroyed while it enriched him. He died in 1729. **Boopthalmus**, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGATE">agate</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> circles in it, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to an ox's eye, from whence it has got this name. **Boops**, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of baleen. See Baleena, Cetology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOSHATTER">Booshatter</a>**, formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a>, famous for the retreat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Cato, lies about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles inland from Porto Farina in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. Nothing remains of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> except <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a large aqueduct, some cisterns, and other magnificent ruins, which cover a large <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of ground, and show it to have been a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The sea, it is known, came up anciently to this city, though now seven miles distant. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOT">Boot</a>**, a leathern cover or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> for the leg, used on horseback, both to keep the body more firm, and defend the part from the injuries of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Boots seem to have taken their name from the resemblance they bear to a sort of jacks or leathern bottles formerly in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, and called botte, in the old French boots. Borel derives the name from the old French word bot, a stump, by reason the boot gives the leg this appearance. The Chinese have a kind of boots made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> or fine stuff, lined with cotton, a full inch thick, which they always wear at home. This people are always booted; and when a visit is made them, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they happen to be without their boots, their guest must wait till they put them on. They never stir out of doors without their boots on; and their scrupulousness in this respect is the more remarkable, as they are always carried in their chairs. The boot was much used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, by the foot as well as by the horsemen. It was called by the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> ocrea; in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, greva, gambria, bainberga, bembarga or benbarga. The boot is said to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the Carians. It was at first made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> both against cuts and thrusts. It was from this that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> called the Greeks braxen-booted. The boot only covered half the leg; some say the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> leg, which was more advanced than the left, it being advanced forwards in an attack with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; but in reality it appears to have been used on either leg, and sometimes on both. Those who fought with darts or other missile weapons, advanced the left leg foremost, so that this only was booted. **<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>-Boots**, are a thick strong sort used in dragging ponds and the like. Hunting-boots, a thinner kind used by sportsmen. Jack-boots, a kind of very strong boots used by the troopers. **Boot**, is likewise a kind of torture for criminals; to extort a confession, by means of a boot, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a>, or buskin of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; which being put on the leg moist, and brought near the fire, in shrinking squeezes the leg violently, and occasions intolerable pain. There is also another kind of boot; consisting of four thick strong boards bound round with cords: two of these are put between the criminal's legs, and the two others placed one on the outside of one leg and the other on the other; then squeezing the legs against the boards by the cords, the criminal's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> are severely pinched, or even broken, &c. The boot is now disused in England and Scotland; but it subsists still in some other countries. **Boot-Tree**, or **Boot-last**, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used by shoemakers to widen the leg of a boot. It is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> slit into two parts, between which, when it is put into the boot, they drive by main force a wedge or quoin. **Bootes**, a constellation of the northern hemisphere, consisting of 23 stars according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>'s catalogue, of 18 in Tycho's, of 34 in Bayer's, of 52 in Hevelius's, and of 54 in Mr Flamstead's catalogue. **Booth, Barton**, a famous English <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> in 1681, and educated in Westminster school under the celebrated Dr Bushby, where his success in the Latin plays customarily performed by the scholars gave him an inclination for the stage. He was intended for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but running away from school to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, he there commenced actor. His first appearance was in the part of Oroonoko, in which he came off with every testimonial of approbation from the audience. From this time he continued daily improving; and after two successful campaigns in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, conceived thoughts of returning to his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and making a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of his abilities on the English stage. To this end, he first, by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, reconciled himself to his friends; and then, as a farther step towards insuring his success, obtained a recommendation from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Fitzhardinge (one of the lords of the bedchamber to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>) to Mr Betterton, who with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> candour and good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> took him under his care, and gave him all the assistance in The first part Mr Booth appeared in at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was that of Maximus in Lord <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>, his reception in which exceeded even his most sanguine expectations; and very soon after his performance of Artaban, in Rowe's Ambitious Stepmother, which was a new tragedy, established his reputation as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> at least to his great instructor, Pyrrhus, in the Distressed Mother, was another part in which he shone without a rival. But he was indebted to a happy coincidence of merit and chance, for that height of fame which he at length attained in the character of Cato, as drawn by Mr Addison, in 1712. For this play being considered as a party one, the Whigs, in favour of those principles it was apparently written, thought it their duty strongly to support it, while at the same time the Tories, who had too much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> to appear to consider it as a reflection on their administration, were still more vehement in their approbation of it, which they carried to such a height, as even to make a collection of 50 guineas in the boxes during the performance, and present them to Mr Booth, with this compliment, "That it was a slight acknowledgment for his honest opposition to a perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, and his dying so bravely in the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>." Besides this, he had a present of an equal sum from the managers, in consideration of the great success of the play, which they attributed in a good <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to his extraordinary merit in the performance; and certain it is, that no one since that time has ever equalled, or even nearly approached, his excellence in that character. But these were not the only advantages which were to accrue to Mr Booth from his success in this part; for Lord Bolingbroke, then one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretaries of state, in a little time after, procured a special license from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, recalling all the former ones, and nominating Mr Booth as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> manager with Wilkes, Gibber, and Dogget; none of whom were pleased at it; but the last especially took such disgust as to withdraw himself from any further share in the management. In 1704, Mr Booth had married a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir William Barkham, Bart. who died in 1710, without issue. Being now established in the management, he once more turned his thoughts towards matrimony; and in the year 1719 united himself to the celebrated Miss Hester Santlow, a woman of a most amiable disposition, whose great merit as an actress, added to the utmost <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> and prudential economy, had enabled her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> up a considerable fortune. During the 20 years in which Mr Booth continued a manager, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> was in the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; and his illness and death, which happened on the 10th of May 1733, contributed not a little to its decline. Mr Booth wrote a dramatic entertainment called Dido and Æneas; but his masterpiece was a Latin inscription to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Mr William Smith, a celebrated actor, who died while he was young. As an actor, his excellency lay wholly in tragedy, not being able to endure such parts as had not strong <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to inspire him. And even in this walk, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, rather than complacency, rage rather than tenderness, seemed to be his taste. For a particular idea of his abilities, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> Mr Cibber has given of him in his Apology; and the admirable character drawn of him by that excellent judge of dramatic perfection, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> Hill, Esq. in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> published by him called the Prompter, which may be seen at length in Theop. Cibber's Lives of the Poets, and Chetwood's History of the Stage. His character as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was adorned with many amiable qualities, among which, a goodness of heart, the basis of every virtue, was remarkably conspicuous; and so particularly was he distinguished and caressed, and his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> sought by the great, that, as Chetwood relates of him, not one nobleman in the kingdom had so many sets of horses at command as he had.

BOOTY

Pages 40-40

whatever is taken from an enemy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. Among the Greeks, the booty was divided in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, the general only claiming a larger share. By the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, spoils taken from the enemy belonged to the republic, particular persons having no <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to them. The generals who piqued themselves on their probity carried it wholly to the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>. Sometimes indeed they divided it among the soldiery, to animate them, and serve in lieu of a reward. But this distribution depended on the generals, who were to conduct themselves herein with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> and moderation; otherwise it became a crime of peculate to lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on the pillage, as regularly belonging only to the state. The consuls <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Vaturnus were condemned for having sold the booty taken from the Equi. Among the Jews, the booty was divided equally between the army and the people, though under the kings a different kind of distribution obtained. Among the Mahometans, two thirds of the spoils are allowed to the army; the other third to God, to Mahomet and his relations, and to the orphans, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the pilgrims. Among us, formerly, the booty was divided among the soldiery. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the general be in the field, everybody takes what he can lay hold on: if the general be absent, the booty is distributed among the soldiery, two parts being allowed to the cavalry and one to the infantry. A <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> is allowed ten shares, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> six, and a cornet four.

BOPPART

Pages 40-40

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and subject to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; it is seated at the foot of a mountain near the Rhine, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 35. N. Lat. 50. 19.

BOPSINGEN

Pages 40-40

a town of Swabia in Germany, seated on the river Egar, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 55. N. Lat. 48. 51.

BOQUINIANS

Pages 40-40

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, so called from Boquinus their founder, who taught that Christ did not die for all mankind, but only for the faithful, and consequently was only a particular Saviour.

BORACK

Pages 40-40

among Mahometans, a fabulous animal, supposed to be of the middle kind between an ass and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>, whereon their prophet was carried in his nocturnal flight from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> into the heavens. This animal the Arabians call Al Borok, q. d. shining. The night when the journey was performed is called Lailat al Mevrada, i.e. the night of ascension; and the flight itself Al Mesra; concerning which there is a multitude of traditions.

BORAX

Pages 40-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in appearance somewhat similar to crystals of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, brought originally from... from the East Indies in an impure state, and afterwards freed from its impurities by certain processes in the European countries. It was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of uncertainty whether this salt be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fictitious substance in those countries from whence it is brought; but it is now beyond a doubt, that it is naturally produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Thibet, from whence other parts of the eastern continent are supplied. According to an account in the Philosophical Transactions, vol. lxxvii., by Mr <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BLANE">Blane</a>, it is produced in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Jumlate, about 30 days journey <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from Betowle, a small principality about 200 miles northeast of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUCKNOW">Lucknow</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it is found is said to be a small valley surrounded with snowy mountains, in which is a lake about six miles in circumference; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of which is constantly so hot that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> cannot bear it for any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Around this lake the ground is perfectly barren, not producing even a blade of grass; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is so full of a saline matter, that after falls of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> or snow it concretizes in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> flakes on the surface like the natron of Hindostan. On the banks of this lake, in the winter season, when the falls of snow begin, the earth is formed into small reservoirs six inches <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>: when these are filled with snow, the hot water from the lake is thrown upon it; which, together with the water from the melted snow, remains in the reservoir, to be partly absorbed by the earth and partly evaporated by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; after which there remains at the bottom a cake of sometimes half an inch thick of crude borax, which is taken up and reserved for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It can only be made in the winter season, because the falls of snow are indispensably requisite, and also because the saline appearances upon the earth are strongest at that time. When once it has been made on any spot, it cannot be made again on the same spot till the snow has fallen and dissolved three or four times, when the saline efflorescence appears as before. See Chemistry and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBETOMAGUS

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Vangiones on the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>; now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">Worms</a>, in Germany. BORBONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BORBORITES

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Gnostics, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, who, besides embracing the errors of these heretics, denied the last judgment. Their name comes from the Greek Borboros, "filth;" on account of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> they had of daubing their faces and bodies with dirt and filth.

BORCH

Pages 41-41

a town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> in Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 14. N. Lat. 52. 25.

BORCHIA

Pages 42-42

CAESAR, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son of Pope Alexander VI. was a brave general, but a most abandoned villain. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">ITALY</a>.—It is incredible what numbers he caused to be taken off by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and it is notorious that swarms of assassins were constantly kept in pay by him at Rome, for the sake of removing all who were either obnoxious or inconvenient to him. He experienced various turns of fortune; and was sometimes very prosperous, sometimes the reverse. He very narrowly escaped dying by poison in 1503; for having concerted with the pope a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of poisoning <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> newly created cardinals at once, for the sake of possessing their effects, the poisoned wine, destined for the purpose, was by mistake brought to and drank by themselves. The pope died of it; but Caesar, by the vigour of his youth, and the force of antidotes, after many struggles, recovered. He only recovered to outlive his fortune and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, to see himself depressed, and his enemies exalted; for he was soon after divested of all his acquisitions, and sent a prisoner to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in order to free Italy from an incendiary, and the Italian princes from those dangers which the turbulent and restless spirit of Cesar made them fear, even though he was unarmed. He escaped from thence; and got safe to Navarre to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> John his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, who was then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with his subjects. Cesar served as a volunteer in that war, and was killed in 1507.

BORCHLOEN

Pages 41-41

a town of the Prussian states in Germany, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 28. N. Lat. 50. 50.

BORCOVIVM

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Ottadini in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; now Berwick on Tweed.

BORD-HALFFENNY

Pages 41-41

a small toll by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the town for setting up boards, tables, booths, &c. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>. Bord-Lands, the demesnes which lords keep in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> for the maintenance of their board <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Bord-Loide, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> required of tenants to carry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> out of the woods of the lord to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It is also used to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of provision which the bordmen paid for their bord-lands. Bord-Service, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> of bord-lands, by which some lands are held of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and the tenants pay sixpence per <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, in lieu of sending provision anciently for their lord's table.

BORDAT

Pages 41-41

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a small narrow stuff, which is manufactured in some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, and Damietta.*

BORDE

Pages 41-41

Andrew, a physician, was born at Pevensey in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, early in the 16th century, and supposed to have been educated at Westminster school. In his Introduction to Knowledge, he says, that he was a student of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; but of what <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> he does not mention. He left the university without a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and entered himself a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of a Carthusian convent in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but not liking the severe <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of that order, he returned to Oxford, and applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after, he embarked for the continent; and, as himself expresses it, "travelled through and round about Christendom, and out of Christendom into some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>." In the years 1541 and 1542, he resided at Montpelier in France, where he was made <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic, and after his return to England was incorporated into the same degree at Oxford. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to his introduction above mentioned, it appears that he had been in Scotland, which probably was soon after his return from France. Having now satisfied his inclination for travelling, he settled first at Pevensey where he was born, afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, and finally in London, where he is said to have become a fellow of the college of physicians, and first physician to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. But notwithstanding his eminence in his profession, he had the misfortune to spend the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the Fleet prison, where he died in the year 1549. As to his character, Wood says that "he was esteemed a noted poet, a witty and ingenious person, and an excellent physician." Pits calls him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of sufficient learning, but too volatile and inconstant. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> and some others, on the contrary, abuse him grossly. His writings are, 1. A book of the introduction of knowledge, the whyle doth teach man to speak part of all manner of languages, &c. Lond. 1547, 4to; dedicated, from Montpelier, to the Lady <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Henry VIII. It is written partly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, and partly in prose, containing 39 chapters, before each of which is a wooden print of a man. 2. The breviary of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, wherein are remedies for all manner of sicknesses and diseases, &c. Lond. 1547, &c. 4to. 3. Dietary of health, Lond. 1576, 8vo. 4. The merry tales of the madmen of Gotham. Printed, says Wood, in the time of Henry VIII, in whose reign, and after, it was accounted a book full of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and mirth by scholars and gentlemen. Afterwards being often printed, it is now only sold on the stalls of ballad-singers. 5. A <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> pleasant and merry <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the mylner of Abington, with his wife and his fair daughter, and of two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> scholars of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. Lond. printed by Richard Jones, 4to. 6. A book of every region, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>; which shows the miles and leagues distant from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> to city, and from town to town, with the noted things in the said cities and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. Wood says that the author <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> the manuscript of this book.

BORDUNI

Pages 41-42
or BORDONE, Paris, an excellent Italian painter, was born at Venice about the year 1512; and, being of a noble family, had a polite education. He was the disciple of Titian; but has been admired more for the delicacy of his pencil than for the truth of his outlines. He was at the court of France in the reign of Francis I. who had a great esteem for him, and for whom he drew not only abundance of history-pieces, but the portraits of several court-ladies, in so fine a manner, that original nature was hardly more charming. He at length returned to Venice, laden with riches and honour; and having gained great reputation in all parts of Italy, died in 1587, aged 75.

BOREAS

Pages 42-42

a Greek name, now in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Pezron observes, that anciently Boreas signified the north-east wind blowing at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice. The Greeks erected an altar to Boreas. He is represented on the temple at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> with his robe before his mouth, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he felt the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> over which he presides, agreeably to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Ovid, who calls him gelidus tyrannus, "the shivering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>," Met. vi. ver. 711. But he is usually described by the Roman poets as violent and impetuous; ibid. ver. 686—ver. 707. In <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he is generally represented like an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> with a horrible look, his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> covered with snow <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hoar <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, with the feet and tail of a dragon. M. Spierlingius has a treatise in praise of Boreas, wherein he shows the honours paid to him by antiquity. Boreas, according to this author, purifies the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, renders it calm and salubrious, preserves buildings from decay, drives away the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> and other noxious diseases, and expels locusts and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a> hurtful to the grounds.

BORELLI

Pages 42-42

JOHN ALPHONSO, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and mathematician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> on the 28th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1608. He was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> in some of the most celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, where he became highly in favour with the princes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Medicis; but having been engaged in the revolt of Messina, he was obliged to retire to Rome, where he spent the remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> under the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTINA">Christina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, who honoured him with her friendship, and by her liberality towards him softened the rigour of his hard fortune. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two years in the convent of the regular clergy of St Pantaleon, called the pious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, where he instructed the youth in mathematical studies. He died there of a pleurisy, the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1679, in the 72nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote in Latin, 1. Euclid restored. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the influence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in medicine, deduced from physical causes. 3. Of percussive force. 4. Of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> motions depending upon gravity. 5. An historical and meteorological account of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of Mount Etna, in the year 1669. 6. Of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of animals; and several other works, some of which are in Italian.

a town of Russia, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kymenegard. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. N. Lat. 60. 34. N. Lat. 44. 50. Borgo San Domino, a town of Italy, in the duchy of Parma, with a bishop's see. E. Long. 10. 31. N. Lat. 41. 53.

BORIA

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 2. N. Lat. 41. 50.

BORING

Pages 43-43

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the art of perforating, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> making a hole through any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> body. Boring of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. The method of boring water-pipes is as follows. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of alder, which is a very useful wood in making pumps, water-pipes, &c., being laid on horses or trassels of a foot height, to rest the augre upon while they are boring, they set up a lathe to turn the least end of the poles, to fit them to the cavities of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> end of the others. They turn the small ends of the poles about five or six inches in length, to the size they intend to bore the bigger ends about the same depth, viz. five or six inches. This is designed to make a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> to shut each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of poles together, the concave <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> being the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> part, and the other the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> of the joint. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the male part, they turn the channel in it, or a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> at a certain distance from the end; and in the female part they bore a small hole to fit over this channel. This being done, they bore the poles through; and to prevent them from boring out at the side, they stick great nails at each end to be a guide in boring. It is usual, however, to bore them at both ends; so that a crooked pole can be bored through and not spoil it. See Boring, Supplement. Boring, in Farriery, a cruel and absurd method of treating a wrenched shoulder. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Boring, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, a method of piercing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with scooping irons, which being drawn back at proper times, bring up with them samples of the different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> through which they have passed; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of which the skilful mineralogist <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be able to guess whereabouts a vein of ore or a stratum of coal may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, or whether it will be worth while to open a mine for the purpose of working it.

BORIQUEN

Pages 43-43

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, near that of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORTO_RICO">Porto Rico</a>. The English formerly had a settlement there, but were driven away by the Spaniards. It is at present without inhabitants, though agreeable and fertile; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> being wholesome, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> good. There are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, whence some have called it Crab <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 64. 35. N. Lat. 18. o.

BORISTHENES

Pages 43-43

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the largest river of Sarmatia Europea, thus described by Me-la, who copies verbatim from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>: "It runs through a cognominal people, is the most pleasant of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, and calmer than all of them in its course, and very agreeable to drink: it feeds very rich pastures, and produces <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fish of the best flavour, and without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; it comes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> way, rising from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> unknown; its course is a distance of 40 days, and so far is it navigable." It is now called the Dnieper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nieper.

BORKELO

Pages 43-43

a strong town in the United Provinces, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, seated on the river Borkel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 30. N. Lat. 52. 15.

BORLASE

Pages 43-44

William, a very ingenious and learned writer, was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in Cornwall, and born at Pendean, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a>, Feb. 2. 1695-6. He was put early to school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and in 1709 removed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1712-13, he was entered at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1719, took a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. In 1720, he was ordained a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and, in 1722, instituted to the rectory of Ludgvan in Cornwall. In 1732, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> presented him to the vicarage of St Just, his native parish; and this, with the rectory aforesaid, were all the preferments he ever had. In the parish of Ludgvan were rich <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> works, which abound with mineral and metallic fossils: and these, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and inquisitive turn, he collected from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and thence was led to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. He was struck at the same time with the numerous monuments of remote antiquity that are to be met with in Cornwall; and enlarging therefore his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, he determined to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> as accurate an acquaintance as possible with the Druid learning, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and customs of the ancient Britons, before their conversion to Christianity. In 1750 he was admitted a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; and, in 1753, published in folio at Oxford his "Antiquities of Cornwall:" a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of which was published, in the same form, at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1769, with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, "Antiquities, historical and monumental, of the county of Cornwall; consisting of several essays on the ancient inhabitants, Druid <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, customs and remains of the most remote antiquity in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and the British isles, exemplified and proved by monuments now extant in Cornwall and the Scilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; with a vocabulary of the Cornu-British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Revised, with several additions, by the author. To which is added a map of Cornwall, and two new plates." His next publication was, "Observations on the ancient and present state of the islands of Scilly, and their importance to the trade of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Britain; Oxf. 1756," 4to. This was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> which had been read before the Royal Society in 1753. In 1758 came out his "Natural history of Cornwall; Oxf." fol. After these publications, he sent a variety of fossils and remains of antiquity which he had described in his works, to be reposed in the Ashmolean <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>: for which, and other benefactions of the same kind, he received the thanks of the university, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from the vice-chancellor, Nov. 18, 1758; and March 1766, the degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws. He died in 1772, aged 77 years, leaving two sons out of six, whom he had by a lady he married in 1724. Besides his literary connections with many ingenious and learned men, he had a particular correspondence with Mr Pope; and there is still existing a large collection of letters written by that poet to Dr Borlase. He furnished Pope with many of the materials which formed his grotto at Twickenham, consisting of curious fossils; and there may at present be seen Dr Borlase's name in capitals, composed of crystals, in the grotto. On which occasion Pope says to Borlase in a letter, "I am much obliged to you for your valuable collection of Cornish diamonds: I have placed them where they may best represent yourself, in a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, but shining;" alluding to the obscurity of the doctor's situation, and the brilliancy of his talents. Besides the above works, he sent many curious papers to the Philosophical Transactions, and had in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> several other works.

BORMIO

Pages 44-44

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> depending on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, formerly on the republic of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a>, but now subject to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and included in the district called the Valtelline. It is 15 miles over both ways; and is divided into five communities, viz. the town of Bormio, the valley of Forbia, the Interior Valley, the Lower Valley, and the Valley of Luvino.
