Bormio, which is the only town in this district, contains about 1000 inhabitants, and is meanly built, but stands in a delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is seated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Adda and Isalacua, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 10. N. Lat. 46. 25.

BORNE

Pages 44-44

a market town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> in England. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 20. N. Lat. 52. 40.

BORNEO

Pages 44-45

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, and one of the three <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUNDA">Sunda</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. It is thought to be the largest island in the world, next to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; being 800 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 700 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. It is seated under the equator, that line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> it almost through the middle. It is almost of a circular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>: abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; and the finest diamonds in the Indies are found in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, being probably washed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills by torrents. Here are also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and tin, and loadstones. Birds nests* are to be had in this island, which are eatable, and reckoned a great delicacy. The beasts are, oxen, buffaloes, deer, goats, elephants, tigers, and monkeys. This island has fine rivers, especially towards the west and south. In their monsoon, from April to September, the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is westerly; and they have continual heavy rains, attended with violent storms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. The rainy season continues for eight months of the year; and as during that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> all the flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> near the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> is overflowed, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is rendered very unhealthful, and the inhabitants are forced to build their houses on floats, which they make fast to trees. The houses have but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, with partitions made with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>; and the roofs are covered with palmetto leaves, the eaves of which reach within four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five feet of the bottom. The west and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east sides of the island are almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, and the east is but little known. The inland parts are very mountainous; and the southeast, for many leagues together, is a stinking morass, which, being overflowed in the wet season, is very unhealthy. The Portuguese, who first discovered Borneo, had arrived in the Indies above 30 years before they knew anything of it more than the name, and its situation, by reason of their frequently passing by its coast. At last one <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Edward Corril had orders to examine it more narrowly; and being once acquainted with the worth of the country, they made frequent voyages thither. They found the coasts inhabited by Malayan Moors, who had certainly established themselves there by conquest; but the original inhabitants still remain in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and are styled Beajus, which in the Malayan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies a wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The most authentic account of these people is the following, which was extracted from the papers of Father Antonio Ventimiglia, an Italian missionary. He was sent to Borneo from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACAO">Macao</a>, on board a Portuguese ship, converted great numbers to Christianity, and died on the island about the year 1691. The Beajus have no kings, but many little chiefs. Some are subject to the Moorish kings, and pay them tribute; but such as live far up the country are altogether independent, and live according to their own customs. They are generally very superstitious, and much addicted to augury. They do not adore idols; but their sacrifices of sweet wood and perfumes are offered to one God, who, they believe, rewards the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> in heaven, and punishes the wicked in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. They marry but one wife; and look upon any <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, either in the man or woman, as a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offence. The Beajus are naturally honest and industrious, and have a brotherly affection for one another. They have a notion of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, which yet does not render them covetous. They sow and cultivate their lands; but in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, each reaps as much as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> serve his family, and the rest belongs to the tribe in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; by which means they prevent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> or disputes. With the Moors on the coasts the Portuguese for some time carried on a considerable trade, and at their request settled a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a> there; which, however, was afterwards surprised and plundered by the Moors, who put most of BORO the people to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town, also called Borneo, is on the north-west side of the island. See BORNEO, Supplement.

BORNHOLM

Pages 45-45

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, to the south-east of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Schonen in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. It is twenty-one miles in length, and above thirteen in breadth. It has three considerable <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, Rattum, Sandwick, and Nexia; with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of villages; and is fertile and populous. It was conquered by the Swedes in 1658: but the inhabitants, under the conduct of Jens Roefods, voluntarily surrendered it to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, on account of the bad usage they received from the former. In 1678, a body of 5000 Swedish troops, in their passage from Pomerania to Sweden, being shipwrecked on this island, such of them as remained were made prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The inhabitants defend the island by their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, without any expense to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It was a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the British, who took it from the Danes in 1809. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 56' N. Lat. 55° 15'.

BORNOU

Pages 45-45

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Zaara in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, extending from 12 to 22 degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and from 17 to 21 degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude. The northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and like the rest of the provinces of Zaara: but all the rest is well watered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> that tumble <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a dreadful noise from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; rendering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> prolific in corn, grass, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and giving it a pleasing aspect. The eastern and western frontiers are divided into mountains and valleys, the latter being all covered with flocks of cattle, fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and millet, and many of the mountains with wood, fruit-trees, and cotton. On the north-west stands the mountain of Tarton, having plenty of good <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and on the south flows the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NIGER">Niger</a>, which, it is said, after running a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many leagues under a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> chain of mountains, rears up its head again, and mingles its streams with the waters of the lake Bornou in its course, from whence it washes the walls of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of this kingdom. The compilers of the Universal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, however, are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that in these mountains the river Niger hath its source, because no river hath been traced to the eastward, except the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, which runs in a different course from north to south, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> river, on the western frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, which is a branch of the Nile. The eastern and western parts of Bornou are inhabited by a people of a roving disposition, who live in tents, and have their women, children, and every thing else, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>; the word <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, or any idea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to it, being utterly unknown among them. They have neither <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, laws, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, nor any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of subordination; and hence they have been supposed by Cluverius to be the lineal descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Garanantes, and this to have been the residence of that people. In these parts, the natives are almost to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> shepherds and husbandmen. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> they go naked, except a short apron before; but in winter they are warmly clothed with the softest sheep-skins, of which they also form their bedclothes; and indeed this is scarce a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> at certain seasons of the year, when a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> piercing <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the northern mountains, that chills the blood in proportion as the pores of the body have been opened by the scorching heats of summer. BAUDRAND and Draper affirm, that the natives are scarce superior in their understanding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>; not even having any names whereby to distinguish each other, except what they take from some personal defect or singularity; such as lean, fat, squinting, humpbacked, &c. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, however, it is acknowledged that they are something more civilized and polite, being many of them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; but of these towns, or indeed of the kingdom in general, very little is known.

BORODINO

Pages 45-45

a village in Russia, near the river Moskwa, about 90 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>; remarkable for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought there on the 7th September 1812, between the French and Russians. The Russian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, of 120,000 men, occupied a position of no great strength. The firing began at six o'clock in the morning, and soon became general in the centre and Russian left. The Russians had extended their line too much; and the French, after making an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> with their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and musketry, pushed forward, regardless of loss, and carried several batteries, about eight o'clock. The Russians resisted obstinately till noon, and even till two o'clock; and during the following night retired from the field. The loss on each side was believed to be about 30,000 men. BOROMÆUS. See Borromeus.

BOROGNONE

Pages 43-43

a celebrated painter, whose true name was Giacomo Cortessi; but he is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Borgognone, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> where he was born, about the year 1605. He was much admired and highly applauded for his admirable gusto and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> manner of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> battles. He had for several years been conversant in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, was an officer of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> his school, and formed all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> from what he had seen performed in the field. His style is roughly noble, full of fire and spirit, and there are a few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> etched by his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he retired to the Jesuits convent at Rome, where he is said to have taken sanctuary to rid his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an ill bargain he had got of a wife; but happily surviving her, he lived in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> till after the year 1675.

BORONDON

Pages 45-45

St, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, mentioned by some writers, particularly Linschotten, in their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Canary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, as something supernatural. It is said to be about 100 leagues distant from Ferro, probably west, though no writer has pretended to lay <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> its exact situation. Here it is affirmed several ships have touched by accident, and all agree in their relations of the state of the inhabitants and island. They affirm, that it is perpetually clothed with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of wood, chiefly fruit-trees; that the valleys are in a perpetual state of verdure. It is said to be peopled by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of their own, apparently combined of a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages. It is remarkable that no ships, expressly sent upon this discovery, were ever fortunate enough to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in with the island of St Borondon, though the Spaniards have several times attempted it from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANARIES">Canaries</a>. Hence it has been called the marvellous island; and hence indeed we may conclude, either that it exists wholly in imagination, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least that it is surrounded with such currents as insensibly carry ships out of their course, and prevent their meeting with it.

BOROUGH

Pages 45-46

in its original Saxon borge, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> borgh, is by some supposed to have been primarily meant of a tithing or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> consisting of ten families, who were bound and combined together as each others pledge. Afterwards, as Verstegan informs us, borough came to signify a town that had something of a wall or inclosure about it: so that all places which among our <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, had the denomination borough, were one way or other fenced or fortified. But, in latter times, the same appellation was also bestowed on several of the ville insigniores, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of more than ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, though not walled. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Saxons, according to Spelman, gave the name burgh to those called, in other countries, cities. But <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> canons being made for removing the Borough episcopal sees from villages and small towns to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities, the name <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> became attributed to episcopal towns, and that of borough retained to all the rest; though these too had the appearance of cities, as being governed by their mayors, and having laws of their own making, and sending representatives to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, and being fortified with a wall and castle, and the like. Borough, or Burgh, is now particularly appropriated to such towns and villages as send burgesses or representatives to parliament. Boroughs are equally such, whether they be incorporate or not; there being <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of our English boroughs not incorporated; and, on the contrary, several corporations that are not boroughs; e.g., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">Deal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENDAL">Kendal</a>, &c. [Merged from HEAD-BOROUGH ALSO, p.46] h also signifies a kind of head <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>, where there are several chosen as his assistants, to serve warrants, &c. See CONSTABLE.

BOROUGHBRIDGE

Pages 46-46

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in England, seated on the river Yore, over which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. The town is not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but commodious, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 15. N. Lat. 54. IO.

BOROUGHS

Pages 46-46

in Scotland. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">LAW</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Boroughs, in Scotland, are corporations made for the advantage of trade, by charters granted by several of their kings; having the privilege of sending commissioners to represent them in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, besides other peculiar privileges. The royal boroughs are not only so many distinct corporations, but do also constitute one entire body, governed by, and accountable to, one general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, anciently called the court of four boroughs, held yearly to treat and determine concerning matters relating to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> advantage of all boroughs. The four boroughs which composed this court were, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, Stirling, Roxburgh, and Berwick; which two last falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the English, Linlithgow and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LANARK">Lanark</a> were put in their places; with a saving to the former whenever they should return to their <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>. But this court not being sufficient to answer the necessities of the royal boroughs, they were all empowered under James III. in 1487, to send commissioners to a yearly convention of their own, which was then appointed to be held at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERKEITHING">Inverkeithing</a>, but is now held at Edinburgh, under the denomination of the convention of boroughs, vested with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> power, and having for their object the benefit of trade, and the general <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the boroughs. BOROUGH-Courts, are certain courts held in boroughs, by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESCRIPTION">prescription</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament: such are the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s court, and court of hustings, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. BOROUGH-English, a customary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of lands or tenements, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> boroughs and copyhold manors, by which the younger son, and not the eldest succeeds to the burgage tenement on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father. For which Littleton gives this reason; because the younger son, by reason of his tender <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, is not so capable as the rest of his brethren to help himself. Other authors have indeed given a much stranger reason for this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the fee had ancienly a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the seventh commandment with his tenant's wife on her wedding night; and that therefore the tenement descended, not to the eldest, but to the youngest son, who was more certainly the offspring of the tenant. But it cannot be proved that this custom ever prevailed in England, though it certainly did in Scotland, (under the name of mercheta, or marcheta), till abolished by Malcolm III. But perhaps a more rational account than either may be brought from the practice of the Tartars; among whom, according to Father Duhalde, this custom of descent to the youngest son also prevails. That <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is composed totally of shepherds and herdsmen; and English the elder sons, as soon as they are capable of leading a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, migrate from their father with a certain allotment of cattle, and go to seek a new habitation. The youngest son, therefore, who continues latest with his father, is naturally the heir of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the rest being already provided for. And thus we find, that among many other northern nations it was the custom for all the sons but one to migrate from the father, which one became his heir. So that possibly this custom, wherever it prevails, may be the remnant of that pastoral state of the ancient Britons and Germans which Caesar and Tacitus describe. BOROUGH-Head, or Head-Borough, called also borough-holder, or bursholder, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the decenna, or hundred, chosen to speak and act in behalf of the rest.

BOROZAIL

Pages 46-46
or the zeal of the Ethiopians, a disease epidemic in the countries about the river Senegal. It principally affects the pudenda, but it is different from the lues venerea. It owes its rise to excessive venery: in the men this distemper is called asab, in women assabatus. BORRACHIO. See CAOUTCHOUK. BORRAGE. See BORAGO, BOTANY Index.

BORREL

Pages 42-42
PETER, a learned physician, was the son of James Borel who published several poems, and was born at Castres in 1620. He applied himself to the study of physic, of which he was created doctor, and practised with great success in the city of Castres. Towards the end of the year 1653, he went to Paris, and was soon after made physician in ordinary to the king. In 1674, he was received into the academy of sciences, and distinguished himself by writing a great number of works. The most esteemed are, 1. Historiarum et observationum medico-physicarum centuria quinque. 2. Bibliotheca chymica, duodecimo. 3. De vero telescopii inventore, cum brevi omnium conspiscillorum historia. He died in 1678.

BORRELISTS

Pages 46-46

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a Christian <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, so denominated from their founder Borrel, a person of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, and Latin tongues. They reject the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the sacraments, public <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, and all other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> acts of worship. They assert, that all the Christian churches of the world have degenerated from the pure apostolical doctrines, because they have suffered the word of God, which is infallible, to be expounded, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather corrupted, by doctors who are not infallible.

BORRICHUS

Pages 46-46

one of the most learned men of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, the son of a Lutheran minister in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, was born in 1626. He applied himself to physic in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, and began to practise during a most terrible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> that made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> havoc in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He travelled: but before his departure, in 1660, he was appointed professor in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; and at his return discharged his duties with great assiduity, of which the works he published afford full <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. He was raised to the office of counsellor in the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, in 1686; to that of counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, in 1689; and died of the operation for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in 1690. He published, i. Lingua pharmacopoeorum. 2. Dissertations de poeticiis Graecis et Latinis. 3. De ortu et progressu chemiae; and several other works.

BORROMEOAN ISLANDS

Pages 46-46

certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the lake Maggiore in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, celebrated for their picturesque <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. See Supplement.

BORROMEOUS

Pages 48-49

churches and chapels have been erected in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Borrowing, this saint, and many <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> instituted and put under his protection. The foregoing particulars are extracted from an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Borromeus, written some years ago by Father Anthony Touron. Upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of this life with that written by Ribadeneira a Spanish Jesuit above a century ago, it appears that the improvement of knowledge has made a very striking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in this kind of biography. Ribadeneira, who lived in the midst of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, did not suspect that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> when the incredible and ridiculous fables he recites could not be believed: his life of this saint, therefore, abounds with particulars which Touron has justly omitted. We are told that a miraculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> was seen over the chamber of Borromeus's mother when she was in labour: That Borromens, seeing two persons carried violently <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> a rapid river on their horses, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> ready to perish, caused their horses suddenly to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> with them out of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, by giving them his benediction: That Octavian Varesi, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, who was confined to his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> by sickness, when Borromeus died, became instantly well, by recommending himself to the saint's intercession. That a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Julius Bonacina was instantly cured of a disorder in her eye, which had taken away the sight of it, by performing an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> in honour of this saint: That a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a> was instantly seized with a violent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> upon speaking irreverently of Borromeus's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, but was cured upon confessing his fault. It would certainly be a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, to new-write the lives of her saints in such a manner as can now be believed, since the lives already written might by that means be gradually superseded, which are a better antidote against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a> than the arguments of the best reasoner in the world.

BORROMEUS

Pages 46-48

ST <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">CHARLES</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>, and archbishop Borromeus, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>; a personage of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a>, and whose sincere piety, simplicity of manners, and zeal for reformation, render him indeed a character equally interesting and instructive to the members of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He was the son of Gilbert Borromeus <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARONA">Arona</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of Medicis, and was born at the castle of Arona upon Lake Maggiore in the Milanese, in October 1538. When he was about 12 years old, Julius Caesar Borromeus resigned an abbacy to him of a considerable revenue, which was considered as an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> inheritance of the family; which Charles accepted, but applied the revenue wholly in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Having acquired a sufficient knowledge of the languages at Milan, he studied the civil and canon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, where he lived like another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a> in Sodom, preserving his innocence among a thousand snares by which it was endangered. He received great advantage from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> and conversation of Francis Alciat, one of the most learned men of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, for whom he afterwards procured the purple. He would accept no new benefice, but upon condition that he should be at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to apply the revenue to public uses. In the year 1554, Charles being then 16 years old, his father died, an event which brought him back to the castle of Arona; where, though he had an elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Count Frederick, he was requested by the family to take upon him the management of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs, to which at length he consented. After some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he returned again to his studies, which, in the year 1559, being then <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> 21, he finished by a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, and took his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The promotion of his uncle to the pontificate, by the name of Pius IV., which happened the year following, seemed to have very little effect upon him; but he was very soon made protonotary, and entrusted both with the public and privy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> state; he was also, at the same time, created cardinal deacon, and soon after archbishop of Milan. In obedience to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of his uncle the pope, he lived in great splendour, having a brilliant retinue and a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of domestics; yet his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> and humility were never brought into question. In order to render even his amusements useful, he established an academy of select and learned persons, as well <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> as laics, from among his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> and dependants, who were employed in some <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> which tended to inspire a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of virtue, and to form a just <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. Each of them was to write on some chosen subject, either in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in prose, and to communicate to each other in frequent conferences the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their studies. The works produced by this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> have been published in many volumes, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Noctes Vaticanae, because these useful assemblies were held at the Vatican, and at night, after the business of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was over. About this time Charles also formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of founding a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Pavia, which should at the same time be a school of science and an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> from the vices and vanities of the world. In prosecution of this design, he raised a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> edifice upon the foundations of several houses which belonged to the family of Borromeus in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; he obtained from the pope several benefices, which he attached to his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; he provided it with all things necessary for the young scholars out of his own revenue; and he dedicated his Borromeus college to Justina virgin and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his only brother Frederick, his relations, his friends, and even the pope himself, advised him to change his state, to quit the church, and marry, that his family might not become extinct. Charles, however, contrary to this advice and the expectations of the world, received the priesthood, and addressed the pope in these terms: "Do not complain of me, Holy Father, for I have taken a spouse whom I love, and on whom my wishes have been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> fixed." From this time he became more fervent in exercises of piety and ecclesiastical knowledge: He perceived that some literati who had departed from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> had also corrupted the writings of some holy doctors of the church, and he thought he should render <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he could restore the genuine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>: He therefore employed <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACHILLES">Achilles</a> Statius, a Portuguese of great learning, in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, whom for that purpose he retained at Rome. To his zeal and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> also is owing the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of eight cardinals, still subsisting, to resolve doubts and obviate difficulties which should arise in explanations of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>. There was a very intimate friendship between Borromeus, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Bartholomew des Martyrs archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>, and author of a work entitled Stimulus Pastorum. This work falling into Borromeus's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> gave him an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire to become a preacher, as he was now convinced that preaching was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> duties of a prelate. An almost inconceivable multiplicity of business, ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, a feeble <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, and a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a>, were no inconsiderable obstacles to his design, yet he surmounted them all; and although his beginnings were weak, yet perseverance crowned them with success. Having obtained permission to visit his church, which the pope had hitherto refused, as he found his presence necessary at Rome, he prepared to set out for Milan. He had before sent thither his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> Ormanetus, whose labours at first had not been unsuccessful, but who soon found opposition so pertinacious and obstinate as to put an end to his hopes: Borromeus therefore <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of going in person, and he was received with the most distinguished honours. He was, however, soon recalled to Rome, where many things made his presence necessary: the pope was gradually dying; and Charles arrived just time enough to administer to him the last sacraments. Pius IV. died on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1566, and 28 days afterwards Cardinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRINE">Alexandrine</a> mounted the papal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and assumed the name of Pius V. the skill and diligence of Borromeus having contributed not a little to prevent the cabals of the conclave. As soon as this event had taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and all was quiet at Rome, Borromeus gave himself wholly up to the reformation of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, where the most flagitious irregularities were openly practised, having first made another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> in his own family. He began by making pastoral visits in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, where the canons were not distinguished for the purity of their manners. He soon restored proper decency and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to divine service, by a variety of wise and necessary regulations: In conformity to the decrees of the council of Trent, he cleared the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of many pomposities. pompous tombs, rich ornaments, banners, arms, and in general of all the trophies with which the vanity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had disfigured the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God; and in order to give a sanction to his zeal by his example, he spared not the monuments of his nearest relations. Nor did his zeal stop here: he divided the nave of the church through its whole length into two parts, by strong thick planks, that the two sexes, being separated, might perform their devotions without any attention to each other, and with a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and recollection more suitable to the place. This pastoral care extended from the cathedral to the collegiate churches, and even to the fraternities or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of penitents, particularly that of St John the Baptist. The duty of this society was to attend criminals to the place of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, to assist, comfort, and prepare them for death; but the spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> was now forgotten, and the wretches who were condemned to death were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> dragged to execution like beasts, without any spiritual assistance or consolation. But the archbishop revived the original fervour of this order, in the exercise of their peculiar duty, and persuaded many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and principal persons of the city to become members of a society appropriated to so eminent a branch of Christian charity. The reformation of the monasteries followed that of the churches, and the vigilance of the pastor soon extended itself from the city to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> round it, which abounded with irregularities that required his correction. The great abuses and irregularities which had overrun the church at this time arose principally from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the clergy; in order therefore to attack these evils at the root, Charles established seminaries, colleges, and communities, for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of young persons intended for holy orders. He met with many difficulties, and much opposition in his endeavours to bring about a reformation of manners; but he prevailed against every obstacle by an inflexible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, tempered with great sweetness of manners. The governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, and many of the senators, were apprehensive that the cardinal's ordinances and proceedings would encroach upon the civil jurisdiction, and become inconsistent with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of his Catholic majesty, to whom the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Milan was then in subjection. And this was a fruitful source of remonstrances, representations, and complaints, which long troubled the courts of Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II., referred entirely to the decision of the pope. But Borromeus had a more formidable opposition to struggle with, that of several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> orders, particularly the Brothers of Humility. Three provosts of the society entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> to cut him off; and one of their confederates, called Jerom Donat, whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> was Farrina, took upon him to carry the design into execution. For this purpose he mixed with the crowd that went into the archiepiscopal chapel, where the cardinal spent an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> every evening in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> with his domestics and other pious persons; and having watched his opportunity, he fired a harquebus at him, which was loaded with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> suited to the bore of the piece, and with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>. It is said that the ball struck him on the spinal bone, but fell <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> at his feet without doing any other damage than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>- ing his rochet, and that one of the shot penetrated his clothes to the skin, and there stopped, without imprinting any wound, which was considered as a miracle, especially as another shot tore away <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a wall, and went quite through a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. In the year 1576, the city and diocese of Milan were visited by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which swept away incredible numbers; and the behaviour of Borromeus, on this occasion, was truly Christian and heroic: He not only <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the spot, but he went about giving directions for accommodating the sick, and burying the dead, with a zeal and attention that were at once ardent and deliberate, minute and comprehensive: and his example stimulated others to join in the good work. He avoided no danger, and he spared no expense; nor did he content himself with establishing proper regulations in the city, but went out into all the neighbouring parishes where the contagion raged, distributing <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the poor, ordering proper accommodations for the sick, and punishing those, especially the clergy, who were remiss in the duties of their calling. Charles, notwithstanding the fatigue and perplexity which he suffered by thus executing his pastoral charge, abated nothing of the usual austerity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, nor omitted any of his stated devotions; for, whatever approached to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> or magnificence, he considered as incompatible with the propriety of his character. It happened, that being once on a visit to the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a> at his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, a very sumptuous entertainment was provided for him. Borromeus, though he had been used to content himself with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, yet sat down at the table, where however he ate but little, and gave sufficient intimation that he was much displeased with such ostentations prodigality; but what was his surprise when he saw the table again covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESSERT">dessert</a>, consisting of whatever was most rare, exquisite, and costly! He immediately rose hastily from his seat, as if he had suddenly recollected some pressing business, and gave orders for his departure, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, and the most earnest entreaties of the archbishop. "My <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>," said the cardinal, "if I should tarry here to-night, you would give me another such treat as that I have just seen, and the poor will then suffer another loss, great numbers of whom might have been fed with the superfluities that have been now set before us." The continual labours and austerities of Borromeus naturally shortened his life; he went to Vercal to put an end, if possible, to the divisions which threatened the most fatal consequences; and, when he was there, he received a message from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy, requesting his presence at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. From Turin he retired to a place called the Sepulchre, on the mountain Varais, where he was seized with an intermittent fever, which scarce permitted him to return alive to Milan, where he arrived on the 3rd of November 1584, and died the next day. He was lamented by the city and the whole province with such marks of sincere sorrow as are rarely seen; and he was immediately worshipped as a saint, without waiting for the pope's approbation. The pope, however, when he was told of it by Cardinal Baronius, gave directions that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> of the people should not be restrained, though Borromeus was not canonized till the 1st of November 1610, in the pontificate of Leo XI. Since that time many churches

BORROWING AND HIRING

Pages 49-49

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, are contracts, by which a qualified <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> may be transferred to the hirer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> borrower; in which there is only this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that hiring is always for a price or stipend, or additional recompense; borrowing is merely gratuitous. But the law in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> is the same. They are both contracts, whereby the possession and transient property is transferred for a particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, on condition and agreement to restore the goods so hired or borrowed, as soon as the time is expired or the use performed, together with the price or stipend (in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of hiring) either expressly agreed upon by the parties, or left to be implied by law, according to the value of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. By this mutual <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, the hirer or borrower gains a temporary property in the thing hired, accompanied with an implied condition to use it with moderation, and not to abuse it; and the owner or lender retains a reversionary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the same, and acquires a new property in the price or reward. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> hires or borrows a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, he has the possession and a qualified property therein during that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which his qualified property determines, and the owner becomes (in case of hiring) entitled also to the premium or price for which the horse was hired. There is one <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this price or reward the most usual of any, but concerning which many good and learned men have in former times very much perplexed themselves and other people, by raising doubts about Borrowing its legality in favo conscientiae. That is, when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> on a contract to receive not only the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sum again, but also an increase by way of compensation for the use, which is generally called interest by those who think it lawful, and usury by those who do not so. But as to this, see the article INTEREST. BORROWSTOWNESS. See BURROWSTOWNNESS.

BORSEHOLDER

Pages 49-49

among the Anglo-Saxons, one of the lowest magistrates, whose authority extended only over one free burgh, tithing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> decenary, consisting of ten families. Every freeman who wished to enjoy the protection of the laws, and not to be treated as a vagabond, was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of being admitted a member of the tithing where he and his family resided; and in order to obtain this admission, it was as necessary for him to maintain a good reputation; because all the members of each tithing being mutual pledges and sureties for each other, and the whole tithing sureties to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> for the good behaviour of all its members, they were very cautious of admitting any into their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> who were of bad or doubtful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Each tithing formed a little state or commonwealth within itself, and chose one of its most respectable members for its head, who was sometimes called the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a> of such a tithing or freeburgh, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, but most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> borseholder, from the Saxon words boh, "a surety," and alder, "a head or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>." This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> had authority to call together the members of his tithing, to preside in their meetings, and to put their sentences in execution. The members of each tithing, with their tithing-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or borseholder at their head, constituted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, in which all the little controversies arising within the tithing were determined. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any dispute of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty or importance happened, or if either of the parties was not willing to submit to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> given in the tithing-court, the cause was referred or appealed to the next superior court, or court of the hundred.

BORSET

Pages 49-49
or BORSETT, celebrated for its baths, a place about half a league from Aix-la-Chapelle in Germany. The abbey here is a very magnificent pile of building. It was formerly a monastery; but serves for a nunnery, whose abbess is a princess of the empire, and lady of Borset. The waters are warm, and of the nature of those of Aix-la-Chapelle; but they are only used as baths for the diseases in which the waters last mentioned are recommended, and also in dropsical and oedematous cases. The waters are distinguished into the upper and lower springs. The former were found by Dr Simmons to raise the thermometer to 158°, the latter to only 127°. All the baths are supplied by the first. Dr Simmons observed, that these waters were much less sulphureous than those of Aix-la-Chapelle, probably on account of their greater heat. He likewise found that they abounded much with selenites, which incrust the pipe through which the water passes, and likewise the sides of the bath. BORYSTHENES. See BORISTHENES.

BOS

Pages 49-50

John Baptist du, a celebrated author and member of the French academy, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> in 1670, and finished his studies at the Sorbonne. In 1695, he was made one of the committee for foreign affairs. affairs under Mr Torez; and was afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with some important transactions in England, Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. At his return to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was handsomely preferred, made an abbé, and chosen perpetual secretary of the French academy. He was the author of several excellent works; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are, 1. Critical reflections upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, 3 vols 12mo. 2. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the four Gordians, confirmed and illustrated by medals. 3. A critical History of the establishment of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">Monarchy</a> among the Gauls, 2 vols 4to, 4 vols 12mo. He died at Paris on the 23d of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1742. Bos, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Janssen, an esteemed painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOIS_LE_DUC">Bois-le-Duc</a>. Having been carefully instructed in the art of painting by the artists of his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he applied himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and rendered himself very eminent for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of his colouring and the neatness of his handling. His favourite subjects were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which he usually represented as grouped, in glasses, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vases of crystal, half filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and gave them so lively a look of nature, that it seemed scarce possible to express them with greater truth or delicacy. It was frequent with this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to represent the drops of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> on the leaves of his objects, which he executed with an uncommon transparency; and embellished his subjects with butterflies, bees, wasps, and other insects, which Sandrart says, were superior to any thing of that kind performed by his cotemporary artists. He likewise painted portraits with very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success; and showed as much merit in that style as he did in his compositions of still <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He died in 1597. BOS. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Bos, in antiquity, was peculiarly used for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> which was didrachmus, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to two drachms. It was so called as having on it the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of an ox, and chiefly obtained among the Athenians and Delians; being sometimes also struck of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. From this arose the phrase Bos in lingua, applied to those who had taken bribes to hold their tongue.

BOSA

Pages 50-50

a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town in the western <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, with a castle, a good port, and a bishop's see. It is seated on the river Bosa, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of an island of the same name; and has good <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> pits. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 30. N. Lat. 40. 19.

BOSCAGE

Pages 50-50

the same with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thicket. Boscage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is that food which trees yield to cattle; as mast, &c. But Manhood says, to be quit of boscage is to be discharged of paying any duty for windfall wood in the forest. Boscage, among painters, denotes a landscape representing much wood and trees.

BOSCAN

Pages 50-50

John, a Spanish poet of the 16th century, born at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a>. He was the friend of Garcilasso de Vega, another Spanish poet. These two were the first who made any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> improvement in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and their pieces were printed together. Boscan, who died about the year 1542, principally succeeded in sonnets.

BOSCAWEN

Pages 50-50

Edward, a brave British <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Hugh late <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> viscount <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>. Having early entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, he was, in 1740, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOREHAM">Shoreham</a>; and behaved with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> intrepidity as a volunteer under Admiral Veonon, Boscawen, at the taking of Porto Bello. At the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1740-1, he had the command of a party of seamen who resolutely attacked and took a batter of 15 twenty-four pounders, though exposed to the fire of another fort of five guns. Lord Aubrey Beaneclerk being killed at the attack of Boca-Chica, Captain Boscawen succeeded him in the command of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Frederic of 70 guns. In May 1742, he returned to England, and married Frances <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of William Glanville, Esq. and the same year was elected representative for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a> in Cornwall. In 1744, he was made captain of the Dreadnought of 60 guns; and soon after he took the Medea, a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> commanded by M. Hoquart, the first <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s ship taken in that war. May 3, 1747, he signalized himself under the admirals Anson and Warren, in an engagement with the French fleet off <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINISTERRE">Finisterre</a>, and was wounded in the shoulder with a musket <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. Here M. Hoquart, who then commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">Diamond</a> of 56 guns, again became his prisoner; and all the French ships of war, which were ten in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, were taken. On the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> he was made rear-admiral of the blue, and commander in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> forces employed on an expedition to the East Indies; and, on the 4th of November, sailed from St Helen's, with six ships of the line, five frigates, and 2000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. On the 29th of July 1748, he arrived at St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, and soon after laid siege to Pondicherry; but the men growing sickly, and the monsoons being expected, the siege was raised, and Mr Boscawen showed himself as much the general as the admiral in his retreat. Soon after he had news of the peace, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MADRAS">Madras</a> was delivered up to him by the French. In April 1750, he arrived at St Helen's in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, and found that in his absence he had been appointed rear-admiral of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. He was the next year made one of the lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, and chosen an elder <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the Trinity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In February 1755, he was appointed vice-admiral of the blue. On the 19th of April, sailing in order to intercept a French squadron bound to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, he fell in with the Alcide and Leys of 64 guns each, which were both taken; on this occasion M. Hoquart became his prisoner a third <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and he returned to Spithead with his prizes and 1500 prisoners. In 1756, he was appointed vice-admiral of the white; and in 1758, admiral of the blue, and commander in chief of the expedition to Cape Breton; when, in conjunction with General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a>, and a body of troops from New England, the important fortress of Louisbourg and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Cape Breton were taken, for which he afterwards received the thanks of the house of commons. In 1759, being appointed to command in the Mediterranean, he arrived at Gibraltar, where hearing that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a> fleet, under M. de la Clue, had passed the Straits, in order to join that at Brest, he got under sail, and on the 18th of August <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, pursued, and engaged the enemy. His ship, the Namor of 90 guns, losing her mainmast, he shifted his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a> to the Newark; and, after, a sharp engagement, took three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ships, and burnt two in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAGOS">Lagos</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and the same year arrived at Spithead with his prizes and 2000 prisoners. On <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 8, 1760, he was appointed general

BOSCH

Pages 50-51
JACOB VANDEN, a painter of still life, was born at Amsterdam, in 1636, and painted summer fruits, of various kinds, peaches, pears, apples, plums, nectarines, and cherries, with extraordinary neatness of pencil. He painted all his objects after nature, and imitated every sort of fruit with so great truth and delicacy, with such natural and transparent colour, that they appeared delicious and almost real. He died in 1676.

BOSCHAERTS

Pages 51-51

THOMAS WILLEBORTS, a celebrated painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-zoom; and, like the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters who flourished at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, began to draw when very young, in the books that were intended for other studies. Preferring his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> to every thing else, he drew his own <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, by his resemblance in a looking-glass, so like, that those who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it were astonished. This he did before he had the least instruction from any one, and when he was only 12 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Upon this his parents sent him to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that he might follow the bent of his genius; but his first master being only an indifferent painter, and incapable of satisfying his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> desire of learning, he left him, and engaged himself with Gerard Segers; under whom, after four years practice, he proved a most accomplished <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> being at that time the seat of arts, where there was a conflux of the most eminent painters, he thought it the fittest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for his improvement; and there executed such a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of noble pieces as added greatly to the splendour of that wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. In 1642, Henry Frederic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, and his son Prince William, employed him in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; in which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> several years, and made those excellent pieces that are to be seen in that prince's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> and other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and painted portraits for most of the persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that were then living. He died in the flower of his age, in 1670.

BOSCO

Pages 51-51
or BOSCHI, a town of Italy, in the Milanese, seated on the river Orbe. E. Long. 9. 44. N. Lat. 44. 53.

BOSCOI

Pages 51-51
or BOSCI, in ecclesiastical history, denotes a species or tribe of monks in Palestine, who fed on grass like the beasts of the fields. The word is Greek, βοσκει, q. d. "grazers;" formed from βοσκω, pasco, "I feed." The Boscoi are ranked among the number of Adamites, not so much on account of their habit, as food. They took no care about provision; but when eating time came, or any of them was hungry, went into the fields, with each his knife in his hand, and gathered and ate what he could find.

BOSCOVICH

Pages 51-69

ROGER <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">JOSEPH</a>, the founder of an original and sublime <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, deserves to be particularly noticed in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but we have to regret that the materials from which our biographical memoir must be compiled, are insufficient to satisfy the curiosity concerning the literary habits, and the characteristic features, of this very illustrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, indeed, as a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, we are enabled to appreciate by perusing some of the immortal works which he hath bequeathed us; but, for a knowledge of his moral character, disposition, and temporal concerns, we can only have recourse to the eulogies of his friends. These are certainly entitled to much of our confidence; and when the names of M. de la Lande, M. Fabroni, Stay, and Zamagna are mentioned, we may be thought fastidious, in implying the least distrust of their testimony. It is our respect for the public and for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and it is our knowledge of the nature of eulogies, which have made us so. We have, therefore, endeavoured, rather to relate the incidents in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Boscoovich, than to give a transcript of friendly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a>; and yet perhaps it may be discovered, that our report is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> with eulogium, whilst its outlines are poorly defined. Boscoovich was born on the 11th of May 1711, at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAGUSA">Ragusa</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Adriatic, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a small republic of the same name, under the protection of the Turks and the Venetians. We know so little of his parents, that we can only conjecture at their circumstances and capacity, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> which they gave to their son being liberal and judicious. It does not appear that our author gave any tokens of superior genius, till he was sent to learn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> and philosophy in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the Jesuits, who were at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> teachers in Ragusa, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>.
