As Rivinus set out with the professed design of imparting facility to botany, he judged very properly in divesting his method of all extraneous matter, and rendering it as simple and uniform as the nature of the science would admit. The distinction into herbs and trees had been adopted by every writer on plants since the time of Aristotle. Rendered in some measure sacred by its antiquity, this distinction maintained a kind of importance to which it was by no means essentially entitled. Rivinus was the first who in this matter dared to think for himself. He was early sensible of the inconveniences to which those who had submitted who employed it as a primary division; and therefore resolved at once to get rid of a distinction that is frequently uncertain, always destructive to uniformity, and in its nature repugnant to the genuine spirit of system, because totally unconnected with the parts of fructification. In the uniformity of its orders or secondary divisions, which are 91 in number, and acknowledge the fruit for their principle, Rivinus's method equals, perhaps excels, all that went before or succeeded it. Only three classes of this method were published by Rivinus himself. These are the 11th, 14th, and 15th, which were offered to the public at different times, illustrated with very splendid figures. The method was completed and published entirely by Heucher, in a work entitled *Hortus Wirtenbergensis*, printed in quarto at Württemberg in 1711. Several German authors have followed Rivinus's method, either wholly or in part, without offering any considerable amendment. The principal of these are, Koenig, in a work on vegetables, published at Basle in 1696; Welch, in his *Basis Botanica*, printed at Leipzig in octavo, in 1697; Gemeinhart, in a catalogue of plants published in 1725; Kramer, in a work entitled *Tentamen Botanicum*, published at Dresden in 1728, and afterwards reprinted with additions at Vienna in 1744; and Heckel in a dissertation on botany published at Hal in Saxony, in 1734. To these may be added Hebenstreit, an ingenious botanist, who in a treatise on plants published at Leipzig in 1731, just before his famous African expedition, established generical characters, which had hitherto been wanting in Rivinus's method. The writers who have attempted to improve upon Rivinus's method are Bernard Ruppius, Christopher Ludwig, and Christian Knaut. Ruppius in his *Flora Jenensis*, published at Francfort in 1718, has arranged the 1200 plants there described by a method partly Rivinus's and partly his own. It consists of 17 classes, and sets out with the same divisions and subdivisions as that of Rivinus's; with this difference, however, that, whereas in Rivinus's method all perfect flowers are divided into simple and compound, in Ruppius the division of regular and irregular flowers precedes that just mentioned, and simple and compound flowers are made subdivisions of the regular flowers only. Christopher Ludwig's method, which was published in 1737, and consists of 20 classes, differs but little from that of Rivinus. The author accompanied Hebenstreit on his expedition to Africa, and seems to have made plants his favourite study. The improvement, however, which he has made on Rivinus's plan, consists only in rendering it more universal, having enriched it with a multitude of genera collected from the works of Tournefort, Ray, Boerhaave, Dillenius, and other eminent botanists, whose generical characters he has likewise adopted. His plan of arrangement has been followed by two succeeding writers: M. Wedel, in a botanical essay published in 1747; and three years after by M. Bochmer, in his catalogue of the plants which grow in the garden of Leipzig. The method of Christian Knaut is much more properly his own, and departs in a much greater degree from that of Rivinus than either of the two former. The regularity and number of the petals furnished the classical divisions in Rivinus's method: in that of Knaut, Christian number takes place of regularity; so that it is very pro-Knaut's perly termed by Linnaeus, "The system of Rivinus inverted." This method was published in 1716; and sets out with a division into flowers which have one petal, and such as have more than one. It consists of the following classes. 1. Monopetalous uniform or regular. 2. Monopetalous difform or irregular. 3. Monopetalous compound uniform or regular. 4. Monopetalous compound difform or irregular. 5. Monopetalous compound uniform and difform together. 6. Dipetalous uniform or regular. 7. Dipetalous difform or irregular. 8. Tripetalous uniform or regular. 9. Tripetalous difform or irregular. 10. Tetrapetalous uniform or regular. 11. Tetrapetalous difform or irregular. 12. Pentapetalous uniform or regular. 13. Pentapetalous difform or irregular. 14. Hexapetalous uniform or regular. 15. Hexapetalous difform or irregular. 16. Polypetalous uniform or regular. 17. Polypetalous difform or irregular. The sections or secondary divisions in Knaut's method are 121, and depend upon the internal divisions of the fruit; and upon this his opinions are somewhat singular. Every kind of fruit, whether pulpy or membranaceous, is termed by our author a capsule. Neither is the term restricted to fruits properly so called: it is extended also to those termed by botanists naked seeds, the existence of which Knaut absolutely denies. Agreeable to this opinion, capsules, he says, with respect to their consistence or substance, are of two sorts; pulpy, or membranaceous. The former correspond to the fruits of the apple, berry, and cherry kind; the latter to the capsules properly so called, and naked seeds of other botanists. Again, with respect to their cells or internal divisions, capsules are either simple or compound. Simple capsules have an undivided cavity or a single cell; compound capsules are internally divided into two or more cells. With other botanists, the umbelliferous flowers bear two, the lip flowers four, naked seeds; according to Knaut, the former produce two, the latter four, simple capsules. Ranunculus, adonis, anemone, herb-bennet, and some other plants, have their flowers succeeded by a number of naked seeds collected into an aggregate or head; each of these seeds passes with Knaut for a simple capsule; so that the whole is an aggregate of several capsules with an undivided cavity or single cell. In numbering the cells or internal divisions of the pulpy fruits, our author has adopted a very singular method. Some fruits of the apple kind enclose a capsule that is divided into five membranaceous cells. It might then be very reasonably expected to find such fruits arranged with compound capsules of five cells: but, instead of this, the author whimsically enough combines in their arrangement the idea both of a simple and compound capsule. The pulpy part is undivided; in other words, it is a simple capsule furnished with one cell; the compound capsule enclosed contains five cells, which added to that of the pulp make the number six; and thus these kinds of fruits are arranged with those having capsules of six cells. By the same kind of reasoning, the fruit of the dogwood, which is of the cherry kind, and contains a stone... stone with two cells or cavities, is placed by Knaut among compound capsules with three cells; the pulp passing for one division, and cavities of the stone or nut for the remaining two. This method of calculation is not the only singularity for which Knaut is remarkable. The essence of the flower is made by Ray, Tournefort, Riviinus, and most other botanists, to consist in the stamens and style. This position Knaut absolutely denies; and has established for a principle, that the flower is essentially constituted by the petals only. With him, the flower cup, stamens, and style, are of little significance: their presence does not constitute a flower, if the petals are wanting; neither is their absence sufficient to destroy its existence, if the petals are present: from this it follows, 1. That there can be no flowers without petals; and, 2. That the regularity or irregularity of the flower can never depend on the stamens and style, which are only occasionally present, and not wise essential to its existence; both of which are evidently false to every botanical reader. Since the time of Riviinus, no leading method in botany has appeared except those of Tournefort and Linnaeus. Tournefort sets out with reviving the distinction of plants into herbs and trees, which had been exploded by Riviinus. His system is founded on the regularity and figure of the petals, together with the twofold situation of the receptacle of the flowers; his orders, on the pistillum or calyx. The classes are, 1. Herbs with simple flowers monopetalous, and bell-shaped. 2. Simple flowers monopetalous, tunnel and wheel-shaped. 3. Simple flowers monopetalous, labiate or lipped. 4. Simple flowers monopetalous, anomalous or irregular. 5. Simple flowers polypetalous cruciform or cross-shaped. 6. Simple flowers polypetalous, and rosette-like. 7. Simple flowers polypetalous, umbellate. 8. Simple flowers polypetalous, caryophyllaceous, or clove-form. 9. Simple flowers polypetalous, lilaceous or lily-form. 10. Simple flowers polypetalous, papilionaceous, or butterfly-form. 11. Simple flowers polypetalous, anomalous or irregular. 12. Compound flowers, flocculous, tubular or whole florets. 13. Compound flowers, semiflocculous, flat or half florets. 14. Compound flowers radiated, like the spokes of a wheel. 15. Apetalous, having no petals. 16. No flower, but bearing seed. 17. No flower nor seed, in the vulgar estimation. 18. Trees with no petals, but bare stamens. 19. Trees with no petals bearing catkins. 20. Trees monopetalous. 21. Trees rosette-like. 22. Trees papilionaceous. The secondary divisions in Tournefort's method, which are 122 in number, have obtained the name of sections. Their general distinctions are founded principally upon the fruit, as those of the classes are upon the flower. Tournefort hath been followed by a vast number of botanical writers, of whom the most considerable are, Dr William Sherard, an eminent botanist of the last and present centuries. In 1689, he published the first sketch of Tournefort's method, under the title of Schola Botanica; or a catalogue of the plants demonstrated by Dr Tournefort, in the royal gardens at Paris. It was not till five years after, that the Elementa Botanica, a work which contains the rudiments and illustration of his method, was published by Tournefort himself. Other writers. Tournefort's method. Father Plumier, termed by way of eminence the Tournefort of America, published in 1703, at Paris, a description of American plants, which he has arranged according to the system of Tournefort. In this work he accurately characterized 96 new genera. Falugi, an Italian, has described, in pretty elegant Latin verse, all the genera of Tournefort, in a work entitled Proprietarum Botanicae, published at Florence, 12mo, 1705. Several celebrated French academicians, particularly Marchant, Dodart, Niffle, Jussieu, and Vaillant, have also occasionally paid their tribute of acknowledgement to this author, from the year 1720 to 1740. The other authors of note who have followed Tournefort's method, are, M. Petit, an ingenious French botanist; Johren, a German, author of a treatise published at Colberg in 1710, entitled Vade mecum Botanicum, seu Odeus Botanicus; Fussile, in his description of the plants of Chili and Peru, published at Paris in quarto, 1714; Christopher Valentin, a German author of a book entitled Tournefortius Contraetus, published at Francfort, in folio, 1715; Ripa, an Italian, in a work entitled Historiae Universalis Plantarum Conferendi Propagium, published in quarto, at Padua, in 1718; Michael Valentini, a German, in his Viridarium Reformatum, published in folio, at Francfort, in 1719; the celebrated Dillenius, professor of botany at Oxford, and author of several much esteemed publications on botany; particularly the Hortus Floraemontis, and History of Mollies, in his Flora Giffensis, printed at Francfort in 1719; Pontedera, an Italian, author of the delineation of a method which combines those of Tournefort and Riviinus, published at Padua, in his botanical dissertations, in 1720; Monti, an Italian, in a work published at Bologna in 1724, under the title of Indices Plantarum Variorum; Dindem, a German, in his Tournefortius Altissimus, first published in 1728; Signor Michel, author of several curious discoveries respecting mollies and mushrooms, in his Nova Genera Plantarum, published in folio at Florence in 1729; Elvebenes, a Swede, in a work published in the Swedish language at Upsal in 1730; Fabricius, a German, author of a work entitled Primitive Florae Butiflaccensis, seu sex Decades Plantarum Rariorum, published in 1743; Sabbati, an Italian, in his catalogue of the plants that grow in the neighbourhood of Rome, published at Rome in 1745; and the ingenious Dr Charles Alston, late professor of botany at Edinburgh, in his Tyrocinium Botanicum, published at Edinburgh in 1753. Of all this numerous list of writers, Father Plumier Plume and Pontedera alone have ventured to quit the track method pointed out by Tournefort. The former, in his arrangement of American plants, has relinquished the distinction into herbs and trees; but the latter has attempted more considerable variations. His classes are, 1. Uncertain. 2. Having no flowers. 3. Without buds, imperfect plants. 4. Anomalous or irregular. 5. Labiate. 6. Bell-shaped. 7. Saucer-shaped. 8. Wheel-shaped. 9. Tunnel-shaped. 10. Flocculous. 11. Semiflocculous. 12. Radiated. 13. Irregular. 14. Papilionaceous. 15. Liliaceous. 16. Caryophyllaceous. 17. Cruciform or cross-shaped. 18. Umbellate. 19. Staminous, or with naked stamens. 20. Bearing buds apetalous, or without petals. 21. Bearing buds irregular. 22. Bearing buds bell-shaped. 23. Bearing

BOTANY-BAY

Pages 411-412

so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> which were discovered by the naturalists who first visited it. See New-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>.

BOTARGO

Pages 412-412

a kind of sausage, made with the eggs and blood of the mullet, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fish <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the Mediterranean. The best kind comes from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> in Barbary: it must be chosen dry and reddish. The people of Provence <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of it, the common way of eating it being with olive <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and lemon juice. There is also a great consumption of it throughout the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>.

BOTE

Pages 412-412

(Sax.), signifies a recompense, satisfaction, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> amends: hence comes manbote, compensation or amends for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> slain, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Ina's laws is declared what rate was ordained for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> of this offence, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the person slain. From hence likewise we have our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> phrase, to-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOT">boot</a>, i.e. compensationis gratia. There are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-bote, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>-bote, &c. privileges to tenants in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> of wood, &c.

BOTELESS

Pages 412-412

(sine remedi). In the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of Hen. I. to Tho. archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, it is said, "that no judgment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> shall acquit him that commits sacrilege; but he is in English called boteless, viz. without emendation." We retain the word still in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> speech; as, It is bootless to attempt such a thing; that is, It is in vain to attempt it.

BOTH

Pages 412-412

John and Andrew, Flemish painters, and pupils of Bloemart. The union of these brothers was very singular; they were inseparable in their studies, travels and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. John painted the landscape <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their pictures in the manner of Lorrain, and Andrew the figures and animals in the style of Bamboche. They both died in 1650. John's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> in landscape is elegant; his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> beautiful; and his execution rich and masterly in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> is not always well distributed; but his figures are excellent. It is to be regretted that we have not more of his works; for they are certainly, upon the whole, among the best landscapes we have.

BOTHNIA

Pages 412-412

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, at the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of the same name. It is divided into two parts, called east and west Bothnia, the former of which belongs to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, and is now subject to Russia. West Bothnia is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, and yet a scarcity of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> is seldom known. Cattle and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> are so <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, salmon and a sort of herrings so plenty, and the trade of skins is so gainful, that the inhabitants can command what they want from their neighbours. There are only two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> worth mentioning, viz. Tornæa and Uma. The inhabitants of this province are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>.

BOTICELLI

Pages 412-413

Sandro, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Alessandro, born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1437, learned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> under Filippo Lippi. He executed several pictures for Pope Sixtus IV. and others for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Florence: for these he received <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, all of which he expended, and died at last in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distress, aged 78. He was not only a painter but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters. Baldini, according to the general report, communicated to him the secret of engraving, then newly discovered by Finiguerra their townsmen. The famous edition of Dante's poem of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">Hell</a>, printed at Florence by Nicholo Lorenzo della Magna, A.D. 1481, and to which, according to some authors, Botticelli undertook to write notes, was evidently intended to have been ornamented with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>, one for each <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTO">canto</a>; and these prints (as many of them as were finished) were designed, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not engraved, by Botticelli. It is remarkable, that the two first plates only were printed upon the leaves of the book, and for want of a blank space at the head of the first canto, the plate belonging to it is placed at the bottom of the page. Blank spaces are left for all the rest; that as many of them as were finished might be pasted on. Mr Wilbraham possesses the finest copy of this book extant in any private library; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of prints in it amounts to nineteen. The two first, as usual, are printed on the leaves; and the other seventeen, which follow regularly, are pasted on the blank spaces; and these apparently were all that Botticelli ever executed. About Botticelli the year 1460, it is said that he engraved a set of plates, representing the Prophets and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBYLS">Sibyls</a>. Basan tells us that he marked these plates with a monogram composed of an A and a B joined together.

BOTRYS

Pages 412-412

Botrus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bostron, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Phoenicia, on the Mediterranean, built by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a>, (a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> at least of antiquity); twelve miles to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Byblus, and twenty to the south of Tripolis. Now almost in ruins, and called Boteron or Boturn, (Postellus). E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 37° 30'. N. Lat. 34° 6'.

BOTTLE

Pages 413-413

a small vessel proper to contain liquors, made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, glass, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The word is formed from butellus or botellus, used in barbarous Latin writers, for a lesser vessel of wine; being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> of bola, which denoted a but or cask of that liquor. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jewish bottles were cags made of goats or other wild beasts skins, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on the inside, well swed and pitched together; an aperture in one of the animals paws serving for the mouth of the vessel. Glass bottles are better for cyder than those of stone. Foul glass bottles are cured by rolling sand or small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> in them; musty bottles, by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them. See Glass. Bottles are chiefly made of thick coarse glass; though there are likewise bottles of boiled leather made and sold by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>-makers. Fine glass-bottles covered with straw or wicker, are called flasks or bettes. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the glass has been sometimes found to affect the liquor in the bottle. Dr Percival cautions against the practice of cleaning of wine bottles with leaden shot. It frequently happens, he thinks, through inattention, that some of the little pellets are left behind; and when wine or beer is again poured into the bottles, this mineral <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> slowly dissolve, and impregnate those vinous liquors with its deleterious qualities. The sweetness which is sometimes perceived in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> port wine may arise from this cause, when such an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADULTERATION">adulteration</a> is neither designed nor suspected.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">Potash</a> is recommended for cleansing bottles: a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> will clean two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>.

BOTTLING

Pages 413-413

the operation of putting up liquors in bottles corked, to keep, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, and improve. The writers on good husbandry give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> rules concerning the bottling of beer, cyder, and the like. The virtues of Spaw, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRMONT">Pyrmont</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCARBOROUGH">Scarborough</a>, and other waters, depend on their being well bottled and corked, otherwise they lose both their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and smell. To preserve them, it is necessary the bottles be filled up to the mouth, that all the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> may be excluded, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy of bottled liquors. The cork is also further secured by a cement. Some improve their bottled beer, by putting crystals of tartar, and wine <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> malt spirits, and others, by putting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> boiled up with the essence of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and cloves, into each bottle. Cyder requires special precautions in the bottling; being more apt to fly, and burst the bottle, than other liquors. The best way to secure them, is to have the liquor thoroughly fine before it be bottled. For want of this, some leave the bottles open a while, or open them after two or three days bottling to give them vent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> one bottle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, through <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, it is best to give them all vent, and cork them up again. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> cyder is apter to break the bottles than rich. Some soak the corks in scalding <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, to render them more pliant and serviceable. Another particular to be observed is, to lay the bottles so as that the liquor may always keep the cork wet and swelled. Something also depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the bottles are set, which ought to be such as exposes them as little as possible to the alterations and impressions of the air; the ground is better for this purpose than a frame; sand better than the bare ground; and a running water, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> often changed, best of all. To hasten the ripening of bottled liquors, they are sometimes set in a warm place, or even exposed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, when a few days <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring them to maturity.

BOTTOM

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, is used to denote as well the channel of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and harbours, as the body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">hull</a> of a ship. Thus, in the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, we say, gravelly bottom, clayey bottom, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> bottom, &c. and in the latter sense, a British bottom, a Dutch bottom, &c. By statute, certain commodities imported in foreign bottoms, pay a duty called petty <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, over and above what they are liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> imported in British bottoms.

BOTTOMRY

Pages 413-414

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, (a practice which originally arose from permitting the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a ship in a foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to hypothecate the ship in order to raise <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to refit,) is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of a mortgage of a ship; when the owner takes up money to enable him to carry on his voyage, and pledges the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bottom of the ship (pars pro toto) as a security for the repayment. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is understood, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ship be lost, the lender loses also his whole money; but if it return in safety, then he shall receive back his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, and also the premium or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> agreed upon, however it may exceed the legal rate of interest. And this is allowed to be a valid <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> in all trading nations, for the benefit of commerce, and by reason of the extraordinary hazard run by the lender. And in this case, the ship and tackle, if brought home, are answerable (as well as the person of the borrower) for the money <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a>. But if the loan is not upon the vessel, but upon the goods and merchandise, which must necessarily be sold or exchanged in the course of the voyage, then also the borrower, personally, is bound to answer the contract; who therefore, in this case, is said to take up the money at respondentia. These terms are also applied to contracts for the repayment of money borrowed, not on the ship and goods only, but on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> hazard of the voyage itself; when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> lends a merchant 100l. to be employed in a beneficial trade, with condition to be repaid with extraordinary interest, in case such a voyage be safely performed; which kind of agreement is sometimes called fenus nauticum, and sometimes usura maritima. But as this gave an opening for usurious and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> contracts, especially upon <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> voyages, it was enacted by the statute 19 Geo. II. c. 37. that all moneys lent on bottomry, or at respondentia, on vessels bound to and from the East Indies, shall be expressly lent only upon the ship, or upon the merchandise; that the lender shall have the benefit of salvage; and that if the borrower has not on board effects to the value of the sum borrowed, he shall be responsible to the lender for so much of the principal as hath not been laid out, with legal interest and all other charges, though the ship and merchandise be totally lost. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOTTOMY">BOTTOMY</a>.** A <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> bottomy, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, terminates nates at each end in three buds, knots, or buttons, resembling, in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, the three-leaved grass; on which account Segging, in his *Tresor Heraldique*, terms it *croix treffle*. It is the badge of the order of St Maurice. See *Heraldry Plates*.

BOTTRIGARO

Pages 414-415

Hercule**, a person eminently skilled in the science of music, though not a musician by profession. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>; and appears, from several letters to him that have been printed, to have had the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a>. He published several controversial pieces on the subject of music. It seems that he entertained strong prejudices in favour of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music; and that he attempted, as Vincentine and others had done, to introduce the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHROMATIC">chromatic</a> genus into practice, but with no better success than had attended the endeavours of others. He corrected Gogavino's Latin version of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> in numberless instances; and that to so good a purpose, that Dr Wallis has in general conformed to it in that translation of the same author which he gave to the world many years after. He also translated into Italian *Boetius de Musica*, and as much of Plutarch and Macrobius as relates to music: besides this, he made annotations upon Aristoxenus, Franchinus, Spataro, Vicentino, Zarlino, and Galisilei; and, in short, on almost every musical treatise he could lay his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on, as appears by the copies which were once his own, and are now reposed in many <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Of Bottrigaro's works it is said, that they contain greater proofs of his learning and skill in music, than of his abilities as a writer, his style being remarkably inelegant: nevertheless, he affected the character of a poet; and there is extant a collection of poems by him, in 8vo, printed in 1557. *Musical Lexicon.* Walther represents him as an able mathematician, and a collector of rarities; and says that he was possessed of a cabinet, which the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand II. had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> desire to purchase. He died in 1609. **Botts**, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> which can be produced and nourished only in the intestines of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. It is there alone they can enjoy the proper temperature of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and receive the nourishment necessary for them. See *Oestrus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*. Besides the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> worms which have been observed in the bodies of horses, there are also short ones.—By these are to be understood what we call botts. All authors, both ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, who have treated of the diseases of horses, have taken notice of these worms; but M. Vallisnieri is the first who has traced them to the last stage of their transformation, and has seen them change into a hairy kind of fly like the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRONE">drone</a>. The flies from which these botts are produced inhabit the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and do not come near houses, at least not near those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>: and therefore horses are never liable to have the worms (i.e. botts) in their bodies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have been kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, especially in a town, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> and autumn. It is in the former of these seasons, and perhaps too in the beginning of the latter, that the females of these flies apply themselves to the anus of horsea, and endeavour to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> admittance, in order there to deposit their eggs, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps their worms. The precise instant of their entrance <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarce admit of an eye-witness, but by the merest chance; yet M. Vallisnieri says, that Dr Gaspari had attained this very uncommon sight. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> (he tells us) was one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> looking at his mares in the field; and from being very quiet, he observed, that on a sudden they became very restless, and ran about in great agitation, prancing, plunging, and kicking, with violent motions of their tails. He concluded, that these extraordinary effects were produced by some fly buzzing about them, and endeavouring to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> upon the anus of one of them; but the fly not being able to succeed, he observed it to go off with less noise than before, towards a mare that was feeding at a distance from the rest; and now the fly taking a more effectual method to obtain its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, passed under the tail of the mare, and so made its way to the anus. Here at first it occasioned only an itching, by which the intestine was protruded with an increasing aperture of the anus; the fly taking the advantage of this, penetrated further, and secured itself in the fold of the intestine;—this effected, it was in a situation proper for laying its eggs. Soon after this, the mare became very violent, running about, prancing, and kicking, and throwing herself on the ground; in short, was not quiet, nor returned to feeding, till after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The fly then, we see, can find means of depositing its eggs, or perhaps its worms (i.e. botts), in the fundament of the horse; which once effectuated, it has done all that it is necessary for them. If these bott-worms are not hatched when first deposited in the horse, but are then only eggs, it will not be long before it happens, from the nutritive heat they there receive. These bott-worms soon make their way into the intestines of the horse: they occupy such parts of this region as are to them most convenient; and sometimes (as we shall see presently) they penetrate even to the stomach. All the hazard they appear to be exposed to, is that of being carried away from the places they have fixed on by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>, which may seem likely to drive all before it. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> has provided for all things; and when we shall have further described these bott-worms, it will seem that they are able to maintain their situation, and to remain in the body of the horse, as long as they please. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when these bott-worms are of themselves desirous to leave this their habitation, it being no longer convenient for them after the purposes of their growth are answered. Their transformation to a fly must be performed out of the horse's body; and accordingly, when the time of their transformation draws near, they approach towards the anus of the horse; and then leave him of their own <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, or with the excrement, with which they then suffer themselves to be carried along. According to M. de Reaumur's observations, the bott-worms have two unequal claws, by which they are enabled to remain in the intestines of the horse in opposition to all efforts of the excrement to force them out.—These claws are a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, differently disposed from those of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> anchors, but contrived to produce the same effect. Besides these two claws, nature has given them a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of triangular spines or bristles, very sufficient to arm them against the coats of the intestines, and to resist the force employed to drive them towards the anus, provided the head be directed towards the stomach of the horse. It will be asked, no doubt, if these bott-worms are not not dangerous to horses?—The mares which afforded M. de Reaumur, for several years, those on which he made his observations, did not appear to be less in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> than those which had none, but it may sometimes happen, that they are in so great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the body of the horse as to prove fatal to him. M. Vallisnieri supposes these bott-worms to have been the cause of an epidemical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> that destroyed a great many horses about <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> in the year 1713. The observations communicated to him by Dr Gaspari sufficiently confirm his supposition. This <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, upon dissecting some horses that died of this distemper, found in their stomachs a surprising quantity of short worms; of which to give us some idea, he compares them to the kernels of a pomegranate opened; each of these, by gnawing on the coat of the stomach, had made to itself a kind of cellule therein, each of which would easily contain a grain of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> wheat. It is easy to imagine by this means the stomach must be reduced to a wretched condition; the outer membranes were inflamed, and the inner ones ulcerated and corrupted; a very small quantity of these worms was found in the small intestines, and only a few in the larger, to which last they were found affixed, but had not corroded them. It is only perhaps when these bott-worms are in great numbers, and thereby incommode each other in the intestines of the horse, that they make their way towards the stomach; and indeed a very few flies must be enough to overstock the inside of a horse, provided they should deposit all their eggs, and such should all be animated, M. Vallisnieri having counted 700 odd in the body of one single fly. When one of these botts has left the anus of the horse, it falls on the ground; and immediately seeks out for some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of safety, where it may retire, to prepare for the last stage of its transformation, by which it is to become a fly. And now by degrees the skin hardens and thickens; and at length forms a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> shell or cod, the form of which scarce differs from that of the worm. It is first of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which changes into chestnut; and at length, by the addition of gradual and successive shades of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, the shell is rendered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. The worm or bott, before it passes into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a>, is of the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; it remains in this form much longer than worms of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-fly kind. M. de Reaumur met with worms that retained this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> five or six days: as yet, one can perceive no traces of the legs, wings, and head of the nymph. Hence he first learned, that those bott-worms do not become nymphs immediately upon their first change; but that, in order to become flies, they must undergo one change more than caterpillars ordinarily do to become butterflies.—For the cure of horses troubled with botts, see Farriery Index.

BOTWAR

Pages 415-415

a town of Germany, in the circle of Suabia, and subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Wirtemberg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 15. N. Lat. 49. 0.

BOTZENBURG

Pages 415-415

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Mecklenburg. It had a castle, which was destroyed by the Danes in 1202. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, and the vessels that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by are obliged to pay a considerable toll. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 48. N. Lat. 53. 34.

BOUCHAIN

Pages 415-415

a fortified town of the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is divided into two parts by the river Scheld. It was taken by the French in 1676: and by the allies under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a> in 1711, which was the last <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> achievement of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> general; but the following year it was retaken by the French. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 15. N. Lat. 50. 17.

BOUCHE OF COURT

Pages 415-415

the privilege of having meat and drink at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> scot-free. The word is also written bouge, bouge, and budge; it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> French, where it signifies mouth.—The French still <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the phrase, Avoir bouche à la cour; that is, to have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> diet at court. This privilege is sometimes only extended to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, beer, and wine; it was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> anciently in use, as well in the houses of noblemen as in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s court. Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> retained Sir John de Ewre, to serve him with ten men at arms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, allowing them bouge of court, with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> of hay and oats, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-shoes and nails. Sir Hugh Meril had the same privilege for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on condition of serving King Edward II.

BOUCHET

Pages 415-415

JOHN, a French poet and historian, flourished in the 16th century. The most considerable of his writings are the Annals of Aquitaine, and his Chapelet des Princes.

BOUDRY

Pages 415-415

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Neufchatel, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a chatelainry of the same name. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7. 5. N. Lat. 47. 11.

BOUFLERS

Pages 415-416
LEWIS FRANCIS, Duke of, a peer and marshal of France, and a general of distinguished reputation, was the son of Francis count of Bouflers. He was born in the year 1644, and entering early into the army, was raised in 1669 to the rank of colonel of dragoons, and in the conquest of Lorraine, served under Marshal Crequi. In the war against Holland he served under the celebrated Turenne, and frequently distinguished himself by his skill and bravery; and when that general was killed, in 1675, he commanded the rear-ass="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard during the retreat of the French army. After performing various military services in Germany, in Flanders, and on the frontiers of Spain, he gradually rose in rank as well as in reputation. In 1690, he was created general of the army of the Moselle. In the following year, he acted as lieutenant-general, under the king in person; and while he invested Mons was wounded in an attack on that place. He conducted the bombardment of Liege, although it was defended by a superior enemy, and he forced the allied generals to abandon Luxemburg. He was entrusted with the command of the covering army, against King William, at the siege of Namur; and for this and many other important services, he was raised in 1693 to the high rank of marshal of France. In 1694, he was appointed governor of French Flanders, and of the town of Lisle. By a skilful manoeuvre he threw himself into Namur, in 1695, and held out for sixty-three days, against the combined armies of the allies under King William. Having agreed to a capitulation, he was arrested prisoner of war, war, because the French had not performed the stipulated terms on which the garrison had surrendered; and when he remonstrated that the garrison should have been retained rather than himself, he received a fine compliment, by being answered, that he was estimated at 10,000 men. In the conferences which were held with the earl of Portland, and which terminated in the peace of Ryswick, he had a principal share. During the following war, when Lisle was again threatened, in 1708, with a siege by the duke of Marlborough and Prince Eugene, Boufflers was appointed to the command, and made a very obstinate resistance of four months. His magnanimity was not less remarkable than his military conduct; for when a partisan represented to him that it would not be difficult to kill Prince Eugene, he was told by the marshal, that he might expect a great reward for taking him prisoner, but the severest punishment if anything were attempted against his life. He was rewarded and honoured by the king for his defence of Lisle, as if he had been victorious. When the affairs of France were threatened with the most urgent danger, though a senior officer to Villars, he made an offer to serve under that general, and was with him at the battle of Malplaquet. Here he again displayed his military skill, by conducting the retreat, so that he lost neither cannon nor prisoners. He died at Fountainbleau in the year 1711, at the age of 68, and left the character of a true patriot, as well as of a great commander. Madame de Maintenon, said of him, "that his heart was the last part that died." His conduct was uninfluenced by private interest, and superior to court intrigue. When he was ordered to take upon him the defence of Lisle, and permitted to have the choice of his lieutenants, he waited not to arrange or regulate his private affairs, or even to take leave of his family, but flew to the place, and carried with him only two officers, one taken from the Bastile, and another who had been in disgrace; preferring merit obscured in the shades of retirement, to the gaudy flatterer in the sunshine of court favour.

BOUGEANT

Pages 416-416

WILLIAM HYACINTH, a famous Jesuit, first taught <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVERS">Nevers</a>, and afterwards settled at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, where he employed himself in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> several works; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which were, 1. A collection of physical observations, extracted from the best authors. 2. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the wars and negociations which preceded the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Westphalia. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>, a philosophical amusement on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of beasts, &c. He died in 1743.

BOUGET

Pages 425-425

DOM JOHN, an ingenious French antiquary, was born at the village of Beaumains near Falaise, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Seez, in 1724. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAEN">Caen</a>, whence he was removed to that university, and pursued his studies with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diligence and success till 1745, when he became a Benedictine monk of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Martin de Seez. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after this, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> claustral of the said abbey, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> six years in that office, when he was nominated prior of Tiron en Perche: whence being translated to the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, in the capacity of sub-prior, he managed the temporalities of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> during two years, as he did their spiritualities for one year longer; after which, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the house, he resigned his office. His superiors, sensible of his merit and learning, removed him thence to the abbey of Bec, where he resided till 1764. He was elected an honorary member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of Antiquaries of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, Jan. 10, 1765; in which year he returned to the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, where he continued to the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. These <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> offices, to which he was promoted on account of his great abilities, enabled him not only to pursue his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities of some of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> Benedictine abbeys in Normandy, but likewise gave him access to all their charters, deeds, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>-books, &c. &c. These he examined with great care, and left behind him in MS. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and accurate accounts of the abbeys of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Jumieges, St Stephen, and the Holy Trinity at Caen (founded by William the Conqueror and his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> Matilda), and a very particular history of the abbey of Bec. These were all written in French. The "History of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Abbey of Bec" (which he presented to Dr Ducarel in 1764) is only an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> of his larger <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> abbey (which hath produced several archbishops of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> and other illustrious prelates of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>) is frequently mentioned by our old historians. The death of our worthy Benedictine (which happened on new-year's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1776) was occasioned by his unfortunate neglect of a hurt he got in his leg by falling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three steps in going from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> to the cloister of the abbey of St Stephen at Caen, being deceived by the ambiguous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> that was placed in the passage. He lived universally esteemed, and died sincerely regretted by all those who were acquainted with him; and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the said abbey, Jan. 3, 1776.

BOUGH

Pages 416-416

denotes much the same with BRANCH.—Green boughs anciently made <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> of altars and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, especially on festival occasions. Oaken boughs were offered to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>; those of laurel, to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>; of olive, to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a>; myrtle, to Venus; ivy, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>; pine, to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>; and cypress to Pluto.

BOUGIE

Pages 416-416

in the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies a wax <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>, and is applied to a machine which (as the wax candle formerly was) is introduced into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-URETHRA">urethra</a> for removing obstructions there. Mons. Daran, a French surgeon, lately boasted of his introducing them as an improvement in his art, and acquired considerable profit by making and selling them. Scultetus, about the middle of the 17th century, used bougies in diseases of the urethra, and Mons. Daran probably took the hint from him. Different compositions have been used, and generally <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of them. Riverins made a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> as follows: Bo ol. oliv. Ib iv. cerae citrin. Ib ii. minii & ceruss. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">aa</a> Ib iss., tereb. venet. & rez. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALB">alb</a>. aa 3 iii. m. Whether the bougies are made up of this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, they must be of different sizes, from the bigness of a knitting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> to that of a goose quill. They are made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> rags, spread with a proper <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, and then rolled up as follows. Having spread any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the linen rag with the composition that is chosen for the purpose, cut it into slips from six to ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and from half an inch to an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: then dexterously roll them on a glazed tile into the form of a waxed candle: and as the end of the bougie that is to be entered first into the urethra should be somewhat smaller than the rest, it would be as well to cut the slips a little tapering. It should also be observed, that when the bougies are rolled up, that side must be outward on which the plaster is spread. Mons. Daran, and some others, attributed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of their bougies to the composition they made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of in forming them. Mr Sharp apprehended, that as much of their efficacy was owing to the compression they made on the affected part, as to any other principle; and Mr Aiken very justly says, As it is evident that bougies of very different compositions succeed equally well in curing the same disorders in the urethra, it is plain, that they do not <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> by means of any peculiar qualities in their composition, but by means of some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. This must be their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> form and texture, therefore their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of action must be simple compression. The efficacy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> compression in many <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of constriction is well known, from the use of sponge tents for widening parts that are straitened by cicatrices; and admitting obstructions in the urethra to be from a constriction formed by cicatrized ulcers, or a projection of the spongy substance of the urethra into the canal, we may easily conceive, that a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> compression <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> overcome the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>. We may also readily account for the inferior efficacy of metallic and whalebone bougies, from their not having the property of swelling with moisture, and therefore not making so equal a compression. As to bougies procuring a discharge of matter, there is no doubt but the mechanical stimulus of a foreign body in such a tender part, though free from disease, must produce it in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and that this will be varied according to the chemically irritating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the composition, and the irritable state of the urethra; but it seems an absurdity to apply a topic, made uniform throughout, to the whole length of a canal, with a view of producing extraordinary effects upon a particular part of it, by means of some powerful quality in the ingredients. That a part of the bougie is particularly covered with matter, is probably owing to the greater irritation of that part of the urethra where the disorder is.

BOUHOURS

Pages 416-417

DOMINIC, a celebrated French critic, Bouhours, tic, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1628; and has been by some considered as a proper person to succeed Malherbe, who died about that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was entered into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Jesuits at the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16; and was appointed to read lectures upon polite literature in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Clermont at Paris, where he had studied; but he was so incessantly attacked with the headache, that he could not pursue the destined task. He afterwards undertook the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of two sons of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Longueville, which he discharged with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. The duke had such a regard for Bouhours, that he would needs die in his arms; and the "Account of the pious and Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>" of this great personage was the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which Bouhours gave the public. He was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a> to the Popish refugees from England; and in the midst of his missionary occupations, found means to compose and publish books. Among these were, "Entretiens d'Ariste et d'Eugene," <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "Dialogues between Aristus and Eugenius;" a work of a critical <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and concerning the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. His book was printed no less than five times at Paris, twice at Grenoble, at Lyons, at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, &c. and embroiled him in quarrels with a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of censors, with Menage in particular, who, however, lived in friendship with our author before and after. The fame of this piece, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> he took in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> it, recommended Bouhours so effectually to the celebrated minister Colbert, that he trusted him with the education of his son the marquis of Segnelai. He wrote afterwards several other works; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of which are, 1. Remarks and doubts upon the French language. 2. Dialogues upon the art of thinking well in works of genius. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of St Ignatius. 4. The art of pleasing in conversation. 5. The life of St Francis Xavier, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> of the Indies and of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>. This last work was translated from the French into English by Mr Dryden, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the year 1668, with a dedication prefixed to James II.'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>.

BOUILLON

Pages 417-417

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Luxembourg, with a fortified castle, which is seated on a rock that is almost inaccessible. The French took it in 1676; upon which it was given to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bouillon. This duchy was a sovereignty, independent of France; and in 1792, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> granted to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> d'Auvergne, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, his license to accept the succession to the said duchy, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, only son of the reigning duke, without issue <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a>, pursuant to a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of his serene highness, in 1791, "at the desire, and with the express and formal consent of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>." Accordingly, Captain d'Auvergne afterwards assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of prince of Bouillon. In May 1794 this town was taken by storm, by General Beaulieu, after defeating a considerable body of republicans, and given up to pillage; 1200 French were killed, and 300 taken prisoners. It is seated near the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 20'. N. Lat. 49° 45'. Bouillon, in the manege, a lump <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> excrescence of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> that grows either upon or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> by the frush, insomuch that the frush shoots out, just like a lump of flesh, and makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> halt; and this is called the flesh blowing upon the frush. Manege horses, that never wet their feet, are subject to these excrescences, which make them very lame. See Frush.

BOULAINVILLIERS

Pages 417-417

HENRY DE, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> of St Saise, and an eminent French writer, was descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble family, and born at St Saise in 1638. His <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was among the fathers of the oratory; where he discovered from his infancy those uncommon abilities for which he was afterwards distinguished. He applied himself principally to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; and his performances in this way are numerous and considerable. He was the author of a history of the Arabians; fourteen letters upon the ancient parliaments of France; a history of France to the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VIII.; the state of France, with historical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> concerning the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Hugh Capet, "written (says M. Montesquieu) with a simplicity and honest freedom worthy of that ancient family from which their author was descended." M. Boulainvilliers died at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1722; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Mahomet.

BOULANGER

Pages 417-418

NICHOLAS ANTHONY, a very singular Frenchman, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1722, and died there in 1759, aged only 37. During his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he is said to have come out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUVAIS">Beauvais</a> almost as ignorant as he entered into it; but struggling hard against his unaptness to learn, he at length overcame it. At seventeen, he began to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; and in three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four years made such a progress, as to be useful to the baron of Thiers, whom he accompanied to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of engineer. Afterwards he had the supervision of the highways and bridges; and he executed several public works in Champagne, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and Lorrain. The author of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in the Dictionnaire des Hommes celebres, writes, that in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> a terrible spirit discovered itself in him, which he himself did not suspect before; and this was, it seems, the spirit of "thinking philosophically." In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, directing and changing the courses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and in breaking up and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a multitude of different substances, which (he thought) evinced the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity of it, and a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of revolutions which it must have undergone. From the revolutions in the globe, he passed to the changes that must have happened in the manners of men, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, in governments, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and he formed many conjectures upon all these. To be farther satisfied, he wanted to know what, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of ages, had been said upon these particulars; and that he might be informed from the fountain-head, he learned first Latin and then Greek. Not yet content, he plunged into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Syriac, Chaldaic, and Arabic; and acquired so immense an erudition, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had lived, he would have been one of the most learned men in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, as we have observed, prematurely took him off. His works are, 1. Traité du Despotism Oriental, 2 vols 12mo; a very bold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but not so bold and licentious, as, 2. L'Antiquité devouée, 3 vols 12mo. This was posthumous. 3. He furnished to the Encyclopédie the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Deluge, Corvet, and Société. 4. He left behind him in MS. a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, which may be regarded as a concordance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. As a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, he is said to have been of a sweet, calm, and engaging temper; which, however, it is very difficult to reconcile with the dark, impetuous, ardent spirit, that appears to have actuated him as a writer. Boulanger, John, an engraver, who flourished towards the end of the last century, was a native of France. His first manner of engraving appears to have been copied, in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, from that of Francis de Poilly; but soon after he adopted one of his own, which, though not original, he however greatly improved: He finished the faces, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and all the naked parts of his figures, very neatly, with dots instead of strokes, or strokes and dots. The effect is singular enough, and by no means unpleasing: only, in some few instances, he has opposed the coarse graving of his draperies and back ground, so violently to the neater work of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, that the outline of the latter is thereby rendered hard, and the general appearance of it flat and chalky. This style of engraving has been carried to its greatest perfection in the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, particularly in England. He did not draw the naked parts of his figures correctly, or with fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. His draperies are apt to be heavy, and the folds not well marked. However, his best <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> possess much merit, and are deservedly held in great esteem.

BOULAY

Pages 418-418

César Egasse Du, in Latin Bulæus, was born at St Ellier, a village of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a> in France; and became professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Navarre, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, rector, and historiographer of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He died in 1678, after having published several works. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of them are, A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the University of Paris, in Latin, 6 vols folio; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">Treasure</a> of Roman Antiquities, in 1 vol. folio.

BOULCOLACA

Pages 418-418

among the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Greeks, denotes the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a> of some wicked person who died excommunicated by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>, reanimated by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, and causing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disturbance among the people; of which many strange stories are told. The word is Greek, and is sometimes written Βουκολακας, bourkola-kos; and supposed to be derived from Βυξες, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Βυξης, "mud," and λαχας, a "ditch," on account of the thinness of the sight.

BOULDER-WALL

Pages 418-418

a kind of wall built of round flints <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pebbles, laid in strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and used where the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> has a beach <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up, or where there are plenty of flints.

BOULETTE

Pages 418-418
