BOVIUM (Itinerary); a town of the Silures, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, fifteen miles to the south of Isca Silurum, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>: Now called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COWBRIDGE">Cowbridge</a>; according to Baudrand, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAERNARVONSHIRE">Caernarvonshire</a>.

BOW

Pages 426-431

(arcus), a weapon of offence made of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which, after being strongly bent, by means of a string fastened to its two ends, in returning to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state throws out an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force. It is also called the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-bow, by way of distinction from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-bow or arbalest. The bow is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and the most universal of of all weapons. It has been found to obtain among the most barbarous and remote people, and who had the least <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the rest of mankind. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the bow and arrow was first abolished in France under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. in 1481, and in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> were introduced the Swiss arms, that is, the halberd, pike, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. The long-bow was formerly in great vogue in England; most of our victories in France were acquired by it; and many laws were made to regulate and encourage its use. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> under Henry VIII. complain "of the disuse of the long-bow, heretofore the safeguard and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and the dread and terror of its enemies." 33 Hen. VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 6. The art of using bows is called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">archery</a>, and those practised therein, archers or bowmen. See ARCHERY. The strength of a bow may be calculated on this principle, that its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, i.e. the power whereby it restores itself to its natural position, is always proportionate to the distance or space it is removed therefrom. The most barbarous nations often excel in the fabric of the particular things which they have the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> offices of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The Laplanders, who support themselves almost entirely by hunting, have an art of making bows, which we, in these improved parts of the world, have never arrived at. Their bow is made of two pieces of tough and strong wood, shaved <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the same size, and flatted on each side; the two flat sides of the pieces are brought closely and evenly together, and then joined by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> made of the skins of perch, which they have in great plenty, and of which they make a glue superior in strength to any which we have. The two pieces, when once united in this manner, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never separate, and the bow is of much more force to expel the arrow, than it could possibly have been under the same dimensions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> made only of one piece. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the bow-string, called τεχνος, was made of horses <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and hence also called ἴππιος; though <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>'s bow-strings are frequently made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> cut into small thongs: whence ἱππικός. The uppermost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bow, to which the string was fastened, was called ξαράντα, being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and the last thing towards finishing the bow. The Grecian bows were frequently beautified with gold or silver; whence we have mention of αὐρεῖος ἀρκευς; and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> is called Ἀγγειοπέδης. But the matter of which they were ordinarily composed, seems to have been wood: though they were anciently, Scythian-like, made of horn, as appears from that of Pandurus in Homer, Iliad. 8. v. 105. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the bow is usually ascribed to Apollo, and was communicated to the primitive inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, who are said to have been the first of mortals who understood the use of bows and arrows. And hence, even in later ages, the Cretan bows were famous, and preferred by the Greeks to all others. Some, however, rather choose to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> Perseus, the son of Perseus, with the invention of the bow; while others ascribe it to Scythus, son of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and progenitor to the Scythians, who were excellent at this art, and by many reputed the first masters of it. From them it was derived to the Grecians, some of whose ancient <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> were instructed by the Scythians in the use of the bow, which in those days passed for a most princely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. It was first introduced into the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. The Indians still retain the bow. In the repository of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> we see a West <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> bow two yards long. The Scythian bow was famous for its incurvation, which distinguished it from the bows of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> and other nations; being so great as to form a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>: whence the shepherd in Athenæus, being to describe the letters in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THESEUS">Theseus</a>'s name, and expressing each of them by some apposite resemblance, compares the third to the Scythian bow; meaning not the more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> character Σ, but the ancient C, which is semicircular, and bears the third place in ΘΗΕΥΓ. Cross-Bow, is also called arbalet or arbalest; which word is derived from arbalaist, i.e. arcubalista, "a bow with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLING">sling</a>." The arbalest consists of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> bow set in a shaft of wood, furnished with a string and a trigger; and is bent with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> fitted for that purpose. It serves to throw bullets, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> arrows, darts, &c. The ancients had large <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> for throwing many arrows at once, called arbalests or balistes. Bow, is also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, for taking the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a>; consisting of a large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of 90° graduated, a shank or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, a side vane, a sight vane, and a horizon vane. It is now out of use. Bow, among builders, a beam of wood or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, with three long screws that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> a lathe of wood or steel to any arch; chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> draughts of ships and projections of the sphere, or wherever it is requisite to draw large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>. Bow, in Music, a small machine, which being drawn over the strings of a musical instrument, makes it resound. It is composed of a small stick, to which are fastened 80 or 100 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> hairs, and a screw which serves to give these hairs a proper tension. In order that the bow may touch the strings briskly, it is usual to rub the hairs with rosin. The ancients do not appear to have been acquainted with bows of hair: in lieu hereof they touched their instruments with a plectrum; over which our bows have great advantage, for giving long and short sounds, and other modifications which a plectrum cannot produce. Bow, among artificers, an instrument so called from its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; in use among gunsmiths, locksmiths, watchmakers, &c. for making a drill go. Among turners it is the name of that pole fixed to the ceiling, to which they fasten the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> that whirls round the piece to be turned. Bow, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a> in England, 188 miles west from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and a little to the west of Crediton, has a weekly market, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the year. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> is commonly kept here. Bows of a Saddle, are two pieces of wood laid archwise to receive the upper part of a horse's back, to give the saddle its due form, and to keep it tight. The fore-bow which sustains the pommel, is composed of the withers, the breasts, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or toes, and the corking. The hind-bow bears the torsequin or quilted roll. The bows are covered with sinews, that is, with bulls pizzles beaten, and so run all over the bows to make them stronger. Then they are strengthened with bands. of iron to keep them tight; and on the lower side are nailed on the saddle-straps, with which they make fast the girths. **Bow (Epaule),** in Ship-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">Building</a>, the rounding part of a ship's side forward, beginning at the place where the planks arch inwards; and terminated where they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, at the stem or prow. It is proved by a variety of experiments, that a ship with a narrow bow is much better calculated for sailing swiftly, than one with a broad bow; but is not so well fitted for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> sea, into which she always pitches or plunges her fore part very deep, for want of sufficient breadth to repel the volume of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> which she so easily divides in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The former of these is called by seamen a lean, and the other a bluff bow. "The bow which meets with the least resistance in a direct course, not only meets with the least resistance in oblique courses, but also has the additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of driving the least to leeward; which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> advantage gained by forming the bow so as to give it that figure which will be least resisted in moving through any medium." *On the Bow,* in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, an arch of the horizon comprehended between some distant object and that point of the compass which is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> a-head, or to which the ship's stem is directed. The phrase is equally applicable when the object is beheld from the ship, or discovered by trigonometrical calculation: As, We <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a fleet at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> three points on the starboard bow: that is, three points from that part of the horizon which is right a-head, towards the right <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. See the article Bearing. **Bow-dye,** a kind of scarlet <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, superior to madder; but inferior to the true scarlet grain for fixedness and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. It was brought into England, and first practised at the village of Bow, near London, by Kephler, a Dutchman, in the year 1643. **Bow-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>,** in the sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, a frame or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> or junks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a>, used to be laid out at the bows, stems, and sides of ships, to preserve them from great flukes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, chiefly when they sail in high <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> or south latitudes. **Bow-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>,** or **Bow-wheel,** an engine for catching fish, chiefly lobsters and craw-fish, made of two round wicker baskets, pointed at the end, one of which is thrust into the other; at the mouth is a little rim, four or five inches broad, somewhat bent inwards. It is also used for catching sparrows. **Bow-legged** or **Bandy-legged.** Some children are bow-legged from their birth; others become so from setting them on their feet too early. The tibia of some is crooked; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> of others are distorted; from a fault in the ankle, the feet of some are turned inwards. These are called vari; and in others, who are called walgi, they are turned outwards. The best method of preventing these disorders in weakly children is to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> them duly, but not violently, by <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> or tossing them about in one's arms; and not setting them much upon their feet, at least not without properly supporting them: if the disorder attends at the birth, or increases after it is begun, apply emollients, then apply boots of strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, wood, &c. so as gradually to dispose the crooked legs to a proper form; or other instruments may be used instead of boots, which, when not too costly, are usually to be preferred. Slighter instances of these disorders yield to careful nursing, without instruments. **Bow-line,** or **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOWLING">Bowling</a>,** a rope fastened near the middle of the leech, or perpendicular edge of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> sails, by three or four subordinate parts called bridles. It is only used when the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is so unfavourable that the sails must be all braced sideways, or close hauled to the wind: in this situation the bow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> are employed to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WINDWARD">windward</a> edges of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sails tight, forward, and steady, without which, they would always be shivering, and rendered incapable of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. To check the bow-line is to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLACKEN">slacken</a> it, when the wind becomes large. **Bow-Pieces,** are the pieces of ordnance at the bow of a ship. **<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a>-Bow.** See **Rain-Bow.** **Bow-Bearer,** an inferior officer of the forest, who is sworn to make <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> of all trespasses against vert or venison, and to attach offenders. **BOWELS,** in Anatomy, the same with intestines. See **Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.** **BOWER,** in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a place under <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a> of trees, differing only from an arbour, as being round or square, and made with a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOME">dome</a> or ceiling at top; whereas the arbour is always built long and arched. **Bower,** in the sea-language, the name of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> carried at the bow of a ship. There are generally two bowers, called first and second, great and little, or best and small bower. See **Anchor.** **BOWESS,** or **BOWET,** in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALCONRY">Falconry</a>, a young hawk, when she draws anything out of her nest, and covets to clamber on the boughs. **BOWL,** denotes either a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of wood, for the use of bowling: or a vessel of capacity, wherein to hold liquors. **BOWLER <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">STONES</a>,** small stones of a roundish figure, and no determinate size, found on the sea-shore, and on banks or rather channels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. **BOWLING,** the art of playing at bowls.—This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> is practised either in open places, as bares and bowling-greens, or in close-bowling-alleys. The skill of bowling depends much on a knowledge of the ground, and the right choice of a bowl suitable to it: for close alleys, the flat bowl; for green swards, plain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, the bowl as round as a ball is preferred. The terms used in bowling are, to **bowl wide,** which is when the bias does not hold, or is not strong enough; **narrow,** when it is too strong, or holds too much; **finely bowled,** is when the ground is well chosen, and the bowl passes near the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, even though it goes much beyond it; **bowling through,** or **a yard over,** is done in order to move the block; an **over-bowl,** that which goes beyond it; a **bowl laid at hand,** is that put down within the gamester's reach, to be in the way of the next bowler, and hinder his having the advantage of the best ground; **bowling at length,** neither bowling through nor short; a **dead length,** a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> or exact one; **throwing or flinging,** is discharging a bowl with a strength purposely too great for a length, in order to carry off either the block or some near bowl; **bowl-room,** or **missing-wood,** is when a bowl has free passage without striking on any other; **get off,** is when a bowl being being narrow, is wanted to be wider; bowl best at block, that nearest the block: drawing a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> or bowl, is to win it by bowling nearer, without stirring either the bowl or block; a bowl is said to rub, when it meets with some obstacle in the ground, which retards its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and weakens its force; it is gone, when far beyond the block. Block signifies a little bowl laid for a mark, also called a jack. Mark, is a proper bowling distance, not under so many yards; and being at least a yard and a half from the edge of the green. Ground, a bag or handkerchief laid down to mark where a bowl is to go. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">Lead</a>, the advantage of throwing the block, and bowling first. Cast, is one best bowl at an end. End, a <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a>, or when all the bowls are out. The game, or up, is five casts or best bowls. Bowling-Green, in Gardening, a kind of parterre in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, laid with fine turf, requiring to be frequently mowed, laid out in compartments of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> figures, with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a>-trees and other decorations. Bowling-greens are of English origin, but have been adopted by the French and Italians, who have them only for ornament; being unacquainted with or not fancying the exercise, on account of which they were first made in England. Bowling-Bridles, are the ropes by which the bowline is fastened to the leech of the sail. Browse, in the sea-language, signifies as much as to hale or pull. Thus browsing upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACK">tack</a>, is hauling upon a tack. Browse away, that is, Pull away all together. Bowsprit, or Boltsprit, a kind of mast, resting slopewise on the head of the main stern, and having its lower end fastened to the partners of the foremast, and farther supported by the fore stay. It carries the sprit-sail, sprit-top-sail, and jack-staff; and its length is usually the same with that of the foremast. Bowyer, William, the most learned printer of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Friars in London, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 17, 1699. His father, whose name also was William, had been eminent in the same profession; and his maternal grandfather (Icabad Dawks) was employed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> the celebrated Polyglott <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a> of Bishop Walton. At a proper age, he was placed for grammatical education under the care of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Bonwicke, a nonjuring clergyman of known piety and learning, who then lived at Headly, near Leatherhead in Surry. Here Mr Bowyer made great advances in literature, and a firm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> commenced betwixt him and his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>. On the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1713, the whole property of the elder Mr Bowyer was destroyed by fire; on which occasion Mr Bonwicke generously undertook the education of his pupil for one year. In 1716, young Mr Bowyer was admitted a sizar at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where Dr Robert Jenkin was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> master. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> at the college of Cambridge under the tuition of the reverend Dr John Newcombe till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1722, during which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he probably took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts; and it appears that he was desirous of obtaining a fellowship, though it is not certain that he ever stood a candidate for that honour. Soon after this he had an opportunity of repaying the kindness which Mr Bonwicke had shown him, by officiating some time after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> in the capacity of a schoolmaster for the benefit of his family. Mr Bowyer now entered into the printing-business along with his father. One of the first books which received the benefit of his correction was the complete edition of Selden, in three volumes folio, by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Wilkins. This edition was begun in 1722, and finished in 1726; and Mr Bowyer's great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to it appeared in his drawing up an epitome of Selden de Synedriis, as he read the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> sheets. In 1727, he drew up an excellent sketch of William Baxter's Glossary of the Roman Antiquities. This was called "A view of a book entitled Reliquiae Baxterianae. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to a friend." A single sheet 8vo. By this first public proof of Mr Bowyer's abilities, Dr Wotton and Mr Clarke were highly pleased; but as it was never published, and a very few copies printed, it is seldom found with the glossary. In 1727 Mr Bowyer lost his mother; on which occasion he received a letter of consolation from Mr Chishull the learned editor of the Antiquitates Asiaticæ. In October 1728 he married Miss Ann Prudom, his mother's niece, a very accomplished lady, by whom he had two sons, William and Thomas: the former of whom died an infant, and the latter survived his father. In 1729 Mr Bowyer published a curious treatise, entitled, "A Pattern for young Students in the University; set forth in the Life of Ambrose Bonwicke, some time scholar of St John's College, Cambridge:" but though this treatise was generally ascribed to Mr Bowyer, it was in reality the production of Mr Ambrose Bonwicke the elder. About this time it appears, that Mr Bowyer had written a pamphlet against the Separatists, though neither the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> nor the occasion of it are now remembered. The same year, through the friendship of the Right Hon. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTHUR">Arthur</a> Onslow, he was appointed printer of the votes of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons; which office he held, under three successive speakers, for near fifty years. In 1731 Mr Bowyer published, and, it is believed, translated, Voltaire's Life of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. This year also his wife died; on which occasion his friends Mr Clarke and Mr Chishull wrote him very affectionate and Christian letters. He remained a widower till 1747, when he married a very benevolent and worthy woman, Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">Bill</a>, by whom he had no children. In 1733 he published a piece in two sheets 4to, entitled, "The Beau and the Academic:" being a translation from a Latin poem recited that year at the Sheldonian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>: and in 1736 he was admitted into the Society of Antiquarians, where he became an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and useful member. In 1737 Mr Bowyer lost his father; and on this occasion Mr Clarke again addressed to him a letter of consolation. In 1742 our author published a translation of Trapp's Latin Lectures on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, in which he was assisted by Mr Clarke, though the latter had a contemptible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the performance. In 1749, Mr Bowyer, along with Dr Burton, was virulently attacked by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> in a piece entitled Elogium famæ inserviens Jacobi Etontensis sive Gigantis: or "The praises of Jack Eaton, commonly called Jack the Giant."—This abuse was probably occasioned by Mr Bowyer's having hinted in conversation some doubts concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s skill in Latin. Our author drew up some strictures in his own defence, which he intended to insert at the conclusion of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to Montesquieu's Reflections; but by Dr Clarke's advice they they were omitted. In 1750, a prefatory critical dissertation and some notes were annexed by our author to Kuster's Treatise De usu verborum mediorum; a new edition of which, with farther improvements, appeared in 1773. He wrote likewise about the same time a Latin preface to Leedes's Veteres poetæ citati, &c.—Being soon after employed to print an edition of Col. Bladen's translation of Caesar's Commentaries, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> received considerable improvements from Mr Bowyer's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with the addition of such notes in it as are signed Typogr. In the subsequent editions of this work, though printed by another person during our author's lifetime, the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a>, though contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, was still retained. In 1751, he wrote a long preface to Montesquieu's "Reflections on the rise and fall of the Roman Empire;" translated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> between Sylla and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>; made several corrections to the work from the Baron's "Spirit of Laws;" and improved it with his own notes. A new edition, with many new notes, was printed in 1759. In 1751 he also published the first translation that ever was made of Rousseau's paradoxical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, which gained the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> at the academy of Dijon in 1750; and which first announced that singular genius to the attention and admiration of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. On the publication of the third edition of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>'s "Remarks on the Life and Writings of Dr Swift," in 1752, Mr Bowyer wrote and printed, but never published, "Two Letters from Dr Bentley in the Shades below, to Lord Orrery in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a> of thick darkness." The notes signed B, in the ninth quarto volume of Swift's works, are extracted from these Letters. In 1753, he endeavoured to allay the ferment occasioned by the Jew bill; with which view he published, in quarto, "Remarks on the speech made in common-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, on the bill for permitting persons professing the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to be naturalized, so far as prophecies are supposed to be affected by it." This little tract was written with spirit, and well received by those who were superior to narrow prejudices. Its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was to show that whatever <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> reasons might be alleged against the bill, Christianity was in no danger of being prejudiced by the intended protection promised to the Jews. The same year some of Mr Bowyer's notes were annexed to Bishop Claton's translation of "A Journal from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> to Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a> and back again."—In 1754, Mr Bower, with a view of lessening his fatigue, entered into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with a relation; but some disagreement arising, the connection was dissolved in three years. On the death of Mr Richardson in 1761, Mr Bowyer succeeded him as printer to the Royal Society, through the favour of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of Macclesfield; and, under the friendship of five successive presidents, enjoyed that office till his death. In 1763, Mr Bowyer published an excellent edition of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, in two vols 12mo. It appeared under the following title: Novum Testamentum Graecum; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> fidem Graecorum solum Codicum MSS. nunc primum impressum, adstipulante Joanne Jacobo Wetstenio, juxta Sectiones Jo. Alberti Bengeli divisum; et nova interpretatione saepius illustratum. Accessere in altero volumine, Emendationes conjecturales virorum doctorum undecunque collectae. This sold with great rapidity: the Conjectural Emendations were well received by the learned, and are thought to be a valuable work. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> and fellows of Harvard college in Cambridge expressed their approbation of this edition in very high terms, in a letter to Mr Bowyer, written in the year 1767. "This work (say they), though small in bulk, we esteem as a rich <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of sacred learning, and of more value than many large volumes of the commentators." A second edition of the Conjectures on the New Testament, with very considerable enlargements, was separately published, in one vol. 8vo, in 1772. Bishop Warburton having censured a passage in the former edition, Mr Bowyer sent him a copy of this book, with a conciliatory letter. Dr Warburton's Divine Legation had received very considerable advantage from Mr Bowyer's corrections; and this even in an edition which was necessarily given to another press. In 1761 he was employed to print his Lordship's Doctrine of Grace. A second edition being soon wanted, and Mr Bowyer not having been intrusted with the care of it, he prepared a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of letters to the bishop in his own defence; of which, together with a few he had formerly received from that great writer, he afterwards printed twelve copies, of which ten have since been destroyed. However, there is the best authority for asserting, that notwithstanding any little alterations which happened, Dr Warburton always retained a sincere regard for our author. In 1763, at the request of Thomas Hollis, Esq. Mr Bowyer wrote a short Latin preface to Dr Wallis's Grammaticæ Linguae Anglicane. He wrote also a large English preface for the same work, which, however, still remains unprinted. In 1766 he entered into partnership with Mr Nichols, who had been trained by him to the profession, and had for several years assisted him in the management of his business. The same year, Mr Bowyer wrote an excellent Latin preface to Joannis Harduini, Jesuïte, ad Censuram Scriotorum veterum Prolegomena. Juxta Autographum. In 1767 he was appointed to print the journals of the house of lords and the rolls of parliament. This year he printed Mr Clarke's excellent and learned work on "The Connection of the Roman, Saxon, and English Coins;" and wrote some notes upon it, which are interspersed throughout the volume with those of the author. Part of the Dissertation on the Roman sestercius was likewise Mr Bowyer's production; and the index, which is an uncommonly good one, was drawn up by him entirely. In January 1771 Mr Bowyer lost his second wife, and again received a letter of consolation from his old friend Mr Clarke, who had sent him one almost forty years before on a similar occasion. In the Philosophical Transactions for this year was printed a very ingenious "Inquiry into the Value of the ancient Greek and Roman <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>," by the late Matthew Raper, Esq. But his opinions not coinciding with those of Mr Bowyer, he printed a small pamphlet, entitled, "Remarks, occasioned by a late Dissertation on the Greek and Roman Money." In 1773 three little tracts were published by him, under the title of "Select Discourses." 1. Of the correspondence of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> months with the Julian, from the Latin of Professor Michaelis. 2. Of the Sabbatical years, from the same. 3. Of the years of Jubilee, from an anonymous writer in Masson's Histoire Critique de la Republique des In 1774 he corrected a new edition of Schrevelius's Greek Lexicon; to which he has added a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of words, distinguished by an asterisk, which he himself had collected in the course of his studies. Considerable additions, still in manuscript, were made by him to the lexicons of Hederic and Buxtorf, the Latin ones of Faber and Littleton, and the English <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> of Bailey; and he left behind him many other proofs of his critical skill in the learned languages. In 1774 was published, "The Origin of printing, in two essays. 1. The substance of Dr Middleton's Dissertation on the Origin of Printing in England. 2. Mr Meerman's Account of the Invention of the art at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, and its progress to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, with occasional Remarks, and an appendix." The original idea of this valuable tract was Mr Bowyer's, but it was completed by Mr Nichols. Although our author, during the last ten years of his life, had been afflicted with the palsy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, he not only preserved a remarkable cheerfulness of temper, but was enabled to support the labour of almost incessant <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>; and he regularly corrected the learned works, especially the Greek books, which came from his press. This he continued to do till within a few weeks of his death, which happened in November 1777, when he had nearly completed his 78th year. For more than half a century Mr Bowyer was unrivalled as a learned printer; and many of the most masterly productions of this kingdom have come from his press. To his literary and professional abilities he added an excellent moral character; and he was particularly distinguished by his inflexible probity, and an uncommon alacrity in relieving the necessitous.

BOWYERS

Pages 431-431

artificers whose business is to make bows: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, bowers stand distinguished from fletchers, who make arrows. The bowyers <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> was incorporated in 1620: and consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, two wardens, twelve assistants, and 30 on the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHERY">ARCHERY</a>.

BOX

Pages 431-431

in its most <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> acceptation, denotes a small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coffer for holding things. Dice-Box, a narrow deep cornet, channelled within, wherein the dice are shaken and thrown. This answers to what the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> called fritillus; whence, crepitantes fritilli; and, in Seneca, resonante fritillo. The same author uses also concutere fritillum, figuratively, for playing. Besides the fritillus, the Romans, for greater security, had another kind of dice-box called pyrgus, πυργός, and sometimes turricula. It was placed immovable in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, being perforated or open at both ends, and likewise channelled within; over the top was placed a kind of funnel, into which the dice were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out upon the fritillus; whence descending, they fell through the bottom on the table; by which all practising on them with the fingers was effectually prevented. For want of some contrivance of this kind, our sharpers have opportunities of playing <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> tricks with the box, as palming, topping, slapping, &c. Box, is also used for an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>: Thus a box of quicksilver contains from one to two hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; a box of prunellas only 14 pounds; a box of rings for keys, two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a>, &c. Box-Tree. See BUXUS, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. African Box. See MYRSINE, BOTANY Index.

BOXERS

Pages 431-431

a kind of athletæ, who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> contend for victory with their fists. Boxers amount to the same with what among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> was called pugiles. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> boxers battled with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force and fury, insomuch as to dash out each other's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and often kill each other. The strange disfigurements the boxers underwent were such that they frequently could not be known, and rendered them the subject of many railleries. In the Greek anthology there are four epigrams of the poet Lucilius, and one of Lucian, wherein their disfigurements are pleasantly enough exposed. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOXING">BOXING</a>.

BOXHORNIUS

Pages 431-431

MARC ZUERIUS, a learned critic, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BERGEN_OP_ZOOM"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol3.html#article-BERGEN">Bergen</a>-op-Zoom in 1612, was professor of eloquence at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, and at length of politics and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the room of Heinsius. He published, 1. Theatrum urbiurn Hollandiae. 2. Scriptores historice Augustae, cum notis. 3. Poetae satyrici minores, cum comment. 4. Notes on Justin, Tacitus; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of other works. He died in 1653, aged 41.

BOXING

Pages 431-432

the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of fighting with the fists, either naked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> or leaden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> grasped in them: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, boxing coincides with the pugilatus of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and what in our amphitheatres is sometimes called <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of manhood. When the champions had ροάγια, or balls, whether of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> or stone, it was properly denominated φορεμαχία. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> boxing differed from the pugna cestuum, in which the combatants had leathern thongs on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and balls to offend their antagonists; though this distinction is frequently overlooked, and fighting with the cestus ranked as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the business of pugiles. We may distinguish three <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of boxing; viz. where both the head and hands were naked; where the hands were armed and the head naked; and where the head was covered with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, called amphotides, and the hands also furnished with the cestus. Boxing is an ancient exercise, having been in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the heroic ages. Those who prepared themselves for it, used all the means that could be contrived to render themselves fat and fleshy, that they might be better able to endure blows: whence corpulent men or women were usually called pugiles, according to Terence: Sigua est habilito paulo, pugilem esse auiunt. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times this art has been in a manner appropriated by the English. About half a century ago it formed as regular an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> as we now see at any of the places of public amusements, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a> alone excepted. It was encouraged by the first ranks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, patronized by the first subjects in the realm, and tolerated by the magistrates. Before the establishment of Bronghton's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, a booth was erected at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TOTTENHAM">Tottenham</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a>, in which the proprietor, Mr George Taylor, invited the professors of the art to display their skill, and the public to be present at its exhibition. The bruisers then had the reward due to their prowess, in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the entrance <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which sometimes was 100l. or 150l. The general <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of sharing was for two-thirds to go to the winning champion, while the remaining third was the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the loser; though sometimes by an express agreement of the parties, the conqueror and the vanquished shared alike. The nobility and gentry having complained of the inconveniences sustained at Taylor's Booth, prevailed on Mr Broughton, who was then then rising into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, as the first bruiser in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, to build a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> better adapted for such exhibitions. This was accordingly done in 1742, principally by subscription, behind <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was called Broughton's New Amphitheatre; and, besides the stage for the combatants, had seats corresponding to the boxes, pit, and galleries, much in the same manner with those at Astley's. After a course of years, however, these exhibitions became gradually less patronized and frequented, owing probably to the refinement of our manners. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago, indeed, they seemed to be revived, and very considerably engaged the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the public; but a fatal issue which attended one of them, brought the practice again into disrepute. One of the combatants was killed on the spot. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> highness the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> was present, and declared that he would have some settlement made on the nearest relation of the deceased, but that, on account of the dreadful example he had then witnessed, he would never more either see or patronize another stage-fight. Boxing, among sailors, is used to denote the rehearsing the several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the compass in their proper order. Boxing is also used for the tapping of a tree, to make it yield its juice. The boxing of maple is performed by making a hole with an axe or chisel into the side of the tree, about a foot from the ground; out of it flows a liquor of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> is made. Boxtehude, a town of Germany, in the circle of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, subject to the Danes. It is seated on the rivulet Esse, which falls into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 35', N. Lat. 53° 40'. Boxtel, a town in Dutch Brabant, with sluices, seated on the river Bommel. E. Long. 5° 15', N. Lat. 51° 30'. Boyar, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANDEE">grandee</a> of Russia and Transylvania. Beeman says that the boyars are the upper nobility; and adds, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CZAR">Czar</a> of Muscovy, in his diplomas, names the boyars before the waywodes. See Waywode. Boyau, in Fortification, a ditch covered with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, which serves as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between two trenches. It runs <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the works of the body of the place; and serves as a line of contravallation, not only to hinder the sallies of the besieged, but also to secure the miners. But when it is a particular cut that runs from the trenches to cover some spot of ground, it is drawn so as not to be enfiladed or scoured by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from the town. Boyd, Mark Alexander, an extraordinary genius, was son of Robert Boyd, who was eldest son of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Boyd of Pinkhill, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Boyd. He was born in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLOWAY">Galloway</a> on the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1562; and came into the world with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>. He learned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Latin and Greek languages at Glasgow, under two grammarians; but was of so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and untractable a spirit, that they despaired of ever making him a scholar. Having quarrelled with his masters, he <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> them both, burnt his books, and forswore learning. While he was yet a youth, he followed the court, and did his utmost to push his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> there; but the fervour of his temper soon precipitated him into quarrels, from which he came off with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and safety, though frequently at the hazard of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He, with the approbation of his friends, went to serve in the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and carried his little patrimony with him, which he soon dissipated at play. He was shortly after roused by that emulation which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> minds, and applied himself to letters with unremitting ardour, till he became one of the most consummate scholars of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He is said to have translated Caesar's Commentaries into Greek in the style of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, and to have written many Latin poems which were little inferior to the first productions of the Augustan age. He also left several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> on philological, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, and historical subjects, in Latin and French, which languages were as familiar to him as his native tongue. He could with facility dictate to three amanuenses at the same time, in different languages, and on different subjects. He was also one of the best Scottish poets of the age. To all this we must add, that his personal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and accomplishments were equal to his mental superiority. He died at Pinkhill in Scotland, in 1601. The following works, which are all that have been printed, were published in the Deliciae Poetarum Scotorum; Amstel. 1637, 12mo. 1. Epigrammata, lib. ii. 2. Heroicum Epistle XIV. lib. ii. 3. Hymni XIV. Boyker, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a>, a well-known glossographer and historiographer, born at Castres in France, in 1664. Upon the revocation of the edict of Nantz, he went first to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, then to Franeker, where he finished his studies; and came finally to England, where he applied himself so assiduously to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and made so great a proficiency therein, that he became an author of considerable note in it, being employed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of several periodical and political works. He was for many years concerned in a newspaper called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">Post</a>-boy, of which he had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> management. He likewise published a monthly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled the Political State of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He wrote a life of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> in folio, which is esteemed a very good <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. But what has rendered him the most known, and has most firmly established his reputation, are the excellent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a> of the French language, which he compiled, and which are still reckoned the best in their kind. He also wrote, or rather translated from the French of M. de Racine, the tragedy of Iphigenia, which he published under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Victim. It was performed with success at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> of Drury-Lane, and is far from being a bad play. Nor can there perhaps be a stronger instance of the abilities of its author, than success in such an attempt; since writing with any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of correctness or elegance, even in prose, in a foreign language, is an excellence not very frequently attained; but to proceed so far in the perfection of it as to be even tolerable in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and more especially in that of the drama, in which the diction and manner of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> require a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and force, and in a language so difficult to attain the perfect command of as the English, is what has been very seldom accomplished. He died in 1729. Boyner, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, a kind of Flemish sloop, or small vessel of burden, having a boltsprit, a castle at each end, and a tall mast; chiefly fit for the navigation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and in many of its parts resembling a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SMACK">smack</a>.

BOYES

Pages 432-433

idolatrous priests among the savages of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> attends a particular idol, and the natives <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> themselves to the priest of that idol to which they intend to pay their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. The idol is invoked in hymns, and his usual offering is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>.

BOYLE

Pages 433-443

Roger, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>, younger <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the former, and the fifth son of Richard, styled the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> earl of Cork, was born April 25. 1621; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of his father with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Faulkland, raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Baron Broghill, when only <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old. He was educated at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, where he soon distinguished himself as an early and promising genius. He afterwards made the tour of France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and at his return assisted his father in opposing the rebellious Irish, in which he behaved with all the spirit of a young, and all the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of an old, officer. Upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, he retired to Marston in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, and hid himself in the privacy of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> retirement; but being at length ashamed to sit the tame spectator of all the mischief that appeared round him, he resolved to attempt something in favour of the king; and under the pretence of going to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPA">Spa</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he determined to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the seas, and apply himself to King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to raise what forces he could in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in order to restore his majesty, and recover his own estate. To this purpose, he prevailed on the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICK">Warwick</a> to procure a license for his going to the Spa; and having raised a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, came up to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to prosecute his voyage; but he had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in town when he received a message from Cromwell, who was then general of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>'s forces, that he intended to wait upon him. The lord Broghill was surprised at this message, having never had the least acquaintance with Cromwell; and desired the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> to let the general know, that he would wait upon his excellency. But while he was waiting the return of the messenger, Cromwell entered the room; and after mutual civilities had passed between them, told him in few words, that the committee of state were apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of going over and applying to Charles Stuart for a commission to raise forces in Ireland; and that they were determined to make an example of him, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he himself had not diverted them from that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. The lord Broghill interrupted him, by assuring him that the intelligence which the committee had received was false, and that he neither was in a capacity nor had any inclination to raise disturbances in Ireland: but Cromwell, instead of making any reply, drew some papers out of his pocket, which were the copies of several letters which the lord Broghill had sent to those persons in whom he most confided, and put them into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. The lord Broghill, upon the perusal of these papers, finding it to no purpose to dissemble any longer, asked his excellency's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for what he had said, returned him his humble thanks for his protection against the committee, and intreated his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> how to behave in such a delicate conjecture. Cromwell told him, that though till this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had been a stranger to his person, he was not so to his merit and character: he had heard how gallantly his lordship had behaved in the Irish wars; and therefore, since he was named lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of Ireland, and the reducing that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was now become his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, he had obtained obtained leave of the committee to offer his lordship the command of a general officer, if he would serve in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and he should have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> engagements imposed upon him, nor be obliged to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> against any but the Irish rebels. The lord Broghill was infinitely surprised at so generous and unexpected an offer. He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, by all the rules of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, to serve against the Irish, whose rebellion and barbarities were equally detested by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> party and the parliament. He desired, however, some time to consider of what had been proposed to him. But Cromwell briskly told him, that he must come to some resolution that very instant: that he himself was returning to the committee, who were still sitting; and if his lordship rejected their offer, they had determined to send him to the Tower. Upon this, the lord Broghill, finding that his liberty and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> were in the utmost danger, gave his word and honour that he would faithfully serve him against the Irish rebels: on which Cromwell once more assured him, that the conditions which he had made with him should be punctually observed; and then ordered him to repair to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, adding, that he himself would soon follow him into Ireland. Lord Broghill, therefore, having settled the business of his command, went over into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; where, by his conduct and intrepidity, he performed many important services, and fully justified the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Cromwell had conceived of him. By his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> he now raised a gallant troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, consisting chiefly of gentlemen attached to him by personal friendship; which corps was soon increased to a complete regiment of 1500 men. These he led into the field against the Irish rebels; and was speedily joined by Cromwell, who placed the highest confidence in his new ally, and found him of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to the interest of the commonwealth. Among other considerable exploits performed by Lord Broghill, the following deserves to be particularly mentioned. Whilst Cromwell laid siege to Clonmell, Broghill being detached to disperse a body of 5000 men who had assembled to relieve the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, he with 2000 horse and dragoons, came up with the enemy at Macroom on the 10th of May 1656; and, without waiting for the arrival of his foot, immediately attacked and routed them, making their general prisoner. Then proceeding to the castle of Carrigdohid, he sent a summons to the garrison to surrender before the arrival of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> cannon, otherwise they were to expect no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. His own <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was surprised at this summons, as knowing he had not one piece of heavy cannon: but Broghill had ordered the trunks of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees to be drawn at a distance by his baggage horses; which the besieged perceiving, and judging from the slowness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> that the guns must be of a vast bore, immediately capitulated. He afterwards relieved Cromwell himself at Clonmell, where that great commander happened to be so dangerously situated, that he confessed, nothing but the seasonable relief afforded him by Lord Broghill could have saved him from destruction. When Ireton sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>, he gave Broghill 600 foot and 400 horse, with orders to prevent Lord Muskerry's joining the pope's nuncio, who had got together a body of 8000 men, and was determined to attempt the relief of Limerick. Muskerry was at the head of 1000 horse and dragoons, and about 2000 foot: notwithstanding which, Lord Broghill fell resolutely upon him. The Irish, having the advantage of the ground and numbers, would have conquered, but for a stratagem of Lord Broghill. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> he desired those about him to repeat what he said; and then cried out as loud as he could, "They run, they run." The first line of the Irish looked round to see if their rear broke; and the rear seeing the faces of their friends, and hearing the shouts of the enemy, imagined that the first line was routed, and fled. The taking of Limerick, which put an end to the war in Ireland, was the consequence of this defeat. When Cromwell became protector, he sent for Lord Broghill, merely to take his advice occasionally. And we are told, that, not long after his coming to England, he formed a project for engaging Cromwell to restore the old <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. The basis of the scheme was to be a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> between the king (Charles II.) and the protector's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. As his lordship maintained a secret correspondence with the exiled monarch and his friends, it was imagined that he was beforehand pretty sure that Charles was not averse to the scheme, or he would not have ventured to have proposed it seriously to Cromwell; who at first seemed to think it not unfeasible. He soon changed his mind, however, and told Broghill that he thought his project impracticable: "For (said he) Charles can never forgive me the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father." In fine, the business came to nothing, although his lordship had engaged Cromwell's wife and daughter in the scheme; but he never durst let the protector know that he had previously treated with Charles about it. On the death of the protector, Lord Broghill <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> attached to his son Richard, till, when he saw that the honesty and good-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of that worthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> would infallibly render him a prey to his many enemies, he did not think it advisable to sink with a man that he could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a>. The dark <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of anarchy seemed now to be hovering over the British <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Lord Broghill saw the storm gathering, and he deemed it prudent to retire to his command in Ireland, where he shortly after had the satisfaction of seeing things take a turn extremely favourable to the design that he had long been a well-wisher to, viz. that of the king's restoration. In this great event Lord Broghill was not a little instrumental; and, in consideration of his eminent services in this respect, Charles created him earl of Orrery by letters-patent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> September 5, 1660. He was soon after made one of the lords justices of Ireland; and his conduct, while at the head of affairs in that kingdom, was such as greatly added to the general esteem in which his character was held before. His lordship's <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and toilsome course of life at length brought upon him some diseases and infirmities which gave him much pain and uneasiness; and a fever which fell into his feet, joined to the gout with which he was often afflicted, abated much of that vigour which he had shown in the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his life: but his industry and application were still the same, and bent to the same purposes; as appears from his letters, which show at once a capacity, and an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to business, which do honour to that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and may serve as an example to this. Notwithstanding Notwithstanding his infirmities, on the king's desiring to see his lordship in England, he went over in 1665. He found the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> in some disorder; where his majesty was on the point of removing the great earl of Clarendon, lord <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>; and there was also a great misunderstanding between the two royal brothers. Lord Orrery undertook to reconcile the king with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; which he effected by prevailing on the latter to ask his majesty's pardon for some steps he had taken in support of the lord chancellor. On his return to Ireland, he found himself called to a new <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of action. The Dutch war was then at its height; and the French, in confederacy with the Hollanders, were endeavouring to stir up the ashes of rebellion in Ireland. The duke de <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUFORT">Beaufort</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> of France, had formed a scheme for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon Ireland; but this was rendered abortive by the extraordinary diligence, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> skill, and prudent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, of Lord Orrery. But, in midst of all his labours, a dispute arose, founded on a mutual jealousy of each other's greatness, betwixt him and his old friend the duke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>, then lord lieutenant; the bad effects of which were soon felt by both disputants, who resorted to England to defend their respective interests and pretensions, both having been attacked by secret enemies who suggested many things to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. This quarrel, though of a private beginning, became at last of a public nature; and producing first an attempt to frame an impeachment against the duke of Ormond, occasioned in the end, by the way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, an actual impeachment against the earl of Orrery. He defended himself, however, so well against a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of high crimes, and even of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> itself, that the prosecution came to nothing. He nevertheless lost his public employments; but not the king's favour: he still came frequently to court, and sometimes to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. After this revolution in his affairs, he made several voyages to and from Ireland; was often consulted by his majesty on affairs of the utmost consequence; and on all occasions gave his opinion and advice with the freedom of an honest plain-dealing man and a sincere friend; which the king always found him, and respected him accordingly. In 1678, being attacked more cruelly than ever by his old enemy the gout, he made his last voyage to England for advice in the medical way. But his disorder was beyond the power of medicine; and having in his last illness given the strongest proofs of Christian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, manly courage, and rational fortitude, he breathed his last on the 16th of October 1679, in the 59th year of his age. His biography wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled "The Art of War." 2. Parthenissa, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a>, in one volume folio. 3. Several poems. 4. Dramatic pieces, two volumes. 5. State-tracts, in one volume folio, &c. Mr Walpole, speaking of this nobleman, says, he never made a bad <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> but as a poet. As a soldier, his bravery was distinguished, his stratagems remarkable. As a statesman, it is sufficient to say, that he had the confidence of Cromwell. As a man, he was grateful, and would have supported the son of his friend; but, like Cicero and Richelieu, he could not be content without being a poet; though he was ill qualified, his writings of that kind being flat and trivial. Boyle, Robert, one of the greatest philosophers as well as best men that our own or indeed any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> has produced, was the seventh son and the 14th child of Richard earl of Cork, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISMORE">Lismore</a> in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in Ireland, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 25, 1626-7. Before he went to school, he was taught to write a very fair <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and to speak French and Latin, by one of the earl's chaplains, and a Frenchman that he kept in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the year 1635, his father sent him over to England, in order to be educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, under Sir Henry Wotton, who was the earl of Cork's old friend and acquaintance. Here he soon discovered a force of understanding which promised great things, and a disposition to cultivate and improve it to the utmost. While he remained at Eton, there were several very extraordinary accidents that befell him, of which he has given us an account; and three of which were very near proving fatal to him. The first was, the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the chamber where he was lodged, when himself was in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>; when, besides the danger he run of being crushed to pieces, he had certainly been choked with the dust during the time he lay under the rubbish, if he had not had presence of mind enough to wrap his head up in the sheet, which gave him an opportunity of breathing without hazard. A little after this, he had been crushed to pieces by a starting horse that rose up suddenly, and threw himself backwards, if he had not happily disengaged his feet from the stirrups, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> himself from his back before he fell. A third accident proceeded from the carelessness of an apothecary's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, who, by mistaking the phials, brought him a strong vomit instead of a cooling julep.
