To this species of knowledge the Brachmans added an infinite number of religious observances, which were adopted by Pythagoras in his school; such as fasting, prayer, silence, and contemplation. They were looked upon as the friends of the gods, because they affected to pay them so much regard; and as the protectors of mankind, because they paid them no regard at all. No bounds were therefore set to the respect and gratitude that were shown them: princes themselves did not scruple to consult these recluses upon any critical conjuncture, from a supposition, no doubt, that they were inspired; since it was impossible to imagine that they had the advantages of experience. We can scarcely, however, deny, that there might be among them some men of real virtue, whose minds relished the pure and ingenious delights of study and science; and who, by nobly raising their thoughts to the contemplation of the First Being, must have had more powerful incitements to render themselves worthy of his care, and none to justify them in deceiving and tyrannizing over their fellow-creatures. There appear still some remains of the ancient brachmans in the east, under the denomination of Bramins. See Bramins.

BRACHYLOGY

Pages 445-445

(from βραχύς and λόγος "<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>"), in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, the expressing any thing in the most concise manner. This, so far as consistent with perspicuity, is a virtue and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of style; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> obscurity be the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, which is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it becomes a blemish and inexcusable defect.—Quintilian gives an instance of brachylogy from Sallust: *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> corpore ingenti perinde armatus*; "Mithridates, as it were, armed with the hugeness of his stature."

BRACHYPRENIUM

Pages 445-445

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of fossils, a genus of septaria, with a short, roundish nucleus. See Septaria.

BRACHYPTERA

Pages 445-445

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by Willoughby, to denote those hawks which have their wings so short as not to reach to the end of the tail. Of this kind are the goss-hawk, sparrow-hawk, &c.

BRACHYTELOSTYLA

Pages 445-445

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name by which Dr Hill calls those crystals which are composed of a short hexangular <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> terminated at each end by an hexangular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>. See Crystal.

BRACKET

Pages 445-445

among carpenters, &c. a kind of wooden stay, serving to support shelves and the like.

BRACKETS

Pages 445-445

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUNNERY">Gunnery</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> of the carriage of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>: they are made of strong planks of wood, of almost a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and bound round with thick <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates; they are fixed to the beds by four bolts, which are called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>-bolts; they rise up on each side of the mortar, and serve to keep her at any elevation by means of some strong iron bolts, called bracket-bolts, which go through these cheeks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brackets.

BRACKLAW

Pages 445-445

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of that name, which is the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Podolia; it is also called Lower Podolia, and is of greater <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> than Upper Podolia, but is more desolate, on account of the neighbourhood of the Tartars.

BRACKLEY

Pages 445-445

a borough-town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, in England, seated on the edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, next Buckinghamshire, on a branch of the river Ouse. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> corporation-town, containing two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches; is governed by a mayor and aldermen; and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, which is turned into a free school. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 15. N. Lat. 52. 0.

BRACON

Pages 445-445

Henry**, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of England in the reign of Henry III. was probably a native of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws, and was made one of the itinerant judges about the year 1244. Ten years after he became chief justice, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> assigned him for his town residence, during the minority of that nobleman. He is said to have filled this important office with singular reputation during 20 years. When he died is not known; probably it was in the reign of Edward I. He wrote *De legibus et consuetudinibus Anglie*, which is one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, and also most methodical books on our laws. His method is copied from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was printed at London in 1569, folio; and in 1640, 4to. The first is very incorrect.

BRACTEA

Pages 445-445

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a thin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> plate of any folium florale, ranged by Linnaeus among the fulera of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. These floral leaves differ in shape and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, from the other folia of the plant; are generally situated on the penduculus, and often so near the corolla as to be easily mistaken for the calyx; than which, however, the bracteae are generally more permanent. Examples of the floral leaves are seen in the tilia, fumaria bulbosa, lavendula and horminum.

BRACTEARIA

Pages 445-445

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of talcs, composed of small plates in form of spangles, each plate either being very thin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fissile into very thin ones. Of this genus there are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, called from their different colours, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a> aurca, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>-glimmer; and mica argentea, silver-glimmer, or cats-silver, &c.

BRADFIELD

Pages 445-445

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 30. N. Lat. 51. 14.

BRADFORD

Pages 445-446

John**, a divine, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a> to the reformation, Bradford formation, was born in the former <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the reign of Henry VIII, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>. Being a remarkable penman and accountant, he became secretary to Sir John <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARRINGTON">Harrington</a>, who was several times employed by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry, and his successor Edward VI, as paymaster to the troops abroad. Bradford at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was a gay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and to support his extravagance made free with the king's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but being at last unable to support the reflection of his guilt, he determined to make restitution, and actually repaid the money. Quitting his employment of secretary, about the year 1547, he took chambers in the inner temple, and for some time studied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but finding in himself an inclination to preach the gospel, in the following year he removed to Catharine-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he applied with such uncommon assiduity to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, that in a much shorter time than usual he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, and soon after made fellow of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>-hall. Bishop Ridley, who, in 1550, was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, charmed with Bradford's application and zeal, now sent for him to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, ordained and appointed him his chaplain. In 1553, he was also made chaplain to Edward VI, during which time he became one of the most popular preachers in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Such a reformer was too dangerous to be suffered in the succeeding reign. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> was hardly in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, before Bradford's persecutions began. He was first confined in the Tower for sedition, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> a year and a half; during which time he wrote several epistles that were dispersed in various parts of the kingdom. He was afterwards removed to other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, and at last brought to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> before that infernal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in which Gardiner sat as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> inquisitor, where he defended his principles to the last, in contempt of their utmost power. They condemned him to the flames; and he was accordingly burnt alive in Smithfield, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1, 1555. His works are, 1. Seventy-two letters, written to various people, whilst the author was in prison; printed in Bishop Cordell's collection. 2. Ten letters, printed in Fox's Acts and Monuments. 3. Complaint of verity, 1559, 8vo. 4. Three examinations before the commissioners, and his private talk with the priests, with the original of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, 1561, octavo. 5. Two notable sermons, 1574, octavo, 1631. 6. Godly meditations and prayers, 1614, 24to. 7. Treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, 1622. With several translations and other pieces.

BRADFORTH

Pages 446-446

a town in the west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the river <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, containing 7767 inhabitants in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 35. N. Lat. 53. 40.

BRADLEY

Pages 446-447

Dr James, a famous English astronomer, was the third son of William and Jane Bradley, and was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHERBORNE">Sherborne</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> in the year 1692. He was educated for the university at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Leach by Mr Egles and Mr Brice, who kept a boarding-school there; and from North Leach he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. His friends intended him for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and his studies were regulated with that view; and as soon as he was of sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> to receive holy orders, the bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>, who had conceived a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for him, gave him the living of Bridstow, and soon after he was inducted to that of Welfrie in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKESHIRE">Pembrokeshire</a>. But notwithstanding these advantages, from which he might <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> himself still farther advancement in the Bradle church, he at length resigned his livings, that he might be wholly at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to pursue his favourite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and particularly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. He was nephew to Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">Pound</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who is well known in the learned world by many excellent observations, and who would have enriched it with more, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the journals of his voyages had not been burnt at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULO">Pulo</a> Condore, when the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was set on fire, and the English who were settled there cruelly massacred, Mr Pound himself very narrowly escaping with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. With this gentleman, Mr Bradley passed all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that he could spare from the duties of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>; and perhaps he sometimes trespassed upon them: he was then sufficiently acquainted with the mathematics to improve by Mr Pound's conversation; yet it does not appear that, in this study, he had any preceptor but his genius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any assistant but his labour. It may be easily imagined, that the example and conversation of Mr Pound did not render Bradley more fond of his profession than he was before; he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, however, as yet to fulfil the duties of it, though at this time he had made such observations as laid the foundation of those discoveries which afterwards distinguished him as one of the greatest astronomers of his age. Though these observations were made as it were by stealth, they gained him at first the notice, and then the friendship, of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> Macclesfield, Mr Newton, afterwards Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, Mr Halley, and many other members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, into which he was soon elected a member. About the same time, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of Savilian professor of astronomy became vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the celebrated Dr Keil; and Mr Bradley was elected to succeed him on the 31st of October 1721, being then <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> 29 years old; and his colleague was Mr Halley, who was professor of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> on the same foundation. Bradley, upon his being elected into this professorship, gave up both his livings, and with great joy quitted a situation in which his duty was directly opposite to his inclination. From this time, he applied himself wholly to the study of his favourite science; and in the year 1727 he published his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the aberration of the fixed stars, which is allowed to be one of the most useful and ingenious discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> astronomy. Three years after this discovery, by which Mr Bradley acquired very great reputation, he was appointed lecturer in astronomy and physics, at the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> of Oxford. He pursued his studies with equal application and delight; and in the course of his observations, which were innumerable, he discovered that the inclination of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>'s axis upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the ecliptic was not always the same, but that it varied backwards and forwards some seconds, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of these variations was <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years. This period seemed altogether unaccountable, as it could not be supposed to have anything in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the revolution of the earth, which is performed in one year. Mr Bradley, however, discovered the cause of this phenomenon in the Newtonian system of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a>. He published this discovery in 1737, so that in the space of about ten years he communicated to the world two of the finest discoveries in modern astronomy, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> for ever make a memorable epocha in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of that science. Mr Bradley always preserved the esteem and friendship of Mr Halley; who, being worn out by age and infirmities, thought he could do nothing farther for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of astronomy, than procure for Mr Bradley the place of regius professor of astronomy at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>, which he had possessed himself many years with the greatest reputation. With this view, he wrote many letters, which have been since found among Mr Bradley's papers, desiring his permission to apply for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of it to him, and even offering to resign in his favour, if it should be thought necessary: but before Mr Halley could bring this kind project to bear, he died. Mr Bradley, however, obtained the place afterwards, by the favour and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Lord Macclesfield, who was afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal Society. As soon as the appointment of Mr Bradley to this place was known, the university of Oxford sent him a diploma creating him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The appointment of astronomer at Greenwich placed Mr Bradley in his proper element, and he pursued his observations with unwearied diligence. However numerous the collection of astronomical instruments at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at Greenwich, it was impossible that such an observer as Dr Bradley should not desire to increase them, as well to answer those particular views, as in general to make observations with greater exactness. In the year 1748, therefore, he took the opportunity of the annual visit made by the Royal Society to the observatory, in order to examine the instruments and receive the professor's observations for the year, to represent so strongly the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of repairing the old instruments, and purchasing new, that the society thought proper to represent it to his majesty, and his majesty gave them £1000. for that purpose. This sum was laid out under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Dr Bradley, who, with the assistance of the late celebrated Mr Graham and Mr <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">Bird</a>, furnished the observatory with as complete a collection of astronomical instruments, as the most skilful and diligent observer could desire. Dr Bradley, furnished with such assistance, pursued his observations with new assiduity, an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of which were found after his death, and put into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Royal Society. It has been already observed, that when Dr Bradley was elected to the professor's chair at Oxford, he gave up his two livings, which were at such a distance, that he could not possibly fulfil the duties of them himself; but it happened that after he was settled at Greenwich the living of that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> became vacant, which is very considerable, and which was offered to him, as he was upon the spot to perform the duty, and had the claim of uncommon merit to the reward. This living, however, Dr Bradley, very greatly to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, refused, fearing the duties of the astronomer would too much interfere with those of the divine. His majesty, however, hearing of the refusal, was so pleased with it, that he granted him a pension of £250l. a-year, in consideration of his great abilities and knowledge in astronomy and other branches of the mathematics, which had procured so much advantage to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, as is particularly mentioned in the grant, which is dated the 15th of February 1752. Dr Bradley, about the same time, was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of the Royal Society. In the year 1748, he was admitted a member of the royal academy of sciences and belles lettres of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, upon the death of M. Crevier, first physician to his Catholic majesty; in the year 1752, a member of the imperial academy at Petersburg; and in 1757, of that instituted at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. Dr Bradley was still indefatigable in his observations, and whatever honour he received became an incitement to obtain new distinction; his corporeal abilities, however, at length declined, though his intellectual suffered no abatement. In the year 1789, he became extremely weak and infirm; and towards the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1762, he was attacked with a total suppression of urine, caused by an inflammation of the reins, which on the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> following put an end to his life, in the 70th year of his age. He was buried at Mitchin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMPTON">Hampton</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> with his mother and his wife. In the year 1744, he married Susannah Peach, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a gentleman of that name in Gloucestershire, by whom he had only one daughter. As to his character, he was remarkable for a placid and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, very uncommon in persons of an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> temper and robust <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. It was still more remarkable, that, with this untroubled equanimity of temper, he was compassionate and liberal in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. Although he was a good speaker, and possessed the rare but happy art of expressing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> with the utmost precision and perspicuity, yet no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was a greater lover of silence, for he never spoke but when he thought it absolutely necessary. He did indeed think it necessary to speak when he had a fair opportunity to communicate any useful knowledge in his own way; and he encouraged those that attended his lectures to ask him questions, by the exactness with which he answered, and the care he took to adapt himself to every capacity. He was not more inclined to write than to speak, for he has published very little; he had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> diffidence, which made him always afraid that his works should injure his character; and therefore suppressed many, which probably were well worthy of the public <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was even known, as it were, in spite of himself; and, in spite of himself, he was known much, and consequently much esteemed. He was acquainted with many of the first persons in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, persons eminent as well for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> as their abilities; he was honoured by all men of learning in general; and there was not an astronomer of any eminence in the world with whom he had not a literary correspondence. Upon the whole, it may be said of Dr Bradley, that no man cultivated great talents with more success, or had a better claim to be ranked among the greatest astronomers of his age.

BRADNINCH

Pages 447-447

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, once a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, but some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago totally destroyed by fire. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 35'. N. Lat. 50° 45'.

BRADS

Pages 447-447

among artificers, a kind of nails used in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which have no spreading heads as other nails have. They are distinguished by ironmongers by six names; as joiner's brads, flooring-brads, batten-brads, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>-brads, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-heads, &c. Joiners-brads are for hard wainscot; batten-brads are for soft wainscot; bill-brads are used when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> is laid in haste, or for shallow <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOISTS">joists</a> subject to warp. See Nail.

BRADSHAW

Pages 447-448

Henry, a Benedictine monk, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, about the middle of the 11th century. Discovering an early propensity to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and literature, he was received while a boy into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of St Werberg in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and having there imbibed the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he was afterwards sent to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he studied <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> with the novices of his order, and then returned to his convent at Chester: here, in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, and wrote several books. He died in the year 1513, the fifth of Henry VIII. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> is not inferior to that of any of his contemporaries. His works are, 1. De antiquitate et magnificentia urbis Cestriae. 2. Chronicon. 3. The life of the glorious virgin St Werberg. Printed Lond. 1521, 4to, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>. The life of St Werberg makes only part of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; for it contains also a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Mercia, life of St Etheldred, the life of St Sexburg, the foundation and history of Chester, and the chronicles of some kings. Possibly this work may include the two first. Bishop Tanner says that he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> in English verse, extracted from Bede, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALMSBURY">Malmsbury</a>, Giraldus, and others. Probably this is the chronicle above mentioned.

BRADWARDIN

Pages 448-448

Thomas, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, was born at Hartfield in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 13th century. He was educated at Mer-ton <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and acquired the reputation of a profound scholar, a skilful mathematician, and consummate divine. Authors are not agreed as to his first preferments. Pitt says he was professor of divinity at Oxford. They agree, however, in asserting, that from being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he became a courtier and confessor to Edward III. whom he constantly attended during his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with France, assisting that victorious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> with his advice, animating the troops, and fervently praying for their success. After his return from the war, he was made prebendary of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and afterwards archbishop of Canterbury. He died at Lambeth in the year 1349, forty days after his consecration; and was buried in St <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>'s chapel, near the south wall. His works are, 1. De causa Dei, printed at London, 1618, published by J. H. Savil. 2. De geometria speculativa, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1495, 1512, 1530. 3. De arithmetica practica, Paris, 1502, 1512. 4. De proportionibus, Paris, 1495. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, 1505, folio. 5. De quadratura circuli, Paris, 1495, folio.

BRADY

Pages 448-448

Nicholas, an excellent divine and poet, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANDON">Bandon</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork, October 28th 1659. He studied at Westminster-school, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. He was a zealous promoter of the Revolution; and, in 1690, when the troubles broke out in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, by his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with McCarty, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James's general, he thrice prevented the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of the town of Bandon. Having quitted several preferments in Ireland, he settled in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he was successively promoted to several livings; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was rector of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAPHAM">Clapham</a>, minister of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, and chaplain to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>'s troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-guards. He wrote <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the new version of the Psalms, now sung in many churches in England and Ireland; the Æneids of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, in 4 vols; and 3 vols of sermons. He died May 20th 1726.

BRADYPUS

Pages 448-448
or Sloth, a genus of quadrupeds, belonging to the order of bruta. See Mammalia Index.

BRAE-MAR

Pages 448-448

a mountainous territory of Scotland, in the shire of Aberdeen, where the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Mar began to raise a rebellion in 1715. It is 27 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Aberdeen. BRAE-Murray, a mountainous and woody tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, lying in the shires of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELGIN">Elgin</a> and Nairn in Scotland.

BRAG

Pages 448-448

an ingenious and pleasant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, where as many may partake as the cards <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> supply; the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> dealing three to each person at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> up the last card all round. This done, each gamester puts <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> three stakes, one for each card.—The first stake is won by the best card turned up in the dealing round; beginning from the ace, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNAVE">knave</a>, and so downwards. When cards of the same value are turned up to two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more of the gamesters, the eldest hand gains; but it is to be observed, that the ace of diamonds wins, to whatever hand it be turned up.—The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> stake is won by what is called the brag, which consists in one of the gamesters challenging the rest to turn up cards equal to his: Now it is to be observed, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of aces is the best brag, a pair of kings the next, and so on; and a pair of any sort wins the stake from the most valuable single card. In this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> consists the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diversion of the game; for, by the artful management of the looks, gestures, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, it frequently happens, that a pair of fives, treys, or even deuces, outbrags a much higher pair, and even some pairs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, to the no small merriment of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. The knave of clubs is here a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> favourite, making a pair with any other card in hand, and with any other two cards a pair royal.—The third stake is won by the person who first makes up the cards in his hand one and thirty; each dignified card going for ten, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> from the pack, as usual in this game.

BRAGA

Pages 448-448

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Entre-minho-duro, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, situated on the river Cavado, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 40. N. Lat. 41. 20.

BRAGANZA

Pages 448-448

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name. It is seated on an eminence, by a brook called Farvenca; and is divided into two parts, the old city and the town. The former is upon an eminence, and fortified with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> wall. That <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> next the town has five bastions, but no ditch; the citadel is on the opposite side joined to the wall. The town is in a plain, and defended by a fort with four bastions. It is seated near the river Sabor, on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 15. N. Lat. 41. 27.

BRAGGOT

Pages 448-448

a kind of drink made of malt, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, and spices, much used in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>.

BRAHE

Pages 448-449

Tycho, a celebrated astronomer, descended of an illustrious family originally of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> but settled at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, was born <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 14. 1546, at at Knudstorp in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Schonen. He was taught Latin when <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years old, and studied five years under private tutors. His father dying, his uncle sent him, in April 1559, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on the 21st of August 1560, happening at the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the astronomers had foretold, he began to look upon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> as something divine; and purchasing the tables of Stadius, gained some notion of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. In 1562, he was sent by his uncle to Leipsic to study <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but astronomy wholly engrossed his thoughts, and in purchasing books on that science he employed all his pocket-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Having procured a small celestial globe, he was wont to wait till his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> was gone to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, in order to examine the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> and learn their names; and when the sky was clear, he spent whole nights in viewing the stars. In 1563, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> arising between Brahe and a Danish nobleman, they fought, and the former had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his nose cut off; which defect he so artfully supplied with one made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver, that it was not perceptible. It was about this time that he began to apply to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, proposing nothing less than to obtain the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. In 1571, he returned to Denmark; and was favoured by his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, Steno Belle, a lover of learning, with a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at his castle of Herritzvad near Knudstorp, for making his observations, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>. His marrying a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> girl, beneath his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, occasioned such a violent quarrel between him and his relations, that the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> was obliged to interpose to reconcile them. In 1574, by his majesty's command, he read lectures upon the theory of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">comets</a> at Copenhagen. The year following he began his travels through Germany, and proceeded as far as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>: he then resolved to remove his family, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>; but Frederic II, king of Denmark being informed of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and unwilling to lose a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that was capable of being such an ornament to his country, promised to enable him to pursue his studies, to bestow upon him for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Huen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">Sound</a>, to erect an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> and laboratory there, and to defray all the expenses necessary for carrying on his designs. Tycho Brahe readily embraced this proposal; and accordingly the first stone of the observatory was laid August 8, 1576. The king also gave him a pension of 2000 crowns out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, a fee in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, and a canonry of Rosechild, which brought him in 1000 more. James VI, of Scotland, afterwards raised to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of England, going to Denmark in order to marry the princess <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, paid a visit to our author in his retirement at Uraniaburg, made him several presents, and with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> wrote a copy of verses in his praise; but, soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King Frederic, he was deprived of his pension, fee, and canonry; upon which, finding himself incapable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the expenses of his observatory, he went to Copenhagen, whither he brought some of his instruments, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his astronomical observations in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, till Valkendorf, chamberlain to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of Christian IV, commanded him by the king's order to discontinue them. He then removed his family to Rostock, and afterwards to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, in order to solicit Henry Ranzou to introduce him to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; and that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> complying with his request, he was received by the emperor at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a> with the utmost civility and respect. That <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> gave him a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, till he could procure one for him more fit for astronomical observations; assigned him a pension of 3000 crowns; and promised upon the first opportunity, a fee for him and his descendants: but he did not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> enjoy this happy situation; for, upon the 24th of October 1601, he died of a retention of urine, in the 55th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and was interred in a very magnificent manner in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Prague, where a noble monument was erected to him. His skill in astronomy is universally known, and he is famed for being the inventor of a new system, which he endeavoured, though without success, to establish upon the ruins of that of Copernicus. He was very credulous with regard to judicial astrology and presages. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he met an old woman when he went out of doors, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a hare upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> in a journey, he used to turn back immediately, being persuaded that it was a bad <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>. When he lived at Uraniaburg, he had at his house a madman, whom he placed at his feet at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and fed himself. As he imagined that everything spoken by mad persons presaged something, he carefully observed all that this man said; and because it sometimes proved true, he imagined it might always be depended on. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> trifle put him in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>; and against persons of the first rank, with whom it was his duty to keep on good terms, he openly discovered his resentment. He was very apt to rally others, but highly provoked if the same <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> was taken with himself. His principal works are, 1. Progymnasmata astronomiae. 2. De mundi ætheri recentioribus phænomenis. 3. Epistolæ armaticarum liber. BRAHMA. See BRAMA.

BRAIDALBIN

Pages 449-450

a district of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a> in Scotland, stretching 32 miles from east to west, and 13 where broadest from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. It is a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, lying among the Grampian hills, supposed to be the country anciently known by the name of Albani; whence the Highlanders to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> call themselves Albinech. It is bounded on the west by Lochaber, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LORN">Lorn</a>, and Knapdale; on the north and east, by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Lochaber and part of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHOL">Athol</a>; and on the south by Strathern and Monteith. It produces plenty of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle; is inhabited by Highlanders said to be the most ferocious in all Scotland; and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to a branch of the Campbell family, which is possessed of a noble and magnificent seat in this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. Much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> is cultivated here. Some years ago, when premiums were given for the greatest crops, from 70 to 120 hogsheads of linseed were annually sown, each peck yielding two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of dressed flax; and when the yarn sold highest, 2000l. worth has been sold out of the country. Oats and potatoes are the other crops. Oats yield from four to six fold at the most, often less; bear from eight to ten, at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> six. The corn raised seldom suffices the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants, so they are often obliged to have recourse to importation. From their potatoes some have distilled a very strong spirit, which has been found cheaper than what is distilled from any grain. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STARCH">Starch</a> is also made from them; and, in some places, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. Corcur, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the lichen omphaloides, is an article of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities have been scraped from the rocks, and exported for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the dyers. Braidalbin at the price of 1s. or 16d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. A good many sheep are reared here, and much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> is sent out of the country. There are few horses raised in this country: such as feed on the tops of the higher hills are often afflicted with a distemper that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> proves fatal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a remedy is not applied within 24 hours. It attacks them in the months of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> and August, usually after a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, or before the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> rises in the morning. An universal swelling spreads over the body; the remedy is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, chafing, or any other method that promotes urine and perspiration. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> this evil to a certain animal that scatters its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> over the grass; but more probably it arises from some noxious vegetable, hitherto unobserved. Before the year 1745, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Braidalbin was obliged to keep a constant <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> for the protection of his vassals cattle, or to retain spies among the thievish clans; having too much spirit to submit to pay an infamous tax, called black mail, to the plundering chieftans, as the price of their safety.

BRAIL

Pages 450-450
or BRAILS, in a ship, are small ropes made use of to furl the sails across: they belong only to the two courses and the mizen-sail; they are reeved through the blocks, seized on each side the ties, and come down before the sail, being at the very skirt thereof fastened to the cringles; their use is, when the sail is furled across, to haul up its bunt, that it may the more easily be taken up or let fall. Hale up the brails, or brail up the sail; that is, Hale up the sail, in order to be furled or bound close to the yard.

BRAIN

Pages 450-450

in Anatomy, is that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, soft, whitish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a>, enclosed in the cranium <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skull; wherein all the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> terminate, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is supposed principally to reside. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BRAIN le Comte, a town of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hainault. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 11. N. Lat. 50. 35.

BRAINTREE

Pages 450-450

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 50. N. Lat. 51. 50.

BRAKE

Pages 450-450

denotes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> fern, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where it grows.—Also a sharp bit or snaffle for horses; and a baker's kneading-trough.—Also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> to bruise <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. See FLAX-Dressing.

BRAKEL

Pages 450-450

a town of Germany, in the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADERBORN">Paderborn</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 8. N. Lat. 51. 46.

BRALLOW

Pages 450-450

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Podolia, seated on the river Bog, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29. 0. N. Lat. 43. 50.

BRAMA

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cyprinus.

BRAMANT

Pages 450-450

a town of Savoy in the valley of Maurich, seated on the river Arck, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 15. N. Lat. 45. 0.

BRAMBER

Pages 450-450

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a> in England, with 95 inhabitants, though formerly of some account; however, it sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 15. N. Lat. 50. 50.

BRAMBLE

Pages 450-450
or Brambling, in Ornithology, the trivial name of a species of Fringilla.

BRAMER

Pages 450-450

LEONARD, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>-painter, was born at Delft in 1596; but learned the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> in the school of Rembrandt, and imitated the manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in small. In the 18th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> he went to Rome for his improvement; but although he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> for some years, and acquired somewhat in his style rather more graceful than Rembrandt, yet he could never divest himself of the Flemish gout. He had a fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is generally good, and in some of his compositions truly noble. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> is delicate, and his colouring very peculiar in the tints, being also remarkably thin in many parts, so as barely to cover the pannel; yet, by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> skill in the management of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHIARO_SCURO">chiaro-scuro</a>, his colouring is bright, bold, and full of lustre; particularly in the vases, which he was fond of introducing in every subject that could admit them, as he knew how to give them a rich and fine relievo. He had accustomed himself to paint with a very thin body of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, especially in the browns and shadowy parts, in order to give his pictures a greater transparency. At <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and other cities of Italy, as well as at Rome, he left many proofs of his extraordinary merit, which rendered his name deservedly famous; and his works are rarely to be met with out of Italy, where he painted most; but whenever they are to be purchased they are bought at considerable prices, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are entire and undamaged. One of the most <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> pictures of Bramer is the Raising of Lazarus, in which there is a charming opposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and shadow; and another is the Denial of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>: They are both painted in his best manner; they are bright, transparent, and finely penciled, and are still preserved at Rome. Likewise at the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Ryswick, there are several valuable paintings by this master; in which the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and execution are highly commendable. But none of his works can be more admired than a small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> representing the story of Pyramus and Thisbe.

BRAMHALL

Pages 450-451

Dr JOHN, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMAGH">Armagh</a>, was born of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family at Pontefract in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, about the year 1593. He was invited over to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> Wentworth; and soon after obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-deaconry of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEATH">Meath</a>, the best in that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1634, he was made bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDONDERRY">Londonderry</a>, which see he improved very much; but the greatest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he did to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Ireland, was by getting, with the deputy's assistance, several acts passed for abolishing fee-farms, recovering appropriations, &c., by which, and by other means, he regained to the church in the space of four years 30,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 40,000l. a-year. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a> he prevailed upon the church of Ireland to unite in the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with the church of England, by adopting the 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Bramhall, cles of that church; and would willingly have introduced the English canons, but could only prevail on their accepting such as they deemed proper. Articles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> were exhibited against him in the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UXBRIDGE">Uxbridge</a> in 1644, the English parliament made it a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> article, that Bishop Bramhall, with Archbishop Laud, and others, should be excepted from the general <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. He went abroad; but on the restoration was appointed archbishop of Armagh, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMATE">primate</a> and metropolitan of all Ireland, and was chosen speaker of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of lords. He died in 1663; and was the author of several works, which are collected in one vol. folio.

BRAMINS

Pages 451-452

the name of the priests among the idolatrous Indians; the successors of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Brachmans. See the article BRACHMANS. Their name is formed from Brama, their particular deity. They are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIAM">Siam</a>, Malabar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, Coromandel, and most other eastern nations anywhere civilized; but their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat is in Indostan*, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the Mogul's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> peculiar to themselves, which they call Shanscrit; in which they have several ancient books, written, as is alleged, by their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> prophet Brahma; as the Shastrum, which is their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIBLE">bible</a>; and Porane, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> which they esteem sacred, and pretend to have been dictated by God himself. There are several orders of Bramins. Those who mix in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> are for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> very corrupt in their morals: they believe that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the Ganges <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> wash away all their crimes; and, as they are not subject to any civil jurisdiction, live without either restraint or virtue, excepting that character of compassion and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> which is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> found in the mild <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The others, who live abstracted from the world, are either weak-minded men or enthusiasts; and abandon themselves to laziness, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. We find in their disputes the very same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> that occur in the writings of our most celebrated metaphysicians; such as, substance, accident, priority, posteriority, immutability, indivisibility, &c. Their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, which was anciently of the allegorical and moral kind, hath degenerated into a heap of extravagant and obscene superstitions, owing to their having realized those fictions which were intended merely as so many symbols and emblems. Were it possible to obtain a sight of their sacred books, the only remains there are of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> antiquities, we might in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be enabled to remove the veil that envelopes those numerous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>; but the following story will show how little reason there is to hope that we shall ever be intrusted with such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Mahmoud Akbar had an inclination to make himself acquainted with the principles of all the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sects throughout his extensive provinces. Having discarded the superstitious notions with which he had been prepossessed by his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, he resolved to judge for himself. It was easy for him to be acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of those systems that are formed upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of making proselytes; but he found himself disappointed in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> when he came to treat with the Indians, who will not admit any person whatever to the participation of their mysteries. Neither the authority nor promises of Akbar could prevail with the Bramins to disclose the tenets of their religion; he was therefore obliged to have recourse to artifice. The stratagem he made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, was to cause a boy, of the name of Feizi, to be committed to the care of these priests, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> orphan of the sacerdotal line, who alone could be initiated into the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. Feizi, having received the proper instructions for the part he was to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a>, was conveyed privately to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>, the seat of knowledge in Indostan; he was received into the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a learned Bramin, who educated him with the same care as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had been his own son. After the youth had spent ten years in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, Akbar was desirous of recalling him; but he was struck with the charms of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his preceptor. The women of the sacerdotal tribe are looked upon as the greatest beauties in Indostan. The old Bramin laid no restraint upon that growing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of the two lovers: he was fond of Feizi, who had gained his affection by his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and docility; and offered him his daughter in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. The young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, divided between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, resolved to conceal the fraud no longer; and falling at the feet of the Bramin, discovered the imposture, and asked <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> for his offence. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, without reproaching him in the least, seized a poniard, which hung at his girdle, and was going to plunge it in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, if Feizi had not prevented him by taking hold of his arm. The young man used every means to pacify him, and declared himself ready to do anything to expiate his treachery. The Bramin, bursting into tears, promised to pardon him on condition that he should swear never to translate the Bedas or sacred volumes, or disclose to any person whatever the symbol of the Bramin creed. Feizi readily promised all that the Bramin required: how far he kept his word is not known; but the sacred books of the Indians have never been translated by him, or any one else, to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. As the Bramins are the only persons who understand the language of the sacred books, their comments on the text are the same as those that have ever been made on religious books; all the maxims which fancy, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, passion, or false zeal can suggest, are to be found in these volumes. See the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> SHASTAH and VEDAM. They own a supreme God, who created Brama, and gave him a power to create the world. They have also their subaltern deities, their pagods or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and idols, whom they fan to defend from flies, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> before them. They also hold a feast in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> considered as the source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, whereby all nature is fecundified. Their pagods or temples consist of three parts. The first is a vaulted <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, supported on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> columns: it lies open, and all persons, without distinction, are allowed to enter into it. It is adorned with symbolical figures made of wood, as elephants, oxen, and horses. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part is open in the daytime, and shut at night. It is fitted with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and monstrous figures, as men with many heads and arms. The third, which is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a>, is kept always shut, with a very strong gate. In this is placed the statue of the deity to whom the pagod is dedicated. A great num- Bramins before they go into the pagod, pull off their shoes, and leave them at the door. The Bramins of Siam and Coromandel maintain that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> will be destroyed by fire; and the former assert that another will arise out of its ashes, in which there shall be no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, nor any change of seasons, but an eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and the latter maintain a plurality of worlds, which are alternately destroyed and renewed. Robert de Nobili, an Italian Jesuit, and one of the Indian missionaries, in the beginning of the 17th century, in order to secure success to his mission, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> and appearance of a Bramin, and at length persuaded the credulous people that he was in reality a member of that venerable order. He forged a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a> in the ancient Indian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, showing that the Bramins of Rome were elder than those of India, and that the Jesuits of Rome descended in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> line from the god Brama. He farther declared on oath, that he derived his origin from this Indian deity. By this imposture he proselyted twelve eminent Bramins, whose influence proved very favourable to his mission. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the Portuguese Jesuits carried on the imposture with very considerable success. These missions, however, were suspended and abandoned in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a papal mandate, issued out in the year 1744, by Benedict XIV. who declared his disapprobation of the artifices that had been used in the conversion of the Indians. See further under the article <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">Observatory</a>.

BRAMPOUR

Pages 452-452
or Brampore, a city of Asia, in Hindostan, and once capital of Candish. It formerly stood on as much ground as London; but it is now greatly decayed, and chiefly inhabited by Banians. The streets are numerous but narrow, with low thatched houses made of earth, though a few are covered with varnished tiles. In rainy weather many of the streets are overflowed. In the market place is the statue of an elephant in red stone, as big as life. On the other side of the river they have built a new town, which is in a better situation. A great trade is carried on in this town, and throughout all the province, where there is made a prodigious quantity of cotton-cloths, as cotton is in greater plenty here than in any other place of the empire. E. Long. 77°25'. N. Lat. 21°10'.

BRAMPTON

Pages 452-452

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> in England, seated not far from the Picts wall, and on the river Irthin. It is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and contained 2043 inhabitants in 1811. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2°40'. N. Lat. 54°50'.

BRAN

Pages 452-452

the skins <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> husks of corn, especially wheat, ground, separated from the flour by a sieve or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLTER">bolter</a>. It contains, besides, a portion of the farinaceous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; this is less glutinous than the finer flour, and is supposed to have a detergent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Infusions of bran are not unfrequently employed in this intention externally, and sometimes likewise taken inwardly. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> bran was used as an erotic, to excite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>. Bran boiled purges scurf, dandruff, and cleanses the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> in lieu of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. The dyers reckon it among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUT">nut</a>-coloured drugs; and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it for making what they call the sour waters, with which they prepare their several dyes. Bran is also used as a medicine for horses. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRANCH

Pages 452-453

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, an arm of a tree, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which, sprouting out from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, helps to form the head or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> thereof. Branches do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> surface of the trunk, but are profoundly rooted therein, so as not only to penetrate into the cortical, but also the woody substance, and even the pith. The constituent parts therefore of a branch are the same as of the trunk, viz. skin, bark, wood, and pith. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. Branches of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDLE">Bridle</a>, in the manege, are two pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> bended, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> between the one and the other, bear the bit-mouth, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-chains, and the curb; so that on one end they answer to the head-stall, and on the other to the reins, in order to keep the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s head in subjection. With regard to their form and structure, branches are either straight, in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a>, for young horses to form their mouth; or after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a> of France's fashion, proper for a horse that carries his head well. Some are in form of a gigot or leg, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> prevent horses from carrying too low: Some are in form of a bent knee, contrived for horses that arm themselves against the operation of the bit; and others after the French fashion, which is hardly above-one third of an inch at the sevile hole, and knead 1½ inch at the jarret or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAM">ham</a>.
