It is to be observed, 1. That the farther the branch is from the horse's neck, the more effect it will have. 2. That short branches, cæteris paribus, are ruder, and their effects more sudden, than those of longer. 3. That the branch is to be proportioned to the length of a horse's neck; and one may sooner err in choosing one too short than too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Branches of Ogives, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of Gothic vaults. These arches, traversing from one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> to another diagonal-wise, form a cross between the other arches, which make the sides of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, of which the arches are diagonal. Branch-Stand, with falconers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to signify the making a hawk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from tree to tree, till the dog <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>. Brancher, among sportsmen, a young hawk, newly taken out of the nest, that can hop from bough to bough. Branchiæ, or Gills, in the anatomy of fishes, the parts corresponding to the lungs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-animals. All fishes, except the cetaceous ones, and the pteronyzum, which have lungs, are furnished with these organs of respiration. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Branchidæ, in Grecian antiquity, priests of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, which was at Didymus in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, towards the Ægean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, upon the frontier of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>. They opened to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-XERXES">Xerxes</a> the temple of Apollo, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> whereof he took away. After which, thinking it unsafe to stay in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, they fled to Sogdiana, on the other side of the Caspian sea, upon the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, where they built a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> called by their own name; but they did not escape the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of their crime; for Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> having conquered <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Persia, and being informed of their treachery, put them all to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and razed their city, thus punishing the impiety of the fathers in their posterity. Branchiostegi, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a term used to express one of the general classes of fishes; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which are, that the rays of the fins are of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> Branchiobony substance, but these fish have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> or ossicula at the branchiae, as the malacoptyerygious and acanthopterygious fishes all have.

BRANCHON

Pages 453-453

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>, seated on the river Mehaigne. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 40'. N. Lat. 50° 32'. BRAND <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, Dimanche des Brandons, in French <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, denotes the first Sunday in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, which is thus called on account of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> practice in the Lyonnais, where the peasants, in the night of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, walked about their orchards, gardens, &c. with torches lighted, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fire-brands in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>; in which plight they visited every tree, and addressing themselves to them one after another, threatened, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they did not bear fruit well the ensuing season, they should be cut <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the ground and burnt. This is evidently a relic of Paganism; the like of which was practised by the ancient idolaters in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of February; hence called Februarius, à februando.

BRANDEIS

Pages 453-453

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14° 25'. N. Lat. 50° 15'.

BRANDENBURG

Pages 453-454

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the marquisate of that name, situated on the river Havel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13° 0'. N. Lat. 52° 25'. It is divided into the old and new town, and was anciently the see of a bishop. The mountain in the neighbourhood, called Marienberg, is planted with vines. Here is a small colony of French Calvinists, with a manufacture of cloth, fustian, and canvas; and a pretty good trade is carried on by the Havel. The fort here looks like a suburb, and contains a riding school, with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> also of the members of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, which still subsists, and is composed of a Lutheran provost, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, senior, subsenior, and three other canons, reside in it. They are distinguished by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> enamelled with violet, terminating in eight <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>; and have a considerable estate. The town contains about 13,000 inhabitants.

BRANDEUM

Pages 454-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> veil put over the tombs of the apostles St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, and left there for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; by which it is supposed to acquire a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of sanctity, so as to be worshipped as a relic; and for that purpose frequently sent by the pope as a present to some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, Brandeum amounts to the same with what was otherwise called sanctuarium, sudarium, orarium, and velum. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of brandea was introduced as a means of diffusing and propagating the virtues and influences of relics, without moving, or any way impairing, the substance of them; the translation of relics in early days being forbidden.

BRANDING

Pages 454-454

in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> on various offences, by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, after the offender hath been once admitted to benefit of clergy.

BRANDON

Pages 454-454

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> in England, seated on the little river Ouse, over which it has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and a ferry at a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>'s distance: whence it is divided into Brandon, and Brandon ferry; which last has the most business, because commodities are brought thither from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> gives the British <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the family of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in Scotland. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1360. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 55'. N. Lat. 52° 30'.

BRANDRITH

Pages 454-454

among builders, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rail about the mouth of a well.

BRANDT

Pages 454-454

GERARD, a learned divine of the reformed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> in 1626, and was successively minister in several places of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. He wrote some works which are esteemed, particularly the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reformation of the Netherlands, 4 vols 4to; and The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Ruyter; both written in the Flemish tongue. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a> in 1685.

BRANDY

Pages 454-454

a spirituous and inflammable liquor, extracted from wine and other liquors by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a>. See Distillation. Wine-brandy, made in France, is esteemed the best in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. They make it wherever they make wine, and for that purpose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> wine that is pricked rather than good wine. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> brandies for foreign trade, and those accounted best, are the brandies of Bordeaux, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>, Cogniac, Charenton, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Rhe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Blasois, Poictou, Touraine, Anjou, Nantz, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, and Champaign.

BRANK

Pages 454-454

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> used in some parts of Scotland, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, for correcting scolding women. It is a sort of head-piece, which opens and encloses the head of the impatient, while an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, sharp as a chisel, enters the mouth, and subdues the more dreadful weapon within. Thus harnessed, the offender is led in triumph through the streets. Dr Plott, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Staffordshire, has favoured the world with a minute <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the instrument*, which is there called a scolding bruckle; and tells us, he looks upon it "as much to be preferred to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCKING">ducking</a>-stool, which not only endangers the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> of the party, but also gives the tongue <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> betwixt every dip; to neither of which this is at all liable."

BRANLIN

Pages 454-454

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of salmon, with several transverse <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> streaks, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of so many fingers.

BRANNODUNUM

Pages 454-454

with a garrison of the Equites Dalmatiae, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, on the Sinus Metaris: now Brancester, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, on the Washes.

BRANOGENIUM

Pages 454-454
or BRANONIUM, a town of the Coritani, a people in the heart of Britain: from the distances of the Itinerary, Camden supposes it to be Worcester.

BRANSKA

Pages 454-454

a town of Transilvania, situated on the river Marish. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 15'. N. Lat. 46°.

BRASIDA

Pages 454-455

an anniversary solemnity at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Brasidas, a Lacedemonian <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>, famous for his achievements at Methone, Pylos, and Amphipolis. It was celebrated with sacrifices and games, wherein none were permitted to attend but free-born Spartans. Whoever neglected to be present at the solemnity was fined.

BRASIDAS

Pages 455-455

a celebrated general of the Lacedemonians, about 424 years before the birth of Christ. He defeated the Athenians by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, took many places, and rendered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> formidable to all the neighbouring states. He conquered the Athenians on their attempting to surprise Amphipolis, but died of the wounds he received in that <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">ATTICA</a> and LACEDEMON.

BRASIL

Pages 455-457

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, being the easternmost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of that continent lying between the equinoctial line and the tropic of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPRICORN">Capricorn</a>. It is about 1560 miles in length, and 1000 in breadth; but measuring along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, it is 2000 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is bordered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that open from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to time, and form good harbours where vessels may <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in safety. It was accidentally discovered by the Portuguese in 1500. Emmanuel <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> had equipped a squadron of 13 sail, carrying 1200 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> and sailors destined for the East Indies, under the conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Alvarez Cabral. This <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, quitting <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> on the 19th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1500, struck out to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to avoid the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and steered his course southward, that he might the more easily turn the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, which projects a good way into the ocean. On the 24th of April, he got sight of the continent of South America, which he judged to be a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at some distance from the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COASTING">Coasting</a> along for some time, he ventured to send a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> on shore; and was astonished to observe the inhabitants entirely different from the Africans in features, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>. It was found, however, impracticable to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon any of the Indians, who retired with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> celerity to the mountains on the approach of the Portuguese; yet, as the sailors had discovered a good harbour, the admiral thought proper to come to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, and called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> Puerto Segura. Next <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> he sent another boat on shore, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to lay hold on two of the natives, whom he clothed and treated kindly, and then dismissed, to make a proper report to their countrymen. The stratagem had the desired effect. The Indians, having heard the relation of the prisoners, immediately crowded to the shore, singing, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and sounding horns of different kinds; which induced Cabral to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and take solemn possession in the name of his Portuguese majesty. As soon as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Lisbon had ordered a survey to be taken of the harbours, bays, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and coasts of Brasil, and was convinced that the country afforded neither <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> nor silver, they held it in such contempt, that they sent thither none but condemned criminals and abandoned women. Two ships were sent every year from Portugal, to carry the refuse of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to this new world, and to bring home parrots and woods for the dyers and cabinet-makers. Ginger was afterwards added; but soon after prohibited, lest it should interfere with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of the same article from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. In 1548, the Jews, many of whom had taken refuge in Portugal, beginning to be persecuted by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, were stripped of their possessions, and banished to Brasil. Here, however, they were not entirely forsaken. Many of them found kind relations and faithful friends; others, who were known to be men of probity and understanding, obtained <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in advance from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of different nations with whom they had formerly had transactions. By the assistance of some enterprising men, they were enabled to cultivate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes, which they first procured from the island of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADEIRA">Madeira</a>. Sugar, which till then had been used only in medicine, became an article of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>. Princes and great men were all eager to procure themselves this new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. This circumstance proved favourable to Brasil, and enabled it to extend its sugar plantations. The court of Lisbon, notwithstanding its prejudices, began to be sensible that a colony might be beneficial to the mother country, without producing gold <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> silver; and this settlement, which had been wholly left to the capricious management of the colonists, was now thought to deserve some kind of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and accordingly Thomas de Souza was sent thither, in 1549, to regulate and superintend it. This able governor began by reducing these men, who had always lived in a state of anarchy, into proper subordination, and bringing their scattered plantations closer together: after which he applied himself to acquire some information respecting the natives, with whom he knew he must be incessantly engaged either in traffic or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This it was no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to accomplish. Brasil was full of small nations, some of which inhabited the forests, and others lived in the plains and along the rivers. Some had settled habitations; but the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them led a roving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and most of them had no intercourse with each other. It is not to be supposed that such a people would be at all disposed to submit to the yoke which the Portuguese wanted to put upon them on their arrival. At first they only declined all intercourse with these strangers: but finding themselves pursued in order to be made slaves, and to be employed in the labours of the field, they took the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and devour all the Europeans they could seize upon. The friends and relations of the savages that were taken prisoners also ventured to make frequent attempts to rescue them, and were sometimes successful: so that the Portuguese were forced to attend to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> employments of labour and war. Souza did not bring a sufficient number of forces to change the situation of affairs. Indeed, by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> San Salvador, he gave a centre to the colony; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of settling, extending, and making it really useful to the mother country, was reserved for the Jesuits who attended him. These men, who for their arts of insinuation and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> have been equalled by none, dispersed themselves among the Indians. When any of the missionaries were murdered, they were immediately replaced by others; and seeming to be inspired only with sentiments of peace and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, the Indians, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, grew not only familiar but passionately fond of them. As the missionaries were too few in number to transact all the business themselves, they frequently deputed some of the most intelligent Indians in their stead. These men having distributed hatchets, knives, and looking-glasses, among the savages they met met with, represented the Portuguese, as a harmless, humane, and good sort of people. The prosperity of the colony of Brasil, which was visible to all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, excited the envy of the French, Spaniards, and Dutch successively. The latter, indeed, bid fairest for the conquest of the whole. Their admiral Henry Lonk arrived, in the beginning of the year 1630, with 46 men of war, on the coast of Fernambuca, one of the largest and best fortified captainships of these parts. He reduced it after several obstinate engagements, in which he was always victorious. The troops he left behind subdued the captainships of Tamaraca, Pareiba, and Rio Grande, in the years 1633, 1634, and 1635. These, as well as Fernambuca, furnished annually a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of sugar, a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of wood for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>, and other commodities. The Hollanders were so elated with the acquisition of this wealth, which flowed to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a> instead of Lisbon, that they determined to conquer all the Brasils, and intrusted Maurice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a> with the conduct of this enterprise. That general reached the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his destination in the beginning of the year 1637. He found the soldiers so well disciplined, the commanders such experienced men, and so much readiness in all to engage, that he directly took the field. He was successively opposed by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUQUERQUE">Albuquerque</a>, Banjala, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Rocca de Borgia, and the Brazilian Cameron, the idol of his people, passionately fond of the Portuguese, brave, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>, cunning, and who wanted no qualifications necessary for a general, but to have learned the art of war under able commanders. These several chiefs exerted their utmost efforts to defend the possessions that were under their protection; but their endeavours proved ineffectual. The Dutch seized upon the captainships of Siara, Serecippe, and the greater part of that of Bahia. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> of the 15 provinces which composed the colony had already submitted to them, and they flattered themselves that one or two campaigns would make them masters of the rest of their enemies' possessions in that part of America; when they were suddenly checked by the revolution happening on the banishment of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> IV., and placing the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a> on the throne. After this, the Portuguese recovering their spirits, soon drove the Dutch out of Brasil, and have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> masters of it ever since. The country of Brasil is divided into the following provinces, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIA">Paria</a>, Maragnano, Sira, Rio Grande, Pareiba, Tamaraca, Fernambuca, Serecippe, Bahia, Porto Seguro, Esperito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Angra, St Vincent, and Del Rey. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. The first aspect of the country from the sea is rather unfavourable, as it appears <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, rough, and unequal; but, on a more narrow inspection, nothing can be more delightful, the eminences being covered with woods, and the valleys and savannahs with the most refreshing verdure. In so vast a tract of land, it cannot be imagined that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found at all equal, or the seasons uniform. The northern provinces are subject to heavy rains and variable winds, like other countries under the same parallels. Tornadoes, storms, and the utmost fury of the elements, wreak their vengeance here; while the southerly regions are blessed with all the comforts which a fine fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and temperate climate can afford. In some of the provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the climate is thought to prove favourable to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of a great variety of poisonous reptiles: some of which, as the liboy or roebuck snake, are said to extend to the length of 30 feet, and to be two or three yards in circumference. The rattlesnake and other reptiles of the same kind, grow likewise to an enormous size; and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> called zibibobaka is affirmed to be 7 yards long, and half a yard in circumference, possessed too of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> instantaneously fatal to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Here also are scorpions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a>-bears, tygers, armadillos, porcupines, janoveras, and an animal called tapirasson, which is the production of a bull and an ass, having a great resemblance to both. No country on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> affords a greater number of beautiful birds, nor variety of the most exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities are Brasil wood, ebony, dyeing woods, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a>, rosin, balsams, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>, sweetmeats, sugar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, gold, diamonds, beautiful pebbles, crystal, emeralds, jasper, and other precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; in all which the Portuguese carry on such an amazing trade as may justly be reputed the support, and indeed the vital fountain, of the mother country. The gold and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are but a recent discovery: they were first opened in the year 1681; and have since yielded above five millions <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a> annually, of which sum a fifth belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. So plentiful are diamonds in this country, that the court of Portugal had found it necessary to restrain their importation, to prevent too great a diminution of their value. They are neither so hard nor so clear as those of the East Indies, nor do they sparkle so much, but they are whiter. The Brazilian diamonds are sold ten per cent. cheaper than the Oriental ones, supposing the weights to be equal. The largest diamond in the world was sent from Brasil to the king of Portugal. It weighs 1680 carats, or 12½ ounces; and has been valued at £6,787,500. Some skilful lapidaries, however, are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that this supposed diamond is only a topaz; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> a very great abatement must be made in its value. The crown revenue arising from this colony amounts to two millions sterling in gold, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> some late writers, besides the duties and customs on merchandise imported from that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. This indeed is more than a fifth of the precious metal produced by the mines; but, every other consequent advantage considered, it probably does not much exceed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The excessive confluence of people to the Brasil colonies, as well from other countries as from Portugal, not only enlarges the imports of gold, but what is of infinitely more importance to Europe in general, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this hemisphere; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are the following. Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> sends woollen manufactures; such as fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> medley cloths, fine Spanish cloths, scarlet and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cloths; serges, duroys, druggets, sagathies, shalloons, camblets, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a> stuffs; black <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a> baise; says, and perpetuanas, called long elle; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, stockings, and gloves. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Germany, and France, chiefly export fine holland, bone-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, and fine thread: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> manufactures, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> tin, and other articles, are also sent from different countries. Besides the particulars already specified, England likewise trades with Portugal, for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Brasils, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, wrought and unwrought <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, and all kinds of hardware: all which articles have so enlarged the Portuguese trade, that, instead of 12 ships usually employed in the Brasil <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, there are now never fewer. fewer than 100 sail of large vessels constantly going and returning to those colonies. To all this may be added the vast slave-trade carried on with the coast of Africa for the use of the Brasil colonies; which, we may believe, employs a great number of shipping, from the multitude of slaves that are annually transported. Indeed the commerce of Brasil alone is sufficient to raise Portugal to a considerable height of naval power, as it maintains a constant nursery of seamen; yet a certain infatuation in the policy of the country has prevented that effect, even amidst all these extraordinary advantages. All the ships in this trade, being under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, have their appointed seasons of going and returning, under convoy of a certain number of men of war. In 1806, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the violence of the French government, the court of Portugal retired to Brasil, where it still remains. In March 1817 a revolt broke out in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERNAMBUCO">Pernambuco</a>. Some individuals, who were marked out for proscription, being apprized of the intention of the government, took up arms, and, supported by the people, drove out the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and got possession of the town. A provisional government was installed, and a republic proclaimed. An <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was then sent against the town, and the republicans being defeated on the 18th May, retired into the interior, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> government was re-established. See Brasil, Supplement. Brasil-Wood, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>-wood, an American wood of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and very heavy. It is denominated variously, according to the places from whence it is brought: Thus we have brasil of Fernambucca, Sappan, Lamon, &c. For its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, &c. see Caesalpinia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BRASLAW

Pages 457-457

a considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, in Lithuania, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WILNA">Wilna</a>, with a castle. It is seated on a small lake, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 5' N. Lat. 55° 45'.

BRASS

Pages 457-458
or, as the French call it, yellow copper, is a factitious metal, composed of copper and zinc. See Chemistry Index, and Brass, Supplement. The first formation of brass, as we are assured by scripture, was prior to the flood, and discovered even in the seventh generation from Adam*. But the use of it was not, as is generally believed, and the Arundelian marbles assert, previous to the knowledge of iron. They were both first known in the same generation, and first wrought by the same discoverer. And the knowledge of them must have been equally carried over the world afterwards, with the spreading of the colonies of the Noachide. An acquaintance with the one or the other was absolutely necessary to the existence of the colonists; the clearing away of the woods about their settlements, and the erection of houses for their habitation. The ancient Britons, though acquainted from the remotest periods with the use of both these metals, remained long ignorant that they were to be obtained in the island. Before this discovery they imported all their iron and brass from the continent. And when they had at length detected the former in their own hills, and had ceased to introduce it, they continued to receive the latter. Their want of the metal remained, and no mines of it were opened in the island. In the earliest ages whose manners have been delineated by history, we find the weapons of their warriors invariably framed of this factitious metal; and the most authentic of all the profane records of antiquity, the Arundelian marbles, for that reason, mistakenly date the first discovery of iron a couple of centuries below the Trojan war. Every military nation, as such, is naturally studious of brightness in its arms; and the Britons, particularly, gloried in the neatness of theirs. For this reason the nations of the world still fabricated their arms of brass, even long after the Arundelian era for the discovery of iron; and the Britons continued to import it from the continent, though they had found iron to be a native of the country, and could have supplied themselves with a sufficient quantity of it. Mr Whitaker * supposes, that when the Britons deprived their iron and brass from the continent, they purchased the latter at an easier expense than the former, &c. The Gauls had many large brass works carried on in the kingdom, but seem to have had but few iron forges within it. And this would naturally induce the Belgae to be less diligent in their inquiry after the veins of copper and calamine at home, than for the courses of iron ore; though the one was equally discoverable in the island as the other, and lay equally within the Belgic regions of it. Brass being thus cheaper than iron, they necessarily formed with it some domestic as well as military implements. Such were common among the Gauls; and such were familiar to the Britons, either imported into the island, as some actually were, or manufactured within it, as others also assuredly were. The Britons had certainly brass foundries erected among them, and minted money and fabricated weapons of brass. In this condition of the works, the Romans entered the island. And seeing so great a demand among the natives for this article, they would speedily instruct them to discover the materials of it among themselves. This must unavoidably have resulted from the conquest of the Romans. The power of surprising their new subjects with so unexpected a discovery would naturally stimulate the pride of the Roman intellect; and the desire of obliging themselves with so cheap a supply of that useful metal, stationary as they were in that kingdom, would also equally actuate the selfishness of the Roman breast. The veins of copper and calamine would be easily found out by any experienced inquirer after them; and the former metal is therefore distinguished among the Welsh, only by the Roman appellation of cyprium, koppr, or copper. And many foundries of brass appear to have been established in the island. Some had been erected before, one perhaps within the confines of every kingdom, and probably in the vicinity of every capital. One at least would be necessary, in order to supply the armory of the principality; and one perhaps was sufficient for most of the British states. But several appear now to have been settled in every kingdom, and one perhaps near every stationary town. Two have been discovered in the single county of Essex, and within a narrow portion of it, at Fifield and Danbury. And a third was placed upon Easterly Moor in Yorkshire, 12 miles to the north-west of York, and in the neighbourhood of Isurium or Aldborough. Corinthian Brass, famous in antiquity, is a mixture of gold, silver, and copper. L. Mummius having sacked and burnt the city of Corinth, 146 years before Christ, it is said this metal was formed from the immense quantities of gold, silver, and copper, wherewith that city abounded, thus melted and run together by the violence of the conflagration. Brass, in the glass trade.—Thrice calcined brass is a preparation which serves the glassmen to give many very beautiful colours to their metal. The manner of preparing it is this: Place thin plates of brass on tiles on the leet of the furnace near the occhis; let it stand to be calcined there for four days, and it will become a black powder sticking together in lumps. Powder this, sift it fine, and recalcine it four or five days more; it will not then stick together, but remain a loose powder, of a russet colour. This is to be calcined a third time in the same manner; but great care must be taken in the third calcination, that it be not overdone nor underdone; the way to be certain when it is right is, to try it several times in glass while melting. If it makes it, when well purified, to swell, boil, and rise, it is properly calcined; if not, it requires longer time. This makes, according to the different proportions in which it is used, a sea-green, an emerald-green, or a turcoise colour. Brass, by long calcination alone, and without any mixture, affords a fine blue or green colour for glass; but they have a method of calcining it also with powdered brimstone, so as to make it afford a red, a yellow, or a chalcedony colour, according to the quantity and other variations in the using it. The method of making the calcination is this: Cut thin plates of brass into small pieces with shears, and lay them stratum super stratum, with alternate beds of powdered sulphur, in a crucible; calcine this for 24 hours in a strong fire; then powder and sift the whole; and finally expose this powder upon tiles for 12 days to a reverberating furnace; at the end of this time powder it fine, and keep it for use. The glass-makers have also a method of procuring a red powder from brass, by a more simple calcination, which serves them for many colours. The method of preparing it is this: They put small and thin plates of brass into the arches of the glass furnaces, and leave them there till they are sufficiently calcined, which the heat in that place, not being enough to melt them, does in great perfection. The calcined matter, powdered, is of a dusky red, and requires no farther preparation. Brass-Colour, one prepared by the braziers and colour-men to imitate brass. There are two sorts of it; the red brass or bronze, and the yellow or gilt brass; the latter is made only of copper-fillings, the smallest and brightest that can be found; with the former they mix some red ochre, finely pulverized; they are both used with varnish.—In order to make a fine brass that will not take any rust or verdigris, it must be dried with a chafing dish of coals as soon as it is applied.—The finest brass-colour is made with powder-brass imported from Germany, diluted into a varnish, made and used after the following manner: The varnish is composed of one pound four ounces of spirit of wine, two quinces of gum-lac, and two ounces of sandarac; these two last drugs are pulverized separately, and afterwards put to dissolve in spirit of wine, taking care to fill the bottle but half full. The varnish being made, you mix such quantity as you please of it with the pulverized brass, and apply it with a small brush to what you would brass over. But you must not mix too much at once, because the varnish being very apt to dry, you would not have time to employ it all soon enough; it is therefore better to make the mixture at several times. After this manner they brass over figures of plaster, which look as well as if they were of cast brass. Brass Leaf is made of copper, beaten out into very thin plates, and afterwards rendered yellow. The German artists, particularly those of Nuremberg and Augsburg, are said to possess the best method of giving to these thin plates of copper a fine yellow colour like gold, by simply exposing them to the fumes of zinc, without any real mixture of it with the metal. These plates are cut into little pieces, and then beaten out fine like leaves of gold; after which they are put into books of coarse paper, and sold at a low price for the vulgar kinds of gilding. The parings or shreds of these very thin yellow leaves being well ground on a marble plate, are reduced to a powder similar to gold; which serves to cover, by means of gum-water, or some other glutinous fluid, the surface of various mouldings or pieces of curious workmanship, giving them the appearance of real bronze, and even of fine gold, at a very trifling expense, because the gold colour of this metallic powder may be easily raised and improved by stirring it on a wide earthen basin over a slow fire. Brass-Lumps, a common name given by miners to the globular pyrites. See Pyrites, Mineralogy Index.

BRASSAW

Pages 458-458
or Cronstadt, a strong town of Transilvania in Burezland; scated on the river Buxel, in E. Long. 22. 35. N. Lat. 46. 30.

BRASSICA

Pages 458-463

Cabbage, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, for the classification of which see Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. But as many of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus are of considerable importance as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food, we shall here lay before our readers a more particular account of their uses and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of culture, under the names known to practical gardeners. The species called campestris grows naturally on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, has a perennial branching stalk, and in this it differs from all the other species. In very severe winters, when the other sorts are destroyed, this is a necessary plant, for the most severe frosts do not injure it. The flower-stalks grow from the end of the branches, and spread out horizontally; but those which arise from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> grow erect, and seldom put out branches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAULIFLOWER">cauliflower</a> has been much more improved in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. In France they rarely have cauliflowers till Michaelmas, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> has been often supplied with them from Britain. In many parts of Germany there were none of them cultivated till within a few years past, and most parts of Europe are supplied with seeds from Britain. That which is generally known by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cole seed is much cultivated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, and some other parts of England, for its seed, from which rape-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is drawn; and it hath also been cultivated of late years, in other places, for feeding of cattle, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> advantage. The cole-seed, when cultivated for feeding of cattle, should be sown about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The ground for this should be prepared for it in the same manner as for turnips. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of seeds for an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is from six to eight pounds; and as the price of the seed is not great, so it is better to allow Brassica. eight pounds; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the plants are too <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> in any part they may be easily thinned when the ground is hoed, which must be performed in the same manner as is practised for turnips, with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, of leaving these much nearer together; for as they have <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots and slender stalks, so they do not require near so much room. These plants should have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hoeing about five or six weeks after the first, which, if well performed in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> entirely destroy the weeds, so they will require no farther culture. Where there is not an immediate want of food, these plants had better be kept as a reserve for hard weather, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> feed, when there may be a scarcity of other green food. If the heads are cut off, and the stalks left in the ground, they will shoot again early in the spring, and produce a good second crop in April; which may be either fed off, or permitted to run to seeds, as is the practice where this is cultivated for the seeds: but if the first is fed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, there should be care taken that the cattle do not destroy their stems, or pull them out of the ground. As this plant is so hardy as not to be destroyed by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>, so it is of great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in hard winters for feeding of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a>; for when the ground is so hard frozen as that turnips cannot be taken up, these plants may be cut off for a constant supply. This will afford late food after the turnips are run to seed; and if it is afterwards permitted to stand for seed, one acre will produce as much as, at a moderate computation, will sell for five pounds, clear of charges. Partridges, pheasants, turkeys, and most other fowl, are very fond of this plant; so that wherever it is cultivated, if there are any birds in the neighbourhood, they will constantly <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> among these plants. The seeds of this plant are sown in gardens for winter and spring salads, this being one of the small salad herbs. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, flat, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>-sided cabbages, are chiefly cultivated for autumn and winter <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The seeds of these sorts must be sown the beginning or middle of April, in beds of good fresh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and when the young plants have about eight leaves, they should be pricked out into shady borders, about three or four inches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, that they may acquire strength, and to prevent their growing long shanked. About the middle of June you must transplant them out, where they are to remain. If they are planted for a full crop in a clear spot of ground, the distance from row to row should be three feet and a half, and in the rows two feet and a half asunder: if the season should prove dry when they are transplanted out, you must <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> them every other evening until they have taken fresh root; and afterwards, as the plants advance in height, you should draw the earth about the stems with a hoe, which will keep the earth moist about their roots, and greatly strengthen the plants. These cabbages will some of them be fit for use soon after Michaelmas, and will continue until the end of February, if they are not destroyed by bad weather; to prevent which, the gardeners near <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> pull up their cabbages in November, and trench their ground up in ridges, laying their cabbages against their ridges as close as possible on one side, burying their stems in the ground: in this manner they let them remain till after Christmas, when they cut them for the market; and although the outer part of the cabbage be decayed (as is often the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in very wet or hard winters), yet, if the cabbages were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and hard when laid, the inside will remain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>. The Russian cabbage was formerly in much greater esteem than at present, it being now only to be found in particular gentlemen's gardens, who cultivate it for their own use. This must be sown late in the spring of the year, and managed as those before directed, with this difference only, that these must be sooner planted out, and must have an open clear spot of ground, and require much less distance every way, for it is but a very small hard cabbage. This sort will not continue long before they will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> and run up to seed. The early and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> loaf cabbages are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> sown for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> use, and are what the gardeners about London commonly call Michaelmas cabbages. The season for sowing of these is about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, or beginning of August, in an open spot of ground; and when the plants have got eight leaves, you must prick them into beds at about three or four inches distance every way, that the plants may grow strong and short shanked; and toward the end of October you should plant them out: the distance that these require is, three feet row from row, and two feet and a half asunder in the rows. The ground must be kept clean from weeds, and the earth drawn up about your cabbage plants. In May, if your plants were of the early kind, they will turn in their leaves for cabbaging; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the gardeners near London, in order to obtain them a little sooner, tie in their leaves close with a slender osier-twig to blanch their middle; by which means, they have them at least a fortnight sooner than they could have if they were left untied. The early cabbage being the first, we should choose to plant the fewer of them, and a greater quantity of the sugar-loaf kind, which comes after them: for the early kind will not supply the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> long, generally cabbaging apace when they begin, and as soon grow hard and burst open; but the sugar-loaf kind is longer before it comes, and is as slow in its cabbaging; and being of a hollow kind, will continue for a good long time. The sugar-loaf kind may be planted out in February, and will succeed as well as if planted earlier; with this difference only, that they will be later before they cabbage. You should also reserve some plants of the early kind in some well sheltered spot of ground, to supply your plantation, in case of a defect; for in mild winters many of the plants are apt to run to seed, especially when their seeds are sown too early, and in severe winters they are often destroyed. The Savoy cabbages are propagated for winter use, as being generally esteemed the better when pinched by the frost: these must be sown about the end of April, and treated after the manner as was directed for the common white cabbage: with this difference, that these may be planted at a closer distance than those; two feet and a half square will be sufficient. These are always much better when planted in an open situation, which is clear from trees and hedges; for in close places they are very subject to be eaten almost up by caterpillars and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, especially if the autumn prove dry. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROCCOLI">broccoli</a> may also be treated in the same manner, but need not be planted above one foot asunder in the rows, and the rows two feet distant; these are ne- ver eaten till the frost hath rendered them tender; for otherwise they are tough and bitter. The seeds of the broccoli (of which there are several kinds, viz. the Roman or purple, the Neapolitan or white, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> broccoli, with some others, but the Roman is preferred to them all), should be sown about the latter end of May, or beginning of June, and when the plants are grown to have eight leaves, transplant them into beds (as was directed for the common cabbage); and towards the latter end of July they will be fit to plant out, which should be done into some well-sheltered spot of ground, but not under the drip of trees: the distance these require is about a foot and a half in the rows, and two feet row from row. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> in which they should be planted ought to be rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than heavy: if your plants succeed well (as there will be little reason to doubt, unless the winter prove extremely hard), they will begin to show their small heads, which are somewhat like a cauliflower, but of a purple <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, about the end of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, and will continue eatable till the middle of April. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or black broccoli is by many persons greatly esteemed, though it doth not deserve a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the kitchen garden where the Roman broccoli can be obtained, which is much sweeter, and will continue longer in season: indeed, the brown sort is much hardier, so that it will thrive in the coldest situations, where the Roman broccoli is sometimes destroyed in very hard winters. The brown sort should be sown in the middle of May, and managed as hath been directed for the common cabbage, and should be planted at the same distance, which is about two feet and a half asunder. This will grow very tall, so should have the earth drawn up to their stems as they advance in height. This doth not form heads so perfect as the Roman broccoli; the stems and hearts of the plants are the parts which are eaten. The Roman broccoli (if well managed) will have large heads, which appear in the centre of the plants like clusters of buds. These heads should be cut before they run up to seed, with about four or five inches of the stem; the skin of the stems should be stripped off before they are boiled. After the first heads are cut off, there will be a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of side-shoots produced from the stems, which will have small heads to them, but are full as well flavoured as the large. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> broccoli hath white heads very like those of the cauliflower, and eats so like it as not to be distinguished from it.—Besides this first crop of broccoli (which is usually sown in the end of May), it will be proper to sow another crop the beginning of July, which will come in to supply the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and the beginning of April; and being very young, will be extremely tender and sweet. In order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> good seeds of this kind of broccoli, you should reserve a few of the largest heads of the first crop, which should be let remain to run up to seed, and all the undershoots should be constantly stripped off, leaving only the main stem to flower and seed. If this be duly observed, and no other sort of cabbage permitted to seed near them, the seeds will be as good as those procured from abroad, and the sort may be preserved in perfection many years. The turnip-rooted cabbage was formerly more cultivated in Britain than at present; for since other sorts have been introduced which are much better flavoured, this sort has been neglected. There are some persons who esteem this kind for soups, but it is too strong for most palates; and is seldom good but in hard winters, which will render it tender and less strong. At the end of June the plants should be transplanted out where they are to remain, allowing them two feet distance every way, observing to water them until they have taken root; and as their stems advance, the earth should be drawn up to them with a hoe, which will preserve a moisture about their roots, and prevent their stems from drying and growing woody, so that the plants will grow more freely; but it should not be drawn very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, for as it is the globular part of the stalk which is eaten, so that should not be covered. In winter they will be fit for use, when they should be cut off, and the stalks pulled out of the ground and thrown away, being good for nothing after the stems are cut off. As food for cattle, however, the cultivation of this species deserves particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. The curled colewort or Siberian broccoli is now more generally esteemed than the former, being extremely hardy, so is never injured by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but is always sweeter in severe winters than in mild seasons. This may be propagated by sowing of the seeds the beginning of July; and when the plants are strong enough for transplanting, they should be planted in rows about a foot and a half asunder, and ten inches distance in the rows. These will be fit for use after Christmas, and continue good until April, so that they are very useful in a family. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a> cabbage. This may be propagated in the same manner as the common cabbage, and should be allowed the same distance: it will be fit for use in October, November, and December; but, if the winter proves hard, these will be destroyed much sooner than the common sort. The common colewort, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a> kale, is now almost lost near London, where their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are usually supplied with cabbage plants instead of them. The best method to cultivate this plant in the fields is, to sow the seeds about the beginning of July, choosing a moist season, which will bring up the plants in about ten days or a fortnight; the quantity of seed for an acre of land is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> pounds: when the plants have got five or six leaves they should be hoed, as is practised for turnips, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> down all the weeds from amongst the plants, and also thinning the plants where they are too thick; but they should be kept thicker than turnips, because they are more in danger of being destroyed by the fly: this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> should be performed in dry weather, that the weeds may be killed. About six weeks after, the plants should have a second hoeing, which, if carefully performed in dry weather, will entirely destroy the weeds, and make the ground clean, so that they will require no farther culture: in the spring they may be either drawn up and carried out to feed the cattle, or they may be turned in to feed upon them as they stand; but the former method is to be preferred, because there will be little waste; whereas, when the cattle are turned in amongst the plants, they will <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a> down and destroy more than they eat, especially if they are not fenced off by hurdles. The two last sorts of cabbages are varieties fit for a botanic garden, but are plants of no use. They are annual Brassica annual plants, and perish when they have perfected their seeds. The best method to save the seeds of all the sorts of cabbages is, about the end of November you should make choice of some of your best cabbages, which you should pull up, and carry to some shed or other covered place, where you should hang them up for three or four days by their stalks, that the water may drain from between their leaves; then plant them in some border near a hedge or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, quite down to the middle of the cabbage, leaving only the upper part of the cabbage above ground, observing to raise the earth about it, so that it may stand a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ground; especially if the ground is wet, they will require to be raised pretty much above the surface. If the winter should prove very hard, you must lay a little straw or pease haulm lightly upon them, to secure them from the frost, taking it off as often as the weather proves mild, lest by keeping them too close they should rot. In the spring of the year these cabbages will shoot out strongly, and divide into a great number of small branches: you must therefore support their stems, to prevent their being broken off by the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and if the weather should be very hot and dry when they are in flower, you should refresh them with water once a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> all over the branches, which will greatly promote their seeding, and preserve them from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILDEW">mildew</a>. When the pods begin to change brown, you will do well to cut off the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> parts of every shoot with the pods, which will strengthen your seeds; for it is generally observed, that those seeds which grow near the top of the shoots, are very subject to run to seed before they cabbage; so that by this there will be no loss, but a great advantage. When your seed begins to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a>, you must be particularly careful that the birds do not destroy it, for they are very fond of these seeds. The best method to prevent this, is to get a quantity of birdlime, and daub over a parcel of slender twigs, which should be fastened at each end to stronger sticks, and placed near the upper part of the seed in different places, so that the birds may alight upon them, by which means they will be fastened thereto; where you must let them remain, if they cannot get off themselves: and although there should not be above two or three birds caught, yet it will sufficiently terrify the rest, that they will not come to that place again for a considerable time after. When your seed is fully ripe, you must cut it off; and after drying, thrash it out, and preserve it in bags for use. But in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> of cabbages for seed, it will be proper never to plant more than one sort in a place, or near one another: for example, never plant red and white cabbages near each other, nor Savoy with white or red cabbages; for they will, by the commixture of their effluvia, produce a mixture of kinds: and it is said to be owing to this neglect, that the gardeners rarely save any good red cabbage seed in Britain, but are obliged to procure fresh seeds from abroad; as supposing the soil or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Britain alters them from red to white, and of a mixed kind betwixt both; whereas, if they should plant red cabbages by themselves for seed, and not suffer any other to be near them, they might continue the kind as good in Britain as in any other part of the world. Cauliflowers have of late years been so far improved in Britain, as to exceed in goodness and magnitude what are produced in most parts of Europe, and by the skill of the gardener are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for several months together; but the most common season for the great crops is in May, June, and July. Having procured a parcel of good seeds, you must sow it about the 21st of August, upon an old cucumber or melon <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, sifting a little earth over the seeds, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an inch thick; and if the weather should prove extremely hot and dry, you should <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> the beds with mats, to prevent the earth from drying too fast, and give it gentle waterings as you may see occasion. In about a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>'s time after sowing, your plants will be fit to prick out: you should therefore put some fresh earth upon your cucumber or melon beds; or where these are not to be had, some beds should be made with a little new dung, which should be trodden down close, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> from getting through it; but it should not be hot dung, which would be hurtful to the plants at this season, especially if it proves hot; into this bed you should prick your young plants at about two inches square, observing to shade and water them at first planting; but do not water them too much after they are growing, nor suffer them to receive too much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> if the season should prove wet, which would be apt to make them black shanked, as the gardeners <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> it, which is no less than a rottenness in their stems, and is the destruction of the plants so affected. In this bed they should continue till about the 30th of October, when they must be removed into the place where they are to remain during the winter season; which, for the first sowing, is commonly under <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> glasses, to have early cauliflowers, and these should be of an early kind: but in order to have a succession during the season, you should be provided with another more late kind, which should be sown four or five days after the other, and managed as was directed for them. In order to have very early cauliflowers, you should make choice of a good rich spot of ground that is well defended from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, east, and west winds, with hedges, pales, or walls; but the first are to be preferred, if made with reeds, because the winds will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> dead in these, and not reverberate as by pales or walls. This ground should be well trenched, burying therein a good quantity of rotten dung; then level your ground, and if it be naturally a wet soil, you should raise it up in beds about two feet and a half, or three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and four inches above the level of the ground; but if your ground is moderately dry, you need not raise it at all: then plant your plants, allowing about two feet six inches distance from glass to glass in the rows, always putting two good plants under each glass, which may be at about four inches from each other; and if you <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> them for a full crop, they may be three feet and a half row from row: but if you intend to make ridges for cucumbers between the rows of cauliflower plants (as is generally practised by the gardeners near London), you must then make your rows about eight feet asunder; and the ground between the rows of cauliflowers may be planted with cabbage plants, to be drawn off for coleworts in the spring. When you have planted your plants, if the ground is very dry, you should give them a little water, and then set your glasses over them, which may remain quite close down over them till Brassica, till they have taken root, which will be in about a week or ten days time, unless there should be a kindly shower of rain; in which case, you may set off the glasses, that the plants may receive the benefit of it; and in about ten days after planting, you should be provided with a parcel of forked sticks or bricks, with which you should raise your glasses about three or four inches on the side toward the south, that your plants may have free <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; in this manner your glasses should remain over the plants night and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, unless in frosty weather, when you should set them down as close as possible; or if the weather should prove very warm, which many times happens in November, and sometimes in December, in this case you should keep your glasses off in the day-time, and put them on only in the night, lest, by keeping the glasses over them too much, you should draw them into flower at that season; which is many times the case in mild winters, especially if unskillfully managed. Toward the latter end of February, if the weather proves mild, you should prepare another good spot of ground to remove some of the plants into, from under the glasses, which should be well dugged and trenched (as before): then set off your glasses; and, after making choice of one of the most promising plants under each glass, which should remain, take away the other plant, by raising it up with a trowel, &c. so as to preserve as much earth to the root as possible; but take care not to disturb or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> the roots of the plants which remain. Then plant the plants which you have taken out at the distance before directed, viz. if for a full crop, three feet and a half, row from row; but if for ridges of cucumbers between them, eight feet, and two feet four inches distance in the rows: then, with a small hoe, draw the earth up to the stems of the plants which were left under the glasses, taking great care not to let the earth fall into their hearts; and set your glasses over them again, raising your props an inch or two higher than before, to give them more air, observing to take them off whenever there may be some gentle showers, which will greatly refresh the plants. In a little time after, if you find your plants grow so fast as to fill the glasses with their leaves, you should then slightly dig about the plants, and raise the ground about them in a bed broad enough for the glasses to stand, about four inches high, which will give your plants a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of room, by raising the glasses so much higher when they are set over them; and by this means they might be kept covered until April, which otherwise they could not, without prejudice to the leaves of the plants; and this is a great advantage to them, for many times we have returns of severe frosts at the latter end of March, which prove very hurtful to these plants, if exposed thereto, especially after having been nursed up under glasses. After you have finished your beds, you may set your glasses over your plants again, observing to raise your props pretty high, especially if the weather be mild, that they may have free air to strengthen them; and in mild soft weather set off your glasses, as also in gentle showers of rain; and now you must begin to harden them by degrees to endure the open air; however, it is advisable to let your glasses remain over them as long as possible, if the nights should be frosty, which will greatly forward your plants; but you must not let your glasses remain upon them in very hot sunshine, especially if their leaves press against the sides of the glasses; for it hath often been observed in such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, that the moisture which hath risen from the ground, together with the perspiration of the plants, which by the glasses remaining over them hath been detained upon the leaves of the plants, when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> hath shone hot upon the sides of the glasses, have acquired such a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> from the beams thereof, as to scald all their larger leaves, to the no small prejudice of the plants: nay, sometimes large quantities of plants have been so affected therewith, as never to be worth any thing after.
