The family of Panmure have now a noble house on the site of the old castle.—Brechin is also remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought near it, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the rebellion raised in 1452, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the earl of Douglas in Stirling castle. The victory fell to the royalists under the earl of Huntly. The malecontents were headed by the earl of Crawford, who, retiring to his castle of Finhaven, in the frenzy of disgrace declared, that he would willingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, to obtain the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> that fell to the share of his antagonist.

BRECKNOCK

Pages 472-472
or Brecon, a town of Brecknockshire in Wales, and capital of the county. It is called by the Welsh Aber Hondey, and is seated at the confluence of the rivers Hondey and Usk, over which there Brecknock is a handsome stone bridge. It is an ancient place, containing three churches, one of which is collegiate, and is seated at the west end of the town. The houses are well built. Here was formerly a stately castle, and a strong wall, through which there were three gates, that are all demolished. It sends one member to parliament. It is well inhabited, which is in some measure owing to its being the town where the assizes are kept; and there is here a considerable woollen manufactory. The markets are well supplied with cattle, corn, and provisions. W. Long, 3. 15. N. Lat. 52. 0.

BRECKNOCKSHIRE

Pages 472-472

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; Cardiganshire and Caernarvonthshire, on the west; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREFORDSHIRE">Herefordshire</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONMOUTHSHIRE">Monmouthshire</a>, on the east; and by Glamorganshire and Monmouthshire, on the south. It is 35 miles in length, 30 in breadth, about 100 in circumference, and contained 37,735 inhabitants in 1811. It is surrounded with hills, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> in the valleys pretty temperate. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> on the hills is very stony, but the streams descending from thence into the valleys render them fruitful both in corn and grass. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities here are corn, cattle, fish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a>'s fur, besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of cloth and stockings. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-USK">Usk</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, and the Yron. The chief <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Brecknock, Bealt, and Hay. Two miles to the east of Brecknock is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, called Brecknock Meer, and by the Welsh Llyn Savaddan; it is two miles in length, and nearly the same in breadth, and contains otters, tench, &c. The county sends one member to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Landaff, and contains 61 parishes, and is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. See Breconshire, Supplement.

BREDA

Pages 472-474

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Dutch Brabant. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, well-built <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, regularly fortified after the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> way, and is one of the strongest places on the Dutch frontiers. It is seated on the river Merck, in a marshy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which may be overflowed and rendered inaccessible to an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is 4000 paces in circumference, and contains upwards of 11,000 inhabitants. The town is of a triangular <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and the ramparts are all planted round with elms. At every <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> there is a gate built with brick. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a noble structure, remarkable for its fine spire, which is 362 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a> of Angelbert II., <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, is a curious piece, adorned with several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> suitable to the occasion. In 1577, the garrison delivered this city to the states-general; but it was taken in 1581 by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> de Barlaimont, assisted by the baron de Fresin, who was prisoner therein. In 1590, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Maurice took it again from the Spaniards. In 1625 it was invested by Spinola; when it endured a siege too remarkable not to deserve a particular detail. The citadel, which formed the residence of the princes of that family, was surrounded by a ditch of prodigious depth filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and a strong wall defended by three great bastions; and the arsenal was celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and the vast quantities of arms and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> stores it contained. Spinola, perfectly acquainted with the strength of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, thought he should expose his whole army to immediate destruction, should he attempt an assault before he had regularly carried Breda carried on his approaches. He even resolved upon reducing the city by famine, as the method attended with least danger to his army; and accordingly began with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> trenches round, for the space of four miles, erecting forts and redoubts at certain distances. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the garrison, consisting of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> thousand infantry, and several troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, composed of English, French, and Dutch <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, took the most vigorous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. The English were under the command of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Morgan, who had frequently distinguished his valour in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the States: the French were directed by Colonel de Hauterive; and the Dutch troops were subject to the immediate orders of Colonel Lohre, though the whole received their instructions from Justin de Nassau, the governor. The first advantage was gained by Baglioni, who seized a large convoy of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and stores coming up the river, converting the boats into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>. This loss dispirited the besieged, and reduced them to a stated allowance of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; and what added to their misfortunes, though they were ignorant of it, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Maurice, from whom they were in hopes of receiving relief. Meanwhile Spinola prosecuted the siege with the utmost diligence and vigour. On his pushing his trenches near the bastions, the besieged began a terrible fire to retard his approaches, and kept it up with such vehemence and obstinacy, that Spinola was in hopes they must soon surrender for want of ammunition. But here he formed a false judgment of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of Justin de Nassau, who finding he could not accomplish his purpose by his firing, resolved to try the effect of water. With this view, he stopped up the course of the river Marek; and having formed a large basin of water, opened the sluices, swept away men, horses, and houses, in an inundation, and overflowed the whole country. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> force of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> fell upon Spinola's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and he exerted his utmost ability to remove the consequences. He dug large pits, and cut out ditches and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> to receive the water; but these being filled, and the whole ground covered over, so as to appear one uniform <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of water, served only to entrap his cavalry. The inundation was augmented by the rains which happened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; a mortality among the soldiers and horses ensued; and of his whole army, Spinola had scarce twelve thousand men fit for service by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>. With these inconsiderable remains, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of vast extent were to be defended, the works were to be advanced, the sallies from the garrison repulsed, and provisions to be conveyed into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, while Spinola, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, was confined to a sick-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. In the garrison, an epidemical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and scarcity likewise prevailed; but the excellent regulations made, and strictly observed, enabled the town to hold out three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four months beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> expected. The magistrates bought the corn for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>; obliging them to sell the bread to the inhabitants and garrison at a fixed price, and returning the overplus of their pay to the soldiers. A variety of other prudent regulations were established by the magistrates and governor, such as we do not find equalled by any instances recorded in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> upon a similar occasion, and all evincing the steadiness, sagacity, courage, and ability of Justin de Nassau. A kind of rivalry appeared between him and Spinola, which should best fulfil their several duties. The Spanish general caused himself to be carried about the works in a litter; he inspected and directed every thing; and displayed the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> at the time his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> was in imminent danger from an acute malady. He ordered several breaches in the lines to be repaired. These the Hollanders had made by sap, with a view of introducing succours to the besieged. He drove piles into all the ditches and canals through which their boats could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. He made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> to clear off the waters of the river Marek; and succeeded in a great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by dint of perseverance, vigilance, and conduct. He was now reinforced with a body of eight thousand foot, and one thousand five hundred horse; many of the sick were perfectly recovered by his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> care; and his army was again become formidable, amounting to twenty-five thousand infantry, and eight thousand cavalry. Nor was Prince Henry idle, who now succeeded to the titles and dominions of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Maurice, and was elected governor of Holland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, Guelderland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, and Overyssel. He pressed France for assistance, and was joined by a body of cavalry under the conduct of the count de Roossi and the marquis de Rambures. With this reinforcement, and a body of German infantry, he attacked the enemy's lines, and after an obstinate conflict was repulsed. He advanced a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time; but Spinola, who entertained a high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his valour and conduct, did not choose to wait for him in his lines; he marched out with the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his army, seized upon a convenient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, and obliged the prince a second time to retire towards Boisleduc. Henry, finding no prospect of being able to relieve the garrison, sent a permission to the governor to surrender on the best conditions he could obtain. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, which was signed with no name, fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the besiegers, and Spinola sent it open, by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, to Justin de Nassau, offering him an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>; but that intrepid governor, suspecting the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> was forged, because it was anonymous, replied civilly, that a permission was not an order to surrender; and that he should better follow the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>'s intentions, and show his respect for Spinola, by continuing to defend the city to the last extremity. By this time the garrison was diminished by disease, fatigue, want, and hardship, to half the original <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; but Justin put on such a countenance, as concealed his situation from Spinola. He frequently saluted out upon Baglioni's quarters, where the Italians were perishing with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, the whole subsistence of the besiegers depending on the contributions raised in the neighbouring territories. This inconvenience produced a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> in the camp, that could not be appeased without applying violent remedies, and executing within sight of the whole army the chief <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a>-leaders. One of the mutineers blew up Spinola's chief <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>, valued at two hundred thousand livres. Urged more by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> than compassion for the besieged, Spinola sent a message to the governor, exhorting him not to force him to extremities, which might be attended with fatal <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to a brave garrison; but Justin, with equal art and dissimulation, answered, that Spinola was certainly ill served by his spies. spies, as he appeared wholly unacquainted with the state of affairs in Breda, which was fully provided for a siege of several months, and defended by soldiers who preferred death to the necessity of surrendering. At that time the besieged were not informed of the death of the prince of Orange. They flattered themselves with the hopes of speedy succour, and were entirely ignorant of Prince Henry's late disappointment. When they wrote to the army an account of their miserable condition, Henry returned an answer, written with his own hand, and signed with his name, apprising them of the death of Maurice, the unsuccessful attempts made to raise the siege and throw in succours, the great inferiority of his troops in point of numbers, and the death of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James, whereby he was disappointed of a strong reinforcement; concluding, that he left the city entirely to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the governor and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers. Justin was thunderstruck with the contents of this letter. He had hitherto concealed the total want of provision and ammunition from the enemy, and his own garrison, except a few officers and other persons in whom he reposed confidence. The colonels Hautevive and Morgan would listen to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>, saying, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of their several countries was concerned, and that they were responsible for the conduct of the English and French forces. They therefore required an express order from the prince of Orange to surrender, notwithstanding they pined under the united pressure of fatigue, scarcity, and disease. Justin acquainted the prince with their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, and he sent back an order to surrender, threatening with capital <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> whoever should disobey; but he requested that the garrison would first acquaint him by a certain number of fires, lighted up in different parts of the city, how many days they should be able to hold out. Upon receipt of this order, eleven fires were kindled; but as the prince had sent a duplicate of the order by another messenger, and this fell into the hands of the enemy, Spinola was now acquainted with the desperate circumstances of the besieged. By this acquisition, he likewise discovered the mystery of the eleven fires: a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> was assembled to deliberate whether they should stay the eleven days, and then oblige the garrison to surrender at discretion, or immediately offer conditions worthy of so brave a garrison. The Spanish officers were of the former opinion; the count de <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERG">Berg</a> and Spinola supported the latter. At last the marquis, determined to pursue the dictates of his noble generosity, sent such terms as could not be refused. The count de Berg conducted the negociation. Two separate capitulations were drawn up, one for the garrison and the other for the city, and both the most honourable and advantageous that could be devised. They were accepted, and the garrison marched out on the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, after having sustained a siege for ten months, whereby they were diminished two thirds; nor was the loss inferior on the part of the inhabitants. Spinola drew up his army to salute them, and, surrounded by his field officers, paid particular compliments to the governor, the colonels Morgan, Hanterive, and Lohre. He distributed <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> among the soldiers, ordered the sick and wounded to be treated with the utmost tenderness, conveyed the rest in the manner most commodious for them to Gertruydenburg, and displayed all the sentiments of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a> in the regard paid to the valour and merits of his enemies. Breda was retaken by the prince of Orange, for the United Provinces, in 1637. There was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> held there, and peace concluded, in 1667, between the Dutch and the English. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. 45. N. Lat. 51. 35. Breda, John Van, painter of history, landscape, and conversations, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1683, the son of Alexander Van Breda, an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> who was much esteemed for landscapes, views of particular scenes in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>, with a variety of animals and figures. He was instructed by his father; and having the advantage of a good example and a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, added to his own great application, he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his studies with his father till he was 18 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Among the variety of capital paintings which were at that time in the possession of John de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">Wit</a> at Antwerp, Breda fixed upon those of Velvet Breughel, which he copied with extraordinary success; and he was also employed for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years in copying the pictures of several other great masters; which he performed with such incredible exactness as scarcely to leave it in the power of any judicious person to distinguish the originals from the copies. Having at length established his reputation in Holland, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> with Rysbrack the sculptor, and there gradually rose into such esteem, that he was visited by persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, and particularly patronized by the unfortunate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Derwentwater, who was beheaded for rebellion in 1715. He found so much encouragement in London, that he was employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and could scarce execute the large demands for his performances. After a residence of some years in England, he returned to Antwerp loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, the honourable testimonies of English liberality, as well as of his own merit; and in the year 1746, when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. arrived in that city, he so far honoured this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> as to purchase four of his pictures: One represented Christ at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Tiberias; another, Christ performing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>; and the other two were landscapes, with a number of figures, so exquisitely drawn and finished that it would be difficult to distinguish them from those of Velvet Breughel. He certainly approached nearer to those great masters, whose manner he imitated, namely, Breughel and Wouvermans, than any other artist of this time. His landscapes are in the style and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the former; and his conversations, historical figures, fairs, skirmishes, or battles, are in the manner of the latter. His colouring is good; his touch neat; his skies and distances <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and beautiful; and his taste of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> agreeable. He had aston's Dic much fire in his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, and perhaps more genius, than Breughel, in those subjects which he painted in the style of that master: his figures are generally well placed; his grounds skilfully broken; every small figure has its particular character, and occupies its proper place; and, in short, he is a painter of such rank, that the value and estimation of his works must always increase. He died in 1750. BREECH of a great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, or cannon, the end next the touch-hole.

BREECHES

Pages 474-475

a garment worn by males, reaching from the girdle to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a>, and serving to cover the hips, thighs, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had nothing in their dress answering to our breeches and stockings; instead of which, under their lower tunics and waistcoats they sometimes bound their thighs and legs round with silken scarves <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fasciae, called tibialia and femoralia. Breeches appear to be a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> peculiar to the barbarous nations, especially those inhabiting the colder countries of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; whence Tacitus calls them barbarum tegmen. We find mention made of them among the ancient Getæ, Sarmate, Gauls, Germans, and Britons; they also obtained among the Medes and Persians, as being a people of Scythian origin; they also afterwards got footing in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, some pretend, as early as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus; but without much foundation, that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s breeches, mentioned by Suetonius, being apparently only swaths tied over his thighs. However, this be, breeches were at last received into Italy, and grew so highly into fashion, that it was thought necessary, under Honorius and Arcadius, to restrain them by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and expel the bracarii or breeches-makers out of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; it being thought unworthy of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> that commanded the world, to wear the apparel of barbarians.

BREECHINGS

Pages 475-475

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> with which the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> guns are lashed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fastened to the ship's side. They are thus called, because made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> round the breech of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>.

BREEDING

Pages 475-475

in a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MORAL_SENSE">moral <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes a person's deportment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaviour in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> offices and decors of social <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. In this sense we say well-bred, ill-bred, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of breeding, &c. Good-breeding is hard to define; none can understand the speculation but those who have the practice. Good-breeding amounts to much the same with what is otherwise called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> urbanity. Good-breeding is near to virtue, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of itself <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a man a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the way towards the same. It teaches him to rejoice in acts of civility, to seek out objects of compassion, and to be pleased with every occasion of doing them good offices. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHAFTESBURY">Shaftesbury</a> compares the well-bred man with the real <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> aim at what is excellent, aspire to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and carry in view the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of what is beautiful and becoming. The conduct and manners of the one are formed according to the most perfect ease, and good entertainment of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; of the other, according to the strictest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of mankind: the one according to his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> in his private station; the other according to his rank and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Horace seems to have united both characters, Quid verum atque decens cura et rogo, et omnis in hoc sum. See the article Good-Manners. BREEDING OF HORSES. See Equus. BREEDING OF FISH. The necessary qualities of a pond, to make it serve well for breeding fish, are very different from those which are to make it serve for the feeding of them, insomuch that some particular ponds serve only for one of these purposes, and others for the other; and scarce ever the same pond is found to answer for them both. In general, it is much more rare to find a good breeding pond than a good feeding one. The best indications of a good breeding pond are these; that there be a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of rushes and grass about its sides, with gravelly shoals, such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-ponds usually have: when a pond has this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and takes to the breeding of fish, it is amazing what a progress will be made in a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The spawn of fish is prodigious in quantity; and where it succeeds, one is able to produce many millions; thus, in one of these breeding ponds, two or three melters, and as many spawners, will, in a very little time, stock the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When these ponds are not meant entirely for breeding, but the owner would have the fish to grow to some size in them, the method is to thin the numbers, because they would otherwise starve one another, and to put in other fish that will prey upon the young, and thin them in the quickest manner. Eels and perch are the most useful on this account; because they prey not only upon the spawn itself, but upon the young fry from the first hatching to the time they are of considerable size. Some fish are observed to breed indifferently in all kinds of waters, and that in considerable plenty; of this nature are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, pike and perch.

BREENBERG

Pages 475-475

BARTHOLOMEW, an excellent painter, was born in 1620. He is best known by the name of Bartolomeo, an appellation bestowed upon him, for distinction sake, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of Flemish painters at Rome called Bentvogels. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>; but in the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> went to Rome. His studies in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> were attended with such success, that his pictures were held in the highest estimation. He greatly excelled in landscapes, and these he enriched with historical subjects. The figures and animals which he introduced were very spirited, and drawn in a masterly manner; especially when they were not larger than the size in which he usually painted them. He died in 1660, aged 40 years. He also etched from his own designs a set of 24 Views and Landscapes, ornamented with Ruins.

BREEZE

Pages 475-475

a shifting <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> that blows from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for some certain hours in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> or night; <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and some parts of the East and West Indies. Breezes differ from etesian or trade-winds, as the former are diurnal, or have their periods each day; and the latter are anniversary, and blow at a distance from land. The sea-breezes rule by day, and the land-breezes by night; so that, dividing their empire, they remain constant as the seasons of the year, or course of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, on which they seem to depend; not but that they appear sooner or later, stronger or weaker, in some places than in others; and vary the alternative according to the several latitudes, situations, and soils, &c. of the countries where they are found. See the article Wind. BREEZE-Fly. See Tabanus, Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BREGENTZ

Pages 475-475
or BERGENTZ, a town of Tyrol in Germany, situated at the east end of the lake of Constance, in E. Long. 9° 40' N. Lat. 47° 36'.

BREHAR

Pages 475-476

one of the Scilly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying almost directly west of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>'s End in Cornwall, about the distance of 30 miles. It lies between the isles of Micarol, Guel, Trescaw, and Samson. It is the roughest and most mountainous of them all, and not many years since, since, there were only two families in it, but now there are 13. There are a few <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> houses, called the town of Brehar; and there are several <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROWS">Barrows</a> edged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in which they buried considerable persons in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times; besides many monuments of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>. Some are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that this with the rest made but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is the reason why so many antiquities are now found in most of them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREHONS">Brehons</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> judges among the ancient Irish, by whom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> was administered, and controversies decided. These sages were a distinct tribe <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> family, to whom competent lands were allowed in inheritance. In criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the brehon had the eleventh <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of all the fines; which could not but be considerable at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when murders, rapes, robberies, and the like offences, were only subject to pecuniary commutations. Brehon-Laws, or Leges Brehonicae, denote the general maxims or rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> observed by the brehons, and having the force of laws throughout all the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. Several fragments of the leges brehonicae are still extant in public and private <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. The most complete collection is that belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Chandos; containing 227 sheets <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> written, full of abbreviated words, and not very legible. By the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a>, made under Edward III., it is enacted that no English subject shall submit to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> by the brehon law, on the penalty of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>. Notwithstanding which, many were still under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of being concluded by the Irish laws and customs, till the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> was settled on an English bottom by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. Bremegarton, a handsome and pretty considerable town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, which, since 1798, forms the head town of a district in the new <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Argau. The inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> chiefly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>; and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is the Roman-catholic. It is divided into the upper and lower <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, and is very advantageously seated on the river Russ. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 25'. N. Lat. 47° 20'. Bremen, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and very strong town of Germany, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, with an archbishop's see, secularized in favour of the Swedes, but now belongs to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. The river Weser runs through the middle, and divides it into the old and new town. In September 1739, while the inhabitants were asleep, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> of powder was set on fire by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, and all the houses were shaken, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there had been a violent earthquake, which threw them into a terrible consternation. The town is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, each of which has a burgomaster; and in the middle there is a large market-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with the statue of Rolando. Bremen drives a very large trade for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, with France, England, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>; and in return takes back other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, with which it supplies Westphalia and the countries about Hanover. It also gets a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> deal by its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>. It contains 53,500 houses, and about 40,000 inhabitants. E. Long. 8° 45'. N. Lat. 53° 40'. Bremen, a duchy of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Weser and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>; of which the former separates it from the duchy of Oldenburg, and the other from that of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile, and well peopled. It formerly belonged to the Swedes, but was afterwards sold to the king of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Hanover, in 1716. In the winter it is subject to inundations. In 1617, on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTMAS_DAY">Christmas-<a </a>class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, several thousand cattle were drowned, besides several hundred of men; and the country was so covered with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, that it has cost immense sums to repair the dykes. Bremen is the capital town. Bremens-Voerd, a town of Germany, in the circle of Lower Saxony, and duchy of Bremen. It is an open town, seated on the river Oost, and was formerly the place of residence of the archbishop. E. Long. 8° 35'. N. Lat. 53° 58'. Brennagium, Brennagium, in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, a kind of tribute paid in lieu of bran, or bran itself, which the tenants were obliged to furnish for the support of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s hounds. The word is also written brenage, brenagium, and brennaige, bernagium, brenaticum, and brennaticum. Brennus, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> among the Gauls, who, about 388 years before the Christian era, entered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> with a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; made great conquests there; defeated the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and sacked Rome. The capitol alone was defended; and Camillus coming to its relief, drove the Gauls not only out of Rome, but out of all Italy. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) Rome. Brent, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, with a market on Saturdays, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, on May 13th and October 10th, for horned cattle. It contains 1230 inhabitants, and lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, being 26 miles south-west from the former, and 198 west by south of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. W. Long. 5° 7'. N. Lat. 50° 30'. Brent-Goose, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of goose with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> neck, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> collar round; usually confounded with the barnacle, though in reality a distinct species. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANAS">Anas</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRENTFORD">Brentford</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, on the great London road to the west. It is divided into old and new Brentford, in which last are the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and market-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> elections are held. It is a long place, well stocked with public houses, and is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a>, 1733. W. Long. 0° 10'. N. Lat. 51° 26'. Brentwood or Burntwood, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a> in England. It stands on a rising ground in the road from London to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a>, and contained 1233 inhabitants in 1811. E. Long. 0° 25'. N. Lat. 51° 38'. Brerewood, Edward, a very learned English mathematician and antiquary, was the son of Robert Brerewood, a tradesman, who was thrice mayor of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>; and born in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the year 1565. He was educated in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> learning at the free school in Chester; and afterwards admitted, in 1581, of Brazen-nose <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In the year 1596, he became the first professor of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> in Gresham-college in London; where he led the same private and retired course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> that he had before done in Oxford. He died there of a fever, upon the 4th of November 1613, much lamented. He was a great searcher into antiquity and curious knowledge; but is remarkable for having never published any thing during his lifetime. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> came out the following works. 1. De ponderibus et pretiis veterum nummorum. 2. Inquiries touching the diversities of languages and religion through the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of the world. 3. Elementa logicæ in grammaticam.

BRESCELLO

Pages 477-477

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>, seated on the river Po, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 25'. N. Lat. 44° 55'.

BRESCHIA

Pages 476-477

a strong and handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with a bishop's see and good citadel. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Bresciano, contains 48,000 inhabitants, and is seated in an agreeable plain on the river Garza, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 5'. N. Lat. 45° 31'.

BRESCIANO

Pages 477-477

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the territories of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRISONS">Grisons</a> and the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>; on the east, by the lake <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GARDA">Garda</a>, the Veronese, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>; on the south, by the duchy of Mantua and the Cremonese; and on the west by the Cremasco, the Bergamasco, and the Valletina. It is watered by several small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which renders it very fertile; and is full of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, of which Brescia is the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>.

BRESCICATE

Pages 477-477

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a kind of baize, in which there is some trade carried on with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a>, between the river <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a> and Sierra Leona. The best sorts for that purpose are the blue and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>.

BRESLAU

Pages 477-477

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of that name, and of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> and Ohlau, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 17° 5'. N. Lat. 51° 4'. It contained 3096 houses in 1794, and has many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> regular squares, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, stately public and private edifices; but the fortifications are of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance. Here are in particular a great many churches and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> belonging to the Catholics; of the former are several also belonging to the Lutherans, one to the Calvinists, and another to the Greeks. The Jews have likewise two synagogues, the bishop a stately <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and the Lutherans two gymnasiaums. The Popish university is a noble structure, nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> desti- tute of magnificence. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is the seat of all the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> colleges; and the third in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, next to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> and Konigsberg, in all the Prussian dominions. The magistracy of it is Lutheran, and its trade and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are very considerable. Several of the monasteries and nunneries are very magnificent; and there are also some good public <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> in it, with two armou- ries, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians, and a mint. Breslau is very populous, and much frequented by Hungarian, Bohemian, Polish, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, having several yearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The city was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1741, and retaken by the Austrians in 1757; but the king of Prussia took it back again in the same year. The suburbs were destroyed when it was taken by the confederates of the French in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1807.

BRESSE

Pages 477-477

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and the Franche Comté; on the east, by Savoy; on the south, by Viennois; on the west, by the principality of Dombes and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOMME">Somme</a>. It is 40 miles from north to south, and 23 from east to west. It is fertile in corn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, has fine pastures, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> with plenty of fish. It is divided into the higher and lower; the first is on the side of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOURGES">Bourges</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> towards St Trivier and the river Sonne. The French got possession of it in 1601. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places are Bourg en Bresse, Montluel, Pont de Vaux, and Coligny.

BREST

Pages 477-477
or Breast, in Architecture, a term sometimes used for the member of a column, more usually called torus. See TORUS. BREST Summers, in timber buildings, are pieces in the outward side thereof, into which the girders are framed: this, in the ground-floor, is called a cell; and, in the garret-floor, a beam.—As to their size, it is the same with that of girders. See GIRDER.

BRESTE

Pages 477-478

the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of, is one of the provinces of Cujava, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>. It lies between the palatinates of Ploesko, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVA">Rava</a>, and Lencici Wiadislaw. It is divid- Breste, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bressici, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the palatinate of Bressici, and of Polesia in Poland, seated on the river Bog, 80 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARSAW">Warsaw</a>, and subject to Poland. It is a fortified town, and has a castle built upon a rock. Here is a famous synagogue, resorted to by the Jews from all the countries in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 24° 0' N. Lat. 41° 35'.

BRET

Pages 478-478

a name the people on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a> give to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> turbot, a fish extremely plentiful with them, and taken in vast abundance. The way of catching them is in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> trailed on the ground by two horses; the one going up to the middle of his body in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the other on shore.

BRETESSE

Pages 478-480

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes a line embattled on both sides. BRETHREN and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">SISTERS</a> OF THE FREE SPIRIT, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an appellation assumed by a new <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a> which sprung up towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the thirteenth century, and gained many adherents in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, France, and Germany. They took their denomination from the words of St Paul, Rom. chap. viii. ver. 2, 14.; and maintained, that the true children of God were invested with the privilege of a full and perfect freedom from the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. They were enthusiasts to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of distraction, both in their principles and practice. They resembled the Beghards, by which name they were sometimes called, in their aspect, apparel, and manner of living. Some of their professed principles resembled those of the Pantheists; for they held, that all things flowed by emanation from God; that rational souls were portions of the Deity, and that the universe was God; and that, by the power of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>, they were united to the Deity, and acquired hereby a glorious and sublime <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, both from the sinful lusts and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> instincts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: and hence they concluded, that the person, who was thus absorbed in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> of the Deity, became a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Godhead, and was the son of God, in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and manner that Christ was, and that he was freed from the obligation of all laws <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> and divine. They treated with contempt all Christian ordinances, and all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> acts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, as unsuitable to the state of perfection at which they were arrived. Some of them were honest but deluded enthusiasts; and they endured the torments inflicted upon them by the inquisitors with astonishing calmness and triumph. Others proceeded to the most extravagant licentiousness of conduct. They held their secret assemblies stark naked, and lay in the same beds with their spiritual sisters, and indiscriminately with other women, without the least scruple <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hesitation: <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and decency being, according to their creed, marks of inward corruption. And some of them proceeded still farther, and maintained, that the divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or believer, could not sin, let his conduct be ever so horrible or atrocious. Many edicts were published against them; but notwithstanding the severities they suffered, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till about the middle of the fifteenth century. They were called by several other names, such as Schwestrones, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICARDS">Picards</a>, Adamites, and Turlupins. BRETHREN and Clerks of the Common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>, a denomination assumed by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> fraternity towards the latter end of the fifteenth century. They lived under the rule of St Augustin, and were eminently useful in promoting the cause of religion and learning. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> was first formed in the preceding century, by Gerard de Groote, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVENTER">Deventer</a>; but did not flourish till about the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> above mentioned, when it obtained the approbation of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, and became very respectable in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, the Lower Germany, and the adjacent provinces. It was divided into two classes; the lettered brethren or clerks, and the illiterate: they lived in separate habitations, but maintained the closest fraternal union. The former applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of polite literature, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of youth; whilst the latter were employed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a> labour, and the mechanic arts. They were frequently called Beghards and Lollards, by way of reproach. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Brethren, fratres albati, were the followers of a leader, about the beginning of the fifteenth century, who was arrayed in a white garment; and as they were also clothed in white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, they were distinguished by this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Their leader was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, who carried about a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, like a standard, and whose apparent sanctity and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> drew together a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of followers. This deluded enthusiast practised many acts of mortification and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, endeavoured to persuade the European nations to renew the holy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and pretended that he was favoured with divine visions. Boniface IX. ordered him to be apprehended and committed to the flames, upon which his followers dispersed. Breton, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> near the eastern continent of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, lying between 45 and 47 degrees of north latitude. It is separated from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a> by a narrow strait called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANSO">Canso</a>, and is about 100 miles in length, and 50 in breadth. It is surrounded with little sharp-pointed rocks, separated from each other by the waves, above which some of their tops are visible. All its harbours are open to the east, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> towards the south. On the other parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> there are but a few anchoring places for small vessels, in creeks, or between islets. Except in the hilly parts, the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> has but little solidity, being everywhere covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> moss, and with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The dampness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is exhaled in fogs, without rendering the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> unwholesome. In other respects, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is very <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; owing either to the prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which cover above half the island, and remain frozen a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; or to the number of forests, that totally intercept the rays of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; the effect of which is besides decreased by perpetual <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. Though some fishermen had long resorted to this island every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, not more than 20 or 30 had ever fixed there. The French, who took possession of it in August 1713, were properly the first inhabitants. They changed its name into that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> Royale, and fixed upon Fort Dauphin for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlement. This harbour was two leagues in circumference. The ships came to the very shore, and were sheltered from winds. Forests affording oak sufficient to fortify and build a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, were near at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; the ground appeared less barren than in other parts, and the fishery was more plentiful. This harbour might have been rendered impregnable at a trifling expense; but the difficulty difficulty of approaching it (a circumstance that had at first made a stronger <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> than the advantages resulting from it) occasioned it to be abandoned, after <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> labour had been bestowed upon the undertaking. They then turned their views to Louisbourg, the access to which was easier; and convenience was thus preferred to security: the fortification of Louisbourg, however, was not begun till 1720. In the year 1714, some fishermen, who till then had lived in Newfoundland, settled in this island. It was expected that their number would soon have been increased by the Acadians, who were at liberty, from the treaties that had been granted them, to remove with all their effects, and even to dispose of their estates; but these hopes were disappointed. The Acadians chose rather to retain their possessions under the dominion of Britain, than to give them up for any precarious advantage they might derive from their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to France. Their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was supplied by some distressed adventurers from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who came over from time to time to Cape Breton, and the number of inhabitants gradually increased to 4000. They were settled at Louisbourg, Fort Dauphin, Port <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, Nerucka, and on all the coasts where they found a proper beach for drying the cod. The inhabitants never applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, the soil being unfit for it. They often sowed corn, but it seldom came to maturity; and when it did thrive so much as to be worth reaping, it had degenerated so considerably, that it was not fit for seed for the next <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. They have only continued to plant a few pot-herbs that are tolerably well tasted, but must be renewed every year from abroad. The poorness and scarcity of pastures has likewise prevented the increase of cattle. In a word, the soil of Cape Breton seemed calculated to invite none but fishermen and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. Though the island was entirely covered with forests before it was inhabited, its wood has scarce ever been an object of trade. A great quantity, however, of soft wood was found there fit for firing, and some that might be used for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; but the oak has always been scarce, and the fir never yielded much resin. The peltry trade was a very inconsiderable object. It consisted only in the skins of a few lynxes, elks, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>-rats, wild cats, bears, otters, and foxes both of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and silver-gray <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Some of these were procured from a colony of Micmac Indians who had settled on the island with the French, and never could raise more than 60 men able to bear arms. The rest came from St John's, or the neighbouring continent. Greater advantages might possibly have been derived from the coal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> which abound in the island. They <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>: and being no more than six or eight feet below the surface, may be worked without <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a> deep, or draining off the waters. Notwithstanding the prodigious demand for this coal from New England, from the year 1745 to 1749, these mines would probably have been forsaken, had not the ships which were sent out to the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> wanted ballast. In one of these mines a fire has been kindled, which could never yet be extinguished. The people of Cape Breton did not send all their fish to Europe. They sent part of it to the French southern islands, on board 20 or 25 ships from 70 to 140 tons burden. Besides the cod, which made at least half their cargo, they exported to the other colonies timber, planks, thin oak-boards, salted salmon and mackerel, train-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-coal. All these were paid for in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> and coffee, but chiefly in rum and molasses. The island could not consume all these commodities. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> took off but a small part of the overplus; it was chiefly bought by the people of New England, who gave in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, vegetables, wood, brick, and cattle. This trade of exchange was allowed; but a smuggling trade was added to it, carried on in flour and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fish. This island, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a> of Canada, was attacked by the English in 1745; and the event is of so singular a nature, that it deserves a particular detail. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of this first invasion was laid at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOSTON">Boston</a>, and New England bore the expense of it. A merchant named Pepperel, who had excited, encouraged, and directed the enterprise, was entrusted with the command of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 6000 men, which had been levied for this expedition. Though these forces, convoyed by a squadron from Jamaica, brought the first news to Cape Breton of the danger that threatened it; though the advantage of a surprise would have secured the landing without opposition; though they had but 600 regular troops to encounter, and 800 inhabitants hastily armed; the success of the undertaking was still precarious. What great exploits, indeed, could be expected from a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> suddenly assembled, who had never seen a siege or faced an enemy, and were to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> under the direction of sea-officers only. These unexperienced troops stood in need of the assistance of some fortunate incident, which they were indeed favoured with in a singular manner. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and repairs of the fortifications had always been left to the care of the garrison of Louisbourg. The soldiers were eager of being employed in these works, which they considered as conducive to their safety, and as the means of procuring them a comfortable subsistence. When they found that those who were to have paid them, appropriated to themselves the profit of their labours, they demanded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. It was denied them, and they were determined to assert their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. As these depredations had been shared between the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> persons of the colony and the subaltern officers, the soldiers could obtain no redress. Their indignation against these rapacious extortioners rose to such a height, that they despised all authority. They had lived in an open rebellion for six months, when the British appeared before the place. This was the time to conciliate the minds of both parties, and to unite in the common cause. The soldiers made the first advances; but their commanders mistrusted a generosity of which they themselves were incapable. It was firmly believed that the soldiers were only desirous of sallying out, that they might have an opportunity of deserting; and their own officers kept them in a manner prisoners, till a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> so ill managed had reduced them to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of capitulating. The whole island shared the fate of Louisbourg, its only bulwark. This valuable possession, restored to France by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle, was again attacked by the British in 1758. On the 2d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, a fleet of 23 ships of the line and 18 frigates, carrying 16,000 well disciplined troops, anchored in Gabarus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, within half a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>. league of Louisbourg. As it was evident it would be to no purpose to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> at a great distance, because it would be impossible to bring up the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and other necessaries for a considerable siege, it had been attempted to render the landing impracticable near the town. In the prudent precautions that had been taken, the besiegers <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the dangers and difficulties they had to expect; but, far from being deterred by them, they had recourse to stratagem, and while by extending their line they threatened and commanded the whole coast, they landed by force of arms at the creek of Cormorant. This place was naturally weak. The French had fortified it with a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a> planted with cannon. Behind this rampart they had posted 2000 excellent soldiers and some Indians. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> they had made such a close hedge with branches of trees, that would have been very difficult to penetrate, even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had not been defended. This kind of pallisade, which concealed all the preparations for defence, appeared at a distance to be nothing more than a verdant plain. This would have preserved the colony, had the assailants been suffered to complete their landing, and to advance with the confidence that they had but few obstacles to surmount. Had this been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, overpowered at once by the fire of the artillery and the small arms, they would infallibly have perished on the shore or in the hurry of embarking; especially as the sea was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> then very rough. This unexpected loss might have interrupted the whole project. But all the prudent precautions that had been taken were rendered abortive by the impetuosity of the French. The English had scarce begun to move towards the shore, when their enemies hastened to discover the snare they had laid for them. By the brisk and hasty fire that was aimed at their boats, and still more by the premature removal of the boughs that masked the forces, which it was so much the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the French to conceal, they guessed at the danger they were going to rush into. They immediately turned back, and saw no other place to effect their landing but a rock, which had been deemed always inaccessible. General Wolfe, though much taken up in reembarking his troops, and sending off the boats, gave the signal to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Scot to repair thither. That officer immediately removed to the spot with his men. His own <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> coming up first, and sinking at the very instant he was stepping out, he climbed up the rock alone. He was in hopes of meeting with 100 of his men who had been sent thither some hours before. He found only ten. With these few, however, he gained the summit of the rock. Ten Indians and 60 Frenchmen killed two of his men, and mortally wounded three. In spite of his weakness, he stood his ground under cover of a thicket, till his brave countrymen, regardless of the boisterous waves and the fire of the cannon, came up to him, and put him in full possession of that important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>, the only one that could secure their landing. The French, as soon as they saw that the enemy had got a firm footing on land, betook themselves to the only remaining refuge, and shut themselves up in Louisbourg. The fortifications were in a bad condition, because the sea sand, which they had been obliged to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is by no means fit for works of masonry. The revetments of the several curtains were entirely crumbled away. There was only one casemate and a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> that were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. The garrison which was to defend the place consisted only of 2900 men. Notwithstanding all these disadvantages, the besieged were determined to make an obstinate resistance. It is scarce credible that the French were confirmed in their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> by the courage of a woman. Madame de Drucourt was continually upon the ramparts, with her purse in her hand; and firing herself three guns every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, seemed to dispute with the governor her husband the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of his office. The besieged were not dismayed at the ill success of their several sallies, or the masterly operations concerted by <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Boscowen and General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a>. It was but at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of an assault, which it was impossible to sustain, that they talked of surrendering.
