The Greek emperors, sensible of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of having such a port as this in Italy, would have restored it to its ancient strength and splendour, had the Normans allowed them time and leisure. The Greeks struggled manfully to keep their ground; but, after many varieties of success, were finally driven out of Brindisi by William I. The frenzy for expeditions to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, though it drained other kingdoms of their wealth and subjects, contributed powerfully to the re-establishment of this city, one of the ports where pilgrims and warriors took shipping. It was also benefited by the residence of the emperor Frederick, whose frequent armaments for the Holy Land required his presence at this place of rendezvous. The loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the Grecian empire, and the ruin of all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> trade after the Turks had conquered the East, reduced Brindisi to a state of inactivity and desolation, from which it has never been able to emerge." E. Long. 18° 5' N. Lat. 40° 52'.

BRINDLEY

Pages 514-515

James, a most uncommon genius for <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> inventions, and particularly excellent in planning and conducting inland navigations, was born, in 1716, at Tunsted in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>: Through the mismanagement of his father (for there was some little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>) his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was totally neglected; and, at seventeen, he bound himself apprentice to a mill-wright, near Macclesfield, in Cheshire. He served his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>, and, afterwards, setting up for himself, advanced the mill-wright business, by inventions and contrivances of his own, to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection which it had not attained before. His fame, as a most ingenious mechanic, spreading widely, his genius was no longer confined to the business of his profession: for, in 1752, he erected a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-engine at Clifton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, for the purpose of draining coal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; and, in 1755, was employed to execute the larger <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> for a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> mill, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGLETON">Congleton</a>, in Cheshire. The potteries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> were also, about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, indebted to him for several valuable additions in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> used by them for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> flint-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. In 1756, he undertook to erect a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STEAM_ENGINE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>-engine near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a> under Line upon a new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; and it is believed that he would have brought this engine to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree of perfection, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> some interested engineers had not opposed him. His <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, however, was soon afterwards called off to another object, which, in its consequences, hath proved of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> importance to trade and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; namely, the projecting and executing "Inland navigations." By these navigations the expense of carriage is lessened; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> is opened from one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> to another, and from each of these parts to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and hence products and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are afforded at a moderate price. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bridgewater hath, at Worsley, about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estate abounding with coal, which had hitherto lain useless, because the expense of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-carriage was too great to find a market for consumption. The duke, wishing to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> these mines, perceived the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of a canal from Worsley to Manchester; upon which occasion Brindley, now become famous, was consulted; and declaring the scheme practicable, an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> for this purpose was obtained in 1758 and 1759. It being, however, afterwards discovered, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> would be more beneficial, if carried over the river Irwell to Manchester, another act was obtained to vary the course of the canal agreeably to the new plan, and likewise to extend a side-branch to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGFORD">Longford</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> in Stretford. Brindley, in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, had begun these great works, being the first of the kind ever attempted in England, with navigable subterraneous tunnels and elevated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>; and as, in order to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the water, it should be free from the usual obstructions of locks, he carried the canal over <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and many large and deep valleys. When it was completed as far as Barton, where the Irwell is navigable for large vessels, he proposed to carry it over that river, by an aqueduct of thirty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet above the surface of the water; and though this project was treated as wild and chimerical, yet, supported by his noble <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, he began his work in Sept. 1760; and the first <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> sailed over it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1761. The duke afterwards extended his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>; and obtained, in 1762, an act for branching his canal to the tideway in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERSEY">Mersey</a>; this part of the canal is carried over the rivers Mersey and Bolland, and over many wide and deep valleys. The success of the duke of Bridgewater's undertakings encouraged a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gentlemen and manufacturers in Staffordshire, to revive the idea of a canal-navigation through that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and Brindley was, therefore, engaged to make a survey from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a> to the Mersey. In 1766, this canal was begun, and conducted under Brindley's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as he lived; but finished after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> Mr Marshall, of whom he had a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, in May 1777. The proprietors called it, "the canal from the Trent to the Mersey;" but the engineer, more emphatically, "the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">Trunk</a> Navigation," Brindley, on account of the numerous branches, which, as he justly supposed, would be extended every way from it. It is 93 miles in length; and, besides a large number of bridges over it, has 76 locks and five tunnels. The most remarkable of the tunnels is the subterraneous passage of Harecastle, being 2880 yards in length, and more than 70 yards below the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. The scheme of this inland-navigation had employed the thoughts of the ingenious part of the kingdom for upwards of 20 years before; and some surveys had been made: but Harecastle hill, through which the tunnel is constructed, could neither be avoided nor overcome by any expedient the most able engineers could <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVISE">devise</a>. It was Brindley alone who surmounted this and other the like difficulties, arising from the variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> and quicksands, as no one but himself would have attempted to conquer. Brindley was engaged in many other similar undertakings; for a fuller account of which, not being consistent with our plan, we refer the reader to the "Biographia Britannica;" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather to a curious and valuable pamphlet, published some years since, and entitled, "The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inland Navigations, particularly that of the duke of Bridgewater." He died at Turnhurst in Staffordshire, September 27, 1772, in his 56th year; somewhat immaturely, as it should seem; but he is supposed to have shortened his days by too intense application, and to have brought on a hectic fever, which <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on him for some years before it consumed him. For he never indulged and relaxed himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> diversions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, as not having the least relish for them; and though once prevailed on to see a play in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, yet he declared that he would on no account be present at another; because it so disturbed his ideas for several days after, as to render him unfit for business. With any extraordinary difficulty occurred to him in the execution of his works, he generally retired to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>; and has been known to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there one, two, or three days, till he has surmounted it. He would then get up, and execute his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> without any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>: for he had a prodigious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and carried everything in his head. As his station in life was low, and his education totally neglected, so his exterior accomplishments were suitable to them. He could indeed read and write, but both very indifferently; and he was perhaps, in his way, as abnormis sapiens—"of mother-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and wise without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>,"—as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> that ever lived. "He is as plain looking man as one of the boors in the Peake, or one of his own carters: but when he speaks, all ears listen; and every mind is filled with wonder, at the things he pronounces to be practicable." The same author gives us also no ungracious idea of his moral make: "being great in himself, he harbours no contracted notions, no jealousy of rivals: he conceals not his method of proceeding, nor asks patents to secure the sole <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a>, which he invents and exposes to public view. Sensible that he must one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> cease to be, he selects men of genius, teaches them the power of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, and employs them in carrying on the various undertakings in which he is engaged. It is not to the duke of Bridgewater only that his services are confined; he is of public utility, and employs his talents in rectifying the mistakes of despairing workmen, &c. His powers shine most in the midst of difficulties; when rivers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> seem to thwart his designs, then appears his vast capacity, by which he makes them subservient to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>."

BRINE

Pages 515-515
or PICKLE; water replete with saline particles. Brine taken out of brine-pits, or brine-pans, used by some for curing or pickling of fish, without boiling the same into salt, and rock salt, without refining it into white salt, are prohibited by I Ann. cap. 21. Brine is either native, as the sea-water, which by coction turns to salt; or factitious, formed by dissolving salt in water. In the salt-works at Upwick in Worcestershire, there are found, at the same time, and in the same pit, three sorts of brine, each of a different strength. They are drawn by a pump; and that in the bottom, first brought up, is called first man; the next, middle man; and the third, last man. Leach-Brine, a name given to what drops from the corned salt in draining and drying, which they preserve and boil again; being stronger than any brine in the pit. There is sand found in all the Staffordshire brines after coction: but naturalists observe, it did not pre-exist in the water, but rather is the product of the boiling. Some steep their seed-wheat in brine to prevent the smut. Brine is also commended as of efficacy against gangrenes.

BRINE ALSO

Pages 515-516

e also denotes a pickle pregnant with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, wherein things are steeped to keep. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINE">Brine</a>-Pans, the pits where the salt-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is retained, and suffered to stand, to bear the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, whereby it is converted into salt. There are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> sorts of salt pans, as the water-pans, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAN">pan</a>, sun-pan; the water being transferred only from one to another. Brine-Pit, in salt-making, the salt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from whence the water to be boiled into salt is taken. There are of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in many places; that at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMPTWICH">Namptwich</a> in Cheshire, is alone sufficient, according to the account of the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, to yield salt for the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but it is under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of certain lords and regulators, who, that the market may not be overstocked, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not suffer more than a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the salt to be made yearly. See the next article. Brine-Springs, are fountains which flow with salt-water instead of fresh. Of these there are a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> in South <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, but though not peculiar to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, are far from being <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in the countries on the continent. There are some of them in several different counties; and perhaps, on a due search, others might be discovered *. The most remarkable of these already known are, one at East Chennock in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>, about 20 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Another at Leamington in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, very near the river Leam; which, however, is but weak. Such a spring likewise runs into the river Cherwell in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>, and several more in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>: but as they are but <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> in most of those counties scarce and dear, no salt is prepared from them. At Borrowdale near Grange, three miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KESWICK">Keswick</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, a pretty strong spring rises in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> near a moss, 16 gallons of the water of which yield one of pure salt; which is the more remarkable, when... when it is considered that the same quantity of salt cannot be obtained from less than 22 gallons of the waters of the German ocean. At a place called Salt-Water Haugh, near Butterby, in the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, there is a multitude of salt-springs which rise in the middle of the river Weare, for the space of about 40 yards in length and ten in breadth; but particularly one out of a rock, which is so strong that in a hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> the surface will be covered with a pure <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> salt. At Weston, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, there are brine pits which afford about a ninth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of very fine white salt. There are others at Enson, St Thomas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Ingrestre, but so weak that they are not wrought; though it is believed, that by <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORING">boring</a>, stronger springs might be found in the neighbourhood. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> there are several salt springs, but (<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except that at Barton, which is as rich as the spring at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NORTHWICH">Northwich</a>) by no means so famous as those of Cheshire, called in general by the name of the witches. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANTWICH">Nantwich</a> on the river Weever, has a noble spring not far from the river, which is so rich as to yield one-sixth part of pure white salt. At six miles distant stands Northwich, at the confluence of the Weever and the Dan; where the brine is still richer, since they obtain six ounces of salt from 16 of water. There are, even at this day, some visible remains of a Roman causeway between these two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, who, before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was incorporated into England, were supplied chiefly, if not solely, with that necessary commodity from these two towns, called the former Hellath Wen, and the latter Hellath Du; i.e. the white and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> salt pit. In 1670, a rock of salt was discovered at a small distance from Northwich, which has been wrought to a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depth, and to a vast <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, so as to be justly esteemed one of the greatest curiosities in England; and it is highly probable, that there is an immense body of fossil salt in the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, under this whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; since, upon boring, brine pits have been found in many places on both sides the river Weever. This is the more likely, since at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLEWICH">Middlewich</a>, which stands at the confluence of the Croke and the Dan, there are salt springs with a fresh brook running between them. The brines from these pits are of unequal strength; but when mixed, they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> obtain four ounces of salt from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of brine. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> shows, that in these springs the water is strongest nearest the bottom, richer in dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> than in wet, and when <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> drawn than when first wrought. But these are no rules in respect to other salt-springs, since in those of Franche Compte the brine is strongest in wet weather. There are several other bodies dissolved in these brines besides salt; in some a sulphureous substance, which sublimes as the brine heats; a sort of dirty ochre which discolours the brine, but if suffered to stand, speedily subsides; and in most brines a calcareous, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather selenitic earth, which settles to the bottom of the pans. To BRING-TO, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, to check the course of a ship when she is advancing, by arranging the sails in such a manner, that they shall counteract each other, and prevent her either from retreating or moving forward. In this situation the ship is said to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> by, or to lie to; having, according to the sea-phrase, some of her sails <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABACK">aback</a>, to oppose the force of those which are full; or having them otherwise shortened by being furled, or hauled up in the brails.

BRINGING-TO

Pages 516-516

is generally used to detain a ship in any particular station, in order to wait the approach of some other that may be advancing towards her; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to retard her course occasionally near any port in the course of a voyage. BRINGING-IN a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>, in the manege, the same as to say, keep <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the nose of a horse that bores and tosses his nose in the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>: this is done by means of a branch.

BRINING OF CORN

Pages 516-516

in husbandry, an operation performed on the wheat-seed, in order to prevent the smut. A liquor is to be prepared for this purpose, by putting 70 gallons of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> into a tub (like a mash-tub used for <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, and a corn-bushel of unslaked <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>. This is to be well stirred till the whole is dissolved, and left to stand for 30 hours; after which it is to be drained off into another tub, in the manner practised for beer. In this way about a hogshead of strong lime-water <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be obtained, to which must be added three pecks of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. The wheat must be steeped in this pickle, by running it gently, and in small quantities, into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>-bottomed <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of about 24 inches in diameter, and 20 inches deep, and stirring it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> seed that floats must be strained off with a strainer, and must not be sown. When the basket has been drawn up, and drained of the pickle, the wheat will be fit for sowing in two hours after the brining. BRINING of hay-ricks, a practice <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, of mixing salt with the hay as it is stacked.

BRIONNE

Pages 516-516

a town of France in Normandy, seated on the river Rille. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 51'. N. Lat. 49° 51'.

BRIOUDE

Pages 516-516

a town of France, in the department of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, formerly Lower Auvergne. There are two Brioudes, three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> from each other; the one is called <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> Brioude, the other Old Brioude. The houses are built after the antique manner, and are badly disposed. The canons are all temporal lords and counts. It is in no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, but depends immediately on the pope. There are several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; and, among the rest, the church of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FERROL">Ferrol</a>, which is highly celebrated. Near the Old Town is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the river <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIER">Allier</a>, which consists of one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>: this is esteemed a stupendous structure, and is thought to be a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. The inhabitants, 5000 in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 25'. N. Lat. 45° 14'.

BRIQUERAS

Pages 516-516

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, seated in the valley of Lucern, three miles from the town of that name, and four south of Pignerol. It had a very strong castle towards the latter end of the 16th century; but when the French got footing in it, it was ruined, that is, before they delivered it up to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy in 1696. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 24'. N. Lat. 44° 41'.

BRISACH

Pages 516-517

New, a town of France, in the department of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, built by order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. over against Old Brisach, and fortified by Vauban. It is 32 miles south of Strasburg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 46'. N. Lat. 48° 5'.

BRISEIS

Pages 517-517
or Hippodamia, in fabulous history, the wife of Mynes king of Lyrnessa. After Achilles had taken that city, and killed her husband, she became his captive. That hero loved her tenderly; but Agamemnon taking her from him, she became the accidental cause of sad disorders in the Grecian army.

BRISGAW

Pages 517-517

a territory of Germany, in the circle of Suabia, on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, about 50 miles in length, and 30 in breadth, now subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BADEN">Baden</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places are Old Brisach, New Brisach, Freyburgh, and Rhinmarck.

BRISIACUS MONS

Pages 517-517

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> east side of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>. Now Brisach, situated on a round hill; a fortified town of Suabia, and distinguished by the name of Old Brisach. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 15'. N. Lat. 48° 10'.

BRISSOT

Pages 517-517

John <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, leader of the Brissotine party in the French revolution. See Supplement.

BRISTLE

Pages 517-517

BRISTOL

Pages 517-518

a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of England, and inferior to none, except <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, for wealth, trade, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants. Bristol is a corruption of Brightstow, as it was called by the Saxons. It is thought to have stood anciently altogether on the west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a> side of the Avon, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> was built; but after that, it came to be partly in Somersetshire and partly in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, until it was made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of itself, though even before that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> rolls, it was always placed in Somersetshire. At present, the east side is by much the largest and most populous. It had anciently a castle, built by Robert <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> son to Henry I., which was demolished by Cromwell; and the ground is now laid out into streets. The corporation consists of a mayor; recorder; twelve aldermen, of whom the recorder is one; two sheriffs; and twenty-eight <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> men. The recorder is generally a serjeant at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and sits as judge in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and all other criminal causes. The mayor, to support his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and defray his extraordinary expense, is entitled to certain fees from ships, which <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago amounted to 500l. or 600l. Bristol is a bishop's see, being one of the six erected by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. out of the spoils of the monasteries and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses which that monarch had got dissolved. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was the church of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of St Austin in Bristol, founded by Robert Fitzharding son to a king of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, once a citizen here, and by him filled with canons regular in the year 1148. At the reformation King Henry VIII. placed therein a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and six prebendaries, which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> still continues. During a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>'s reign, this see was held in commendam by the bishop of Gloucester. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> was formed chiefly out of the diocese of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>, with a small part from the dioceses of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. It contains most of the city of Bristol, and all the county of Dorset, in which are 236 parishes, of which 64 are appropriated. It hath only one archdeaconry, viz. of Dorset; is valued in the king's books at 33l. 8s. 4d. and is computed to be annually worth 1500l. including its commendams. The tenths of the clergy are 353l. 18s. 4½d. This see hath yielded to the state one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> privy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>. The revenues of the abbey of St Augustine, or St Austin, in Bristol, were valued at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> at 6700l. 13s. 1½d. when it was erected into a cathedral by King Henry VIII. by the name of the Cathedral Church of the Holy Trinity. To this cathedral belong a bishop, a dean, an archdeacon, a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, six prebendaries, and other inferior officers and servants. Besides the cathedral, there are 18 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-churches; and here are dissenters of all denominations, of whom the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a> are very respectable both for their wealth and numbers. Of the parish-churches, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Ratcliff is reckoned one of the finest, not only here, but in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In this church, besides two monuments of the founder William Cannings, who had been five times mayor of this city, one in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and another in that of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> (for in his latter days he took orders), there is one of Sir William Penn, father to the famous Quaker. The old bridge over the Avon consisted of four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, with houses on both sides like those formerly on London bridge; but this has been lately pulled <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and another erected in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. No carts or waggons are admitted into Bristol, for fear of damaging the vaults and gutters made under ground for carrying the filth of the city into the river. Queen's-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in this city, is larger than any in London, except <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn Fields, and has in the centre an equestrian statue of King William III. All the gates of the city remain entire, and a part of the walls; the rest were razed in the reign of William Rufus. It is almost as broad as long; and, including the out-parishes, is supposed to contain 100,000 inhabitants. Of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> That called Queen Elizabeth's, in which 100 boys are taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>; six of whom, when they go out, have 10l. and the rest 8l. 8s. to bind them apprentices: the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> is allowed 45l. a-year, for the maintenance of the boys. 2. Colston's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>; in which 100 boys are maintained for <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years, and taught and apprenticed, as in Queen Elizabeth's. 3. Another founded by the same <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> in 1691, for 12 men and 12 women, with an allowance of 3s. per <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and 24 sacks of coals in the year. This <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> cost the founder 25,000l. 4. Another founded partly by Mr Colston and partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, in which 18 men on account of the merchants, and 12 men and women on account of Mr Colston, are maintained. 5. An infirmary, which was opened in 1736 for the sick, lame, and distressed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of the city, which is maintained by subscription, besides 500l. bequeathed to it by John Eldridge, Esq., formerly comptroller of the customs at this port. There are, besides these, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a>, several almshouses, and charity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. There is also a guildhall for the sessions and assizes; the mayor's and sheriffs' courts; a council-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the mayor and aldermen meet every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, except Sundays, to administer <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; a handsome new <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, with three entrances, about two-thirds as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as that in London, and a quay half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> in length, the most commodious in England for shipping and landing goods, for which purpose it is provided with several cranes. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>-green is a stately <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, with the effigies of several kings round it. In Winch-street is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>-house, with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. As to the trade of this city, it was computed many years ago to be much greater in proportion, especially to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> and the West Indies, than that of London. Fifty sail, some of them ships of considerable burthen, have arrived here at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, or very near one another, from the West Indies. For this trade, and that to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, it is much better situated than London, besides the great advantages it possesses of an inland navigation by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>. Their trade extends to the Baltic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and the Straits. The largest ships are discharged at Kingroad, four miles below the city, and the goods are brought to the quay by lighters. For <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, equipping, and repairing ships, there are docks, yards, rope-walks, and shipwrights. In 1809 various improvements were completed upon the harbour, which cost 600,000l. Here are some considerable woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>; and no less than 15 glass-houses, for which Kingswood and Mendip furnish the coals. The city companies are 13: 1. The merchant adventurers. 2. The merchant tailors. 3. The mercers. 4. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> boilers. 5. The tobacconists. 6. The butchers. 7. The barbers. 8. The tylers. 9. The holliers, who are the sled-men. 10. Shoemakers. 11. Coopers. 12. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BAKERS">Bakers</a>. 13. Smiths. For supplying the city with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> there are six public conduits. There are also stage coaches, which set out every day for Bath, London, and other places. A mile below the city, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the river, is the hot well, whose waters are specific for the diabetes, and good in phthisical, scorbutic, and inflammatory disorders. Hither is a great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of invalids, as well as other <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; for whose accommodation and entertainment there is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a>-room, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>-room, coffee-house, with taverns, and a great number of elegant lodging houses, both below on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the well, and above in the delightful village of Clifton, which is situated on the brow of a hill, from whence there are <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">downs</a> extending several miles, where the company ride out for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. Nothing can be more pure and salutary than the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> of these downs, which afford a variety of the most romantic and agreeable prospects, comprehending Kingroad, with the ships at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, the mouth of the Severn, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. In the rocks above the well are found those six-cornered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> called Bristol-stones; but they are not so plentiful now as in Camden's days, when, he says, whole bushels might have been easily gathered. In this city is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, where plays are acted almost every night during the recess of the comedians from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. There are two annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, to which the concourse is so great, that the neighbouring inns have filled 100 beds a piece with their guests. In the winter season there is an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> every Thursday for the gayer part of the citizens of both sexes. About half way betwixt Bristol and Bath, at a place called Warmly, a company of Bristol merchants have erected a noble manufacture of pins and other <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> utensils, which employs a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, including about 200 children of both sexes from seven to twelve or thirteen years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>. All the different operations of melting, plitting, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, hammering, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>, &c. are performed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> worked with water, which is raised by two fire engines of a very curious mechanism. The city of Bristol gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of earl to the family of Hervey, and sends two members to parliament. It is worth observing, that whoever marries a citizen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> becomes free of the city. New-Bristol, the capital of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, situated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a>, about 20 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>, in W. Long. 75° N. Lat. 40° 45'. Bristol Water. Of the four <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> warm waters naturally produced in England, this is the least so. As the Bath waters are proper where the secretions are defective, so the Bristol water is of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> where they exceed the requirements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The Bath water warms; the Bristol cools. Bath water helps the stomach, intestines, and nerves; the Bristol favours the lungs, kidneys, and bladder. Except a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>-attend, the Bristol water may be of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DROPSY">dropsy</a> by its drying and diuretic qualities. Dr Winter asserts, that there is no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in Bristol water: and that its mineral contents are chalk, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">lapis</a> calcareus and calaminaris. Five gallons of this water, after <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, afforded only 3 iii. and gr. 2. of mineral substances. The diseases in which this water is useful are internal hemorrhages, immoderate menses, internal inflammations, spitting blood, dysentery, purulent ulcers of the viscera, consumption, dropsy, scurvy with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, gravel, strangury, habitual gout, atrophy, slow fever, scrofula, gleets, and diabetes, in which last it is a specific, and may be drank as freely as the thirst requires it. The hotter months are the best for using it. The Bristol and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATLOCK">Matlock</a> waters are of exactly the same qualities. Doctors <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a> and Lane first established the reputation of Bristol waters in diseases of the kidneys and bladder.

BRITAIN

Pages 608-627

BRITAIN The many affronts and indignities which administration had of late been obliged to put up with now rendered it absolutely necessary to fall upon some method to show that their authority was not altogether lost. For this purpose a committee was appointed by ballot of the house of commons to inquire into the reason why there had been so many obstructions to the authority of the house of commons. This committee having sat from the 28th of March to the 30th of April, at last gave in the following report. "Your committee beg leave to observe, that in the diligent search they have made in the journals, they have not been able to find an instance that any court or magistrate has presumed to commit, during the sitting of parliament, an officer of the house for executing the orders of the house. They further beg leave to observe, that they have not been able to find, that there ever has been an instance wherein this house has suffered any person, committed by order of this house, to be discharged, during the same sittings, by any authority whatever, without again committing such persons. As therefore, with regard to J. Millar, who was delivered from the custody of the messenger by the lord mayor, who for the said offence is now under the censure of the house, it appears to your committee, that it highly concerns the dignity and power of the house to maintain its authority in this instance, by retaking the said J. Millar; the committee recommend to the consideration of the house, whether it may not be expedient that the house should order that the said J. Millar should again be taken into custody of the sergeant at arms; and that his deputy or deputies be strictly enjoined to call upon the magistrates, officers of the peace, and other persons, who by the speaker's warrant are required to be aiding and assisting him in the execution thereof, for such assistance as the said sergeant, his deputy or deputies, shall find necessary, to enable him or them to take into custody the said J. Miller." Nothing could have been more imprudent than the urging with such violence a contest against such contemptible adversaries; and in which they were finally baffled. What they intended for punishment really afforded the criminals matter of triumph and exultation. Every honour that the city of London could bestow was conferred upon the magistrates, while the complaints and execrations of the people at large became louder than ever. Every step taken about this time by administration seemed calculated to add to the public ill humour. Towards the end of the session a bill was brought in "for enabling certain persons to enclose and embank part of the river Thames, adjoining to Durham-yard, Salisbury-street, Cecil-street, and Beaufort-buildings in the county of Middlesex." This bill was opposed, as appearing contrary to the ancient rights and privileges of the city of London; but was easily carried through both houses, though it produced a protest in the upper house; and a few days before the rising of the session, the city of London petitioned against it. In this petition it was complained of as a violent and unjust transaction; totally unprecedented; being an invasion of the property which the city claimed in the foal or bed of the river. It was afterwards complained of in a remonstrance, as an infringement of the rights of the people, and urged as a reason for the dissolution of parliament. The only other transaction of moment during this East India session related to the East India Company. It was now proposed to raise 2000 men in England for the service of the company, the officers to be appointed by the king, and to be paid by the company. But after much speculation, it was rejected as unconstitutional and dangerous to keep an armed force in the kingdom which was not paid by government; and that, however inconsiderable the number proposed was at present, it might soon be increased on any frivolous pretence. It was likewise urged, that it would prove an obstruction to the recruiting service for our own army, on account of the superior advantages of enlisting in the company's service. The advocates for the bill urged the inconvenience of sending out a sufficient number of men annually to recruit the Indian forces; and that, unless parliament should adhere to the promise they formerly made of afflicting the company in recruiting, they would be daily exposed to vast loss and expense from the tricks of recruiting parties. The session rose on the 8th of May. In the speech from the throne, it was observed, that the satisfaction obtained from his Catholic majesty for the injury done this kingdom, and the proofs of the pacific disposition which the courts of France and Spain had given by laying aside their armaments, enabled us to reduce our forces by sea and land. The zeal manifested by parliament could not fail to convince the world of its affectionate attachment to the crown and regard to the interests of the country. His majesty's endeavours were promised to put an end to the troubles which still prevailed in some parts of the continent; thanks were given to the commons for the unanimous cheerfulness, and public spirit with which they had granted the supplies; and an apology was made for the extraordinary demands which had been made. The speech concluded with advising the members to use their best endeavours, in their respective stations and counties, to render the national happiness complete, by discouraging needless suspicions and domestic disturbances. His majesty had no other objects, and could have no other interests, than to reign in the hearts of a free and happy people; and it was his earnest wish that his subjects might not be prevented, by mistakes or animosities among themselves, from enjoying the happiness they had in their power. The many defeats that had been received by opposition during this and the foregoing sessions now began to discourage them from proceeding such lengths in the cause of patriotism as they had formerly done. Many of them had also lost much of their popularity by taking an active part against the printers; and as every motion had been carried in favour of administration by nearly two to one, a general discouragement and languor began to take place among the popular party. The only gainers indeed by the late contentions were the city magistrates and printers who had been punished by the house of commons. On the rising of the parliament, when the lord mayor and aldermen were released... released from the Tower, they were welcomed by every mark of congratulation. The city was illuminated; and the mob, as usual, took vengeance on the refractory by breaking their windows. A committee was even appointed to carry on a prosecution against the speaker of the house of commons; but as this did not seem likely to afford any redress, they determined once more to have recourse to the throne. Accordingly, on the 16th of July 1771, another petition and remonstrance was presented, the subjects of which were the embankments on the Thames, the proceedings against the magistrates; and a speedy dissolution of parliament was requested. But this met with an unfavourable answer as before. His majesty replied, that he was ready to put an end to the real grievances of his faithful subjects; but he was sorry to find that a part of them still renewed requests which he had repeatedly refused to comply with. In the speech from the throne, when the parliament met, January 21, 1772, his majesty observed, that the performance of the king of Spain's engagements, and the behaviour of the other European powers, promised a continuance of peace; and though the necessity of keeping up a respectable naval force was evident, yet no extraordinary aid for that purpose would be necessary; and he concluded with recommending the most vigilant and active attention to the concerns of the country, with an assurance of the interposition of the crown to remedy abuses or supply defects. Little dispute was made about the addressees in answer to this speech, though an ample subject of altercation very soon occurred. This was a motion made by administration, intimating the necessity of raising 25,000 seamen for the service of the current year; it being always necessary, they said, for us to preserve a superiority to the French in the East Indies, which had not been the case since they sent a considerable fleet thither. "It was equally necessary (they added) to preserve the present strength of the West Indies unimpaired; as the Spaniards knew the importance of our settlements there too well not to make an attack upon them first if ever a rupture should take place. Twenty of the best ships in the navy were also now employed as guard-ships, and wanted nothing but men to fit them for actual service." A declaration of this kind, coming immediately after the assurances of peace that had been given from the throne, was said to be a contradiction; that the peace establishment would thus be augmented till we were overburdened by it; 300,000 would thus be added to the national expenses; and as the same augmentation might every year be made on similar pretences, we should thus be obliged to submit to the hardships of war in time of a profound peace. If the assurance of peace from the throne were well founded, the force in the East Indies was already too great; if, on the contrary, a war was at hand, it would be too small notwithstanding the proposed augmentation; and the same way Jamaica was likely to suffer from the inferiority. These remonstrances were by no means sufficient to put a stop to any measure which had at this time been suggested by administration. The question for the augmentation was carried without a division; after which the subject of religion came to be discussed. This was occasioned by the general tendency to Arianism or Socinianism, which had for some time prevailed to a great degree, and had at last infected the enlightened church in such a manner, that the subscription to her standards was reckoned intolerable by many of the clergy. Meetings had been frequently held by the discontented members, in order to consider of some mode of relief; and in the beginning of February 1772, Petition about 250 of them, with several professors of law and gainful subjects, joined in a petition to the house of commons, expressing their dissatisfaction with subscription to any human forms, and praying for relief. In this petition they asserted, that they held certain rights and privileges from God alone, without being subject to any other authority; such as the exercise of their own reason and judgment, by which they were instructed and confirmed in their belief of the Christian religion, as contained in the Holy Scriptures. They accounted it a blessing to live under a government which maintained the sufficiency of the Scriptures to instruct in all things necessary to salvation. Hence they concluded, that they had a right from nature, as well as from the principles of the reformed religion, to judge for themselves what was or was not contained in the Scriptures. From this invaluable privilege, however, they found themselves in a great measure precluded by the laws relative to subscription; by which they were enjoined to acknowledge certain articles and confessions of faith framed by fallible men as entirely agreeable to Scripture. They prayed therefore to be relieved from such an imposition, and to be restored to their undoubted right of interpreting Scripture for themselves, without being bound by any human explanation of it, or being required to acknowledge by subscription or declaration the truth of any formulary of religious faith and doctrine whatever, excepting the Holy Scripture itself. The affair of subscription they looked upon to be not only a grievance to themselves, but an encroachment on their rights as men and members of a Protestant establishment, as well as a great hinderance to the spreading of the Christian religion, tending to discourage further inquiry into the true sense of Scripture, to divide communions, and to cause a mutual dislike between fellow Protestants; giving occasion for unbelievers to reproach and vilify the clergy, by representing them as guilty of prevarication, and of accommodating their faith to lucrative views and political considerations. It afforded also to Papists, and others disaffected to the religious establishment of the church of England, an occasion of reflecting upon it as inconsistent, and authorizing doubtful and precarious doctrines, at the same time that the Scripture alone was acknowledged to be certain and sufficient for salvation. It had likewise a tendency to divide the clergy among themselves; subjecting one part, who affirmed their privilege as Protestants, to be reviled both from the pulpit and the press, by another who seemed to judge the articles they had subscribed to be of equal authority with the Scripture itself; and, lastly, it occasioned scruples and embarrassments of conscience to those who were about to enter into the ministry, or prevented the cheerful exercise of it to those who were already entered. By reason of these embarrassments, the clerical part of the petitioners found themselves under der great difficulties, being obliged in some sense to join with the adversaries of revelation, in supposing the one true sense of Scripture to be expressed in the present established system of faith; or else to incur the reproach of having deserted their subscription, &c., while such of the petitioners as had been educated with a view to the professions of civil law and physic could not but think it a great hardship to be obliged, as they all were in one of the universities, even at their first matriculation and admission, though at an age very improper for such important dispositions, to subscribe their assent to a variety of theological tenets, concerning which their private opinions could be of no consequence to the public, in order to entitle them to academical degrees in those faculties; more especially as the course of their studies and attention to their practice did not afford them leisure sufficient to examine how far these tenets were consonant to the word of God. This petition was presented by Sir William Meredith, who, along with the other members who favoured the cause, enforced it by many arguments drawn from the principles of toleration. They maintained also that nothing but hypocrisy and prevarication could arise from obliging men to subscribe what they did not believe; that the repeal of the laws for subscription would prevent the increase of dissenters, so very conspicuous at this time, and incline many of them to return to the church. The articles themselves were said to have been compiled in a hurry; that they contained doctrines highly controversial; and that this restraint on the consciences of men was of all others the greatest hardship. The majority of parliament, however, were found inimical to the petition, though some who opposed it at present wished for time to consider it more deliberately, or to refer it to a committee of the clergy. By the rest it was urged, that the matter of the petition was a violent infraction of the laws of the English religion; and that if this was granted, another would soon follow against the liturgy. The conduct of many of the petitioners, instead of being founded in any regard for religion, had its origin in hypocrisy and dissoluteness, and certainly proceeded in many instances from a disbelief of the Trinity, and of the divinity of our Saviour. The complaints of men were to be disregarded when they wished to profit by the emoluments of the church without subscribing to its laws; besides, the king was bound by his coronation oath to continue the church-government without alteration. It was likewise urged, that if people were to be restrained by no other article than an assent to the truth of the scriptures, the church would soon be overrun with impiety. Many had already founded blasphemous tenets on the right of private opinion; and though it could not be denied that every man has this right for himself, yet none has a right to obtrude his singularities upon others; and if any of the clergy found the delicacy of their consciences affected after they had accepted of benefices, they were welcome to leave them. Some of the more moderate opposers of the petition endeavoured to vindicate the character of the clergy from the imputations laid upon them; and contended that the legislature had a controlling power over the articles of the union, and confirmed their affections by mentioning the act against occasional conformity, as well as another against elective patronages, both of them passed since the union: and it seemed to be the general wish of the house that the professors of law and physic might be relieved from subscription, though they did not consider their share in the matter as of any great importance to the public. It was at last rejected, thrown out by a majority of near 150. The rejection of the subscription bill was followed by that of a bill for quieting the possessions of his majesty's subjects from dormant claims of the church; after which the attention of parliament was called to one of the utmost importance, and which was introduced by a message from the king. This was the famous royal marriage-bill, occasioned by the marriage of the late duke of Cumberland with Mrs Horton, a widow lady, daughter of Lord Irnham, and sister to Colonel Luttrell, and that of the duke of Gloucester with the countess-dowager of Waldegrave. By the message it was recommended to both houses to take it into their consideration, whether it might not be expedient to supply the defects of the laws then in being, and by some new regulations more effectually to prevent the descendants of his late majesty (excepting the issue of the princesses who had married, or might hereafter marry, into foreign families) from marrying without the consent of his majesty, his heirs, and successors. In consequence of this a bill was brought in, declaring all such marriages, without the consent above mentioned, to be null and void. The descendants of his majesty, however, if above the age of 25 years, might marry without the royal consent, provided they gave intimation twelve months beforehand to the privy council, and no opposition to the match was made by parliament during that interval. This bill met with the most violent and powerful opposition. The principal arguments against it were gained, expressed in two protests from the upper house, and were to the following purpose: 1. The doctrine that marriages in the royal family are of the highest importance to the state, and that therefore the kings of this realm have ever been trusted with the care thereof, is both absurd and unconstitutional; though it would from that period have the force of a parliamentary declaration. The immediate tendency of this was to create as many prerogatives to the crown as there are matters of importance in the state; and to extend them in a manner as vague and exceptionable as had ever been done in the most despotic period. 2. The enacting part of the bill had an inconvenient and impolitic extent; namely, to all the descendants of Geo. II. In process of time, that description might become very general, and comprehend a great number of people; and it was apprehended that it would be an intolerable grievance, for the marriages of so many subjects, perhaps dispersed among the various ranks of civil life, to be subject to the restrictions of this act; especially as the abettors of this doctrine had also maintained, that the care and approbation of the marriage also included the education and custody of the person. This extensive power might in time make many of the first families of the kingdom entirely dependent on the crown; and it was regretted that all endeavours to limit, in some degree, the generality of that description, had proved ineffectual. 3. The time of nonage for the royal family appeared to be improperly extended beyond... yond the limit of 21 years; a period which the wisdom of the constitution seems with great wisdom to have assigned to minority. 4. The deferring their marriage to the age of 26 might also be attended with other bad consequences, by driving them into a disorderly course of life, which ought to be particularly guarded against in those of such an exalted station. 5. The power given by this bill to a prince to marry after the age of 26, is totally defeated by the proviso which declares the consent of parliament to be ultimately necessary. Thus great difficulties must be laid on future parliaments, as their silence in such a case must imply a disapprobation of the king's refusal; and their concurrence with it might prove a perpetual prohibition from marriage to the party concerned. 6. The right of conferring a discretionary power of prohibiting all marriages, appears to be above the reach of any legislature whatever, as being contrary to the inherent rights of human nature; which, as they are not derived from, or held under, the sanction of any civil laws, cannot be taken away by them in any case whatever. The legislature no doubt has a right to prescribe rules to marriage as well as to every other kind of contract; but there is an essential difference between regulating the mode by which a right may be enjoyed, and establishing a principle which may tend entirely to annihilate that right. To disable a man during life from contracting marriage, or, which is the same thing, to make his power of contracting such marriage dependent neither on his own choice nor on any fixed rule of law, but on the arbitrary pleasure of any man, or set of men, is exceeding the power permitted by Divine Providence to human legislature, and directly contrary not only to the divine command, but also to the rights of domestic society and comfort, &c. 7. This bill has a natural tendency to produce a disputed title to the crown. If those who are affected by it are in power, they will easily procure a repeal of this act, and the confirmation of a marriage made contrary to it; and if they are not, it will at least be the source of the most dangerous faction that can exist in any country, viz., one attached to a pretender to the crown; whose claim, he may assert, has been set aside by no other authority than that of an act to which the legislature was not competent, as being contrary to the common rights of mankind. 8. The bill provides no security against the improper marriages of princes married into foreign families, and those of their issue: which may fall as materially affect the interest of this nation as the marriages of princes residing in the dominions of Great

Britain was to sink in utter disgrace and contempt by their mere secession, without making any account of their exploits in the field, which could not fail to equal those of the heroes of antiquity. On the same principles the event of the skirmish at Lexington was magnified by the one into a "disgraceful defeat" on the part of the British; and by the other treated with absolute unconcern, as if no regard whatever was to be paid to it, nor any inference drawn from thence concerning the fate of the war in general. Thus also the battle at Bunkers Hill, and all the transactions of the year 1775, were unfairly stated by both parties; and the only consequence ensuing from these misrepresentations was the inflaming to a violent degree the resentment betwixt the two parties; one of which deprecated the Americans to the rank of consummate poltroons, while the other exalted them almost to that of demi-gods. While these altercations continued to agitate the minds of the superior classes of people in
