He was some time rector of Sturston in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, where he married a wealthy widow; and afterwards, when the king visited Cambridge 1728, became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws. He was in 1733 presented by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to the rectory of Pulham in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, which he held with Oakley Magna in Suffolk, given him by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Cornwallis, to whom he was chaplain, and who added the vicarage of Eye in Suffolk; he then resigned Pulham, and retained the other two. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his life he grew again poetical, and amused himself with translating Odes of Anacreon, which which he published in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>. He died at Bath in 1745.

BROOMING

Pages 817-817
or Breathing of a Ship, the washing and burning off all the filth she has contracted on her sides, with weeds, straw, broom, &c. when she is on the careen, or on the ground. See Careening.

BROSSARD

Pages 817-817

Sebastian de, an eminent French musician. In the former <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he had been prebendary and chapel-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Strasburg; but afterwards became <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-chaplain, and also maître de chapelle in the cathedral of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>. There is extant of his a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled Prodromus Musicalis. He was author also of a very useful book, entitled Dictionnaire de Musique, printed at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, in folio, 1703; and afterwards at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in octavo, without a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>. At the end of this book is a catalogue of authors <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, to the amount of 900, who have written on music, divided into classes; wherein are interspersed many curious observations of the author relating to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of music. By Mr Boivin's Catalogue General des Livres de Musique for the year 1729, it appears that Brossard was the author of two sets of motets, as also of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> Leçons de Tenebres therein mentioned. It seems that these several publications were at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when the author was far advanced in years; for Walther takes notice that in the Mercure Galante, he is mentioned as an abbé and composer, so early as the year 1678.

BROTHEL-HOUSES

Pages 817-817

lewd places, being the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> habitations of prostitutes. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, in the 37th year of his reign, suppressed all the stews <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> brothel-houses which had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>-side in Southwark, contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> of God and of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>*. A brothelman was a loose idle fellow; and a femme bordelier, or brothelier, a common whore. And bordelain is a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> for brothel-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. See Bawdy-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>.

BROTHER

Pages 817-819

Frater, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation between two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> children, sprung from the same father, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mother, or both. Scaliger and Vossius derive frater from Φατερ, for Φατερικός, which properly signifies a person who draws <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the same well; Φατερικός, in Greek, signifying well, and Φατερικός, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of people who have a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to draw water out of the same well. The word, it is said, came originally from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, where there were only a few <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> distributed in certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the city, to which those of the same neighbourhood alone repaired. By the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> stand in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>; by the canon law, they are in the first degree.—By the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic law</a>, the brother of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who died without issue was obliged to marry the widow of the deceased. Deuter. xxv. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> applied the term brother indifferently to almost all who stood related in the collateral line, as uncles and nephews, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> germans, &c.—This we learn not only from a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, but also from profane authors: Cicero, in his Philippics, says, "Antonia was both wife and sister of Mark Antony; because she was <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of his brother C. Antonius." And as to cousins, Tullus Hostilius, in Dionysius <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, calls the Horatii and Curiatii, brothers; because they were sisters children. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Jews, Bishop Pearson observes, included in the name of brethren not only the strict relation of fraternity, but also the larger of consanguinity. We are brethren, says <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, Gen. xiii. 8. whereas Lot was only his nephew.—So <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> told Rachel that he was her father's brother, Gen. xxix. 12. where he was only her father's nephew.—This consideration has been urged with good advantage against the Antidicomarianites, who, from the mention made of the brethren of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, John ii. 12. Matth. xii. 46. have impugned the perpetual virginity of the mother of Christ. Among us, it is customary for kings to give the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> brother to each other; the unction in coronation being esteemed to create a kind of brotherhood. Nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENANDER">Menander</a> mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of Cosroes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, beginning thus: Cosroes, king of kings, &c. to the emperor Justinian my brother.—Kings now also give the same appellation to the electors of the empire; and the like was given by the king of France to the late king of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, while only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Savoy. In the civil law, brothers, fratres, in the plural, sometimes comprehends sisters: as Lucius et Titia, fratres; tres fratres, Titius, Maevius, et Seia. Foster-BROTHERS, those who sucked the same nurse. The French call them fratres du lait, or brothers by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; which is most properly used in respect of a person who sucked a nurse at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with the nurse's own child. BROTHERS-German, Fratres Germani. See German. BROTHER was also used, in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, for a comes, or governor of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. BROTHER is applied, in a less proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, to denote a person of the same profession. In which sense, judges, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, priests, &c. call each other brothers. BROTHER is also a customary term for priests of the same persuasion to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> one another by: But it is more particularly used to denote the relation between monks of the same convent; as Brother Zachary: in English, we more usually say, Friar Zachary, from the French word, frere, brother.—Preachers also call their hearers, my brethren, or my dear brethren. This appellation is borrowed from the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who all called each other brothers. But it is now principally used for such of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> as are not priests; those in orders are generally honoured with the title of father, whereas the rest are only simply brothers. BROTHER is also an appellation more peculiarly given to certain orders of religious: Thus, the Brothers of St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a>, in the low countries, were an order of persons who attended on those who lay dying, and took care of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of the dead. See also Brethren of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> BROTHERS, in the charity-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, a denomination given to decayed gentlemen, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 8c, who are subsisted with diet, clothing, and lodging, on the establishment. The poor brothers are to be gentlemen by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, come to poverty; or decayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, or officers of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>. The conditions of admission are, that they have no estate. Brother estate for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> worth 200l. nor coming in viis et modis, 24l. per annum; and that they be 50 years old, unless they have been maimed in the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the age of 40 suffices. They wear a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a> within doors. Brothers of Arms, an appellation given those who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a kind of fraternity in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, obliging themselves to the mutual service and assistance of each other. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> orders, the knights are also called brothers.—In the order of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, there is a particular class, who are called serving brothers; consisting of such as cannot give <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. In Latin they are denominated fratres clientes. Brothers of the rosy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. See Rosycrucians. Brouage, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of Saintonge in France. It consists of five or six streets which terminate in a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. It is famous for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-works, which are the finest in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 0'. N. Lat. 45° 50'. Broushaven, a port-town of the United Provinces, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Schonen in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the island, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in E. Long. 3° 35'. N. Lat. 51° 50'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROUGH">Brough</a>, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a> in England, seated under Stanmore-hill. W. Long. 2° 50'. L. Lat. 54° 40'. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, being a Roman fortress; but is now much decayed. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> in 1811, 758. Brough'ton, Thomas, a learned divine, and one of the original writers of the Biographia Britannica, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 5, 1704, in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Andrew, Holborn; of which parish his father was minister. At an early age he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETON">Eton</a> school, where he soon distinguished himself by the acuteness of his genius, and the studiousness of his disposition. Being superannuated on this foundation, he removed about 1722 to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; and, for the sake of scholarship, entered himself of Gonville and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. Here two of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> were, the acquisition of the knowledge of the modern languages, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, under the famous Professor Sanderson. May 28, 1727, Mr Broughton, after taking the degree of bachelor of arts, was admitted to deacon's orders. In the succeeding year, September 22d, he was ordained <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and proceeded to the degree of M. A. At this time he removed from the university, to the curacy of Offley, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>. In 1739, he was instituted to the rectory of Stepington, otherwise Stibington, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Huntingdon, on the presentation of John duke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>, and was appointed one of that nobleman's chaplains. Soon after he was chosen reader to the Temple, by which means he became known to Bishop Sherlock, then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of it, and who conceived so <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of our author's merit, that in 1744, this eminent prelate presented Mr Broughton to the valuable vicarage of Bedminster, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, together with the chapels of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Redcliff, St Thomas, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEIGH">Leigh</a>, annexed. Some short time after, he was collated, by the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, to the prebend of Bedminster and Redcliff, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALISBURY">Salisbury</a>. Upon receiving this preferment, he removed from London to Bristol, where he married the daughter of Thomas Harris, clerk of that city, by whom he had <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> children, six of whom survived him. He resided Broughton, on his living till his death, which happened <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 21, 1774, in the 71st year of his age. He was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Mary Redcliff. From the time of Mr Broughton's quitting the university, till he was considerably advanced in life, he was engaged in a variety of publications, of which a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> is given in the Biographia Britannica, 2d edition. Some little time before his death, he composed "A short view of the principles upon which Christian churches require, of their respective clergy, subscription to established <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>;" but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> never appeared in print. He possessed, likewise, no inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, as is evident from many little fugitive pieces in manuscript, found among his papers; and particularly from two unfinished tragedies, both written at the age of 17. When he was at Eton school, Mr Broughton was of the same year with Dr Ewer, late bishop of Bangour; Dr Sumner, late provost of King's college, Cambridge; and Dr Sleech, late provost of Eton; and during his residence in London, he enjoyed the esteem and friendship of most of the literary men of his time. He was a great lover of music, particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; which introduced him to the knowledge and acquaintance of Mr Handel; whom he furnished with the words for many of his compositions. In his public character, Mr Broughton was distinguished by an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> zeal for the Christian cause, joined with a moderation of mind. In private life, he was devoted to the interests and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his family; and was of a mild, cheerful, and liberal temper. This disposition, which is not always united with eminent literary abilities, attended him to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>. In 1778, a posthumous "volume of sermons, on select subjects," was published by his son, the Rev. Thomas Broughton, M. A. of Wadham college, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of Tiverton, near Bath. Brookhusius, Jonus, or John Broekhui-zen, a distinguished scholar in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, was born November 20, 1649, at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, where his father was a clerk in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>. He learned the Latin tongue under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> Junius, and made a prodigious progress in polite literature; but, his father dying when he was very young, he was taken from literary pursuits, and placed with an apothecary at Amsterdam, with whom he lived some years. Not liking this, he went into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, where his behaviour raised him to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a>; and, in 1674, was sent with his regiment to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> in the fleet under <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> de Ruyter, but returned to Holland the same year. In 1678, he was sent to the garrison at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, where he contracted a friendship with the celebrated Gravius; and here, though a person of an excellent temper, he had the misfortune to be so deeply engaged in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, that, according to the laws of Holland, his life was forfeited: but Gravius wrote immediately to Nicholas Heinsius, who obtained his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a>. Not long after, he became a captain of one of the companies then at Amsterdam; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> placed him in an easy situation, and gave him leisure to pursue his studies. His company being disbanded in 1697, a pension was granted him, upon which he retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-house near Amsterdam, where he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> but little company, and spent his time among books. He died December 15, 1707. As a classical editor, he is distinguished by his labours upon Tibullus and Propertius; the latter was published in 1702, the former in 1708. He was an excellent Latin poet himself; a volume of his poems was published at Utrecht, 1684, in 12mo; but a very noble edition of them was given by Van Hoogstretton at Amsterdam, 1711, in 4to. His "Duteh poems" were also published at Amsterdam, 1712, in 8vo, by the same person, who prefixed his life, extracted from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Burman's funeral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> upon him. Broukhusius was also an editor of Sannazarus's and Palearius's Latin works. With regard to his Latin poems, the authors of the "Journal de Trevoux" have delivered themselves thus (and what they have said may be applied to the bulk of modern Latin poems): "His verses are written in good enough Latin; but they want fire. The author was a poet by art, not by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>."

BROUNCKER

Pages 819-819
or Brounker, William, lord viscount of Castle-Lyons, in Ireland, and the first president of the Royal Society, was the son of Sir William Brounker, knt. and born about the year 1620. He was distinguished by his knowledge of the mathematics, and by the considerable posts of honour and profit he enjoyed after the Restoration; for he had at the same time the office of chancellor to the queen, and the keeping of her great seal, that of one of the commissioners of the navy, and master of St Catharine's hospital near the Tower of London. He wrote, 1. Experiments of the recoiling of guns. 2. An algebraical paper upon the squaring of the hyperbola; and several letters to Dr Usher, archbishop of Armagh. He died in 1684.

BROWER

Pages 819-819

Adrian, a famous Dutch painter, born either at Oudenard <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Haerlem, in 1603, of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> parentage. He became the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Francis Hals, under whom he proved an inimitable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. His subjects were taken from low <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, always copied from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; as droll conversations, drunken brawls, boors at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, or surgeons dressing the wounded. Brower was apprehended at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> as a spy; where being discovered by Rubens, he procured his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, took him home, clothed him, and endeavoured to acquaint the public with his merit; but the levity of his temper made him quit his benefactor; and he died not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after, in 1649, destroyed by a dissolute course of life.

BROWN

Pages 829-829

among dyers, painters, &c. a dusky <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> inclining towards redness. Of this colour there are various shades <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> degrees, distinguished by different appellations; for instance, Spanish-brown, a sad-brown, a tawny-brown, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> brown, a clove-brown, &c. Spanish-brown is a dark dull <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> colour. It is an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and is of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among painters, being generally used as the first and priming colour that they lay upon any kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. That which is of the deepest colour, and freest from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, is the best. Though this is of a dirty brown colour, yet it is much used, not to colour any garment, unless it be an old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>; but to shadow vermillion, or to lay upon any dark ground behind a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, or to shadow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> berries in the darkest places, when you want lake, &c. It is best and brightest when burnt in the fire till it be red hot; although, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you would colour any hare, horse, dog, or the like, it should not be burnt; but, for other uses, it is best when it is burnt; as for colouring wood, posts, bodies of trees, or any thing else of wood, or any dark ground of a picture. BROWNIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BROWNISTS

Pages 829-830

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, which sprung out of the Puritans, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the 16th century. Their leader, Robert <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>, wrote <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> books in their behalf, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of good parts, and some learning. He was born of a good family in Rutlandshire, and related to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Burleigh. He had been educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; but first published his notions, and began to inveigh openly against the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and ceremonies of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWICH">Norwich</a>, in the year 1580; from which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he underwent divers prosecutions from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>; insomuch that he boasted he had been committed to no less than 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a>, in some of which he could not see his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at noon-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. At length, with his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>, he left the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and settled at Middleburgh in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>; where they obtained leave of the states to worship God in their own way, and form a church according to their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; which they had not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> done, before this handful of men, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> delivered from the severities of the bishops, began to differ among themselves and crumble into so many parties, that Brown their pastor grew weary of his office; and, returning to England in 1589, renounced his principles of separation, and was preferred to the rectory of a church in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, and died, after leading a very idle and dissolute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in 1630. The revolt of Brown was attended with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the church at Middleburgh; but the seeds of Brownism, which he had sown in England, were so far from being destroyed, that Sir Walter Raleigh, in a speech in 1592, computes no less than 20,000 followers of it. The occasion of their separation was not any fault they found with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, but only with the discipline and form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, of the other churches in England. They equally <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> corruption on the Episcopal form, and on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, by consistories, classes, and synods: nor would they join with any other reformed church, because they were not assured of the sanctity and regeneration of the members that composed it; on account of the toleration of sinners, with whom they maintained it an impiety to communicate. They condemned the solemn celebration of marriages in the church; maintaining that matrimony being a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> thereof ought to come from the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. They would not allow any children to be baptized of such as were not members of the church, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of such as did not take sufficient care of those baptized before. They rejected all forms of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>; and held that the Lord's prayer was not to be recited as a prayer, being only given for a rule or model whereon all our prayers are to be formed. The form of church-government which they established was democratical. When a church was to be gathered, such as desired to be members of it made a confession of it, and signed a covenant, by which they obliged themselves to walk together in the order of the gospel. The whole power of admitting and excluding members, with the decision of all controversies, was lodged in the brotherhood. The church officers were chosen from among themselves, for preaching the word, and taking care of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and separated to their several offices by fasting, prayer, and imposition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of some of the brethren. But they did not allow the priesthood to be any distinct order, or to give any indelible character. As the vote of the brotherhood made a man a minister, and gave him authority to preach the word and administer the sacraments among them, so the same power could discharge him from his office, and reduce him to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> layman again. And as they maintained Brownists, maintained the bounds of a church to be no greater than what could meet together in one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and join in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, so the power of these officers was prescribed within the same limits. The minister or pastor of one church could not administer the Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> to another, nor baptize the children of any but those of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. Any lay-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> was allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of prophesying, or of giving a word of exhortation to the people; and it was usual for some of them, after sermon, to ask questions, and reason upon the doctrines that had been preached. In a word, every church on the Brownists model is a body corporate, having full power to do every thing which the good of the society requires, without being accountable to any classis, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>, or other jurisdiction whatever. Most of their discipline has been adopted by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, a party which afterwards arose from among the Brownists. The laws were executed with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> severity on the Brownists; their books were prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and their persons imprisoned, and many of them were hanged. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR_CHAMBER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>-chamber, in fine, distressed them to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they resolved to quit their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Accordingly, many families retired and settled at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, where they formed a church, and chose Mr Johnson their pastor; and after him Mr Ainsworth, author of the learned <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>. Their church flourished near 100 years. See Independents.

BROWNRIGG

Pages 830-830

WILLIAM, M.D. F.R.S. was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, and born about the year 1712. Of the early <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> we have had no opportunity of obtaining information. Being destined for the medical profession, after the previous studies in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> to finish his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. This university was then in its highest splendour; <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBINUS">Albinus</a> in anatomy, Euler in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> was occupied by the all-accomplished Boerhaave. Having made at Leyden a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and happy residence, and taken his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, he returned to his native country, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITEHAVEN">Whitehaven</a>, married a lady of singular good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and possessing an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> so versatile and superior as never failed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> in whatever circle it was exerted. He was author of an inaugural dissertation De Praxi medica incunda, 4to, Lugd. Bat. 1737; of a treatise "On the Art of making <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">Common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a>," printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, in 1748, in 8vo; which procured for him the addition of F.R.S.; a book now long out of print, but not out of recollection. He also published "An Enquiry concerning the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Spirit contained in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPA">Spa</a> in Germany;" and, lastly, a treatise, published in 1771, "On the Means of preventing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">Communication</a> of Pestilential Contagion." A trip to the Spas of Germany suggested to him the idea of analyzing the properties of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRMONT">Pyrmont</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, and of some others, and actually led him to that train of disquisition, which terminated in the de-elementizing one of our elements, and fixing its invisible fluid form in a palpable and visible substance. That Dr Brownrigg was the legitimate father of these discoveries was not only known at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to his intimate and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> circle, but also to the then <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, Sir John Pringle; who, when called upon to bestow upon Dr Priestley the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> medal for his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> of "Discoveries of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> and Properties of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">Air</a>," thus observed; "And it is no disparagement to the learned Dr Priestley, that the vein of these discoveries was <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon, and its course successfully followed up, some years ago, by my very learned, very penetrating, very industrious, but modest, friend, Dr Brownrigg." To habits of too much diffidence, and to his scrupulousness of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the world has to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the fewness of his publications, and the difficulties which always impeded his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to the press. The writer of this article has grounds for saying, that a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cumberland was one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s literary projects, and that he had made several arrangements subservient to such an undertaking, particularly in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> history. As a medical practitioner, his works were more numerous, and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not equally celebrated, they were of a character more endearing within the sphere of their utility. His system of treating <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> formed an epoch in the annals of medical practice. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and the rich had everywhere somewhat for which they thanked him; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> seemed only one of the blessings which he had to dispense. By these means the doctor passed into the summit of professional <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> without rival <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> competitor, without controversy or detraction, but not without applications and requests from fellow students and followers from distant parts, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, foreign and domestic, entreating permission to enrol his name among their respective communities. In his younger days, though the classics of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, Rome, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, were present to his fancy, and enlivened and enriched his conversation, yet the Sacred Scriptures were the topics of his delight, and the objects of his veneration: and as his quotations of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> bore testimony to the elegance of his taste, and the fervour of his genius; so, when <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> and Isaiah were brought forward, he shewed what his imagination would aspire at, in the ranges of sublimity. In the ordinary occurrence of good things, he never failed to give God the praise; and in the more solemn dispensations, he closed his observations or repressed his feelings, by a purpose of resignation to God's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. To his seat at Ormethingwaite, near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KESWICK">Keswick</a>, he had retired about 20 years before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, withdrawing himself as much from the practice of physic as his numerous connexions, his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> character, and his friendly disposition would permit: and purposing to divide his time and his-taste between the romantic scenery of this delicious spot, and his researches in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In this retirement he died at the venerable <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 88, lamented by the poor, to whom he was always a beneficent friend, and regretted by all. (<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">Month</a>. Mag.)

BROWNY

Pages 830-831

the name of a serviceable kind of sprite, who, according to a superstitious notion formerly prevalent in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> and Highlands of Scotland (as well as among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people in England, where he had the name of Robin Goodfellow), was wont to clean the houses, helped to churn, thrashed the corn, and would belabour all that pretended to make a jest of him. He was represented as stout and blooming, had fine <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> flowing <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and went about with a wand in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He was the very counterpart of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>'s Lubber Fiend, who Tells how the drudging goblin swet, To earn his cream-bowl duly set, When When in one night, ere glimpse of morn, His shadowy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAIL">flail</a> hath thrash'd the corn That ten <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-lab'lers could not end; Then lays him <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Lubber Fiend, And stretch'd along the chimney's length, Basks at the fire his hairy strength.

BROWSE

Pages 831-831

the tops of the branches of trees, whereon beasts feed. This is sometimes also called brouce and bruttle; probably from the French brout, which signifies the same thing.

BROWSE MORE PROPERLY

Pages 831-831

E more properly denotes the food which deer find in young copses, continually sprouting anew.

BRUCE

Pages 831-835

James, F. R. S. the celebrated traveller, was born at Kinnaird-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Stirling, Scotland, in the year 1729. The Bruces of Kinnaird are a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. They were descended from a younger son of Robert de Bruce, and have been in possession of that estate for three centuries, connected during this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> with some of the most distinguished houses of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Mr Bruce was instructed in grammatical learning at the school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">Harrow</a> on the Hill in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, where he acquired a considerable share of classical knowledge. Returning to Scotland, he applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the laws of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; but soon contracting a dislike to his situation, he determined to push his fortune in the East Indies, and for that purpose went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. Being disappointed in his views of procuring an appointment in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, he engaged in trade, and entered into <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with a wine merchant in London of the name of Allen, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> he married. That lady falling into a bad state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, Mr Bruce took her abroad, in hopes that travelling would be attended with beneficial effects, but in these he was disappointed, as she died within a year after her <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. He was induced, in order to dispel his grief, to continue his travels, during which his father dying (at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> 4th May 1758), the inheritance of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> devolved upon him, and he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. Some of his subsequent transactions shall now be related in his own words: "Every one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> remember that period, so glorious to Britain, the latter end of the ministry of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHATHAM">Chatham</a>. I was then returned from a tour through the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, particularly through the whole of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, between whom there was then the appearance of an approaching <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. "I was about to retire to a small patrimony I had received from my ancestors, in order to embrace a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of study and reflexion, nothing more <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> appearing within my power, when chance threw me unexpectedly into a very short and very desultory conversation with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Chatham. "It was a few days after this, that Mr Wood, then under secretary of state, my zealous and sincere friend, informed me that Lord Chatham intended to employ me upon a particular service; that, however, I might go <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for a few weeks to my own country to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> my affairs, but, by all means, to be ready upon a call. Nothing could be more flattering to me than such an offer, when so young; to be thought worthy by Lord Chatham of any employment, was doubly a preference. No <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> was lost on my side; but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> after receiving orders to return to London, his Lordship had gone to Bath, and resigned his office. "This disappointment, which was the more sensible to me that it was the first I had met with in public life, was promised to be made up to me by Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EGREMONT">Egremont</a> and Mr George Grenville. The former had been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> my friend; but unhappily he was then far gone in a lethargic indisposition, which threatened, and did very soon put a period to his existence. With Lord Egremont's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> my expectations vanished. Further particulars are unnecessary; but I hope that, at least in part, they remain in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> where they naturally ought to be, and where I shall ever think, not to be long forgotten is to be rewarded. "<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> eight months were passed in an expensive and fruitless attendance in London, when Lord <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> was pleased, not only to propose but to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for me, a journey of considerable importance, and which was to take up several years. His lordship said, that nothing could be more ignoble than, at such a time of life, at the height of my <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, health, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, I should as it were, turn <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>, and voluntarily <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> myself in obscurity and idleness; but though war was now <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> fast to an end, full as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> a competition remained among men of spirit, which should acquit themselves in the dangerous line of useful adventure and discovery. "He observed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Barbary, which might be said to be just at our door, was yet but partially explored by Dr Shaw, who had only illustrated (very judiciously indeed) the geographical labours of Sanson; that neither Dr Shaw nor Sanson had been, or pretended to be, capable of giving the public any detail of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and magnificent remains of ruined <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, which they both vouch to have seen in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities, and of exquisite elegance and perfection, all over the country. Such had not been their study, yet such was really the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> that was required in the present times. He wished, therefore, that I should be the first, in the reign just now beginning, to set an example of making large additions to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> collection; and he pledged himself to be my support and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and to make good to me, upon this additional merit, the promises which had been held forth to me by former ministers for other services. "The discovery of the source of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a> was also a subject of these conversations; but it was always mentioned to me with a kind of diffidence, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> to be expected from a more experienced traveller. Whether this was but another way of exciting me to the attempt, tempt, I shall not say; but my heart, in that instant, did me <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to suggest, that this too was either to be achieved by me, or to remain as it had done for these last two thousand years, a defiance to all travellers, and an opprobrium to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">geography</a>. "Fortune seemed to enter into this scheme. At the very instant, Mr Aspinwall, very cruelly and ignominiously treated by the dey of Algiers, had resigned his consulship, and Mr Ford, a merchant, formerly the dey's acquaintance, was named in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Mr Ford was appointed, and, dying a few days after, the consulship became vacant. Lord Halifax pressed me to accept of this, as containing all sorts of conveniences for making the proposed expedition. "This favourable event finally determined me. I had all my life applied unweariedly, perhaps with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> than <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a>, to drawing, the practice of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and especially that part necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. The transit of Venus was at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. It was certainly known, that it would be visible once at Algiers, and there was great reason to expect it might be twice. I had furnished myself with a large <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of instruments, the completest of their kind, for the observation. In the choice of these, I had been assisted by my friend <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Campbell, and Mr Russel, secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> company: every other necessary had been provided in proportion. It was a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> now to know, that it was not from a rock or wood, but from my own house at Algiers, I could deliberately take <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to place myself in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of men of science, of all nations who were then preparing for the same scientific purpose. "Thus prepared, I set out for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, through France; and though it was in time of war, and some strong objections had been made to particular passports, solicited by our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> from the French secretary of state, Mousieur de Choiseul most obligingly waived all such exceptions with regard to me, and most politely assured me, in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> accompanying my <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSPORT">passport</a>, that those difficulties did not in any shape regard me, but that I was perfectly at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through or remain in France, with those that accompanied me, without limiting their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, as short or as long a time as should be agreeable to me. "On my arrival at Rome, I received orders to proceed to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, there to wait his majesty's further commands. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Saunders, then with a fleet before <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a>, had orders to visit <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> before he returned to England. It was said, that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of that order had behaved so improperly to Mr Harvey (afterwards Lord <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>) in the beginning of the war, and so partially and unjustly between the two nations in the course of it, that an explanation on our part was become necessary. The grand master no sooner heard of my arrival at Naples, than, guessing the errand, he sent off Chevalier Mazzini to London, where he at once made his peace and his compliments to his majesty upon his accession to the throne. "Nothing remained now but to take possession of my consulship. I returned, without loss of time, to Rome, and from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>, where having embarked on board the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTREAL">Montreal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of war, I proceeded to Algiers. "After a year spent at Algiers, constant conversation with the natives while abroad, and with my <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> within doors, had qualified me to appear in any part of the continent without the help of an interpreter. Ludolf had assured his readers, that the knowledge of any oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> would soon enable them to acquire the Ethiopic; and I needed only the same number of books to have made my knowledge of that language go hand in hand with my attainments in the Arabic. My immediate project of setting out on my journey to the inland parts of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, had made me <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> my diligence; night and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> there was no relaxation from these studies, although the acquiring any single language had never been with me either an object of time or difficulty." At Algiers Mr Bruce was detained longer than he expected, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a dispute with the dey concerning Mediterranean passes. This being adjusted, he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MAHON">Mahon</a>, and from Mahon to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. He next visited <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and travelled over the interior parts of these states. At Benghazi, a small town on the Mediterranean, he suffered shipwreck, and with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty saved his life, though with the loss of all his baggage. He afterwards sailed to the isles of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a> and Cyprus, and proceeding to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, travelled through a considerable part of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>, visiting Hassia, Latakea, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, and Tripoli, near which last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> he was again in imminent danger of perishing in a river. The ruins of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALMYRA">Palmyra</a> and Baalbec were next carefully surveyed and sketched by him; and his drawings of these places are deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s library at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>: "the most magnificent present, in that line," to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his own words, "ever made by a subject to his sovereign." It is much to be regretted, that Mr Bruce published no particular account of these various journeys; from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the places visited, and the abilities of the man, much curious and useful information might have been expected. Some manuscript accounts of different parts of them are said to have been left by him, but whether in such a state as to be fit for publication is very uncertain. In these various travels some years were passed; and Mr Bruce now prepared for the grand expedition, the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of which had ever been nearest his heart, the discovery of the sources of the Nile. In the prosecution of that dangerous object, he left <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a> on the 15th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1768, and arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> on the 20th of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. He proceeded from thence to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the 12th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> following, when he embarked on the Nile, and sailed up the river as far as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYENE">Syene</a>, visiting in the course of the voyage the ruins of Thebes. Leaving Kenné on the Nile, 16th February 1769, he crossed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> of the Thebaid to Cosseir on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JIDDA">Jidda</a> on the 3rd of May. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix he remained, not without making several excursions, till the 3rd of September, when he sailed from Loheia, and arrived on the 19th at Masuah, where he was detained near two months by the treachery and avarice of the naybe of that place. It was not till the 15th of November that he was allowed to quit Arkeeko, near Masuah; and he arrived on the 15th of February 1770 at Gondar, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, where he ingratiated himself with the most considerable persons of both sexes belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. Several months were were employed in attendance on the king; and in an unsuccessful expedition round the lake of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMBEA">Dembea</a>. Towards the end of October, Mr Bruce set out for the sources of the Nile, at which long-desired spot he arrived on the 14th of November, and his feelings on the accomplishment of his wishes cannot better be expressed than in his own words: "It is easier to guess than to describe the situation of my mind at that moment; standing in that spot which had baffled the genius, industry, and inquiry, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> and moderns for the course of near 3000 years. Kings had attempted this discovery at the head of armies; and each expedition was distinguished from the last only by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the numbers which had perished, and agreed alone in the disappointment which had uniformly, and without exception, followed them all. Fame, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, had been held out for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of ages to every individual of those myriads those princes commanded, without having produced one man capable of gratifying the curiosity of his sovereign, or wiping off this stain upon the enterprise and abilities of mankind, or adding this desideratum for the encouragement of geography. Though a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> private Briton, I triumphed here in my own mind over kings and their armies; and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> was leading nearer and nearer to the presumption, when the place itself where I stood, the object of my vain-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, suggested what depressed my short-lived triumphs. I was but a few minutes arrived at the source of the Nile, through numberless dangers and sufferings, the least of which would have overwhelmed me, but for the continual goodness and protection of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">providence</a>; I was, however, but then half through my journey, and all those dangers which I had already passed awaited me again on my return. I found a despondency gaining ground fast upon me, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLASTING">blasting</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of laurels I had too rashly woven for myself." When he returned to rest the night of that discovery, repose was sought for in vain. "Melancholy reflections upon my present state, the doubtfulness of my return in safety, were I permitted to make the attempt, and the fears that even this would be refused, according to the rule observed in Abyssinia with all travellers who have once entered the kingdom; the consciousness of the pain that I was then occasioning to many worthy individuals, expecting daily that information concerning my situation which it was not in my power to give them; some other thoughts, perhaps, still nearer the heart than those, crowded upon my mind, and forbade all approach of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>. "I was, at that very moment, in possession of what had for many years been the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of my ambition and wishes; indifference, which, from the usual infirmity of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> nature, follows, at least for a time, complete enjoyment, had taken place of it. The marsh, and the fountains, upon comparison with the rise of many of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, became now a trifling object in my sight. I remembered that magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> in my own native country, where the Tweed, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNAN">Annan</a>, rise in one hill; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THREE_RIVERS">three rivers</a> I now thought not inferior to the Nile in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, preferable to it in the cultivation of those countries through which they flow; superior, vastly superior to it in the virtues and qualities of the inhabitants, and in the beauty of its flocks, crowding its pastures in peace, without fear of violence from man or beast. I had seen the rise of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, and the more magnificent sources of the Saone; I began, in my sorrow, to treat the inquiry about the source of the Nile as a violent effort of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">dis</a>-tempered fancy: 'What's Hecuba to him, or he to Hecuba, 'That he should weep for her?' Grief and despondency now rolling upon me like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, relaxed, not refreshed, by unquiet and imperfect sleep, I started from my <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a> in the utmost agony. I went to the door of my <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. Everything was still; the Nile, at whose head I stood, was not capable either to promote or to interrupt my slumber, but the coolness and serenity of the night braced my nerves, and chased away those phantoms that while in bed had oppressed and tormented me. "It was true, that numerous dangers, hardships, and sorrows, had beset me through this half of my excursion; but it was still as true, that another Guide, more powerful than my own courage, health, or understanding, if any of them can be called man's own, had uniformly protected me in all that tedious half. I found my confidence not abated, that still the same Guide was able to conduct me to my wished-for home. I immediately resumed my former fortitude, considered the Nile as indeed no more than rising from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> as all other rivers do, but widely differing in this, that it was the palm for 3000 years held out to all the nations of the world as a detur dignissimo, which in my cool hours I had thought was worth the attempting at the risk of my life, which I had long either resolved to lose, or lay this discovery a trophy in which I could have no competitor, for the honour of my country, at the feet of my sovereign, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> I was." The object of Mr Bruce's wishes being now gratified, he bent his thoughts on his return to his native country. He arrived at Gondar 19th November 1770; but found, after repeated solicitations, that it was by no means an easy task to obtain permission to quit Abyssinia. A civil war in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time breaking out, several engagements took place between the king's forces and the troops of the rebels, particularly three actions at a place called Serbraxos on the 16th, 20th, and 23rd of May 1771. In each of them Mr Bruce acted a considerable part, and for his valiant conduct in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> received, as a reward from the king, a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, of 184 links, each link weighing $3\frac{1}{2}$ dwt. or somewhat more than $2\frac{1}{2}$ lbs. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">troy</a> in all. At Gondar, after these engagements, he again preferred the most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties to be allowed to return home, entreaties which were long resisted; but his health at last giving way, from the anxiety of his mind, the king consented to his departure, on condition of his engaging by oath to return to him in the event of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, with as many of his kindred as he could engage to accompany him. After a residence of nearly two years in that wretched country, Mr Bruce left Gondar on the 16th of December 1771, taking the dangerous way of the desert of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, in place of the more easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> of Masuah, by which he entered Abyssinia. He was induced to take this rout, from his knowledge and former <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of the cruel and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> temper of the naybe of Masuah. Arriving at Teawa the 21st <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1773, Mr Bruce had the misfortune to find the sheikh Fidele at Atbara, the counterpart of the naybe of Masuah, in every bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; by his intrepidity and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, however, and by making good use of his foreknowledge of an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, which happened on the 17th of April, he was permitted to depart next day, and he arrived at Sennaar on the 29th of the same month. Mr Bruce was detained upwards of four months at that miserable and inhospitable place; the inhabitants of which he describes in these expressive words: "War and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> seem to be the only employment of these horrid people, whom heaven has separated by almost impassable deserts from the rest of mankind, confining them to an accursed spot, seemingly to give them an earnest in time of the only other worse which he has reserved to them for an eternal hereafter." This delay was occasioned by the villany of those who had undertaken to supply him with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but at last, by disposing of 178 links of his gold chain, the well-earned trophy of Serbraxos, he was enabled to make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for his dangerous journey through the deserts of Nubia. He left Sennaar on the 5th of September, and arrived on the 3rd of October at Chendi, which he quitted on the 24th, and travelled through the desert of Gooz, to which village he came on the 26th of October. On the 9th of November he left Gooz, and entered upon the most dreadful and dangerous part of his journey; the perils attending which he has related with a power of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> not unworthy of the greatest masters. All his camels having perished, Mr Bruce was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of abandoning his baggage in the desert, and with the greatest difficulty reached Assouan upon the Nile on the 29th of November. After some days rest, having procured fresh camels, he returned into the desert, and recovered his baggage, among which is particularly to be remarked a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a> (of three feet radius) supplied by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XV. from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> academy at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>; by means of which noble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, now deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> at Kinnaid, Mr Bruce was enabled with precision and accuracy to fix the relative situations of the several remote places he visited. On the 10th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1773, after more than four years absence, he arrived at Cairo, where, by his manly and generous behaviour, he so won the heart of Mahomet Bey, that he obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRMAN">firman</a>, permitting the commanders of English vessels belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> to bring their ships and merchandise to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, a place far preferable in all respects to Jidda, to which they were formerly confined. Of this permission, which no European <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> could ever before acquire, many English vessels have since availed themselves; and it has proved peculiarly useful both in public and private dispatches. Such was the worthy conclusion of his memorable journey through the desert; a journey which, after many hardships and dangers, terminated in obtaining this great national benefit. At Cairo Mr Bruce's earthly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> had nearly been concluded by a disorder in his leg, occasioned by a worm in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>. This accident kept him five weeks in extreme agony, and his health was not re-established till a twelvemonth afterwards, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> of Porretta in Italy. On his return to Europe, Mr Bruce was received with all the admiration due to so exalted a character. After passing some considerable time in France, particularly at Montbard, with his friend the comte de Buffon, by whom he was received with much hospitality, and is mentioned with great applause, he at last revisited his native country, from which he had been upwards of twelve years absent. It was now expected that he would take the earliest opportunity of giving to the world a narrative of his travels, in which the public curiosity could not but be deeply interested.
