But still it seems to our author unreasonable to exclude them from the place which the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and facts ascertained by constant observation, assign to them in the great and diversified sphere of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, sensation, and intelligence;—he does not, however, consider them as beings whose actions actions are directed to moral ends, nor consequently as accountable and proper subjects for reward or punishment in a future world. That brute animals possess reflection and sentiment, and are susceptible of the kindly as well as the irascible passions, independently of sexual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> and natural affection, is evident from the numerous instances of affection and gratitude daily observable in different animals, particularly the dog. Of these and other sentiments, such as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, and even a sense of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, the elephant exhibits proofs equally surprising and indubitable, as the reader may see under the article Elephas. As to the natural affection of brutes, says an ingenious writer, "the more I reflect on it, the more I am astonished at its effects. Nor is the violence of this affection more wonderful than the shortness of its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Thus every hen is in her turn the virago of the yard, in proportion to the helplessness of her brood; and will fly in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of a dog or a sow in defense of those chickens which in a few weeks she will drive before her with relentless cruelty. This affection sublimes the passions, quickens the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>, and sharpens the sagacity of the brute creation. Thus a hen, just become a mother, is no longer that placid <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> she used to be, but with feathers standing on end, wings hovering, and clocking <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, she runs about like one possessed. Dams will throw themselves in the way of the greatest danger, in order to avert it from their progeny. Thus a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a> will tumble along before a sportsman, in order to draw away the dogs from her helpless covey. In the time of nidification the most feeble birds will assault the most rapacious. All the hirundines of a village are up in arms at the sight of a hawk, whom they will persecute till he leaves that district. A very exact observer has often remarked, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of ravens nestling in the rock of Gibraltar would suffer no vulture or eagle to rest near their station, but would drive them from the hill with amazing fury: even the blue thrush at the season of breeding would dart out from the clefts of the rocks to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> away the kestrel or the sparrow-hawk. If you stand near the nest of a bird that has young, she will not be induced to betray them by an inadvertent fondness, but will wait about at a distance with meat in her mouth for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> together. The flycatcher builds every year in the vines that grow on the walls of my <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. A pair of these little birds had one year inadvertently placed their nest on a naked bough, perhaps in a shady time, not being aware of the inconvenience that followed; but a hot sunny season coming on before the brood was half fledged, the reflection of the wall became insupportable, and must inevitably have destroyed the tender young, had not affection suggested an expedient, and prompted the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>-birds to hover over the nest all the hotter hours, while with wings expanded and mouths gaping for breath they screened off the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> from their suffering offspring. A farther instance I once <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> of notable sagacity in a willow-wren, which had built in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> in my fields. This bird, a friend and myself had observed as she sat in her nest; but were particularly careful not to disturb her, though we saw she eyed us with some degree of jealousy. Some days after, as we passed that way, we were desirous of remarking how this brood went on, but no nest could be found, till I happened to take up a large bundle of long green moss as it were carelessly thrown over the nest, in order to dodge the eye of any impertinent intruder." A wonderful spirit of sociality in the brute creation, independent of sexual attachment, has been frequently remarked. Many horses, though quiet with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, will not stay one minute in a field by themselves: the strongest fences cannot restrain them. A horse has been known to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> out at a stable window, through which dung was thrown, after company; and yet in other respects is remarkably quiet. Oxen and cows will not fatten by themselves; but will neglect the finest pasture that is not recommended by society. It would be needless to instance in sheep, which constantly flock together. But this propensity seems not to be confined to animals of the same species. In the work last quoted, we are told of "a doe still alive, that was brought up from a little fawn with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAIRY">dairy</a> of cows; with them it goes a-field, and with them it returns to the yard. The dogs of the house take no notice of this deer, being used to her; but if strange dogs come by, a chase ensues; while the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> smiles to see his favourite securely leading her pursuers over hedge, or gate, or style, till she returns to the cows, who with fierce lowings and menacing horns drive the assailants quite out of the pasture." Even great disparity of kind and size does not always prevent social advances and mutual fellowship. Of this the following remarkable instance is given in the same work: "A very intelligent and observant person has assured me, that in the former part of his life, keeping but one horse, he happened also on a time to have but one solitary hen. These two incongruous animals spent much of their time together in a lonely orchard, where they saw no creature but each other. By degrees an apparent regard began to take place between these two sequestered individuals. The fowl would approach the quadruped with notes of complacency, rubbing herself gently against his legs; while the horse would look <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with satisfaction, and move with the greatest caution and circumspection, lest he should trample on his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>. Thus by mutual good offices each seemed to console the vacant hours of the other; so that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, when he puts the following sentiment in the mouth of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, seems to be somewhat mistaken: Much less can bird with beast, or fish with fowl, So well <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>, nor with the ox the ape. In the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1788 we have the following anecdotes of a raven, communicated by a correspondent who does not sign his name, but who says it is at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the doubtful. The raven alluded to "lives, or did live three years since, at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> Lion at <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGERFORD">Hungerford</a>; his name, I think, is Rafe. You must know then, that coming into that inn, my chaise run over or bruised the leg of my Newfoundland dog; and while we were examining the injury done to the dog's foot, Rafe was evidently a concerned spectator; for the minute the dog was tied up under the manger with my horse, Rafe not only visited but fetched him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and attended upon him with particular and repeated marks of kindness. The bird's notice of the dog was so marked, that I observed it to the hostler;" hostler; for I had not heard a word before of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this benevolent creature. John then told me, that he had been bred from his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a>-feather in intimacy with a dog; that the affection between them was mutual; and that all the neighbourhood had often been witnesses of the innumerable acts of kindness they had conferred upon each other. Rafe's poor dog, after a while, unfortunately broke his leg; and during the long time he was confined, Rafe waited upon him constantly, carried him his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> daily, and never scarce left him alone! One night by accident the hostler had shut the stable door, and Rafe was deprived of the company of his friend the whole night; but the hostler found in the morning the bottom of the door so pecked away, that had it not been opened, Rafe would in another hour have made his own entrance-port. I then inquired of my landlady (a sensible woman), and heard what I have related confirmed by her, with several other singular traits of the kindnesses this bird shows to all dogs in general, but particularly to maimed or wounded ones. I hope, and believe, however, the bird is still living; and the traveller will find I have not overrated this wonderful bird's merit." To these instances of attachment between incongruous animals from a spirit of sociality or the feelings of sympathy, may be added the following instance of fondness from a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, recounted by Mr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">White</a>, in the work already so frequently quoted. "My friend had a little helpless leveret brought to him, which the servants fed with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> in a spoon; and about the same time his cat kittened, and the young were dispatched and buried. The hare was soon lost, and supposed to be gone the way of most foundlings, or to be killed by some dog or cat. However, in about a fortnight, as the master was sitting in his garden in the dusk of the evening, he observed his cat, with tail erect, trotting towards him, and calling with little short inward notes of complacency, such as they use towards their kittens, and something gambling after, which proved to be the leveret, which the cat had supported with her milk, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to support with great affection. Thus was a graminivorous animal nurtured by a carnivorous and predatory one! "Why so cruel and sanguinary a beast as a cat, of the ferocious genus of Felis, the murium leo, as Linnæus calls it, should be affected with any tenderness towards an animal which is its natural prey, is not so easy to determine. This strange affection probably was occasioned by that desiderium, those tender maternal feelings, which the loss of her kittens had awakened in her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; and by the complacency and ease she derived to herself from the procuring her teats to be drawn, which were too much distended with milk, till from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> she became as much delighted with this foundling as if it had been her real offspring. "This incident is no bad solution of that strange circumstance, which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> historians as well as the poets assert, of exposed children being sometimes nurtured by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> wild beasts that probably had lost their young. For it is not one whit more marvellous that <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> and Remus, in their infant state, should be nursed by a she-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, than that a poor little sucking leveret should be fostered and cherished by a bloody grimalkin. But besides the different qualities enumerated, besides reflection and sagacity often in an astonishing degree, and besides the sentiments and actions prompted by social or natural attachments, certain brutes seem on many occasions inspired with a superior faculty, a kind of presentiment or second-sight as it were, with regard to events and designs altogether unforeseen by the rational beings whom they concern. Of the faculty alluded to various instances will probably consist with the knowledge or the recollection of most of our readers: We shall therefore only recite the following, on account of its unquestionable authenticity. At the seat of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Lichfield, three miles from <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLENHEIM">Blenheim</a>, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTRAIT">portrait</a> in the dining-room of Sir Henry <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">Lee</a>, by Johnston, with that of a mastiff dog which saved his life. It seems a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> had formed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of assassinating his master and robbing the house; but the night he had fixed on, the dog, which had never been much noticed by Sir Henry, for the first time followed him up stairs, got under his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, and could not be got from thence by either master or man: in the dead of night, the same servant entered the room to execute his horrid design; but was instantly seized by the dog, and being secured confessed his intentions. There are ten quaint <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in one corner of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, which conclude thus: But in my dog, whereof I made no store, I find more love than those I trusted more. Upon what hypothesis can we account for a degree of foresight and penetration such as this? Or will it be suggested, as a solution of the difficulty, that a dog may possibly become capable in great <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of understanding human discourse, and of reasoning and acting accordingly; and that, in the present instance, the villain had either uttered his design in soliloquy, or imparted it to an <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLICE">accomplice</a>, in the hearing of the animal? It has been much disputed whether the brutes have any language whereby they can express their minds to each other; or whether all the noise they make consists only of cries inarticulate, and unintelligible even to themselves. We are, however, too little acquainted with the intellectual faculties of these creatures to be able to determine this point. Certain it is, that their passions, when excited, are generally productive of some peculiar cry; but whether this be designed as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> to others, or only a mechanical motion of the muscles of the larynx occasioned by the passion, is what we have no means of knowing. We may indeed, from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, conclude, with great reason, that some of the cries of beasts are really expressions of their sentiments; but whether one beast is capable of forming a design, and communicating that design by any kind of language to others, is what we submit to the judgment of the reader, after giving the following instance, which among others is brought as a proof of it by Father Bougeant. "A sparrow finding a nest that a martin had just built, standing very conveniently..."

Pages 846-846

Stephen Junius, the disguised author of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Vindiciae contra tyrannos. See Languet.

BRUYERE

Pages 846-846

John de la, a celebrated French author, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOURDAN">Dourdan</a> in the year 1664. He wrote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, describing the manners of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>: which characters were not always imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> general, but descriptive, as was well known, of persons of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. In the year 1693, he was by an order of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> chosen a member of the French Academy; and died in the year 1696.—"The characters of Bruyere (says Voltaire), may justly be ranked among the extraordinary productions of this age. Antiquity furnishes no examples of such a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. A style rapid, concise, and nervous; <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> animated and picturesque; an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> altogether new, without offending against its established rules, struck the public at first; and the allusions, which are crowded in almost every page, completed its success. When La Bruyere showed his work in manuscript to Malesieux, this last told him, that the book would have many readers, and its author many enemies. It somewhat sunk in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of men, when that whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> whose follies it attacked were passed away; yet as it contains many things applicable to all times and places, it is more than probable that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be forgotten."

BRUYIERS

BRYAN

holy see was in agitation. He was <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of the privy chamber to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. and to his successor Edward VI. in the beginning of whose reign he marched with the protector against the Scots; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUSSELBURGH">Musselburgh</a>, in which he commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, was made banneret. In 1548, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> governor of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, where he married the countess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a>. He died soon after, and was buried at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>. He wrote, 1. Lond. 1565. 2. Letters written from Rome concerning the king's divorce; manuscript. 3. Various letters of state; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a>. Wood says he had seen. 4. A dispraise of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of a courtier, &c. Lond. 1548, 8vo, from the French.

BRYANT

Sir Francis, a soldier, statesman, and a poet of no inconsiderable fame in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born of a genteel family, educated at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards spent some time in travelling abroad. In the year 1522, the 14th of Henry VIII., he attended in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a> in his expedition to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Brittany; and commanded the troops in the attack of the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORLAIX">Morlaix</a>, which he took and burnt. For this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he was knighted on the spot by the earl. In 1528, he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; but on what service is doubtful. In 1529, he was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to France; and the year following to Rome, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s divorce. He had also been there in 1522, in the same capacity, when <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> to the holy...

BRYE

Pages 847-847

JOHN THEODORE DE, an excellent engraver, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>; but he resided chiefly at Franckfort, where he carried on a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a>. It does not appear when he was born, nor to what <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> he owed his instructions in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> and engraving. He worked almost entirely with the graver, and seldom called in the assistance of the point. He acquired a neat free style of engraving, excellently well adapted to small subjects, in which many figures were to be represented; as funeral parades, processions, and the like, which he executed in a charming manner. He also drew very correctly. His heads in general are spirited and expressive, and the other extremity of his figures well marked. His back-grounds, though frequently very slight, are touched with a masterly <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. He died, as his sons inform us in the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Boissard's collection of portraits, on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 27th, 1598; the two first parts of which collection were engraved by himself, assisted by his sons, who afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> it.

BRYENNIUS

Pages 847-847

MANUEL, a Greek writer on music, is supposed to have flourished under the elder Palaeologus, viz. about the year of Christ 1120. He wrote three books of Harmonics; the first whereof is a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on Euclid, as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third are on <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. He professes he has studied perspicuity for the sake of young men. Meibomius had given the public expectations of a translation of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; but not living to complete it, Dr Wallis undertook it; and it now makes a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the third volume of his works, published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in three volumes folio, 1699. Bryennius, Nicephorus, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> distinguished by his courage, probity, and learning, was born at Orechia in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>; where his father by rebellion provoked the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to send his general <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXIS">Alexis</a> Comnenus against him, who ordered his eyes to be pulled out; but being charmed with his son Bryennius, he married him to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Comnena his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, so famous by her writings. When Alexis came to the throne, he gave Bryennius the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Caesar; but would not declare him his successor, though solicited to it by the empress Irene; and was therefore succeeded by his son John Comnenus, to whom Bryennius behaved with the utmost fidelity. Being sent, about the year 1137, to besiege Antioch, he fell sick; and, returning, died at Constantinople. This prince wrote the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Alexis Comnenus, which he composed at the request of his mother-in-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a> the empress Irene.

BUA

Pages 847-847

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, near the town of Trau; called likewise the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PARTRIDGE">Partridge</a>-island, because frequented by those birds. It is called Babus by Pliny. In the times of the decay of the empire it was called Boas; and several illustrious men that fell under disgrace at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> were banished to this island; among whom were Florentius, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the offices of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Julian, Immentinus de Valenti, and the heretic Jovinian. The emperors of Constantinople either were not much acquainted with this pretended <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> were willing to treat the banished with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a>. It is certain that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this island is exceedingly mild; the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> perfectly good; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and fruit excellent; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> around it abounds in fish, and the port is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and secure. Neither is it so small that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> has not room to walk and ride about as much as he pleases; for it is ten miles in length, and about 25 in circuit; nor can it be said to be rugged, though rather <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and mountainous.

N. Lat. 43. 47.

BUBALIS

Pages 847-847

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of the buffalo, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">bos</a>. See Bos.

BUBASTIS

Pages 847-848

in the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, one of the names of Isis <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. The Egyptians bestowed different names on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, either to characterize his effects or his relations with respect to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; they followed the same method respecting the moon. Cheremon, a sacred writer of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, leaves no doubt on this subject. "Every thing which is published of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> and Isis, all the sacerdotal fables, allude only to the phases of the moon, and the course of the sun." Bubastis was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> attributes of Isis. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a> having personified her, formed of her a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, in whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of that name was built, as described by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, and where the people collected from all parts of Egypt, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of the year. A cat was the symbol of this deity. The priests fed it with sacred food; and when it died, they embalmed its body, and carried it in pomp to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> prepared for it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> have explained this worship variously. The Greeks pretend that when Typhon declared <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the gods, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> transformed himself into a vulture, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a> into an ibis, and Bubastis into a cat, and that the veneration of the people for the latter animal took rise from that <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>; but they ascribe their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> to the Egyptians, who thought very differently. However that may be, the cat was greatly honoured in Egypt, and a Roman soldier having imprudently killed one, was immediately put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by the populace. Bubastis, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the priests, was deemed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Isis, and even represented her in cer- Bubastis, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> circumstances. It is for this reason that the Greeks, who honoured the moon by the name of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a>, bestowed it also on this Egyptian divinity. Bubastis, says Herodotus, is called Diana by the Greeks. The Egyptians attributed to her the virtue of assisting pregnant women. The Greeks and Latins, disciples of the Egyptians, ascribed the same power to Diana; and Horace does not think it unworthy of his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> the following strophe to her: Montium custos nemorumque, Virgo, Quae laborantes utero puellas Ter vocata audis, adimisque letho, Diva Triformis. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> seek for the origin of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> worship in the laws imposed by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> on women, and which in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> follow the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> revolutions. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> philosophers and the poets buried it under allegories unintelligible to the people. A perfect resemblance, however, does not exist between the two deities we have been speaking of. The Greeks constituted Diana <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a> and of the forests; an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the Egyptians did not acknowledge in Bubastis. The former added, that she was the daughter of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LATONA">Latona</a>, and Bubastis was produced by Osiris and Isis. A barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was introduced at the festivals celebrated in honour of Bubastis, called by the Greeks also Ilithyia, or Lucina, to mark her presiding over childbirth. The Egyptians adored her under this name in the city of Ilithyia, situated near Latopolis. It remains to resolve a question which naturally arises here: How could Bubastis be called the daughter of Isis, since she also was a symbol of the moon? The Egyptian theology easily explains these apparent contradictions. Isis was the general appellation of the moon, Buhastis a particular attribute. The sun, in conjunction with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the night, formed the celestial <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Osiris and Isis; the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> which appears three days after was allegorically called their daughter. It is in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> that the Hebrews called this same phenomenon the birth of the moon, and that Horace says, Calo supinas si tuleris manus, Nascente <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUND">lund</a> rustica Phidyle, &c. &c. These observations inform us, why in the city of Ilithyia, where Bubastis was adored, the third <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the lunar <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> was consecrated by a particular worship. In fact, it is three days after the conjunction, that the moon, disengaged from the rays of the sun, appears as a crescent, and is visible to us. The Egyptians celebrated therefore a solemnity in honour of Bubastis, which in their tongue signified new moon. The crescent with which her head was crowned, expresses palpably the intention of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in creating this symbolical divinity.

BUBBLE

Pages 848-848

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a cant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> given to a kind of project for raising <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> on imaginary grounds, much practised in France and England in the years 1719, 1720, and 1721. The pretence of those schemes was the raising a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> for retrieving, setting on foot, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> carrying on, some promising and useful branch of trade, manufacture, machinery, or the like. To this end proposals were made out, showing the advantages to be derived from the undertaking, and inviting persons to be engaged in it. The sum necessary to manage the affair, together with the profits expected from it, were divided into shares or subscriptions, to be purchased by any disposed to adventure therein. Bubbles, by which the public have been tricked, are of two kinds, viz. 1. Those which we may properly enough term trading bubbles; and, 2. Stock or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUND">fund</a> bubbles. The former have been of various kinds; and the latter at different times, as in 1719 and 1720.

BUBONOCELE

or Hernia inguinalis, in Surgery, a tumour in the inguen, formed by a prolapsus of the intestines, omentum, or both, through the processus of the peritoneum and rings of the abdominal muscles. See SURGERY Index.

BUC

Pages 848-848

GEORGE, a learned English antiquarian, flourished in the beginning of the 17th century. In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. he was made one of the gentlemen of his majesty's privy-chamber, and knighted: he was also constituted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the revels. What he mostly distinguished himself by was his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, 1. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the reign of Richard III.; in which he takes <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to wipe off the bloody stains that have blotted his character, and represents the person and actions of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in a much less odious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> than other historians have done. He also wrote, 2. A Treatise of the Art of Revels; and, 3. A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled The Third Universitie of England.

BUCAANEER

Pages 848-856

one who dries and smokes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fish after the manner of the Indians. The name was particularly given to the first French settlers on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of St Domingo, whose sole employment consisted in hunting bulls or wild boars, in order to sell their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and flesh. The name has also been applied to those famous piratical adventurers, chiefly English and French, who joined together to make depredations on the Spaniards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. Of both these we shall give an account. 1. The Bucaneers of St Domingo. The Spaniards had not been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the possession of the West Indies and the continent of America, when other nations, especially the English and French, began to follow them there. But though the Spaniards were unable to peo- ple such extensive countries themselves, they were resolved that no others should do it for them; and therefore made a most cruel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on all those of any other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> who attempted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in any of the Antilles or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The French, however, were at last lucky enough to acquire some footing in the island of St Christopher's; but by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they began to subside into a regular form of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, the Spaniards found means to dislodge them. Upon this the wretched fugitives, considering at how <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a distance they were from their mother-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and how near to the island of Hispaniola or St Domingo, the northern parts of which were then uninhabited and full of swine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, immediately resolved to take possession of that country, in conjunction with several other adventurers of their own and the English nation; especially as the Dutch, who now began to appear in these seas, promised to supply them plentifully with all kinds of necessaries they might require, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for the hides and tallow they should procure by hunting. These new settlers obtained the name of buccaneers, from their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of buccanning their beef and pork in order to keep it for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, or for their own consumption, the method of which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be presently described. But some of them soon grew tired of this new way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and took to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a>; while many more chose to turn pirates, trusting to find among those who remained on shore a quick sale for all the plunder they could make at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This new body of adventurers were called freebooters, from their making free prey or booty of whatever came in their way. The colony now began to thrive at a great rate, by the cheap and easy manner in which the freebooters acquired the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>, and the profusion with which they distributed them among their old companions, the buccaneers and planters, for the merest trifles. This brought numbers of settlers from Old France in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of indented servants, though they toiled rather like slaves during the three years for which they generally bound themselves. One of these men presuming to represent his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, who always fixed upon a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a> for sending him with skins to the port, that God had forbidden such a practice, when he had declared, "Six days shalt thou labour, and on the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> shalt thou rest:" "And I (replied the brutish buccaneer) say to thee, Six days shalt thou kill bulls, and strip them of their skins, and on the seventh day shalt thou carry their hides to the sea-shore." This command was followed by blows, which sometimes enforce obedience, sometimes disobedience, to the laws of God. Thus the colony consisted of four classes: buccaneers; freebooters; planters; and indented servants, who generally remained with the buccaneers or planters. And these four orders composed what they now began to call the body of adventurers. These people lived together in a perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> under a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a>: every freeman had a despotic authority over his own family; and every <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> was a sovereign in his own ship, though liable to be discarded at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the crew. The planters settled chiefly in the little island of Tortuga on the northern <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Hispaniola: but it was not long before some of them going to the great island to hunt with the buccaneers, the rest were surprised by the Spaniards; and all, even those who had surrendered at discretion in hopes of mercy, were put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> or hanged. The next care of the Spaniards was to rid the great island of the buccaneers; and for this reason they assembled a body of 500 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>-men, who, by their seldom going fewer than 50 in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, obtained the name of the Fiflies from their enemies, whose manners and customs we shall now enter upon. The buccaneers lived in little huts built on some spots of cleared ground, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> enough to dry their skins on, and contain their buccanning houses. These spots they called Boucans, and the huts they dwelt in Ajoupas, a word which they borrowed from the Spaniards, and the Spaniards from the natives. Though these ajoupas lay open on all sides, they were very agreeable to the hardy inhabitants, in a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> where <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> are so very desirable things. As the buccaneers had neither wife nor child, they associated by pairs, and mutually rendered each other all the services a master could reasonably expect from a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>, living together in so perfect a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, that the survivor always succeeded his deceased partner. This kind of union or fellowship they called s'ematelotet [insailoring], and each other matelot [sailor], whence is derived the custom of giving, at least in some parts of the French Antilles, the name matclotage [sailorage], to any kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> formed by private persons for their mutual advantage. They behaved to each other with the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and openness of heart: it would have been a crime to keep any thing under lock and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>; but, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the least pilfering was unpardonable, and punished with expulsion from the community. And indeed there could be no great temptation to steal, when it was reckoned a point of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, never to refuse a neighbour what he wanted; and where there was so little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, it was impossible there should be many disputes. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any happened, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> friends of the parties at variance interposed, and soon put an end to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>. As to laws, the buccaneers acknowledged none but an odd jumble of conventions made between themselves, which, however, they regarded as the sovereign rule. They silenced all objections by coolly answering, that it was not the custom of the coast; and grounded their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of acting in this manner, on their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> under the tropic, which freed them, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, from all obligations antecedent to that marine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. The governor of Tortuga, when that island was again settled, though appointed by the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, had very little authority over them; they contented themselves with rendering him from time to time some slight homage. They had in a manner entirely shaken off the yoke of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and thought they did a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in not wholly forgetting the God of their fathers. We are surprised to meet with nations, among whom it is a difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to discover any trace of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship; and yet it is certain, that had the buccaneers of St Domingo been perpetuated on the same footing they subsisted at the time we are speaking of, the third or fourth <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of them would have had as little religion as the Caffres and Hottentots of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, or the Topinambous and Cannibals of America. They even laid aside their surnames, and assumed nick-names, or martial names, most of which have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCANEER">Bucaneer</a> continued in their families to this day. Many, however, on their marrying, which seldom happened till they turned planters, took care to have their real surnames inserted in the French <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; and this practice gave occasion to a proverb, still current in the French Antilles, *a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is not to be known till he takes a wife.* Their dress consisted of a filthy greasy shirt, dyed with the blood of the animals they killed; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of trousers still more nasty; a thong of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> by way of belt, to which they hung a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> containing some Dutch knives, and a kind of very short sabre called *manchette*; a hat without any brim, except a little flap on the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> to take hold of it by; and shoes of hogskin all of a piece. Their guns were four feet and a half in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>, and of a bore to carry balls of an ounce. Every man had his contract servants, more or fewer according to his abilities; besides a pack of 20 or 30 dogs, among which there was always a couple of beagles. Their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> employment at first was ox-hunting; and, if at any time they chased a wild <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>, it was rather for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASTIME">pastime</a>, or to make provision for a feast, than for any other advantage. But in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, some of them took themselves entirely to hunting of hogs, whose flesh they buccanned in the following manner: First, they cut the flesh into long pieces, an inch and a half thick, and sprinkled them with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, which they rubbed off after 24 hours. Then they dried these pieces in stoves over a fire made of the skin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the beast, till they grew as hard as a board, and assumed a deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. Pork prepared in this manner will keep in casks a twelvemonth and longer; and when steeped but a little while in lukewarm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, becomes plump and rosy, and yields moreover a most grateful smell, either broiled or boiled, or otherwise dressed, enough to tempt the most languid appetite and please the most delicate palate. Those who hunt the wild boar, have of late been called simply *hunters*. In hunting, they set out at day-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a>, preceded by the beagles, and followed by their servants with the rest of the dogs; and as they made it a point never to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALK">balk</a> their beagles, they were often led by them over the most frightful precipices, and through places which any other mortal would have deemed absolutely impassable. As soon as the beagles had roused the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, the rest of the dogs struck up and surrounded the beast, stopping it, and keeping a constant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARKING">barking</a> till the buccaneer could get near enough to shoot it; in doing this, he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> aimed at the pit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; when the beast fell, he hamstring it, to prevent its rising again. But it has sometimes happened that the creature, not wounded enough to tumble to the ground, has run furiously at his pursuer, and ripped him open. But, in general, the buccaneer seldom missed his aim; and when he did, was nimble enough to get up the tree behind which he had the precaution to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> himself. What is more; some of them have been seen to overtake the beast in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, and hamstring it without any further ceremony. As soon as the prey was half-skinned, the master cut out a large bone, and sucked the marrow for breakfast. The rest he left to his servants, one of whom always remained behind to finish the skinning, and bring the skin with a choice piece of meat for the huntsman's dinner. They then continued the chase till they had killed as many beasts as there were heads in the company. The master was the last to return to the boucan, loaded buccaneer-like the rest with a skin and a piece of meat. Here the buccaneers found their tables ready: for every one had his separate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; which was the first thing, any way fit for the purpose, that came in their way, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of a tree, and the like. No table-cloth, no napkin, no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> or wine, graced their board; not even potatoes or bananas, unless they found them ready to their hand. When this did not happen, the fat and lean of the game, taken alternately, served to supply the place. A little pimento, and the squeeze of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, their only sauce; contentment, peace of mind, a good appetite, and abundance of mirth, made everything agreeable. Thus they lived and spent their time, till they had completed the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hides for which they had agreed with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; which done, they carried them to Tortuga, or some port of the great island. As the buccaneers used much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, and fed only on flesh meat, they generally enjoyed a good state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. They were indeed subject to fevers, but either such as lasted only a day, and left no sensible <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> the day following; or little slow fevers, which did not hinder them from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and were of course so little regarded, that it was usual with the patient, when asked how he did, to answer "Very well, nothing ails me but the fever." It was impossible, however, they should not suffer considerably by such fatigues, under a climate to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of which few of them had been early enough inured. Hence the most considerate among them, after they had got <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> enough for that purpose, turned planters. The rest soon spent the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their labour in taverns and tippling-houses; and many had so habituated themselves to this kind of life, as to become incapable of any other. Nay, there have been instances of young men, who having early embarked through <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> in this painful and dangerous profession, persisted in it afterwards, merely through a principle of libertinism, rather than return to France and take possession of the most plentiful fortunes. Such were the buccaneers of St Domingo, and such their situation, when the Spaniards undertook to extirpate them. And at first they met with great success; for as the buccaneers hunted separately, every one attended by his servants, they were easily surprised. Hence the Spaniards killed numbers, and took many more, whom they condemned to a most cruel <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. But whenever the buccaneers had time to put themselves into a state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, they fought like lions, to avoid falling into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a nation from whom they were sure to receive no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; and by this means they often escaped: nay, there are many instances of single men fighting their way through numbers. These dangers, however, and the success of the Spaniards in discovering their boucans, where they used to surprise and cut the throats of them and their servants in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, engaged them to cohabit in greater numbers, and even to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> offensively, in hopes that by so doing they might at last induce the Spaniards to let them live in peace. But the fury with which they behaved whenever they met any Spaniards, served only to make their enemies more intent on their destruction; and assistance coming to both parties, the whole island was turned into a slaughter-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and so much blood spilt on both sides, that many places, on account of the carnage of which Bucaner, which they had been the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">theatres</a>, were entitled, of the massacre: such as the hill of the massacre; the plain of the massacre; the valley of the massacre; which names they retain to this day. At length the Spaniards grew tired of this way of proceeding, and had recourse to their old method of surprise, which, against enemies of more courage than vigilance, was like to succeed better. This put the bucaners under a necessity of never hunting but in large parties, and fixing the boucan in the little islands on the coast, where they retired every evening. This expedient succeeded; and the boucans, by being more fixed, soon acquired the air and consistency of little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. When the bucaners had once fixed themselves, as related, each boucan ordered scouts every morning to the highest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the island, in order to reconnoitre the coast, and see if any Spanish parties were abroad. If no enemy appeared, they appointed a place and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of rendezvous in the evening, and were never absent if not killed or prisoners. When therefore any one of the company was missing, it was not lawful for the rest to hunt again till they had got intelligence of him if taken, or avenged his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> if killed. Things continued in this situation for a long time, till the Spaniards made a general hunt over the whole island; and, by destroying their game, put the bucaners under a necessity of betaking themselves to another course of life. Some of them turned planters; and thereby increased some of the French settlements on the coast, and formed others. The rest, not relishing so confined and regular a life, entered among the freebooters, who thereby became a very powerful body. France, who had hitherto disclaimed for her subjects these ruffians whose successes were only temporary, acknowledged them, however, as soon as they formed themselves into settlements; and took proper <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> for their government and defence. See the article St Domingo. The hunting both of the bull and boar is at this day carried on, and proves of considerable importance. That of the former furnishes France with the finest hides brought from America. The bucaners put the hides in packs which they call loads, mixing together hides of full grown bulls, of young bullocks, and of cows. Each of these loads is composed of two bull-hides, or of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a>; that is to say, either of two real bull hides, or of one bull-hide and two cow-hides, or of four cow-hides, or of three young bullocks hides; three bullocks hides being reckoned equivalent to two full-grown bulls hides, and two cows hides equivalent to one bull's hide. These bulls they commonly call oxen in France, though they be not gelt. Each load is commonly sold for six pieces of eight rials, which is a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, the French coin being but little current, or not at all, in the island of St Domingo. The boar meat bucanned in the manner above mentioned is sold by the bundle or pack, weighing commonly 60 pounds, at the rate of six pieces of eight per pack. The palmetto leaves serve to pack it up in; but their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> is deducted, so that there must be in each pack 60 pounds of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> flesh. These bucaners have also a great trade of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> of boars, which they melt, and gather in large pots called potiches. This lard, which is called mantegua, is also sold for about eight pieces of eight per pot. There is a great trade, and a great consumption of each of these merchandises in the French settlements of the island of St Domingo, and in those of Tortuga: besides which, they used to send great quantities of them to the Antilles, and even into the continent of French America. There is also a great deal of it sold for the support of the crews of the ships that come from France for trading, or which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a> of Tortuga fit out for cruising against the Spaniards. The Spaniards, who have large settlements in the island of St Domingo, have also their bucaners there, whom they call matadores or monteros. Their chase has something noble, which savours of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>: the huntsman being on horseback uses the lance to strike the bull, thinking it beneath his courage to shoot him at a distance. When the servants who are on foot, have discovered the beast, and with their dogs have driven it into some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVANNAH">savannah</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>, in which the master waits for them on horseback, armed with two lances, the matador goes and hamstring it with the first lance, the head of which is made like a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> or half-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, and extremely sharp, and kills it afterwards with the other lance, which is a common one. The chase is very agreeable; the huntsman making commonly, in order to attack the bull, the same turns and the same ceremonics which are practised in those festivals so famous in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, wherein the greatest lords expose themselves sometimes to the view of the people, to make them admire their dexterity and intrepidity in attacking those furious animals: but then it is a very dangerous chase; those bulls, in their fury, often running directly against the huntsman, who may think himself very happy if he comes off only with the loss of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and if he himself is not mortally wounded. The Spaniards dress their hides like the French, who have learned it from them; and these hides being carried to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVANNAH">Havannah</a>, a famous harbour in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, are a part of the trade of that celebrated town. The flota and the galleons scarce ever fail touching there, on their return from Vera Cruz and Porto Bello, and load there those hides which they carry into Spain, where they are sold for Havannah hides, the most esteemed of any that are brought from America into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. II. Bucaneers, the Pirates. Before the English had made any settlement at Jamaica, and the French at St Domingo, some pirates of both nations, who have since been so much distinguished by the name of Bucaneers, had driven the Spaniards out of the small island of Tortuga; and, fortifying themselves there, had with an amazing intrepidity made excursions against the common enemy. They formed themselves into small companies, consisting of 50, 100, or 150 men each. A <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, of a greater or smaller size, was their only armament. Here they were exposed night and day to all the inclemencies of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; having scarce room enough to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> independence, the greatest blessing to those who are not proprietors of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, rendered them averse from those mutual restraints which the members of society impose upon themselves for the common good; some of them chose to sing, while others were desirous of going to sleep. As the authority they had conferred on their captain was confined Bucaneer, to his giving orders in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, they lived in the greatest confusion. Like the savages, having no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of want, nor any care to preserve the necessaries of life, they were constantly exposed to the severest extremities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> and thirst. But deriving, even from their very distresses, a courage superior to every danger, the sight of a ship transported them even to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of frenzy. They never deliberated on the attack, but it was their custom to board the ship as soon as possible. The smallness of their vessels, and the skill they showed in the management of them, screened them from the fire of the greater ships; and they presented only the fore-part of their little vessels filled with fusileers; who fired at the port-holes with so much exactness, that it entirely confounded the most experienced gunners. As soon as they threw out the grappling, the largest vessel seldom escaped them. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> necessity, they attacked the people of every nation, but fell upon the Spaniards at all times. They thought that the cruelties the latter had exercised on the inhabitants of the new world justified the implacable aversion they had sworn against them. But this was heightened by a personal pique, from the mortification they felt in seeing themselves debarred from the privileges of hunting and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, which they considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>. Such were their principles of justice and religion, that, whenever they embarked on any expedition, they used to pray to heaven for the success of it; and they never came back from the plunder, but they constantly returned thanks to God for their victory. The ships that sailed from Europe to America seldom tempted their avidity. The merchandise they contained would not easily have been sold, nor been very profitable to those barbarians in those early times. They always waited for them on their return, when they were certain they were laden with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, jewels, and all the valuable productions of the new world. If they met with a single ship, they never failed to attack her. As to the fleets, they followed them till they sailed out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Bahama; and as soon as any one of the vessels was separated by accident from the rest, it was taken. The Spaniards, who trembled at the approach of the buccaneers, whom they called devils, immediately surrendered. Quarter was granted, if the cargo proved to be a rich one; if not, all the prisoners were thrown into the sea. The buccaneers, when they had got a considerable booty, at first held their rendezvous at the island of Tortuga, in order to divide the spoil; but afterwards the French went to St Domingo, and the English to Jamaica. Each person, holding up his hand, solemnly protested that he had secreted nothing of what he had taken. If any one among them was convicted of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, a case that seldom happened, he was left, as soon as an opportunity offered, upon some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> island, as a traitor unworthy to live in society. Such brave men among them as had been maimed in any of their expeditions, were first provided for. If they had lost a hand, an arm, a leg, or a foot, they received 26l. An eye, a finger, or a toe, lost in fight, was valued only at half the above sum. The wounded were allowed 2s. 6d. per day for two months, to enable them to have their wounds taken care of. If they had not money enough to answer these several demands, the whole company were obliged to engage in some fresh expedition, and to continue it till they had acquired a sufficient stock to enable them to satisfy such <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> contracts. After this act of justice and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, the remainder of the booty was divided into as many shares as there were buccaneers. The commander could only lay claim to a single share with the rest; but they complimented him with two or three, in proportion as he had acquitted himself to their satisfaction. Favour never had any influence in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the booty; for every share was determined by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>. Instances of such rigid justice as this are not easily met with; and they extended even to the dead. Their share was given to the man who was known to be their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> when alive, and therefore their heir. If the person who had been killed had no intimate, his part was sent to his relations when they were known. If there were no friends or relations, it was distributed in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and to the churches, which were to pray for the person in whose name these benefactions were given. When these duties had been complied with, they then indulged themselves in all kinds of profusion. Unbounded licentiousness in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, wine, women, every kind of debauchery, was carried to the utmost pitch of excess, and was stopt only by the want which such profusion brought on. Those men who were enriched with several millions, were in an instant totally ruined, and destitute of clothes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. They returned to sea; and the new supplies they acquired were soon lavished in the same manner. The Spanish colonies, flattering themselves with the hopes of seeing an end to their miseries, and reduced almost to despair in finding themselves a perpetual prey to these ruffians, grew weary of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. They gave up all the power, conveniences, and fortune, which their connections procured them, and formed themselves almost into so many distinct and separate states. They were sensible of the inconveniences arising from such a conduct, and avowed them; but the dread of falling into the hands of rapacious and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> men, had greater influence over them than the dictates of honour, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and policy. This was the rise of that spirit of inactivity which continues to this time. This despondency served only to increase the boldness of the buccaneers. As yet they had only appeared in the Spanish settlements, in order to carry off some provisions when they were in want of them. They no sooner found their captures begin to diminish, than they determined to recover by land what they had lost at sea. The richest and most populous countries of the continent were plundered and laid waste. The culture of lands was equally neglected with navigation; and the Spaniards dared no more appear in their public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, than sail in the latitudes which belonged to them. Among the buccaneers who signalized themselves in this new <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of excursions, Montbar, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, particularly distinguished himself. Having by chance, in his infancy, met with a circumstantial account of the cruelties practised in the conquest of the new world, he conceived an aversion which he carried to a degree of frenzy against that nation which BUC which had committed such enormities. The enthusiasm this spirit of humanity worked him up to, was turned into a rage more cruel than that of the religious fanaticism, to which so many victims had been sacrificed. The manes of these unhappy sufferers seemed to rouse him, and call upon him for vengeance. He had heard some account of the buccaneers, who were said to be the most inveterate enemies to the Spanish name; he therefore embarked on board a ship, in order to join them. In the passage they met with a Spanish vessel; attacked it; and, as it was usual in those times, immediately boarded it. Montbar, with a sabre in his hand, fell upon the enemy; broke through them; and, hurrying twice from one end of the ship to the other, levelled every thing that opposed him. When he had compelled the enemy to surrender, leaving to his companions the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of dividing so rich a booty, he contented himself with the savage <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of contemplating the dead bodies of the Spaniards, lying in heaps together, against whom he had sworn a constant and deadly hatred. Fresh opportunities soon occurred, that enabled him to exert this spirit of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, without extinguishing it. The ship he was in arrived at the coast of St Domingo; where the buccaneers on land immediately applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> some provisions for brandy. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> they offered were of little value, they alleged in excuse, that their enemies had overrun the country, laid waste their settlements, and carried off all they could. "Why (replied Montbar) do you tamely suffer such insults?" "Neither do we (answered they in the same tone); the Spaniards have experienced what kind of men we are, and have therefore taken advantage of the time when we were engaged in hunting. But we were going to join some of our companions, who have been still worse treated than we; and then we shall have warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>." "If you approve of it (answered Montbar), I will head you, not as your commander, but as the foremost to expose myself to danger." The buccaneers perceiving from his appearance that he was such a man as they wanted, cheerfully accepted his offer. The same day they overtook the enemy, and Montbar attacked them with an impetuosity that astonished the bravest. Scarce one Spaniard escaped the effects of his fury. The remaining part of his life was equally distinguished as on this day. The Spaniards suffered so much from him, both by sea and land, that he acquired the name of the Exterminator. His savage disposition, as well as that of the other buccaneers who attended him, having obliged the Spaniards to confine themselves within their settlements, these freebooters resolved to attack them there. This new method of carrying on the war required superior forces; and their associations in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> became more numerous. The first that was considerable was formed by L'olonois, who derived his name from the sands of Olones the place of his birth. From the abject state of a bondsman, he had gradually raised himself to the command of two canoes, with 22 men. With these he was so successful as to take a Spanish frigate on the coast of Cuba. He then repaired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PORT_AU_PRINCE">Port-au-<a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, in which were four ships, fitted out purposely to sail in pursuit of him. He took them, and threw all the crews into the sea, except one man, whom he saved, in order to send him with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the governor of Bucaneer, the Havannah, acquainting him with what he had done, and assuring him that he would treat in the same manner all the Spaniards that should <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into his hands, not excepting the governor himself, if he should be so fortunate as to take him. After this expedition, he ran his canoes and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>-ships <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>, and sailed with his frigate only to the island of Tortuga. Here he met with Michael de Basco, who had distinguished himself by having taken, even under the cannon of Porto-Bello, a Spanish ship, estimated at 218,500l. and by other actions equally brave and daring. These two gave out, that they were going to embark together on an expedition equally glorious and profitable; in consequence of which they soon collected together 440 men. This body of men, the most numerous the buccaneers had yet been able to muster, sailed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Venezuela, which runs up into the country for the space of 50 leagues. The fort that was built at the entrance of it for its defence was taken; the cannon were nailed up; and the whole garrison, consisting of 250 men, put to death. They then reimbarked, and came to Maracaybo, built on the western coast of the lake of the same name, at the distance of ten leagues from its mouth. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which had become flourishing and rich by its trade in skins, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, and cocoa, was deserted.
