The inhabitants had retired with their effects to the other side of the bay. If the buccaneers had not lost a fortnight in riot and debauch, they would have found at Gibraltar, near the extremity of the lake, everything that the inhabitants had secreted to secure it from being plundered. On the contrary, they met with fortifications lately erected, which they had the useless satisfaction of making themselves masters of, at the expense of a great deal of blood; for the inhabitants had already removed to a distance the most valuable part of their property. Exasperated at this disappointment, they set fire to Gibraltar. Maracaybo would have shared the same fate, had it not been ransomed. Besides the sum they received for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, they also carried off with them all the crosses, pictures, and bells of the churches; intending, as they said, to build a chapel in the island of Tortuga, and to consecrate this part of their spoils to sacred purposes. Such was the religion of these barbarous people, who could make no other offering to heaven than that which arose from their robberies and plunder. While they were idly dissipating the spoils they had made on the coast of Venezuela, Morgan, the most renowned of the English buccaneers, sailed from Jamaica to attack Porto-Bello. His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of operations was so well contrived, that he surprised the city, and took it without opposition. The conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> was an object of much greater importance. To secure this, Morgan thought it necessary to sail in the latitudes of Costa-Ricca, to procure some guides in the island of St Catharine's, where the Spaniards confined their malefactors. This place was so strongly fortified, that it ought to have held out for ten years against a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Notwithstanding this, the governor, on the first appearance of the pirates, sent privately to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> measures how he might surrender himself without incurring the imputation of cowardice. The result of this consultation was, that Morgan, in the nighttime, should Bucaneer attack a fort at some distance, and the governor should sally out of the citadel to defend a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of so much consequence; that the assailants should then attack him in the rear, and take him prisoner, which would consequently occasion a surrender of the place. It was agreed that a smart firing should be kept on both sides, without doing mischief to either. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> was admirably carried on. The Spaniards, without being exposed to any danger, appeared to have done their duty; and the bucaniers, after having totally demolished the fortifications, and put on board their vessels a prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of warlike ammunition which they found at St Catharine's, steered their course towards the river Chagre, the only channel that was open to them to arrive at the place which was the object of their utmost wishes. At the entrance of this considerable river, a fort was built upon a steep rock, which the waves of the sea constantly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> against. This bulwark, very difficult of access, was defended by an officer whose extraordinary abilities were equal to his courage, and by a garrison that deserved such a commander. The bucaniers, for the first time, here met with a resistance that could only be equalled by their perseverance; it was a doubtful point, whether they would succeed or be obliged to raise the siege, when a lucky accident happened that proved favourable to their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and their fortune. The commander was killed, and the fort accidentally took fire; the besiegers then taking advantage of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> calamity, made themselves masters of the place. Morgan left his vessels at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, with a sufficient number of men to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> them; and sailed up the river in his sloops for 33 miles, till he came to Cruces, where it ceases to be navigable. He then proceeded by land to Panama, which was only five leagues distant. Upon a large and extensive plain that was before the city, he met with a considerable body of troops, whom he put to flight with the greatest ease, and entered into the city, which was now abandoned. Here were found prodigious treasures concealed in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and caves. Some valuable commodities were also taken upon the boats that were left aground at low water; and in the neighbouring forests were also found several rich deposits. Having burnt the city, they set sail with a great number of prisoners, who were ransomed a few days after, and came to the mouth of the Chagre with a prodigious booty. In 1603, an expedition of the greatest consequence was formed by Van <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSTEND">Ostend</a>, but who had served all his life among the French. His intrepidity would never let him suffer the least signs of cowardice among those who associated with him. In the heat of an engagement, he went about his ship; successively observed his men; and immediately killed those who shrank at the sudden report of a pistol, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, or cannon. This extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> had made him become the terror of the coward and the idol of the brave. In other respects, he readily shared with the men of spirit and bravery the immense riches that were acquired by so truly warlike a disposition. When he went upon these expeditions, he generally sailed in his frigate, which was his own property. But these new designs requiring greater numbers to carry them into execution, he took to his assistance Gramont, Bucaneer, Godfrey, and Jonqué, three Frenchmen distinguished by their exploits; and Lawrence de Graff, a Dutchman, who had signalized himself still more than they. Twelve hundred bucaniers joined themselves to these famous commanders, and sailed in six vessels for Vera Cruz. The darkness of the night favoured their landing, which was effected at three leagues from the place, where they arrived without being discovered. The governor, the fort, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, and the posts of the greatest consequence, every thing, in short, that could occasion any resistance, was taken by the break of day. All the citizens, men, women, and children, were shut up in the churches, whither they had fled for shelter. At the door of each <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> were placed barrels of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a> to blow up the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. A bucanier, with a lighted <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a>, was to set fire to it upon the least appearance of an insurrection. While the city was kept in such terror, it was easily pillaged; and after the bucaniers had carried off what was most valuable, they made a proposal to the citizens who were kept prisoners in the churches to ransom their lives and liberties by a contribution of 437,500l. These unfortunate people, who had neither ate nor drank for three days, cheerfully accepted the terms that were offered them. Half of the money was paid the same day; the other part was expected from the internal parts of the country; when there appeared on an eminence a considerable body of troops advancing, and near the port a fleet of 17 ships from Europe. At the sight of this armament, the bucaniers, without any marks of surprise, retired quietly, with 1500 slaves they had carried off with them as a trifling indemnification for the rest of the money they expected, the settling of which they referred to a more favourable opportunity. Their retreat was equally daring. They boldly sailed through the midst of the Spanish fleet; which let them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without firing a single gun, and were in fact rather afraid of being attacked and beaten. The Spaniards would not probably have escaped so easily and with no other inconvenience but what arose from their fears, if the vessels of the pirates had not been laden with silver, or if the Spanish fleet had been freighted with any other effects but such merchandise as was little valued by these pirates. A year had scarce elapsed since their return from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, when, on a sudden, they were all seized with the rage of going to plunder the country of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>. It is probable that the hopes of finding greater treasures upon a sea little frequented, than on one long exposed to piracies of this kind, was the cause of this expedition. But it is somewhat remarkable, that both the English and French, and the particular associations of these two nations, had projected this plan at the same time, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>, intercourse, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of acting in concert with each other. About 4000 men were employed in this expedition. Some of them came by Terra Firma, others by the straits of Magellan, to the place that was the object of their wishes. If the intrepidity of these barbarians had been directed, under the influence of a skilful and respectable commander, to one single uniform end, it is certain that they would have deprived the Spaniards of this important But their natural character was an invincible obstacle to so rare an union; for they always formed themselves into several distinct bodies, sometimes even so few in number as ten or twelve, who acted together, or separated, as the most trifling caprice directed. Grognier, Lecuyer, Picard, and Le Sage, were the most distinguished officers among the French; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Samms, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Wilner, and Towley, among the English. Such of these adventurers as had got into the South sea by the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a>, seized upon the first vessel they found upon the coast. Their associates, who had sailed in their own vessels, were not much better provided. Weak, however, as they were, they beat several times the squadrons that were fitted out against them. But these victories were prejudicial to them, as they interrupted their navigation. When there were no more ships to be taken, they were continually obliged to make descents upon the coasts to get provisions, or to go by land in order to plunder those cities where the booty was secured. They successively attacked Seppa, Puebla-Nuevo, Leon, Realejo, Puebla-Viejo, Chiriquita, Lesparso, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, Villia, Nicoy, Tecanteca, Mucmeluna, Chiloteca, New-Segovia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUAYAQUIL">Guayaquil</a>, the most considerable of all these places. Many of them were taken by surprise; and most of them deserted by their inhabitants, who fled at the sight of the enemy. As soon as they took a town, it was directly set on fire, unless a sum proportioned to its value was given to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> it. The prisoners taken in battle were massacred without mercy, if they were not ransomed by the governor or some of the inhabitants: gold, pearls, or precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, were the only things accepted of for the payment of their ransom. Silver being too common, and too weighty for its current value, would have been troublesome to them. The chances of fortune, that seldom leave guilt unpunished, nor adversity without a compensation for its suffering, atoned for the crimes committed in the conquest of the new world, and the Indians were amply revenged of the Spaniards. While such piracies were committed on the southern ocean, the northern was threatened with the same by Gramont. He was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, by birth a gentleman, and had distinguished himself in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> capacity in Europe; but his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for wine, gaming, and women, had obliged him to join the pirates. He was, however, affable, polite, generous, and eloquent; he was endowed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> judgment, and was a person of approved valour; which soon made him be considered as the chief of the French buccaneers. As soon as it was known that he had taken up arms, he was immediately joined by a number of brave men. The governor of St Domingo, who had at length prevailed upon his master to approve of the project, equally wise and just, of fixing the pirates to some place, and inducing them to become cultivators, was desirous of preventing the concerted expedition, and forbade it in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s name. Gramont, who had a greater share of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than his associates, was not on that account more inclined to comply, and sternly repelled: "How can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> disapprove of a design he is unacquainted with, and which has been planned only a few days ago?" This answer highly pleased all the buccaneers; who directly embarked, in 1685, to attack <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPEACHY">Campeachy</a>. They landed without opposition. But at some distance from the coast, they were attacked by 800 Spaniards, who were beaten and pursued to the town; where both the parties entered at the same time. The cannon they found there was immediately levelled against the citadel. As it had very little effect, they were contriving some stratagem to enable them to become masters of the place, when intelligence was brought that it was abandoned. There remained in it only a gunner, an Englishman; and an officer of such signal courage, that he chose rather to expose himself to the greatest extremities, than basely to fly from the place with the rest. The commander of the buccaneers received him with marks of distinction, generously released him, gave him up all his effects, and besides complimented him with some valuable presents: such influence have courage and fidelity even on the minds of those who seem to violate all the rights of society. The conquerors of Campeachy spent two months in searching all the environs of the city, for 12 or 15 leagues, carrying off every thing that the inhabitants, in their flight, thought they had preserved. When all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> they had collected from every quarter was deposited in the ships, a proposal was made to the governor of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, who still kept the field with 900 men, to ransom his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city. His refusal determined them to burn it, and demolish the citadel. The French, on the festival of St Louis, were celebrating the anniversary of their king; and in the transports of their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIOTISM">patriotism</a>, intoxication, and national love of their prince, they burnt to the value of a million of logwood; a part, and a very considerable one too, of the spoil they had made. After this singular and extravagant instance of folly, of which Frenchmen only could boast, they returned to St Domingo. In 1697, 1200 buccaneers were induced to join a squadron of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ships that sailed from Europe under the command of Pointis, to attack the famous city of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. This was the most difficult enterprise that could be attempted in the new world. The situation of the port, the strength of the place, the badness of the climate, were so many obstacles that seemed insurmountable to any but such men as the buccaneers were. But every obstacle yielded to their valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>: the city was taken, and booty gained to the amount of 1,750,000l. Their rapacious commander, however, deprived them of the advantages resulting from their success. He scrupled not, as soon as they set sail, to offer 5250l. for the share of those who had been the chief instruments in procuring him so considerable a spoil. The buccaneers, exasperated at this treatment, resolved immediately to board the vessel called the Sceptre, where Pointis himself was, and which at that time was too far distant from the rest of the ships to expect to be assisted by them. This avaricious commander was upon the point of being massacred, when one of the malecontents cried out: "Brethren, why should we attack this rascal? he has carried off nothing that belongs to us. He has left our share at Carthagena, and there we must go to recover it." This proposal was received received with general applause. A savage joy at once succeeded that gloomy melancholy which had seized them; and without further deliberation all their ships sailed towards the city. As soon as they had entered the city without meeting with any resistance, they shut up all the men in the great church; and exacted payment of 218,750l. the amount of their share of booty which they had been defrauded of; promising to retreat immediately upon their compliance, but threatening the most dreadful vengeance if they refused. Upon this, the most venerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in the city mounted the pulpit, and made <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all the influence his character, his authority, and his eloquence gave to him, to persuade his hearers to yield up without reserve all the gold, silver, and jewels they had. The collection which was made after the sermon, not furnishing the sum required, the city was ordered to be plundered. At length, after amassing all they could, these adventurers set sail; when unfortunately they met with a fleet of Dutch and English ships, both which nations were then in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with Spain. Several of the pirates were either taken or sunk, with all the cargo they had on board their ships; the rest escaped to St Domingo. Such was the last memorable event in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the buccaneers. The separation of the English and French, when the war, on account of the prince of Orange, divided the two nations; the successful means they both made use of to promote the cultivation of land among their colonies, by the assistance of these enterprising men; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> they showed in fixing the most distinguished among them, and entrusting them with civil and military employments; the protection they were both under the necessity of affording to the Spanish settlements, which till then had been a general object of plunder: all these circumstances, and various others, besides the impossibility there was of supplying the place of these remarkable men, who were continually dropping off, concurred to put an end to a society as extraordinary as ever existed. Without any regular system, without laws, without any degree of subordination, and even without any fixed revenue, they became the astonishment of that <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which they lived, as they will be also of posterity.

BUCCELLARIUS

Pages 856-856

an order of soldiery under the Greek emperors, appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> and distribute the ammunition <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>; though authors are somewhat divided as to their office and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Among the Visigoths buccellarius was a general name for a client <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vassal who lived at the expense of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. Some give the denomination to parasites in the courts of princes, some make them the body-guards of emperors, and some fancy they were only such as emperors employed in putting persons to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> privately.

BUCCELLATUM

Pages 856-856

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> writers, denotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> biscuit baked hard and dry, both for lightness and keeping. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">Soldiers</a> always carried with them enough for a fortnight, and sometimes much longer, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that military <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> was kept up.

BUCCINA

Pages 856-856

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> musical and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. It is usually taken for a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is confirmed by Festus, by his defining it a Buccina crooked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, played on like a trumpet. Vegetius observes, that the buccina was bent in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a>, in which respect it differed from the tuba <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trumpet. It is very hard to distinguish it from the cornu or horn, unless it was something less, and not quite so crooked; yet it certainly was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, because we never read of the cornu in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with the watch, but only the buccina. Besides, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the buccina was sharper, and to be heard much farther than either the cornu or the tuba. In Scripture, the like instrument, used both in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and in the temple, was called rams-horns, kiren jobel, and sepheroth hagigobelim. This instrument was in use among the Jews to proclaim their feast-days, new-moons, jubilees, sabbatic years, and the like. At Lacedemon, notice was given by the buccina when it was <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and the like was done at Rome, where the grandees had a buccina blown both before and after they sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. The sound of the buccina was called buccinum, or bucinus; and the musician who played on it was called buccinator.

BUCCLEUGH

Pages 856-856

a village in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Selkirk in Scotland, from which the noble family of Scott have the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a>.

BUCENTAUR

Pages 856-856

a galeas <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> galley of the doge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, adorned with fine pillars on both sides, and girt over from the prow to the stern. This vessel is covered over head with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, made of purple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. In it the doge receives the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> lords and persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> that go to Venice, accompanied with the ambassadors and counsellors of state, and all the senators seated on benches by him. The same vessel serves also in the magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of Ascension <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, on which the doge of Venice throws a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RING">ring</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to espouse it, and to denote his dominion over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Venice. Bucentaurs is also the name of a ship, as great and as magnificent as that of the Venetians, built by order of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and launched on a lake which is six leagues in length.

BUCEPHALA

Pages 856-858
or Bucephalos, in Ancient Geography, a town built by Alexander, on the west side of the Hydaspis, a river of the Hither India, in memory of his horse Bucephalus, which was killed in the action with Porus, after crossing that river. Others say, this horse died of age, 30 years old; and not in the battle, but some time after. His being branded or marked on the buttock with the head of an ox, gave rise to his name (Hesychius).—This generous animal, who had so long shared the toils and dangers of his master, had formerly received signal marks of royal regard. Having disappeared in the country of the Uxii, Alexander issued a proclamation, commanding his horse to be restored, otherwise he would ravage the whole country with fire and sword. This command Bucer was immediately obeyed, "So dear," says Arrian, "was Bucephalus to Alexander, and so terrible was Alexander to the Barbarians." Bucer, Martin, one of the first authors of the reformation at Strasburg, was born in 1491, in Alsace; and took the religious habit of St Dominic, at seven years of age: but meeting afterward with the writings of Martin Luther, and comparing them with the Scriptures, he began to entertain doubts concerning several things in the Romish religion. After some conferences with Luther at Heidelberg in 1521, he adopted most of his sentiments; but in 1532, he gave the preference to those of Zwinglius. He assisted in many conferences concerning religion; and in 1548 was sent for to Augsburg to sign the agreement between the Papists and Protestants, called the interim. His warm opposition to this project exposed him to many difficulties and hardships; the news of which reaching England, where his fame had already arrived, Cranmer archbishop of Canterbury gave him an invitation to come over, which he readily accepted. In 1549, a handsome apartment was assigned him in the university of Cambridge, and a salary to teach theology. King Edward VI. had the greatest regard for him. Being told that he was very sensible of the cold of the climate, and suffered much for want of a German stove, he sent him 100 crowns to purchase one. He died of a complication of disorders in 1551; and was buried at Cambridge with great funeral pomp. Five years after, in the reign of Queen Mary, his body was dug up, and publicly burnt, and his tomb demolished; but it was afterwards set up by order of Queen Elizabeth. He composed many works, among which are commentaries on the evangelists and gospels. Buceros. See Ornithology Index. Buchan, a district of Scotland, lying partly in the shire of Aberdeen and partly in that of Banff: it gives the title of earl to the noble and ancient family of Erskine. Buchanan, George, the best Latin poet of his time, perhaps inferior to none since the Augustan age, was born in February 1506. This accomplished scholar and distinguished wit was not descended of a family remarkable for its rank. He had no occasion for the splendour of ancestry. He wanted not a reflected greatness, the equivocal, and too often the only ornament of the rich and noble. The village of Killearn, in Stirlingshire, Scotland, was the place of his nativity; and the abject poverty in which his father died might have confined him to toil at the lowest employments of life, if the generosity of an uncle had not assisted him in his education, and enabled him to pursue for two years his studies at Paris. But that short space was scarcely elapsed, when the death of his benefactor made it necessary that he should return to his own country, and forsake, for a time, the paths of science. He was yet under his 20th year, and surrounded with the horrors of indigence. In this extremity, he enlisted as a common soldier under John duke of Albany, who commanded the troops which France had sent to assist Scotland in the war it waged, at this period, against England. But nature had not destined him to be a hero. He was disgusted with the fatigues of one campaign; and, fortunately, John Major, then Buchanan professor of philosophy at St Andrew's, hearing of his necessity and his merit, afforded him a temporary relief. He now became the pupil of John Mair, a celebrated teacher in the same university, under whom he studied the subtleties of logic: and contracting an attachment to his master, he followed him to Paris. There, after having encountered many difficulties, he was invited to teach grammar in the college of St Barbe. In this slavish occupation he was found by the earl of Cassillis; with whom having remained five years at Paris, he returned to Scotland. He next acted as preceptor to the famous earl of Murray, the natural son of James V. But while he was forming this nobleman for public affairs, he found that his life was in danger; and from enemies, whose vindictive rage could suffer no abatement, and who would not scruple the most dishonourable means of gratifying it. The scandalous lives of the clergy had, it seems, excited his indignation; and, more than reasoning or argument, had estranged him from the errors of Popery. The Franciscan monks, in return to the beautiful but poignant satires he had written against them, branded him with the appellation of atheist; a term which the religious of all denominations are too apt indiscriminately to lavish where they have conceived a prejudice; and, not satisfied with the outrage of abuse and calumny, they conspired his destruction. Cardinal Beaton gave orders to apprehend him, and bribed King James with a very considerable sum to permit his execution. He was seized upon accordingly; and the first genius of his age was about to perish by the halter, or by fire, to satisfy a malignant resentment, when, escaping the vigilance of his guards, he fled into England. Henry VIII. at all times the slave of caprice and passion, was then burning, on the same day, and at the same stake, the Lutheran and the Papist. His court did not suit a philosopher or a satirist. After a short stay, Buchanan crossed the sea to France; and, to his extreme disappointment, found at Paris, Cardinal Beaton, as ambassador from Scotland. He retired privately to Bourdeaux, dreading, perhaps, new misfortunes, and concerned that he could not prosecute his studies in obscurity and silence. Here he met Andrew Govea, a Portuguese of great learning and worth, with whom he had formerly been acquainted during his travels, and who was now employed in teaching a public school. He disdained not to act as the assistant of his friend; and during the three years he resided at this place, he composed the tragedies which do him so much honour. It was here, also, that he wrote some of the most pleasant of those poems, in which he has rallied the muses, and threatened to forsake them, as not being able to maintain their votary. About this time, too, he presented a copy of verses to the emperor Charles V. who happened to pass through Bourdeaux. His enemies, meanwhile, were not inactive. Cardinal Beaton, wrote about him to the archbishop of Bourdeaux; and by every motive which a cunning and a wicked heart can invent, he invited him to punish the most pestilential of all heretics. The archbishop, however, was not so violent as the cardinal. On inquiring into the matter, he was convinced that the poet had committed a very small impropriety; and allowed Buchanan lowered himself to be pacified. But fortune was not long to continue her smiles. Andrew Govea being called by the king of Portugal, his master, to establish an academy at Coimbra, he entreated Buchanan to accompany him. He obtained his request; and had not been a year in his own country, when he died, and left his associate exposed to the malice of his inveterate enemies the monks. They loudly objected to him, that he was a Lutheran; that he had written poems against the Franciscans; and that he had been guilty of the abominable crime of eating flesh in Lent. He was confined to a monastery till he should learn what these men fancied to be religion; and they enjoined him to translate the Psalms of David into Latin verse; a task which every man of taste knows with what admirable skill and genius he performed. On obtaining his liberty, he had the offer of a speedy promotion from the king of Portugal: the issue of which, his aversion to the clergy did not allow him to wait. He hastened to England; but the perturbed state of affairs during the minority of Edward VI. not giving him the promise of any lasting security, he set out for France. There he had not been long, when he published his Jephtha, which his necessities made him dedicate to the marshal de Brissac. This patron did not want generosity, and could judge of merit. He sent him to Piedmont, as preceptor to his son Timoleon de Cossi. In this employ he continued several years; and during the leisure it afforded him, he fully examined the controversies which now agitated Europe; and put the last hand to many of the most admired of his smaller poems. When his pupil had no longer any use for him, he passed into Scotland, and made an open profession of the reformed faith. But he soon quitted his native country for France; which appears to have been more agreeable to his taste. Queen Mary, however, having determined that he should have the charge of educating her son, recalled him: and till the prince should arrive at a proper age, he was nominated to the principality of St Andrew's. His success as James's preceptor is well known. When it was reproached to him, that he had made his majesty a pedant; "It is a wonder (he replied) that I have made so much of him." Mackenzie relates a story concerning his tutelage of his pedantic majesty, which shows under what authority Buchanan held his pupil, and at the same time the degree of his veneration for royalty. The young king being one day at play with his fellow pupil the master of Erskine, Buchanan, who was then reading, desired them to make less noise. Finding that they disregarded his admonition, he told his majesty, if he did not hold his tongue, he would certainly whip his breech. The king replied, he would be glad to see who would bell the cat, alluding to the fable. Buchanan, in a passion, threw the book from him, and gave his majesty a sound flogging. The old countess of Mar, who was in the next apartment, rushed into the room, and taking the king in her arms, asked how he dared to lay his hand on the Lord's anointed. Buchanan's answer is too indelicate to be repeated. On the misfortunes that befell the amiable but imprudent Mary, he went over to the party of the earl of Murray; and at his earnest desire he was prevailed upon to write his "Detection;" a work which his greatest admirers have read with regret. Having been Buchanan sent with other commissioners to England, against his mistress, he was, on his return, rewarded with the abbacy of Cross Regal; made director to the chancery; and some time after lord privy s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council and privy seal. He was likewise rewarded by Queen Elizabeth with a pension of 100l. a-year. The last twelve years of his life he employed in composing his History of Scotland. After having vied with almost all the more eminent of the Latin poets, he contested with Livy and Sallust the palm of eloquence and political sagacity. But it is to be remembered with pain, that, like the former of these historians, he was not always careful to preserve himself from the charge of partiality. In the year 1582, he expired at Edinburgh, in the 76th year of his age. Various writers who have mentioned this author, speak of him in very different language, according to their religious and political principles. From his works, however, it is evident, that, both as a Latin poet and prose writer, he hath been rarely equalled since the reign of Augustus; nor is he less deserving of remembrance as a friend to the natural liberties of mankind, in opposition to usurpation and tyranny. "The happy genius of Buchanan (says Dr Robertson), equally formed to excel in prose and verse, more various, more original, and more elegant, than that of almost any other modern who writes in Latin, reflects, with regard to this particular, the greatest lustre on his country." To his memory an obelisk 100 feet high was erected by subscription in 1788, at Killearn the place of his nativity, designed by Mr J. Craig, nephew to the celebrated poet Thomson. The following is a list of his works. 1. Rerum Scoticarum, &c. 2. Psalmorum Davidis paraphrasis poetica. 3. De jure regni apud Scotos Dialogus. 4. Psalmus civ. cum judicio Barclaii, &c. 5. Psalmus cxx. cum analysi organica Beuzeri. 6. Baptistes, sive Calumnia. 7. Alcestis, tragedia. 8. Tragediae sacrae et externae. 9. De Caleto recepto carmen, apud Stephan. 10. Franciscanus et Fratres, &c. 11. Elegia, Silvae, &c. 12. De spera Herbornae. 13. Poemata. 14. Satyra in cardinalem Lotharingium. 15. Rudimenta grammatices, Tho. Linacri ex Anglico sermone in Latinum versae. 16. An admonition to the true lords. 17. De prosodia. 18. Chamaleon, 1572. 19. Ad viros sui seculi epistolae. 20. Literae reginae Scoticae ad com. Bothwell. 21. A detection of the doings of Mary queen of Scots, and of James earl of Bothwell, against Henry Lord Darnly. 22. Vita ab ipso scripta biennio ante mortem, cum commentario D. Rob. Sibbaldi, M.D. 23. Life of Mary queen of Scots. These have been severally printed often, and in various countries. An edition of them all collected together was printed at Edinburgh in 1704, in 2 vols folio.

a small town of Suabia in Germany, seated on the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a>, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9° 20'. N. Lat. 47° 41'.

BUCHANNESS

Pages 858-858

a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> promontory of Scotland, which is the farthest point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERHEAD">Peterhead</a>, and the most eastern of all Scotland. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 30. N. Lat. 57. 28.

BUCHAREST

Pages 858-859

a pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, seated in the middle of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, and the ordinary residence of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPODAR">hospodar</a>. The houses are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> and very ill built, except a few that belong to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons. In 1716, a party of Germans sent from Transylvania entered this town, and took the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> prisoner with all his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and carried them off. This expedition was the more easily performed, as several lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> had a secret intelligence with the governor of Transylvania. This prince had no other way to regain his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, but by giving up that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Walachia, which lies between the river Aluth and Transylvania, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of Germany, by the peace concluded at Passarowitz in 1718. The Germans again entered the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of his dominions, and levied excessive contributions. But affairs took another turn after the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Crotska in 1737; for the emperor was obliged to restore this part of Walachia to the hospodar. Bucharest contains about 62,000 inhabitants. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26° 30'. N. Lat. 44° 32'.

BUCHAW

Pages 858-858

a town of Germany, seated on the river Tedesse, 22 miles south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ULM">Ulm</a>. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>, whose abbess had formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in the diets of the empire. The town is subject to Wirtemberg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 37. N. Lat. 48. 5.

BUCIOCHE

Pages 859-859

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of woollen cloth manufactured in Provence in France, which the French ships carry to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>.

BUCK

Pages 859-859

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> horned beast of venery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> is denominated a doe. See Cervus and Buck-Hunting. Buck, is also applied to the male of the hare and rabbit kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEPUS">Lepus</a>, and Hare-Hunting. BUCK-Bean. See Menyanthes, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BUCK-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THORN">Thorn</a>. See Rhamnus, Botany Index. BUCK-Wheat. See Polygonum, Botany Index.

BUCKENHAM

Pages 859-859

New, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> in England, which formerly had a strong castle, but now demolished. It is seated in a flat, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 10'. N. Lat. 52° 30'. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 656 in 1811.

BUCKET

Pages 859-859

a small portable vessel to hold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, often made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> for its lightness and easy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of fire. It is also the vessel let <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> into a well, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the sides of ships, to fetch up water.

BUCKING

Pages 859-859

the first operation in the whitening of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> yarn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cloth.

BUCKINGHAM

Pages 859-859

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town of Buckinghamshire in England, stands in a low ground, on the river Ouse, by which it is almost surrounded, and over which there are three handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-bridges. The town contained 3500 inhabitants in 1811, and sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It seems, however, to have been but an inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> at the Conquest; for, according to Doomsday-book, it paid only for one hide, and had but 26 burgesses. Edward the elder fortified it in the year 918 against the incursions of the Danes, with a rampart and turrets. It also had formerly a castle in the middle of the town, of which no vestiges now remain. The shrine of St Rumbald, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of fishermen, preserved in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, was held in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>-gaol stands in this town, and here the assizes are sometimes kept. It was formerly a staple for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, but that advantage it hath now lost. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a> and 12 burgesses, who are the sole electors of the members. In its neighbourhood are many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> upon the Ouse. W. Buckingham-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 58°. N. Lat. 51° 30'.

BUCKINGHAM-SHIRE

Pages 859-859

(supposed to derive its name from the Saxon word Buc, denoting a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">hart</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> buck) an inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of England. During the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the landing of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> it was included in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of Catteuchlani; and after their conquest it was included in their third <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Flavia Cesariensis. During the heptarchy it belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Mercia, which commenced in 582, and terminated in 827, having had 18 kings; and it is now included in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> circuit, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>, and the province of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>; south by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a>; east by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>; and west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. It is of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, whose greatest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> is from north to south. It contains 441,000 acres; has above 111,400 inhabitants, 185 parishes, 73 vicarages; is 49 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, 18 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and 109 in circumference. It has 15 market-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AYLESBURY">Aylesbury</a>, the county towns, Marlow, Newport-Pagnell, Winslow, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WENDOVER">Wendover</a>, Beaconsfield, Wiccomb, Chesham, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERSHAM">Amersham</a>, Stony <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRATFORD">Stratford</a>, Colnbrook, Ivingho, Oulney, Risborough; besides the considerable villages of Eaton and Fenny Stratford, and 613 others inferior. It is divided into eight <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>, provides 560 men for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>, sends 14 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>-men, and pays 12 parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, Ouse, Coln, Wicham, Amersham, Isis, Tame, and Loddon. Its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> produce is bone-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, corn, fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, and breeding rams. The most noted places are the Chiltern Hills, Vale of Aylesbury, Bernwood Forrest, Wooburn-Heath, and 15 parks. The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> is generally good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> mostly chalk or marle. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Buckinghamshire amounted to 117,650 in 1811. See Buckinghamshire, Supplement.

BUCKLE

Pages 859-859

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>. The buckle was so much esteemed in former times, that few persons of repute and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> wore their girdles without it; and it may be considered, in coats of arms, as a token of the surety, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the bearer.

BUCKLER

Pages 859-860

a piece of defensive armour used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. It was worn on the left arm, and composed of wickers woven together, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> wood of the lightest sort, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and fortified with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or other metal. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> was sometimes round, sometimes oval, and sometimes almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. Most of the bucklers were curiously adorned with all sorts of figures of birds and beasts, as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, lions; nor of these only, but of the gods, of the celestial bodies, and all the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was derived from the heroic times, and from them communicated to the Grecians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and Barbarians. The scutum, or Roman buckler, was of wood, the parts being joined together with little plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and BUCKLER and the whole covered with a bull's hide. An iron plate went about it without, to keep off blows; and another within, to hinder it from taking any damage by lying on the ground. In the middle was an iron boss or umbo jutting out, very serviceable to glance off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and darts; and sometimes to press violently upon the enemy, and drive all before them. They are to be distinguished from the clypei, which were less, and quite round, belonging more properly to other nations, though for some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> used by the Romans. The scuta themselves were of two kinds; the ovata, and the imbricata: the former is a plain oval figure; the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> inward like half a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>. Polybius makes the scuta four feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and Plutarch calls them ἀποδεξιας, reaching <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the feet. And it is very probable that they covered almost the whole body, since in Livy we meet with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who stood on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, sometimes sleeping with their head on their shield, having fixed the other <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. Votive Bucklers: Those consecrated to the gods and hung up in their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, either in commemoration of some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>, or as a thanksgiving for a victory obtained over an enemy; whose bucklers, taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, were offered as a trophy.

BUCKOR

Pages 860-860

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul. It is seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a>, on the banks of which there are corn and cattle; but the west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, which is bounded by Sagestan in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>. The inhabitants are strong, robust, and apt to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a>; for which reason the Mogul has a garrison at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town called Buckor, which is seated in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> made by the river Indus. They are all Mahometans, and drive a great trade in cotton cloth and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> commodities. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 70. 5. N. Lat. 28. 20.

BUCKRAM

Pages 860-860

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth stiffened with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a>, used in the making of garments to keep them in the form intended. It is also used in the bodies of women's gowns; and it often serves to make wrappers to cover cloths, serges, and such other merchandises, in order to preserve them, and keep them from the dust, and their colours from fading. Buckrams are sold wholesale by the dozen of small pieces <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remnants, each about four ells <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> according to the piece from which they are cut. Sometimes they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> new pieces of linen cloth to make buckrams, but most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> old sheets and old pieces of sails.

BUCKSTALL

Pages 860-860

a toil to take deer, which must not be kept by any body that has not a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a> of his own, under penalties.

BUCOLIC

Pages 860-860

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a kind of poem relating to shepherds and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> affairs, which, according to the most generally received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, took its rise in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Bucolics, says Vossius, have some conformity with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>. Like it, they are pictures and imitations of ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; with this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, however, that comedy represents the manners of the inhabitants of cities, and bucolics the occupations of country people. Sometimes, continues he, this last poem is in form of a monologue, and sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. Sometimes there is <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTION">action</a> in it, and sometimes only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a>; and sometimes it is composed both of action and narration. The hexameter <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> is the most proper for bucolics in the Greek and Latin tongues. Moschus, Bion, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, are the most renowned of the ancient bucolic poets.

BUDA

Pages 860-861

the Beglerbegliec of, was one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> governments of the Turks in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It included all the countries of Upper <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Teisse and Danube, and between <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIA">Agria</a> and Novigrad; all Lower Hungary from Gran and Canisca, the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Slavonia, and almost all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>: but a good part of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> now belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. BUDÆUS, WILLIAM, the most learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in France in the 15th century, was descended of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and illustrious family, and born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1467. He was placed young under masters; but barbarism prevailed so much in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of Paris, that Budæus took a dislike to them, and spent his whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in idleness, till his parents sent him to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. Here he passed three years without adding to his knowledge; for his parents sending for him back to Paris, found his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> no less than before, and his reluctance to study, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> and other useless pleasures, much greater. They talked no more to him of learning of any kind; and as he was heir to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fortune, left him to follow his own inclinations. He was passionately fond of hunting, and took <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in horses, dogs, and hawks. The fire of youth beginning to cool, and his usual pleasures to pall upon his senses, he was seized with an irresistible <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for study. He immediately disposed of all his hunting equipage, and even abstracted himself from all business to apply himself wholly to study; in which he made, without any assistance, a very rapid and amazing progress, particularly in the Latin and Greek languages. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which gained him greatest reputation was his treatise de Asse. His erudition and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> birth were not his only advantages; he had an uncommon share of piety, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, gentleness, and good-breeding. The French <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, Francis I. often sent for him; and at his persuasion, and that of Du Bellay, founded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of France, for teaching the languages and sciences. The king sent him to Rome with the character of his <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to Leo X. and in 1522 made him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of requests. The same year he was chosen provost of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. He died at Paris in 1540. His works, making four volumes in folio, were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1557. BUDDÆUS, JOHN FRANCIS, a celebrated Lutheran divine, and one of the most learned men Germany has produced, was born in 1667, at Anclam, a town of Pomerania, where his father was minister. He was at first Greek and Latin professor at Colburg; afterwards professor of morality and politics in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>; and at length, in 1705, professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Jena, where he fixed, and where he died, after having acquired a very great reputation. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works are, 1. A large historical German <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>. 2. Historia ecclesiastica Veteris Testamenti, 2 vols 4to. 3. Elementa philosophiae practice, instrumentalis, et theoreticae, 3 vols 8vo, which has had a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of editions, because in most of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of Germany the professors take this work for the text of their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a>. 4. Selecta juris naturae et gentium. 5. Miscellanea sacra, 3 vols 4to. 6. Isagoge historico-theologica <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AD">ad</a> theologiam universam, singulare ejus partes, 2 vols 4to; which is much valued by the Lutherans. 7. A treatise on atheism and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>.

BUDDESDALE

Pages 861-861
or BETTISDALE, a town of Suffolk in England, seated in a dale or valley, and its street takes in a good part of Ricking, all which together make up the town; for of itself it is but a hamlet, having a small chapel, and an endowed grammar-school, to which belong certain scholarships, assigned to Bennet or Corpus Christi college in Cambridge, being the gift of Sir Nicholas Bacon, lord keeper of the great seal. E. Long. 1. 8. N. Lat. 52. 25.

BUDDLE

Pages 861-861

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> frame of boards, used in washing metallic ores. BUDDLEIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BUDELICH

Pages 861-861

a town of Germany, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It is seated on the little river Traen, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 55. N. Lat. 49. 52.

BUDGE-BARRELS

Pages 861-861

among engineers, small barrels well hoop'd, with only one head; on the other end is nailed a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, to draw together upon strings like a purse. Their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is for carrying powder along with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>; being less dangerous, and easier carried, than whole barrels. They are likewise used upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of mortars for holding <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> powder.

BUDGELI

Pages 861-862

EUSTACE, Esq. an ingenious and polite writer, was the son of Gilbert Budgell, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and was born at St Thomas, near <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a>, about the year 1685. He was educated at Christchurch <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; from which he removed to the Inner Temple, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: but instead of studying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>, for which his father intended him, he applied to polite literature; kept <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with the gentlest persons in town; and particularly contracted a strict intimacy with the ingenious Mr Addison, who was first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to his mother, and who, on his being made secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wharton, lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, took him with him as one of the clerks of his office. Mr Budgell, who was about 20 years of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and had read the classics, and the works of the best English, French, and Italian authors, now became concerned with Sir Richard Steele and Mr Addison in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the Tatler, as he had, soon after, a share in writing the Spectators, where all the papers written by him are marked with an X; and when that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was completed, he had likewise a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">Guardian</a>, where his performances are marked with an asterisk. He was afterwards made under secretary to Mr Addison, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> secretary to the lords justices of Ireland, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. Soon after, he was chosen a member of the Irish <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and in 1717, Mr Addison, having become <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> secretary of state in England, procured him the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of accountant and comptroller general of the revenue in Ireland. But the next year, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Bolton being appointed lord-lieutenant, Mr Budgell wrote a lampoon against Mr Webster, his secretary, in which his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> himself was not spared; and upon all occasions treated that <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> with the utmost contempt. This imprudent step was the primary cause of his ruin: for the duke of Bolton, in support of his secretary, got him removed from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of accountant-general; upon which, returning to England, he, contrary to the advice of Mr Addison, published his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in a pamphlet, entitled, "A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the lord * * *, from Eustace Budgell, Esq. accountant-general," &c. Mr Addison had now resigned the seals, and was retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> for the sake of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>: Mr Budgell Budgell had also lost several other powerful friends who had been taken off by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; particularly the lord <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Sunderland: he, however, made several attempts to succeed at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but was constantly kept <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by the duke of Bolton. In the year 1720 he lost 20,000l. by the South-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> scheme, and afterwards spent 5000l. more in unsuccessful attempts to get into parliament. This completed his ruin. He at length employed himself in writing pamphlets against the ministry, and wrote many papers in the Craftsman. In 1733, he began a weekly pamphlet, called The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEE">Bee</a>; which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for above 100 numbers, printed in eight volumes 8vo. During the progress of this work, Dr Tindal's death happened, by whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> Mr Budgell had 2000l. left him; and the world being surprised at such a gift from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> entirely unrelated to him, to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the next heir, a nephew, and the continuator of Rapin's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of England, immediately imputed it to his making the will himself. Thus the satirist: Let Budgell <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> low Grub-street on my quill, And write whate'er he please except my will. It was thought he had some hand in publishing Dr Tindal's Christianity as old as the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">Creation</a>; for he often talked of another additional volume on the same subject, but never published it. After the cessation of the Bee, Mr Budgell became so involved in law-suits, that he was reduced to a very unhappy situation. He got himself called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and attended for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the courts of law; but finding himself unable to make any progress, and being distrest to the utmost, he determined at length to make away with himself. Accordingly, in the year 1736, he took a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> at Somerset-stairs, after filling his pockets with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; ordered the waterman to shoot the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and, while the boat was going under, threw himself into the river. He had several days before been visibly distracted in his mind. Upon his bureau was found a slip of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, on which were these words: What Cato did, and Addison approv'd, Cannot be wrong. Besides the above works, he wrote a Translation of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">Characters</a>. He was never married; but left one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, who afterwards assumed his name, and became an actress in Drury-lane.

BUDINUS

Pages 862-862

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a mountain of Sarmatia Europæa, from which the more northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the Borysthenes is said to take its rise, according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. But this is contradicted by later accounts. Now Podolia. BUDNÆANS, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, so called from the name of their leader, Simon Budnaeus. They not only denied all kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> worship to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, but asserted, that he was not begotten by any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> of divine power; being born, like other men, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> way. Budnaeus was deposed from his ministerial functions in the year 1584, and publicly excommunicated, with all his disciples; but afterwards abandoning his peculiar sentiments, he was readmitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-SOCINIAN">Socinian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. Crellius ascribes the origin of the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Neuser. BUDOÀ, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, with a bishop's see, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It is seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CATTARO">Cattaro</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Dulugno, on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>; and is an important fortress, where the Venetians formerly kept a strong garrison. In 1667, it suffered greatly by an earthquake; and in 1686 was besieged by Soliman, basha of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCUTARI">Scutari</a>; but General Cornaro obliged him to raise the siege. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19. 22. N. Lat. 42. 12.

BUDRIO

Pages 862-862

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the Bolognese. The adjacent fields produce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, which renders the town of more <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> than larger places. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11. 35. N. Lat. 44. 27.

BUDUN

Pages 862-862

is the name of one of the Ceylonese gods: he is supposed to have arrived at supremacy, after successive transmigrations, from the lowest state of an insect, through the various <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of living animals. There have been three deities of this name, each of which is supposed to reign as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> removes a hill of sand, half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and six miles round, by a single grain in a thousand years. See SAKRADAWENDRA.

BUDWEIS

Pages 862-862

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a> in Germany. It is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and well built, surrounded with strong walls, fortified with a good rampart, and might be made an important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> in 1744, but he did not keep it very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>. E. Long. 14. 19. N. Lat. 42. 15. BUDZIAC <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, lies on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Neister, Bog, and Nieper; having <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> and Russia on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, Little Tartary on the east, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south, and Bessarabia on the west. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Ocjakow. It is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>.

BUENA VISTA

Pages 862-863

one of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying in N. Lat. 15. 56. It is also called Bonvista and Bonnevue; but the first is the true appellation, the others being only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> and corruptions of the original name, which signifies a good prospect, intimating the beautiful appearance it makes to ships at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is reckoned near 20 leagues in circumference, and is distinguished on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side by a ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rocks that bound it. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> that stretches east and north-west is terminated with sundry banks to the sea; but the interior <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is chiefly mountainous.
