From the northern point there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ridge of rocks projecting near a whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> into the sea, against which the waves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> with incredible fury. Another point of rocks stretches into the sea on the southern point of the island eastward, a league and a half beyond that point; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for shipping. BUENOS Ayres, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to the Spaniards. This name, given from the pleasantness of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, is extended to all that country lying between <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUCUMAN">Tucuman</a> on the east, Paraguay on the north, and Terra Magellanica on the south, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERTEX">vertex</a> of that triangular point of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> which composes South America. The country is watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> river La Plata; first discovered in 1515 by Juan Diaz de Solis, who with two of his attendants was massacred by the natives; and partly subdued by Sebastian Gaboto, who gave the great river the appellation of La Plata, from the abundance of the precious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METALS">metals</a> he procured from the inhabitants, imagining them to be the produce of the country, though in fact they they were brought from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>.—No country in the world abounds more in horned cattle and horses than Buenos Ayres, where the greatest expense of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or cow is in the catching it, and they are frequently to be had at the small price of two or three rials. In such abundance are these useful animals, that the hide alone is deemed of any value, as this constitutes a main article in the trade of the country. All rove wild in the fields; but they are now become more difficult of access, the terrible havoc made among them having taught the cautious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a> to keep at a greater distance. All kinds of fish are in the same abundance; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> produced by every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe grow up here in the utmost perfection; and for the salubrity of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>, a finer country cannot be imagined. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities are Buenos Ayres the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTE_VIDEO">Monte Video</a>, Corrientes, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SANTA_FE">Santa Fe</a>. See BUENOS AYRES, Supplement.

BUENOS AYRES

Pages 863-863

Neustra Senhora de, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Buenos Ayres, in South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, was founded in the year 1535, under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">Don</a> Pedro de Mendoza, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governor. It stands on a point called <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANCO">Blanco</a>, on the south side of the Plata, fronting a small river, in S. Lat. 34° 34' 38", according to the observations of Father Ferville. The situation is in a fine plain, rising by a gentle ascent from the river; and truly paradisaical, whether we regard the temperature of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that beautiful verdure which overspreads the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country, of which the inhabitants have a prospect as far as the eye can reach. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is very considerable in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, containing according to some 40,000, according to others 60,000 inhabitants. The streets are straight, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and pretty equal in the heights and dimensions of the buildings; one very handsome <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> adorns it, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> being a castle in which the governor holds his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, and presides over a garrison of 3000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. The city was taken by the British in 1806, but retaken by the inhabitants a few weeks after.

BUFALMACO

Pages 863-863

Boramico, an Italian painter; the first who put labels to the mouths of his figures, with sentences; since followed by bad masters, but more frequently in caricature engravings. He died in 1340.

BUFF

Pages 863-863

in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> prepared from the skin of the buffalo; which dressed with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, after the manner of shammey, makes what we call buff-skin. This makes a very considerable article in the French, English, and Dutch commerce at Constantinople, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and all along the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. The skins of elks, oxen, and other like animals, when prepared after the same manner as that of the buffalo, are likewise called buffs. Of buff-skin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> buff-leather, are made a sort of coats for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or gens d'armes of France, bandoliers, belts, pouches, and gloves. In France, there are several manufactories designed for the dressing of those sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, particularly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORBEIL">Corbeil</a>, near <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIORT">Niort</a>, at Lyons, at Rome, at Etanepus, at Cone.

BUFFALO

Pages 863-863

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>. BUFFET was anciently a little apartment, separated from the rest of the room by slender wooden columns, for the disposing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a>, glass-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c. It is now properly a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in a dining-room, called also a side-board, for the plate, glasses, bottles, basons, &c., to be placed on, as well for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the table as for magnificence. In houses of persons of distinction in France, the buffet is a detached room, decorated with pictures relative to the subject, with fountains, cisterns, and vases. It is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> faced with marble <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRONZE">bronze</a>.

BUFFIER

Pages 863-863
Claude, a French writer, born in 1661, became a Jesuit in 1679, and died at Paris in 1737. There are many works of this author, which show deep penetration and accurate judgment; the principal of which is, Un Cours des Sciences, &c.; that is, "a Course of Sciences upon principles new and simple, in order to form the language, the understanding, and the heart, 1732," in folio. This collection includes an excellent "French grammar upon a new plan; a philosophical and practical treatise upon eloquence; an art of poetry," which, however, is not reckoned the best part of this miscellany; "elements of metaphysics; an examination into vulgar prejudices; a treatise of civil society; and an exposition of the proofs of religion:" all full of reflections, just as well as new. He was the author of other works, in verse and prose, of which no great account is had; and it is remarkable, that his style in both is rather easy than accurate and correct, notwithstanding the precepts in his "Grammar," which is really philosophic.

BUFFON

Pages 863-864

George <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> Le Clerc, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> of, a celebrated naturalist, was born at Montbard, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the 9th of September 1707: his father was a counsellor of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Dijon, and the son was destined to the same office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> science had not drawn him away from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAW">law</a>. He studied at Dijon; and his eager <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, his acuteness, penetration, and robust <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, fitted him to pursue business and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> with equal ardour. His early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> was for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and the young Le Clerc was never without Euclid in his pocket. At the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty, he went with an English nobleman and his governor to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; but he overlooked the choicest remains of art, and, amidst the ruins of an elegant and luxurious people, he first felt the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, whose zealous and successful admirer he afterwards proved. On his return to France, he fought, on some occasional quarrel, with an Englishman, whom he wounded, and was obliged to retire to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. He there translated Newton's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">Fluxions</a> from the Latin, and Hales's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STATICS">Statics</a> from the English, into the French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He afterwards came to England, at the age of 25; and this journey concluded his travels: he staid there about three months. At the age of 21, he succeeded to the estate of his mother, which was valued at about 300,000 livres (above 12,000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>); and he was one of those whose easy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> affluent circumstances urge on to literary pursuits, and clear the path of some of its thorns. Perhaps this was the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of his retirement to Montbard, where he spent much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and where his leisure was little interrupted: while in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, his office of intendant of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s garden and cabinet engaged much of his time. He loved much <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, and was partial to the fair; but he loved <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> more. He spent 14 hours every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; and, when we examine the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of his knowledge, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his works, we wonder at his having executed so much much even in this time. At five in the morning he retired to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a> in his vast gardens, and he was then inaccessible. This was, as <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> called it, the cradle of natural history; but she was indifferently accommodated. The walls were naked; an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INK">ink</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, and an elbow <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, were the only furniture of his study. His <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> were in a cabinet in another <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and he went occasionally from one to the other. The eras of Buffon's works are pretty well known. When each was finished it was put aside, in order that he might forget it, and he then returned to it with the severity of a critic. He was anxious to have it perspicuous; and if those to whom he read his works hesitated a moment, he changed the passage. The works of others he at last read like Magabechi, the titles, the contents, and the most interesting parts; but he read M. Neckar's Compte Rendu, and the Administration of the Finances, at length; he spoke of them also with no little enthusiasm. His favourite authors were Fenelon, Montesquieu, and Richardson. M. de Buffon's conversation was unadorned, rarely animated, but sometimes very cheerful. He was exact in his dress, particularly in dressing his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. He sat <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> at table, and then seemed at his ease. His conversation was, at this time, unembarrassed, and his guests had frequently occasion to notice some happy turn of phrase, or some deep reflection. His complaisance was very considerable: he loved praise, and even praised himself; but it was with so much frankness, and with so little contempt of others, that it was never disagreeable. Indeed, when we consider the extent of his reputation, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of his works, and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> with which they were always received, we do not wonder that he was sensible of his own value. It would perhaps have displayed a stronger mind to have concealed it. His father lived to 93, and almost adored his son; his grandfather to 87; and the subject of the present article exceeded only 80. He died in April 1788. Fifty-six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> were found in his bladder; but if he had consented to the operation, he might probably have lived longer. He left one son; who near a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower in the gardens of Montbard has placed a low <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, with the following inscription: Excelse Turri Humilis Columna, Parenti suo Fil. Buffon. This son fell a victim to the tyranny of Robespierre during the late revolution in France.

BUFFOON

Pages 864-864

a droll, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mimic, who diverts the public by his pleasantries and follies. Menage after Salmasius, derives the word from buffo; a name given to those who appeared on the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> with their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a> blown up; that, receiving blows thereon, they might make the greater noise, and set the people a laughing. Others, as Rhodiginus, make the origin of buffoonery more venerable; deriving it from a feast instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Erectheus, called buphonia. Buffoons are the same with what we otherwise find denominated scurræ, gelasiani, mimilogi, ministelli, go-liardi, joculatores, &c. whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> is laid at the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men. Gallienus never sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to meat without a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of buffoons by him; Tiberinus also renders pantomimes by buffoons. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> he observes, the shows of the buffoons were taken away by Domitian, restored by Nerva, and finally abolished by Trajan.

BUFONITA

Pages 864-864

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the toad-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. This has been received not only among the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a> by the generality of authors, but even has held a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> among the gems, and is still worn in rings by some people; though undoubtedly it is an extraneous fossil. There has been a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in the world, that it was found in the head of an old toad; and that this animal voided it at the mouth, on being put on a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> cloth. The general <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the bufonita is a deep dusky <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; but it varies greatly in this respect in several specimens, some of which are quite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, others of an extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> simple brown, a chestnut colour, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> colour, black-gray, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whitish. The bufonita are usually found immersed in beds of stone; and so little doubt is there of what they have originally been, viz. the petrified <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the lupus piscis, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>-fish, that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the jaw of the fish has sometimes been found with the teeth petrified in it. The bufonita are said to be cordial and astringent; many other fanciful virtues are ascribed to them, which the present practice has rejected.

BUG

Pages 864-864
or BUGG. See CIMEX, Entomology Index. Cheap, easy, and clean mixture for effectually destroying BUGGS. Take of the highest rectified spirit of wine, (viz. lamp-spirits) that will burn all away dry, and leave not the least moisture behind it, half a pint; new distilled oil, or spirit, of turpentine, half a pint: mix them together; and break into it, in small bits, half an ounce of camphire, which will dissolve it in a few minutes; shake them well together; and with a piece of sponge, or a brush dipt in some of it, wet very well the bed or furniture wherein these vermin harbour and breed, and it will infallibly kill and destroy both them and their nits, although they swarm never so much. But then the bed and furniture must be well and thoroughly wet with it (the dust upon them being first brushed and shaken off), by which means it will neither soil, stain, nor in the least hurt, the finest silk or damask bed that is. The quantity here ordered of this mixture (that costs but about a shilling) will rid any one bed whatever, though it swarms with bugs. If any bugs should happen to appear after once using it, it will only be for want of well wetting the lacing, &c. of the bed, or the folding of the linens or curtains near the rings, or the joints or holes in and about the bed or head-board, wherein the bugs and nits nestle and breed; and then their being wetted all again with more of the same mixture, which dries in as fast as you use it, pouring some of it into the joints and holes where the brush or sponge cannot reach, will never fail absolutely to destroy them all. Some beds that have much wood-work can hardly be thoroughly cleared without being first taken down; but others that can be drawn out, or that you can get well behind, to be done as it should be, may. The smell this mixture occasions will be all gone in two or three days; which yet

BUGGERY

Pages 864-865
or SODOMY, is defined by Sir Edward Coke to be a carnal copulation against nature, either by a confusion of species, that is to say, either a man or woman with a brute beast; or sexes, as a man with a man, or a man unnaturally with a woman. It is said this sin against God and nature was first brought into England by the Lombards. As to its punishment, the voice of nature and of reason, and the express law of God †, determines it to be capital. Off Levit. xx. this we have a signal instance, long before the Jewish dispensation, by the destruction of two cities by fire from heaven; so that this is an universal, not merely a provincial, precept. Our ancient law, in some measure, imitated this punishment, by commanding such miscreants to be burnt to death; though Flota says, they should be buried alive; either of which punishments was indifferently used for this crime among the ancient Goths. But now the general punishment of all felonies is the same, namely, by hanging: and this offence (being in the times of Popery only subject to ecclesiastical censures) was made felony without benefit of clergy by statute 25 Hen. VIII. c. 6. revived and confirmed by 5 Eliz. c. 17. And the rule of law herein is, that, if both parties are arrived at the years of discretion, agentes et consentientes pari pena plectantur, “all are liable to the same punishment.”

BUGIA

Pages 865-865

by the Africans called Bugeiah, a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Algiers, and once the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of that name. It is supposed to be the Saldae of Strabo, built by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It hath a handsome port formed by a narrow neck of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> running into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of whose promontory was formerly faced with a wall of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; where was likewise an aqueduct, which supplied the port with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, discharging it into a capacious basin; all which now <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in ruins. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> itself is built on the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one, at the foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain that looks towards the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east; a great part of whose walls run up quite to the top of it; where there is also a castle that commands the whole town, besides two others at the bottom, built for a security to the port. The inhabitants drive a considerable trade in ploughshares, mattocks, and other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> tools, which they manufacture from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The town is watered by a large river, supposed to be the Nasava of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is populous; and hath a considerable market for iron <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and wax, which is carried on with great tranquillity; but is no sooner over than the whole place is in an uproar, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> seldom concludes without some flagrant instance of barbarity. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4. N. Lat. 35. 30.

BUGIE

Pages 865-865

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, situated on the western shore of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> almost opposite to Ziden, the port town to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, and about 100 miles west of it. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 36. N. Lat. 22. 15. BUGLE. See AJUGA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. BUGLOSS. See ANCHUSA, BOTANY Index. Vipers BUGLOSS. See ECHIUM, BOTANY Index.

BUILDING

Pages 865-866

BUILDING, a fabric erected by art, either for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>, magnificence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conveniency. Building is also used for the art of constructing and raising an edifice; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it comprehends as well the expences as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and execution of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> buildings are much more commodious, as well as beautiful, than those of former times. Of old they used to dwell in houses, most of them with a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> staircase, low ceilings, and dark windows; the rooms built at random, without any thing of contrivance, and often with steps from one to another; so that one would think the people of former ages were afraid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and fresh <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a>; whereas the genius of our times is altogether for light staircases, fine sash-windows, and lofty ceilings. And such has been our builders industry in point of compactness and uniformity, that a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> after the new way <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford, on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of ground, almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the conveniences which could be had from an old one. By <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ACT">act</a> 11 Geo. I. and 4 Geo. III. for the regulation of building within the weekly bills of mortality, and in other places therein specified, party walls are required to be erected of brick or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which shall be two bricks and a half thick in the cellar, two bricks thick upwards to the garret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, &c., and other limitations are enacted respecting the disposition of the timbers, &c. And every building is to be surveyed; and the person who offends against the statute in any of the particulars recited, is liable to a forfeit of £250l., to be levied by warrant of justices of the peace. The other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> statutes relating to building are 19 Car. II. c. 3. 22 Car. II. c. 11. 5 Eliz. c. 4. 35 Eliz. c. 6. 6 Ann. c. 31. 7 Ann. c. 17. 33 Geo. II. c. 30. and 6 Geo. III. c. 37. Building of Ships. See Ship-Building. Builth, or Bealt, a town of South <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> in Brecknockshire, pleasantly seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WYE">Wye</a>, over which there is a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> that leads into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 52. 8. Buis, a territory of France, in Dauphiny. It is a small mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, but pretty fertile; and Buis and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NIONS">Nions</a> are the principal places.

BUKARI

Pages 866-866

a small well-built town of Hungarian <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, situated on the Golfo di Bikeriza, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20. 53. N. Lat. 45. 20.

BUKHARIA

Pages 866-868

a general name for all that vast tract of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> lying between Karazm and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Kobi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY_DESERT"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> bordering on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. It derives its name of Bukharia from the Mogul word Bukhar, which signifies a learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; it being formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for those who wanted instruction in the languages and sciences to go into Bukharia. Hence this name appears to have been given to it by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOGULS">Moguls</a> who under Jenghiz Khan conquered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is nearly the same with that called by the Arabs Mawaralnahr, which is little other than a translation of the word Transoxana, the name formerly given to those provinces. This region is divided into Great and Little Bukharia. Great Bukharia (which seems to comprehend the Sogdiana and Bactriana of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, with their dependencies) is situated between the 34th and 46th degrees of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, and between the 76th and 92d degrees of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>. It is Bukharia, bounded on the north by the river Sir, which separates it from the dominions of the Eluths or Kalmucs; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Kashgar in Little Bukharia, on the east; by the dominions of the great Mogul and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> on the south; and by the country of Karazm on the west; being about 770 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> from west to east, and 730 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from south to north. It is an exceeding rich and fertile country; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> abound with the richest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; the valleys are of an astonishing fertility in all sorts of fruit and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>; the fields are covered with grass the height of a man; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with excellent fish; and wood, which is scarce over all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, is here in great plenty. But all these benefits are of little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to the Tartar inhabitants, who are naturally so lazy, that they would rather go rob and kill their neighbours than apply themselves to improve the benefits which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> so liberally offers them. This country is divided into three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> provinces, viz. Bukharia proper, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMAR">Samar</a>-cand, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALK">Balk</a>; each of which generally has its proper khan. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bukharia proper is the most western of the three; having on the west Karasm, on the north a desert called by the Arabs Guzznah, on the east the province of Samar-cand, and on the south the river Amu. It may be about 390 miles long, and 320 broad. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Bokhara, Zam, Wardansi, Karakul, Siunjbala, Karshi, Zaruj, Nersem, Karmina, &c. Little Bukharia is so called, not because it is less in dimensions than the other, for in reality it is larger; but because it is inferior to it as to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its cities, goodness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, &c. It is surrounded by deserts; it has on the west, Great Bukharia; on the north, the country of the Kalmucs; on the east, that of the Moguls subject to China; on the south, Thibet, and the north-west corner of China. It is situated between the 93d and 118th degrees of east longitude, and between 35° 30' and 45° of north latitude; being in length from east to west about 850 miles, and in breadth from north to south 580: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> its dimensions be taken according to its semicircular course from the south to the north-east, its length <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 1200 miles. It is sufficiently populous and fertile; but the great elevation of its land, joined to the height of the mountains which bound it in several parts, particularly towards the south, renders it much colder than from its situation might naturally be expected. It is very rich in mines of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver; but the inhabitants reap little benefit from them, because neither the Eluths nor Kalmucs, who are masters of the country, nor the Bukhars, care to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in them. Nevertheless, they gather abundance of gold from the beds of the torrents formed by the melting of the snow in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and from hence comes all that gold dust which the Bukhars carry into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, China, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>. Much <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSK">musk</a> is likewise found in this country; and all sorts of precious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, even diamonds; but the inhabitants have not the art of either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> or polishing them. The inhabitants both of Great and Little Bukharia, are generally those people called Bukhars. They are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-burnt and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>-haired; although some of them are very fair, handsome, and well made. They do not want <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and are addicted to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; Bukharia; which they carry on with China, the Indies, Persia, and Russia: but those who <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with them will be sure of being overreached, if they do not take great care. The habits of the men differ very little from those of the Tartars. Their girdles are like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">Poles</a>. The garments of the women differ in nothing from those of the men, and are commonly quilted with cotton. They wear bobs in their ears 12 inches long; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> and twist their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> in tresses, which they lengthen with black ribbands embroidered with gold or silver, and with great tassels of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and silver, which hang <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to their heels; three other tufts of a smaller size cover their breasts. Both sexes carry about with them prayers written by their priests, which they keep in a small leathern purse by way of relics. The girls, and some of the women, tinge their nails <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> with the juice of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> called by them kena: they dry and pulverize it; then mixing it with powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, expose it in the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIR">air</a> for 24 hours before they use it, and the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> lasts a long <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Both sexes wear <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> breeches, and boots of Russia <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and without heels, or leather soles; putting on galoches, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-headed slippers like the Turks, when they go abroad. They wear also the same sort of bonnets and covering for the head; only the women set off theirs with trinkets, small pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and Chinese pearls. Wives are distinguished from maids by a long piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> worn under their bonnets; which, folding round the neck, they tie in a knot behind, so that one end of it hangs down to the waist. The Bukhar houses are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and pretty good; but their moveables consist mostly of some China trunks plated with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Upon these, in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>-time, they spread the quilts they have made use of at night, and cover them with a cotton carpet of various colours. They have likewise a curtain sprigged with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and various figures; also a sort of bedstead half a yard high, and four yards long, which is hidden in the daytime with a carpet. They are very neat about their victuals; which are dressed in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>'s chamber by his slaves, whom the Bukhars either take or buy from the Russians, Kalmycs, or other neighbours. For this purpose there are in the chamber, according to the largeness of the family, several iron pots, set in a kind of range near a chimney. Some have little ovens, made, like the rest of the walls, with a stiff clay or bricks. Their utensils consist of some plates and porringer made of cagua wood or of china, and some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> vessels. A piece of coloured calico serves them instead of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>-cloth and napkins. They use neither chairs nor tables, knives nor forks; but sit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged on the ground; and the meat being served up, they pull it to pieces with their fingers. Their spoons resemble our wooden ladles. Their usual food is minced meats, of which they make pies of the form of a half <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: these serve for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> when the Bukhars go long journeys, especially in winter. They carry them in a bag, having first exposed them to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; and when boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, they make very good broth. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> is their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMMON">common</a> drink, of which they have a black sort prepared with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; eating <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> with it, when they have any. As the Bukhars buy their wives, paying for them more or less according to their handsomeness; so the surest way to be rich is to have many daughters. The persons to be married must not see or speak to each other from the time of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> to the day of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. This is celebrated with three days feasting, as they do great annual festivals. The evening before the wedding, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of young girls meet at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and divert themselves till midnight, playing, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and singing. Next morning the guests assemble, and help her to prepare for the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>. Then, notice being given to the bridegroom, he arrives soon after, accompanied by ten or twelve of his relations and friends. These are followed by some playing on flutes, and by an Abus (a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>), who sings, while he beats two little timbrels. The bridegroom then makes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; which being ended, he distributes the prizes, six, eight, or twelve, in number, according to his ability. They consist of damasks, sables, fox-skins, calico, or the like. The parties do not see each other while the marriage ceremony is performing, but answer at a distance to the questions asked by the priest. As soon as it is over, the bridegroom returns home with his company; and after dinner carries them to the bride's house, and obtains leave to speak to her. This done, he goes back, and returns again in the evening, when he finds her in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>; and in presence of all the women, lays himself down by her in his clothes, but only for a moment. The same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARCE">farce</a> is acted for three days successively; but the third night he passes with her entirely, and the next day carries her home. Although the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> throughout all Little Bukharia is the Mahometan, yet all others enjoy a perfect toleration. The Bukhars say, that God first communicated the Koran to mankind by Moses and the prophets; that afterwards Mahomet explained, and drew a moral from it, which they are obliged to receive and practise. They hold Christ to be a prophet, but have no notion of his sufferings. Yet they believe in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a>, but cannot be persuaded that any mortal shall be eternally damned: on the contrary, they believe, that as the demons led them into sin, so the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on them. They believe, moreover, that at the last day every thing but God will be annihilated; and, consequently, that all creatures, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>, and Christ himself, will die. Likewise, that, after the resurrection, all men, excepting a few of the elect, will be purified or chastised by fire, every one according to his sins, which, will be weighed in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>. They say there will be eight different paradises for the good; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> hells, where sinners are to be purified by fire; that those who will suffer most, are liars, cheats, and others of that kind: that the elect who do not feel the fire will be chosen from the good; viz. one out of 100 men, and one out of 1000 women; which little troop will be carried into one of the paradises, where they shall enjoy all manner of felicity, till it shall please God to create a new world. It is a sin, according to them, to say, that God is in heaven. God, say they, is everywhere; and therefore it derogates from his omnipresence to say that he is confined to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. They keep an annual fast of 30 days, from the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the middle of August, during which time they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> nothing all day; but eat twice in the night, at sunset and midnight; Bukharia nor do they drink anything but tea, all strong liquors being forbidden. Whoever transgresses these ordinances is obliged to emancipate his most valuable slave, or to give an entertainment to 60 people: he is likewise to receive 85 strokes on the back with a leathern strap called dura. The common people, however, do not observe this fast exactly, and workmen are allowed to eat in the daytime. The Bukhars say prayers five times a-day; before morning, towards noon, after noon, at sunset, and in the third <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night. Jenghis Khan, who conquered both the Bukharias from the Arabs, left the empire of them to his son Jagatay Khan. He died in the year 1240, and left the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to his son Kara Kulaku, and of Little Bukharia to Amul Khoja Khan. A long succession of khans is enumerated in each of these families, but their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is uninteresting. They are long since extinct, and the Kalmyk Tartars are masters of the country. See Bukhara, Supplement.

BULAC

Pages 868-868

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, situated on the eastern shore of the river <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, about two miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, of which it is the port town, and contains about 4000 families. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade, as all the vessels going up and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the Nile make some stay here. It is also at this place that they cut the banks of the river every year, in order to fill their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> and overflow the neighbouring ground, without which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> would produce neither grain nor herbage. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 32° N. Lat. 30°.

BULAFO

Pages 868-868

a musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, consisting of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of wood tied together with thongs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, so as to form a small interstice between each pipe. It is used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>.

BULAM

Pages 868-869
or Bulama, an island on the western coast of Africa, at the mouth of the Rio Grande, in N. Lat. 11° and W. Long. 15°. This island, which is about 18 leagues long, and four broad, forms part of a cluster of islands, which have been known by the name of Bissagos, and are supposed to be the Hesperides of the ancients. This island was purchased in 1792 by a society instituted for similar purposes with those of the Sierra Leone association. The sum of 9000l. was subscribed for the establishment of the colony, and the management of it is intrusted to a committee who sailed from Spithead in April 1792, and having arrived at Bulama, took possession of the new purchase, and left a body of settlers consisting of 49 men, 13 women, and 25 children, under a superintendant, with a supply of stores and provisions necessary for an infant settlement. The following account of the climate, soil, and productions of Bulama, drawn up by Mr. Johansen, gives a flattering picture of this island. The climate, says he, on the whole, may be deemed salubrious, and will become more so in proportion to the increase of cultivation. The mornings and evenings are temperate and pleasant; the middle of the day is hot, but the fine sea breeze which then sets in tends greatly to cool and refresh the air. The heat of the sun is not so excessive or intolerable as has been generally supposed; indeed nature has most admirably adapted our mechanical and physical qualities to the exigencies of different regions; and man, who is the inhabitant of every climate, may, in some measure, render himself indigenous to every soil. Here the only danger arises from too sudden an exposure to the operation of the vertical rays of the sun, or an excess of labour; both of which the first settlers ought most studiously to avoid. "It appears from Mr. Beaver's observations at noon, between the 20th of July 1792, and the 28th of April 1793, that the thermometer, when lowest, was at 74°; the medium heat 85°; and that it never exceeded 96°, except at one time when it rose to 100°, during a calm that occurred in the interval between the north-east breeze in the morning and the south-west in the evening of the 19th of February 1793. The difference between the heat of noon and that of the morning and evening is from 20 to 30 degrees. On the 23rd of October 1792, hail of the size of a pin's head fell during two minutes, although not a cloud was to be seen during this phenomenon. The mercury in the thermometer then stood at 85°; the wind was at north-east in the morning and south-west in the evening. "Immediately after sunset a dew constantly begins to fall, which induces some to light a fire in their houses; they at the same time put on warmer clothing. There is little or no twilight; and night and day are nearly equal: the earth has therefore time to cool during twelve hours absence of the sun. "None of these terrible and destructive hurricanes so frequently experienced in the West Indies are to be met with here. The tornadoes, which arise chiefly from the eastern point of the compass, are but of short duration, seldom lasting above an hour, and may be readily foreseen some time previously to their commencement. They occur at the beginning and close of the wet season, and are highly beneficial, as they purify the air, and dispel the noxious vapours with which it would otherwise abound. "The rains set in about the latter end of May or the beginning of June, and discontinue in October or November. They do not fall every day, for there is often a considerable interval of clear weather, during which the atmosphere is beautifully serene; the showers in the first and last months occur but seldom; and are far from being violent; while, on the other hand, they sometimes resemble torrents, more especially towards the middle of the season. During the whole of this period, Europeans should, if possible, confine themselves to their habitations, as the rains prove injurious to health, more especially, if those exposed to them neglect to wipe their bodies dry, and to change their clothes immediately on their return home. It is deemed prudent also not to dig the earth until the expiration of a month after the return of fair weather, as this is considered to be unhealthy. "During the continuance of the dry season, a dew falls during the night, in sufficient quantity to answer all the purposes of vegetation. "Every stranger is generally here, as well as in the West Indies, subject to a fever or seasoning on his arrival. This is not infectious; it proceeds perhaps from an increased perspiration and a sudden extension of the pores of the human body, in consequence of the heat, by which means it is rendered more liable to imbibe the abundant exhalations that arise from the animal, vegetable, getable, and mineral kingdoms; but even this, slight as it is, might doubtless be avoided by means of a proper regimen, and a short seclusion from the full action of the open air, more especially at noon, and during the evening, till the climate has been rendered familiar. "Bulama is admirably adapted for all the purposes of an extensive commerce, being not only happily situated at the mouth of the Rio Grande, but in the vicinity of several other navigable rivers; so that a trade with the internal parts of Africa is thereby greatly facilitated. The landing is remarkably easy and safe, there being no surge; the ebb and flow is regular, and there is an increase of 16 feet of water at spring tide. The bay opposite the Great Bulama is adorned with a number of islands, covered with trees, and forms a most excellent harbour, sufficiently capacious to contain the whole navy of Great Britain, which might ride there in safety. The settlement in general is well supplied with water. A number of springs have been lately discovered in different places; and besides a draw-well in the fort which was erected for the defence of the colony, there is a small stream, which runs into Lewis Bay, near the new settlement called Hesper Eleusis; this is admirably situated for the supply of shipping. "The island is beautifully surrounded and interspersed with woods: lofty fruit and forest trees, mostly free from underwood and brambles, form a verdant belt, in some places two or three miles broad, which entirely encircles it, in such a manner as to represent a plantation artificially formed around a park. Within this the fields are regularly divided by trees, so as to resemble the hedge-rows in England. The beach has in some places the appearance of gravel walks; it is fringed with mangrove-trees, which forming a line with the high-water mark dip their branches into the sea, and thus afford nourishment to the oysters that often adhere to their extremities. "The soil is abundantly rich and deep; stones do not here impede the labours of the farmer; and indeed none have hitherto been discovered, but a small sort, resembling pieces of ore, which are to be met with on the shore. There are many savannahs or natural meadows, so extensive that the eye can scarcely descry their boundaries. These are admirably adapted for the rearing of stock and feeding of cattle of every kind. "Cotton, indigo, rice, and coffee, grow spontaneously on this coast; the sugar cane is indigenous to many parts of Africa, and might be cultivated here by the labour of freemen, in equal perfection, and to much greater advantage than in the exhausted islands of the West Indies. All kinds of tropical productions, such as pine-apples, limes, oranges, grapes, plums, cassada, guava, Indian wheat, the papaw, water-melon, muskmelon, the punkin, tamarind, banana, and numbers of other delicious fruits, also flourish here. The adjoining territories produce many valuable sorts of spices, gums, and materials for dyeing: all of which, it is but fair to suppose, might be readily cultivated in a kindred climate and a congenial soil. "The neighbouring seas abound with a variety of fish, highly agreeable to the palate. The lion, tyger, jackal, &c., are natives of the continent; but in Bulama no animals have been discovered, the wolf, some buffaloes, a few elephants, and a species of the deer, Bulama excepted. "The woods abound with doves, guinea fowls, and a variety of birds, celebrated for the beauty of their plumage." The settlement was abandoned a short time after it was formed.

BULARCHUS

Pages 869-869

a Greek painter; the first who introduced (among the Greeks at least) different colours in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>. He flourished in 740 B.C.

BULB

Pages 869-870

in the anatomy of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bud, generally produced under the ground, upon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> near the root of certain herbaceous plants, hence denominated bulbous. A bulb is defined by Linnæus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of hybernaculum, produced upon the descending caudex or root; consisting of stipule, petioli, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the former leaves, and scales or bark. To elucidate this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, it is proper to remark, that every bud contains, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> or embryo, a plant, in every respect similar to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> upon which it is seated. Plants therefore are perpetuated in the buds, as well as in the seeds; and the species may be renewed with equal efficacy in either way. The tender rudiments of the future vegetable, of which the bud is composed, are inclosed, and during the severities of winter defended from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> injuries, by a hard bark or rind, which generally consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of scales placed over each other like tiles, and fastened together by means of a tenacious, resinous, and frequently odoriferous, substance. Thus defended, the buds remain upon different parts of the mother plant till the ensuing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and are, therefore, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> propriety, denominated by Linnæus the hybernaculum or winter-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the future vegetable. With respect to their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, buds are situated either upon the stem and branches, or upon the roots: the former are styled gemmæ, or buds properly so called; but as they subsist several years by their roots, may be furnished with the other species of hybernaculum called bulbs, which, according to the definition, are seated upon the descending caudex or root. Again, trees which are perennial, with a woody and durable stem or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, have generally proper buds or gemmæ, but no bulbs. In bulbous plants, as the tulip, onion, or lily, what we generally call the root, is in fact a bulb or hybernaculum, which incloses and secures the embryo or future shoot. At the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this bulb may be observed a fleshy knob or tubercle, from whence proceed a number of fibres or threads. This knob, with the fibres attached to and hanging from it, is, properly speaking, the true root; the upper part being only the cradle or nursery of the future stem, which after the bulb has repaired a certain number of times, it perishes; but not till it has produced at its sides a number of smaller bulbs or suckers for perpetuating the species. One part of Linnæus's definition still remains obscure. The bulb, says he, is composed of the remains or rudiments of the former leaves of the plant; è rudimenta foliorum præteritorum. It is easy to comprehend that buds contain the rudiments of the future leaves; but how can bulbs be said to contain the rudiments of leaves that, to all appearance, are already perished? To explain this, let it be observed, that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of very eminent botanists, the root, in a very great number of perennial herbs, is annually renewed or repaired out of the trunk or stalk itself; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> only, roots are properly said to descend. In the perennials alluded to, the basis of the stalk continually, and by insensible degrees, descends below the surface of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and is thus changed into a true root; which root, by the continuance of the said <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the stalk, also descends; and thus, according to the durableness of its substance, becomes a longer or shorter root; the elder or lower part rotting off in proportion as the upper is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> out of the stalk. Thus, in brownwort, the basis of the stalk, sinking <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> by degrees till it is hid under the ground, becomes the upper part of the root; and continuing still to sink, the next year becomes the lower part, and the following year rots away. This is exactly what obtains in bulbous roots, as well as in the far greater number of other herbaceous perennials; as arum, valerian, tansy, samphire, primrose, wood-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, and others. The immediate visible cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> is the string-roots which this kind of trunks frequently puts forth; which descending themselves directly into the ground, serve like so many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> for pulling the trunk after them. Hence the tuberous roots of iris are sometimes observed to reascend a little upon the rotting or fading away of the string roots which hang at them. In bulbous roots, where the stalk and former leaves of the plant are sunk below, and formed into what is called the bulb or wintering of the future vegetable, the radicles or small fibres that hang from the bulb are to be considered as the root; that is, the part which furnishes nourishment to the plant: the several rinds and shells, whereof chiefly the bulbs consist, successively perish, and shrink up into so many dry skins; betwixt which, and in their centre, are formed other leaves and shells, and thus the bulb is perpetuated. What has been said of the descent of roots by the sinking of the stalk, is further confirmed by the appearance of certain roots; as of valerian, plantago <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>'s bit, in which the lower part appears bitten or chopped off. In these the lower part rotting off as the upper descends, the living remainder becomes stumped, or seems bitten. All bulbous roots, says the learned Dr Grew in his anatomy of plants, may be considered as hermaphrodite roots, or root and trunk both together; for the radicles or strings only are <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> roots; the bulb actually containing those parts which springing up make the body or leaves of the plant; so that it may be regarded as a large bud under ground. Bulbous roots are said to be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, when composed of one uniform lump of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>: tunicated, when formed of multitudes of coats surrounding one another; squamose, when composed of, or covered with, lesser flakes; duplicate, when there are only two to each plant: and aggregate, when there is a congeries of such roots to each plant. **BULBOCASTANUM.** See **BUNIUM**, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BULBOSE

Pages 870-870
or Bulbous. See BULB. **BULEUTÆ**, in Grecian antiquity, were magistrates answering to the decurions among the Romans. See Decurio. **BULFINCH.** See Loxia, Ornithology Index.

BULGARIA

Pages 870-870

a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Wallachia, on the east by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, on the south by Romania and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, and on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>. It is very narrow, but 325 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> on the side of the Danube, from Servia till it falls into the Black sea. The Bulgarians anciently inhabited the plains of Sarmatia that extended along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>. Thence they migrated, about the middle of the 7th century of the Christian era, in quest of new settlements. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> body of them passed the Danube, and took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> adjacent to the western <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Euxine sea. Several attempts were made by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to dispossess and extirpate them: But they defended themselves with equal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and success. Constantine III. being defeated and intimidated, concluded an ignominious peace with them (A.D. 78), and purchased their friendship by the payment of an annual tribute. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a> II. refused to comply with these dishonourable terms, and invaded their territories (A.D. 687); but he was defeated, and constrained to renew the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a> was carried on, almost without interruption, between them and the eastern emperors, during the course of several centuries. After a long and doubtful struggle, the Romans prevailed; and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> reduced Bulgaria to the form of a province (A.D. 1019). From this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Bulgarians remained in subjection, and were governed by Roman dukes, until the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Angelus, when they revolted (A.D. 1186). The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Bulgaria, in the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, scarcely merits <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Stephen IV. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>, having defeated the Bulgarians, obliged them to acknowledge him as their sovereign. His successors were styled kings of Hungary and Bulgaria; and this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was transmitted, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Hungary, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. By the aid of the eastern emperors they threw off the Hungarian yoke; and, in return, they assisted their ally in an attempt to recover <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a> (A.D. 1369). Provoked by this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a>, Amurath invaded their country; and Bajazet, his successor, completed the conquest of it (A.D. 1396). Bulgaria still remains a province of the Ottoman empire. The inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; but extremely ignorant, insomuch that they seem to know nothing of Christianity but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and fasting. It is divided into four sangliacates; Byden, Sardice, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a>, and Silistria. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are of the same names, except Sardice, which is now called Sophia. **BULGARIAN <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>**, the same with the Slavonic.

BULIMY

Pages 870-870

a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> in which the patient is affected with an insatiable and perpetual desire of eating; and, unless he is indulged, he often falls into fainting fits. It is also called *fomes canina*, canine appetite. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

BULITHUS

Pages 870-871

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a> found either in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a>-bladder, BULK of a SHIP, the whole content in the hold for the stowage of goods. BULK-HEADS are partitions made athwart the ship with boards, by which one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is divided from the other; as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cabin, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUN">gun</a>-room, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-room, and several other divisions. The bulk-head afore is the partition between the forecastle and gratings in the head.

BULL

Pages 871-876

George, bishop of St <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">Wells</a>, in 1634; and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXETER">Exeter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. The first benefice he enjoyed was that of St George's, near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, whence he rose successively to be rector of Suddington in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, prebendary of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>, archdeacon of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LLANDAFF">Llandaff</a>, and in 1705 bishop of St David's. This <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> he enjoyed about four years, and died in 1709. During the usurpation of Cromwell, he adhered steadily, though still with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, to the forms of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England; and in the reign of James II. preached very strenuously against the errors of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPERY">Popery</a>. He wrote, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the Nicene <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. 2. Apostolical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>. 3. Primitive apostolical <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>; and other works. BULL. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOS">Bos</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Wild Bulls. The wild bulls, now so numerous on the continent of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, are said to have sprung from one bull and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> cows, which were carried thither by some of the first conquerors. For the manner of hunting these, see Bucaneers. Bull, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>. See Astronomy Index. Bulls Eye, among seamen, a small, obscure, sublime cloud, ruddy in the middle, that sometimes appears to mariners, and is the immediate forerunner of a great storm at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. Bull-Fighting, a sport <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> much in vogue among the Spaniards and Portuguese, consisting in a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a> of a cavalier or torreadore against a wild bull, either on foot or on horseback, by riding at him with a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>. The Spaniards have bull-fights, i.e. feasts attended with shows, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of St John, the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, &c. This sport the Spaniards received from the Moors, among whom it was celebrated with great eclat. Some think that the Moors might have received the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and they from the Greeks. Dr Plot is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the Tavgora-kaivovv npevov among the Thessalians, who first instituted this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, and of whom Julius Caesar learned and brought it to Rome, were the origin both of the Spanish and Portuguese bull-fighting, and of the English bull-running. This practice was prohibited by Pope Pius V. under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> incurred ipso facto. But succeeding popes have granted several mitigations in behalf of the torreadores. From the following account of a bull-feast in the Coliseum at Rome 1332, extracted from Muratori by Mr Gibbon, the reader may form some idea of the pomp, the ceremonies, and the danger which attended these exhibitions. "A general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> as far as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIMINI">Rimini</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a> invited the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> to exercise their skill and courage in this perilous adventure. The Roman ladies were marshalled in three squadrons, and seated in three balconies, which on this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the third of September, were lined with scarlet cloth. The fair Jacova di Rovers led the matrons from beyond the Tiber, a pure and native <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who still represent the features and character of antiquity. The remainder of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was divided between the Colonna and Ursini families: the two factions were proud of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> bands; the charms of Savella Ursini are mentioned with praise; and the Colonna regretted the absence of the youngest of their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, who had sprained her ankle in the garden of Nero's tower. The lots of the champions were drawn by an old and respectable citizen; and they descended into the arena or pit, to encounter the wild bulls, on foot as it should seem, with a single spear. Amidst the crowd, our annalist has selected the names, colours, and devices of 20 of the most conspicuous knights. Several of the names are the most illustrious of Rome and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> State; Malatesta, Polenta, della Valle, Cafarello, Savelli, Cappoccio, Conti, Annibaldi, Altieri, Corsi. The colours were adapted to their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and situation. And the devices are expressive of hope or despair, and breathe the spirit of gallantry and arms. "I am alone, like the youngest of the Horatii," the confidence of an intrepid stranger; "I live disconsolate," a weeping widower; "I burn under the ashes," a discreet lover; "I adore Lavinia or Lucretia," the ambiguous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>: "My faith is as pure," the motto of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIVERY">livery</a>: "Who is stronger than myself?" of a lion's hide: "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> I am drowned in blood, what a pleasant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>!" the wish of ferocious courage.
