Of those who were allowed the rites of burial, some were distinguished by particular circumstances of disgrace attending their interment: thus persons killed by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> were buried apart by themselves, being thought odious to the gods; those who wasted their patrimony forfeited the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of being buried in the sepulchres of their fathers; and those who were guilty of self-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> were privately deposited in the ground, without the accustomed solemnities. Among the Jews, the privilege of burial was denied only to self-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>, who were thrown out to rot upon the ground. In the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, though good men always desired the privilege of interment, yet they were not, like the heathens, so concerned for their bodies, as to think it any detriment to them, if either the barbarity of an enemy, or some other accident, deprived them of this privilege. The primitive Christian church denied the more solemn rites of burial only to unbaptized persons, self-murderers, and excommunicated persons who <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> obstinate and impenitent, in a manifest contempt of the church's censures. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of burial among the Jews was never particularly determined. We find they had graves in the town and country, upon the highways, in gardens, and upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. Among the Greeks, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were made repositories for the dead in the primitive ages; yet the general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> in latter ages, with them, as well as with the Romans and other heathen nations, was to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> their dead without their cities, and chiefly by the highways. Among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, burying in cities was not allowed for the first 300 years, nor in churches for many ages after, the dead bodies being first deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATRIUM">atrium</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, and porches and porticoes of the church; <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> burying-places were forbidden till the 12th century. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of burial, with all the ceremonies accompanying it, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNERAL_RITES">Funeral Rites</a>.

BURICK

Pages 882-882

a town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>. It was taken by the French in 1672, who demolished the fortifications. It is agreeably seated on the river <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, over against Wesel, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6. 8. N. Lat. 51. 38.

BURIDAN

Pages 882-882

John, a native of Bethune, in Artois, was one of the most celebrated philosophers of the 14th century. He taught in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; and wrote commentaries on logic, morality, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. Aventinus relates, that he was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Ockam; and that, being expelled Paris by the power of the Realists, which was superior to that of the Nominalists, he went into Germany, where he founded the university of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. From him came the proverb of the ass of Buridan, so famous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. Buridan supposed a hungry ass fixed at an exactly equal distance between two bushels of oats; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an ass, as much pressed by thirst as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, between a bushel of oats and a pail of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, each of them acting equally on his senses. Having made this supposition, he desired to know what the ass would do? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he was answered that he would remain immovable, then he concluded he would die of hunger between two bushels of oats, or of both hunger and thirst, with corn and water within his reach. This appeared absurd, and brought the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUGHTER">laughter</a> on his side; but if it was replied, that the ass would not be so stupid as to die of hunger or thirst in such a situation, Then (said he), the ass has free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, or is it possible that of two equal weights one should outweigh the other? These two consequences appeared equally absurd; and thus Buridan, by this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOPHISM">sophism</a>, perplexed the philosophers, and his ass became famous in the schools.

BURNTISLAND

Pages 839-839

a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a> in Scotland, situated on the frith of Forth, eight miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 5. N. Lat. 56. 12. It has the best harbour on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which is formed by a rocky <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> eked out with piers, for there are none on this side the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> entirely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>. This is dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a steeple rising in the centre. The old castle, built by the Duries, commanded both town and harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has a natural strength, which, with the conveniency of a port opposite to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, made it, during the troubles of 1560, a most desirable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a>. The French, allies of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> regent, fortified it strongly. In 1715, it was surprised and possessed by the rebels, who here formed the bold <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of passing over a body of troops to the opposite shore, which was in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> executed under the command of Brigadier Macintosh, notwithstanding all the efforts of the men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to prevent it. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 1934 in 1811.

CLASSIS XXI

In this class the stamens and pistils are found in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> on the same plant. The flowers that have stamens, but want pistils, are, according to the principles of Linnæus's sexual system, which we have adopted, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> flowers; whereas the flowers that have pistils, but want stamens, are styled <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers. In the following account of the genera the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the male flowers is marked (1), and that of the female flowers (2). 1429. *Ægophricon.* (1) Cal. 3-fidus. One <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; viz. palustris. 1035. CERATOCARPUS. One species; viz. arenarius. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>. 1426. ARTOCARPUS, or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a>-fruit. Two species; viz. incisa, integriflora.—It has a cylindric amentum or catkin, which thickens gradually, and is covered with flowers; the male and female in a different amentum. In the male, the calyx is two-valved, and the corolla is wanting. In the female, there is no calyx nor corolla; the stylus is one, and the drupa is many-celled. Though this tree had been mentioned by many voyagers, particularly by Dampier, by Rumphius, and by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Anson, yet very little notice seems to have been taken of it till the return of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Wallis from the South seas, and since that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> by others who have touched at Otaheite and some countries in the East Indies. Captain Dampier relates, that in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUAM">Guam</a>, one of the Ladrones <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, "there is a certain fruit called the bread-fruit, growing on a tree as big as our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> apple-trees, with dark leaves. The fruit is round, and grows on the boughs like apples, of the bigness of a good <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>-loaf; when ripe, it turns <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, soft, and sweet; but the natives take it green, and bake it in an oven till the rind is <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; then they scrape off, and eat the inside, which is soft and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, like the inside of new baked bread, having neither seed nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it is kept above 24 hours it is harsh. As this fruit is in season eight months in the year, the natives feed upon no other sort of bread during that time. They told us that all the Ladrones islands had plenty of it. 'I never heard of it in any other <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.'" Rumphius, after describing the tree, observes, that "the fruit is shaped like a heart, and increases to the size of a child's head. Its surface or rind is thick, green, and covered everywhere with warts of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRILATERAL">quadrilateral</a> or hexagonal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, like cut diamonds, but without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. The more flat and smooth these warts are, the fewer seeds are contained in the fruit, and the greater is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pith, and that of a more glutinous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. The internal part of the rind, or peel, consists of a fleshy substance, full of twisted fibres, which have the appearance of fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>; these adhere to, and in some <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> form it. The fleshy part of this fruit becomes softer towards the middle, where there is a small cavity formed without any nuts or seeds, except in one species, which has but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, and this sort is not good, unless it is baked or prepared some other way; but if the outward rind be taken off, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> dried and afterwards boiled with meat as we do cabbage, it has then the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of artichoke bottoms. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOYNA">Amboyna</a> dress it in the liquor of cocoa nuts; but they prefer it roasted on coals till the outward part or peel is burnt. They afterwards cut it into pieces, and eat it with the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a> of the cocoa-nut. Some people make fritters of it, or fry it in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and others, as the Sumatrans, dry the internal soft part, and keep it to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> instead of bread with other food. It affords a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nourishment, and is very satisfying, therefore proper for hard-working people: and being of a gentle astringent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, is good for persons of a laxative <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body. It is more nourishing boiled in our manner with fat meat than roasted on coals. The milky juice which distils from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, boiled with the cocoa-nut oil, makes a very strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>-lime. This tree is to be found on the eastern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and in the Malay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is called soccus and soccum copus. It grows likewise about the town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BANTAM">Bantam</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, and in Ballega and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MADURA">Madura</a>, and is known there by the name of soccum." In Anson's voyage we are informed, "that the rima, or bread-fruit tree, is common in all the Ladrones islands and some of the Philippines. It is somewhat larger than our apple tree, and bears a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> dark-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> with five indentures on each side. The fruit hangs on the boughs like apples; and is of the size of a penny loaf, with a thick tough rind, which when full ripe turns yellow. The natives gather it before it is quite ripe, and bake it till the crust is pretty black; when they rasp it, and there remains a pretty loaf, with a tender yellow crust, and the crumb of it is soft and sweet as a new baked roll: it is without any seeds or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. This fruit the inhabitants enjoy for about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> months; during which they never eat any other kind of bread: but they are obliged to bake it every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for when it grows a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STALE">stale</a>, it becomes harsh and husky, somewhat like the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a> bread made in the west of England. There is, however, a remedy for this; which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the loaf into slices when it is new, and drying it in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, by which it is changed into the pleasantest rusk that can be eaten." Captain Cook, in his voyage, observes, that this fruit not only serves as a substitute for bread among the inhabitants of Otaheite and the neighbouring islands, but also, variously dressed, composes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of their food. It grows on a tree that is about the size of a middling oak; its leaves are frequently a foot and a half long, of an oblong shape, deeply sinuated like those of the fig-tree, which they resemble in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and consistence, and in the exuding of a milky juice upon being broken. The fruit is about the size and shape of a new-born child's head; and the surface is reticulated, not much unlike a truffle; it is covered with a thin skin, and has a core about as big as the handle of a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. The eatable part lies between the skin and the core; it is as white as snow, and somewhat of the consistence of new bread; it must be roasted before it is eaten, being first divided into three or four parts; its taste is insipid, with a slight sweetness, somewhat resembling that of the crumb of wheaten bread mixed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> artichoke. This fruit is also cooked in a kind of oven, which renders it soft, and something like a boiled potato; not quite so farinaceous as a good one, but more so than those of the middling sort. Of the bread-fruit they also make three dishes, by putting either <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> or the milk of the cocoa nut to it, then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> it to a paste with a stone pestle, and afterwards mixing it with ripe plantains, bananas, or the sour paste which they call mahie. The mahie, which is likewise made to serve as a succedaneum for ripe bread-fruit before the season comes on, is thus made: The fruit of the bread-tree is gathered thered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> before it is perfectly ripe; and being laid in heaps, is closely covered with leaves: in this state it undergoes a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and becomes disagreeably sweet; the core is then taken out entire, which is done by gently pulling out the stalk, and the rest of the fruit is thrown into a hole which is dug for that purpose, generally in the houses, and neatly lined in the bottom and sides with grass: the whole is then covered with leaves and heavy stones laid upon them; in this state it undergoes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fermentation, and becomes sour, after which it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> suffer no change for many months. It is taken out of the hole as it is wanted for use; and being made into balls, it is wrapped up in leaves and baked; after it is dressed, it will keep five or six weeks. It is eaten both <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hot; and the natives seldom make a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> without it, though to Europeans the taste is as disagreeable as that of a pickled olive generally is the first time it is eaten. The fruit itself is in season eight months in the year, and the mahie supplies the inhabitants during the other four. To procure this principal article of their food (the bread fruit), costs these happy people no trouble or labour except climbing up a tree: the tree which produces it does not indeed grow spontaneously; but if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> ten of them in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> time, which he may do in about an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, he will as completely fulfil his duty to his own and future generations, as the native of our less temperate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> can do by ploughing in the cold of winter, and reaping in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, as often as these seasons return; even if, after he has procured bread for his present <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, he should convert a surplus into <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and lay it up for his children. We have said that there are two species of artocarpus, viz. the incisa, with gashed leaves; and the integripila, with entire leaves. There is also said to be another distinction, into that which bears fruit with stones or seeds, and that in which the fruit has none. The parts of fructification of that tree which bears the fruit without stones are defective. The amentum, or catkin, which contains the male parts, never expands. The styli, or female parts of the fruit, are likewise deficient. From which it follows, that there can be no stones or seeds, and therefore that this tree can be propagated only by suckers or layers; although it is abundantly evident, that it must have originally proceeded from the seed-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> bread-fruit tree. Instances of this kind we sometimes find in European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; such as the barberry, and the Corinthian grape from Zant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called currants, which can therefore be increased only by layers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTINGS">cuttings</a>. Dr Solander was assured by the oldest inhabitants of Otaheite and the adjoining islands, that they well remembered there was formerly plenty of the seed-bearing bread-fruit; but they had been neglected upon account of the preference given to the bread-fruit without seeds, which they propagate by suckers. The British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> sent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Bligh in the Bounty in 1787 to Otaheite to procure and transport to our West <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> colonies this valuable plant. The project was at that time unsuccessful, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> of the ship's crew, who seized the vessel, and carried her back to Otaheite. The object, however, was accomplished at a future <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and the bread-fruit is now reared in Jamaica and the other West India islands. Plants of this genus have also been brought to his majesty's gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>. The taste of the fruit is said to be a sort of medium between the tate of common wheaten bread, and the taste of a boiled potato. Those who prefer potatoes to ordinary bread also prefer the bread-fruit to it. 1033. Cynomorium. One species; viz. coccineum. Jamaica. Nipa. New BRITAIN

Pages 804-805

New BRITAIN, a large country of North America, called also Terra Labrador, has Hudson's bay and strait on the north and west, Canada and the river St Lawrence on the south, and the Atlantic ocean on the east. It is subject to Great Britain, but yields only skins and furs. The following is the best description of this country that hath yet appeared. It was drawn up by the commander of the Otter sloop, and communicated to the Royal Society, by the honourable Daines Barrington in 1774. "There is no part of the British dominions so little known as the immense country of Labrador. So few have visited the northern parts of this vast country, that almost from the straits of Belleisle until you come to the entrance of Hudson's bay, for more than ten degrees of latitude, no chart which can give any tolerable idea of the coast hath been hitherto formed. The barrenness of the country explains why it has been so seldom frequented. Here avarice has but little to feed on. Perhaps, without an immoderate share of vanity, I may venture to presume, that, as far as I have been, which is to the latitude of 59° 10', the draught which I have been able to form is by much the best of any that has hitherto been made. Others have gone before me, blest with abilities superior to mine, and to whom I hope to be thought equal only in assiduity. But I had advantages of which they were destitute: with a small vessel, and having an Indian with me, who knew every rock and shoal upon the coast, I was enabled to be accurate in my observations; and these are the reasons why I deem my own sketch preferable to all others. As this country is one of the most barren in the whole world, so its sea coast is the most remarkable. Bordered by innumerable islands, and many of them being a considerable distance from the main land, a ship of burden would sail a great way along the coast without being able to form any notion of its true situation. Hence it is that all the charts of it have been so extremely erroneous; and hence arose those opinions that some of the inlets extended a vast distance into the country, if not quite into the sea of Hudson's bay. Davis's inlet, which has been so much talked of, is not 20 leagues from the entrance of it to its extremity. The navigation here is extremely hazardous. Towards the land, the sea is covered with large bodies and broken pieces of ice; and the farther you go northward, the greater is the quantity you meet with. Some of those masses, which the seamen call islands of ice, are of a prodigious magnitude; and they are generally supposed to swim two-thirds under water. You will frequently see them more than 100 feet above the surface; and to ships in a storm, or in thick weather, nothing can be more terrible. Those prodigious pieces of ice come from the north, and are supposed to be formed by the freezing of cataracts upon the lands about East Greenland and the pole. As soon as the severity of the winter begins to abate, their immense weight breaks them from the shore, and they are driven to the southward. To the miserable inhabitants of Labrador, their appearance upon the coast serves as a token of the approach of summer. This vast tract of land is extremely barren, and altogether incapable of cultivation. The surface is everywhere uneven, and covered with large stones, some of which are of amazing dimensions. There are few springs; yet throughout the country there are prodigious chains of lakes or ponds, which are produced by the rains and the melting of the snow. These ponds abound in trout, but they are very small. There is no such thing as level land. It is a country formed of frightful mountains, and unfruitful valleys. The mountains are almost devoid of every sort of herbage. A blighted shrub and little moss is sometimes to be seen upon them, but in general the bare rock is all you behold. The valleys are full of crooked low trees, such as the different pines, spruce, birch, and a species of cedar. Up some of the deep bays, and not far from the water, it is said, however, there are a few flicks of no inconsiderable size. In a word, the whole country is nothing more than a prodigious heap of barren rocks. The climate is extremely rigorous. There is but little appearance of summer before the middle of July; and in September the approach of winter is very evident. It has been remarked, that the winters within these few years have been less severe than they have been known heretofore. The cause of such an alteration it would be difficult to discover. All along the coast there are many rivers that empty empty themselves into the sea, and yet there are few of any consideration; and you must not imagine that the largest are any thing like what is generally understood by a river. Custom has taught us to give them this appellation; but the greatest part of them are nothing more than broad brooks or rivulets. As they are only drains from the ponds, in dry weather they are everywhere fordable; for running upon a solid rock, they become broad without having a bed of any depth below the surface of the banks. "The superficial appearance of this country is extremely unfavourable. What may be hidden in its bowels, we cannot pretend to suggest: probably it may produce some copper; the rocks in many places being impregnated with an ore of that resemblance. Something of a horny substance, which is extremely transparent, and which will scale out into a number of small sheets, is often found amongst the stones; there are both black and white of this sort, but the black is the most rare. It has been tried in fire, but seems to be nowise affected by heat. "The species of wood here are not very various: excepting a few shrubs which have as yet received no name from the Europeans, the principal produce of the country are the different sorts of spruce and pine. Of these, even in the more southern parts, there is not abundance; as you advance northwards they gradually diminish; and by the time you arrive at the 60th degree of latitude, the eye is not delighted with any sort of herbage. Here the wretched residents build their miserable habitations with the bones of whales. If ever they cheer their aching limbs with a fire, they gather a few sticks from the sea-shore, which have probably been washed from Norway or Lapland. Here a vast quantity of snow remains upon the land throughout the year. "Although the winter here is so excessively rigid, in summer the heat is sometimes disagreeable; and in that season the weather is very moderate, and remarkably serene. It is but seldom foggy, speaking comparatively between this and Newfoundland; nor are you so frequently liable to those destructive gales of wind which visit many other parts of the globe. "It is in general high land, and sometimes you meet with mountains of an astonishing height; you are also frequently presented with prospects that are really awful, and extremely romantic. "The inhabitants of New Britain are called Eskimauks." See Greenland and Hudson's Bay.
